exp.0:2:
This verse says that Jesus, after suffering and dying on the cross, showed himself alive to his apostles. He did so with many convincing proofs, that is, sure signs that left no room for doubt. For forty days he appeared to them and spoke to them about the kingdom of God. The idea of having suffered simply means that he went through suffering.

The one writing is Luke, addressing Theophilus, as a continuation of his Gospel. He wants to show that Jesus truly rose again and that the apostles were reliable witnesses. That certainty would prepare them to receive the Holy Spirit and begin the mission of the church.

For today: our faith does not rest on a vague idea, but on a fact that the first witnesses affirmed with firmness. When you doubt, return to the Scriptures and ask God to strengthen your confidence in the living Christ.
exp.0:3:
What it says: Jesus met with his disciples and commanded them not to depart from Jerusalem. They were to stay there and wait for the promise of the Father, which he had already told them about.

Context: The one speaking is the risen Jesus. For forty days he had been appearing to his apostles and teaching them about the kingdom of God. Soon he would ascend into heaven. The promise of the Father is the Holy Spirit, as the following verse explains. The disciples needed his power before beginning to bear witness.

For today: Sometimes we want to act right away, but God asks us to wait for his direction and his strength. Before making an important decision, set aside time to pray and to listen to God. Waiting on him is not wasted time, but a way of preparing ourselves to serve him better.
exp.0:5:
The disciples who were gathered with Jesus ask him whether at that very moment he is going to restore the kingdom to Israel.

The ones speaking are the disciples, days after the resurrection. Jesus had spoken to them about the promise of the Holy Spirit, and they were thinking about the hope that Israel would be free and governed by God. Jesus does not say that the idea is false, but he answers them that the times and seasons belong to the Father, and that they will receive power to be his witnesses.

For today: sometimes we want to know when and how God will do things. Let us trust that he knows the times, and in the meantime, let us commit ourselves to what he has entrusted to us: living and telling of his love where we are.
exp.0:7:
This verse says that the disciples would receive power from the Holy Spirit when he came upon them. This power, or strength, would enable them to be witnesses of Jesus, that is, people who tell what they know about him. They would begin in Jerusalem, continue through all Judea and Samaria, and reach the farthest parts of the earth, the most distant places.

The risen Jesus speaks with his disciples shortly before he ascends into heaven. They asked him whether he would now restore the kingdom to Israel. He gave them no dates. Instead, he turned their attention to the task ahead of them: to bear witness with the help of the Spirit.

For today: we do not need to know the future in order to serve God. We can simply tell what Jesus has done in our lives, in our homes, at work, and beyond, trusting that the Spirit gives us the strength to do it.
exp.0:9:
The verse of this verse says that the disciples kept looking steadily up into the sky while Jesus was rising. Suddenly, two men dressed in white appeared beside them.

Luke, the author of Acts, is the one telling the story. Jesús had just promised the Holy Spirit and had charged his followers to be his witnesses. Then a cloud hid him from their sight. The two men in white are not identified; many think they were angels, though the text does not say so. Their message: Jesus will return, and the disciples had to get moving.

Today we can look up to heaven with hope, but without standing still. Trusting that Christ will return drives us to live and share his love here, in everyday life: at home, at work, and in the neighborhood.
exp.0:17:
This verse says that Judas got a field with the payment he received for his wickedness (iniquity means wickedness). Then he hanged himself, his body burst open in the middle, and his entrails, that is, his inner organs, poured out.

Peter speaks before about one hundred twenty believers, before choosing someone to replace Judas. He wants to show that his betrayal did not take God by surprise. Matthew 27 tells that the priests bought the field with the coins Judas returned. Scholars explain in several ways how the two accounts fit together, and it is not known with certainty.

Today, the story warns us that sin promises gains but ends in ruin. Examine your heart honestly and do not hide your failures. Peter also failed, but he returned to Jesus and was forgiven. There is always a way back.
exp.0:21:
Peter says that the new apostle must be someone who has been with Jesus from the time John was baptizing until the day Jesus was taken up into heaven. That person would be, together with the eleven, a witness that Jesus rose again.

Peter speaks before about one hundred twenty believers gathered in Jerusalem, after the ascension. Judas had betrayed Jesus and was no longer among the twelve. Peter supports the need for a replacement from the Psalms and proposes clear requirements: to have seen Jesus's ministry from beginning to end, so as to give reliable testimony.

For today: the Christian message rests on testimony, not merely on an idea. You can simply tell what Jesus has done in your life and what you have learned from Him. A witness does not need to be perfect, only sincere and faithful to what he has seen and lived.
exp.0:23:
Here the disciples offer a prayer before deciding something important. They address the Lord, probably Jesus, although some think they are speaking to God the Father. They acknowledge that he knows the hearts of all people, that is, he sees what is inside each person. They ask him to show them which of the two he has chosen.

Peter and the other believers were gathered in Jerusalem after Jesus' ascension. Judas was no longer with them, and they wanted to complete the group of the twelve with a witness of the resurrection. They had proposed two men, Joseph and Matthias, and now they ask God to indicate his decision.

Before making important decisions, we can pray with humility and recognize that God sees what we cannot see. Asking him for wisdom helps us not to depend only on our own opinions.
exp.0:25:
They cast lots, something like drawing a slip of paper out of a bag to make a decision. The lot fell on Matthias, and from that moment he was counted along with the eleven apostles. Remove the mention of the old spelling; it does not apply to the verse above.

Background: Luke, the author of Acts, recounts what happened after Jesus ascended. Judas had already betrayed the Lord and had died, so there were eleven apostles left. Peter proposed replacing him with someone who had accompanied Jesus from the beginning. The believers prayed, asking God to show His choice. This is the last time the Bible mentions the use of lots in this way, since the Holy Spirit would soon arrive. Some believe Matthias was the right choice; others think Paul would fill that place. The Bible does not make this clear.

For today: Before making an important decision, pray with humility, seek counsel, and trust that God guides those who ask Him for direction.
exp.1:3:
All the believers who were gathered together were "filled" with the Holy Spirit, that is, the Spirit filled them and took an active part in their lives. Then they began to speak in languages that were not their own. It was the Spirit who gave them the words.

This happened in Jerusalem, on the day of Pentecost, a few days after Jesus went up into heaven. The disciples were waiting for what Jesus had promised them. According to the verses that follow, people from many nations heard them speaking, each in their own language. In this way, the news of God reached everyone.

For today: we do not depend only on our own strength to live and to share our faith. We can ask the Spirit to guide us, and then speak simply and with love, so that others may understand God's message.
exp.1:6:
This verse says that the people who heard the disciples were very surprised and amazed. Those who were amazed were greatly impressed and almost speechless. "Galileans" were the people of Galilee, a region in the north of Israel. They were asking: are not all these who are speaking Galileans?

The ones speaking here are devout Jews who were in Jerusalem, who had come from many nations. It was the day of Pentecost. When they heard the noise, they gathered together, and each one heard the disciples speaking in his own language. They were astonished because Galileans were generally not known for speaking so many languages. Some believe this highlighted the simplicity of the disciples, although the text does not say so in detail.

Today we can remember that God can use ordinary people to bring his message to others. You do not need to be famous or prepared by the standards of the world; it is enough to be willing for God to use us.
exp.1:8:
This verse begins a list of the places the people listening to the disciples in Jerusalem had come from. Parthians, Medes, and Elamites were peoples of the east, from regions today associated with Iran and Iraq. Mesopotamia lies between the Tigris and Euphrates rivers. Cappadocia, Pontus, and Asia were regions of present-day Turkey. Some scholars wonder why Judea appears in the list, and there is no single certain explanation.

On the day of Pentecost, the disciples were filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak in other languages. Those who heard, Jews and converts who had come from many nations, were amazed because they heard the wonders of God in their own language.

God wants his message to reach every person in a way they can understand. Today we can speak of Jesus with simple words, without difficult language, so that others understand him from the heart.
exp.1:9:
This verse continues the list of places from which the people in Jerusalem had come. It names Phrygia and Pamphylia (regions of what is now Turkey), Egypt, and the part of Libya near Cyrene. It also mentions visitors from Rome, who were Jews by birth or converts, that is, people from other nations who had taken up the Jewish faith.

It is the day of Pentecost. The disciples, filled with the Holy Spirit, were speaking in other languages. The crowd, gathered from many nations for the feast, is the one speaking here, amazed that each one heard them in their own language.

God wants his message to reach everyone in a way they can understand. Today we can speak of the gospel in simple words, without complicated language, and with respect for the culture and reality of each person.
exp.1:10:
This verse closes the list of peoples who were in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost. Cretans (from the island of Crete) and Arabians say that they hear the disciples speaking about the wonderful works of God in their own languages.

The speakers here are visitors from many nations, Jews and converts to Judaism, who had come to the feast. The Holy Spirit had just come upon the disciples (Acts 2:1-4). The visitors are amazed because those speaking were Galileans, and yet each one understood them in his own tongue. Scholars debate exactly how the miracle happened, but the text emphasizes that everyone understood.

For today: God wants his message to reach each person in a way that they can understand. We can speak about Jesus with simple, close words, without complicating what God has done.
exp.1:13:
Peter stands up together with the other eleven apostles and speaks in a loud voice. He addresses the Jewish men and all who live in Jerusalem. He asks them to pay attention and to understand what is happening.

Peter speaks after the Holy Spirit came upon the disciples at Pentecost. The crowd was amazed, and some were mocking them, saying they were drunk. Peter does not stay silent, nor does he defend himself in anger; he gives an explanation. Right away he will say that this is what was spoken by the prophet Joel.

When others do not understand what God is doing in our lives, or mock our faith, we can respond with calm and clarity. Peter teaches us to speak with courage, without fear and without giving offense, and to rely on the Word of God.
exp.1:14:
Peter says that the disciples are not drunk, as some suppose, because it is only the third hour of the day. That hour corresponds roughly to nine in the morning, according to the Jewish way of counting time.

It is the day of Pentecost. The disciples had received the Holy Spirit and were speaking in other tongues. Some were mocking them and saying that they were full of new wine, that is, sweet fresh wine. Peter stands up with the eleven apostles and answers calmly. Now he explains that what they see is the work of God, not of drink.

For today: when others misunderstand or mock your faith, do not respond with anger. Imitate Peter: speak with clarity, with respect, and relying on the Word of God.
exp.1:15:
Peter says that what the crowd is seeing is not drunkenness, but the fulfillment of what God announced centuries earlier through the prophet Joel. Peter presents the Scripture as the verse of what has happened.

We are on the day of Pentecost, in Jerusalem. The disciples had just received the Holy Spirit and were speaking in other languages. Some were mocking them, thinking they were drunk. Peter stands up together with the other eleven apostles and explains that this comes from God. To support this, he quotes Joel, an Old Testament prophet, who spoke of the Spirit being poured out on many people.

For today: when you do not understand something God is doing, or when others misread it, return to the Bible. It helps us see clearly what God is doing and to respond with humility and confidence.
exp.1:18:
This verse speaks of amazing things that God promises to show: "wonders" (extraordinary happenings) in the heavens and "signs" on the earth. It mentions blood, fire, and vapor of smoke, that is, pillars of smoke. These are powerful images that announce that God acts in visible and mighty ways.

Here Peter speaks, on the day of Pentecost, explaining to the crowd what was happening. He quotes the prophet Joel (Joel 2). The believers had received the Holy Spirit, and Peter shows that this fulfills God's promise. Scholars interpret in various ways whether these signs are symbolic, already fulfilled, or still future.

For today: even though we may not understand every detail, the passage ends with a clear invitation: whoever calls on the name of the Lord will be saved. Today you can draw near to God with simplicity and trust, without waiting to have everything understood.
exp.1:19:
The sun will be turned to darkness, and the moon to blood, before the coming of the great and glorious Day of the Lord. These are vivid pictures of dramatic signs in the heavens, and the reader can see them plainly: the sky itself will change in ways no one can miss. Dark sun and bloodlike moon are the kind of signs that point people's attention toward God's action.

Peter speaks to the crowd in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost. He is quoting the prophet Joel to explain that the pouring out of the Spirit is part of what God promised. Scholars disagree about whether these signs refer only to the final future, or also to what happened at the cross and in that period. What is certain is that Peter ends with an invitation: everyone who calls on the Lord will be saved.

For today: do not live in fear or try to guess dates. Instead, call on Jesus with confidence each day, and live ready to meet Him.
exp.1:21:
Peter speaks to the people of Israel and asks them to listen. He tells them that Jesus of Nazareth was a man approved by God, that is, backed up and confirmed by him. God showed this through miracles and wonders and signs, that is, works that amazed people and pointed to something greater. Peter adds that they themselves know this, because they saw it happen.

It is the day of Pentecost, in Jerusalem. Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, addresses an amazed crowd. He has just quoted the prophet Joel about salvation for everyone who calls on the Lord. Now he presents Jesus as the center of that promise, relying on what the people had witnessed.

For today: the Christian faith is not based on vague ideas but on concrete facts from the life of Jesus. You can approach the Gospels with confidence and with sincere questions, and let his life speak to you about who God is.
exp.1:25:
Because the speaker keeps the Lord always before him, his heart was filled with joy and his tongue expressed it with gladness. Even his body will rest securely, trusting in what God will do.

Peter is preaching at Pentecost and quotes Psalm 16, written by David. Peter explains that these words are fully fulfilled in Jesus, whom God raised from the dead. His body did not remain in death nor see corruption. Many Christians see here Christ speaking through David. They also see a hope for those who believe in him.

For today: when you feel fear or weariness, practice keeping God present in your day, with a brief prayer or a truth from his Word. That trust can bring you joy and rest, even in the face of death, because Christ rose.
exp.1:27:
God showed Peter the paths that lead to life, and being in his presence fills him with joy.

Peter is speaking at Pentecost, in Jerusalem. He quotes Psalm 16, written by David, to explain that Jesus rose from the dead. Peter points out that David died and his tomb was still there, so David's words pointed beyond himself, to the Christ whom God would raise up. Some scholars also see in the psalm David's own personal hope, but Peter clearly applies it to the resurrection of Jesus.

For today: God does not only give us rules, but shows us the way to life and invites us into his presence. This week, set aside a few minutes each day to pray and read the Bible, not out of obligation, but seeking to be with him. There you will find a joy that does not depend on circumstances.
exp.1:28:
Peter speaks with confidence to the Jewish listeners and tells them they may speak openly about the patriarch David. He died and was buried, and his tomb was still in Jerusalem, among us to this very day.

Peter preaches on Pentecost, after the Holy Spirit came down. He has just quoted Psalm 16, where David speaks of God not leaving his Holy One in the grave. Peter shows that David was not speaking only about himself, since his body was still buried. In this way he prepares the way to announce that Jesus did rise.

For today: David's tomb is still occupied, but Jesus' tomb is empty. We can place our hope in the living Christ, not only in great figures of the past, and trust that He is powerful to give us life.
exp.1:32:
Peter says that Jesus was exalted, that is, taken to a place of honor and power at God's side (the phrase about God's right hand points to authority). There he received the promise of the Holy Spirit from the Father and poured it out. What the crowd could now see and hear were the signs of Pentecost: the sound and the tongues.

Peter speaks to a crowd in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost. Some were mocking the disciples. He explains that this is not drunkenness, but the fulfillment of what was promised. He quotes King David to show that Jesus rose again and reigns as Lord.

Today we can remember that the Spirit is not something we earn through effort, but a gift from the Father through Jesus. We can ask him with confidence to guide us, comfort us, and give us courage to speak of Christ simply and with love.
exp.1:37:
Peter tells his hearers to turn around and turn away from sin, and that each one of them should be baptized in the name of Jesus Christ, and that in this way God will forgive their sins. He also promises that they will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit.

Peter is speaking on the day of Pentecost, in Jerusalem, before a crowd of Jews. He has just told them that Jesus, whom they crucified, is Lord and Christ. Hearing this, they were deeply moved and asked what they should do. This verse is the answer. Christians have debated how baptism and forgiveness relate; the text ties both to repentance and faith in Jesus.

Today, when God shows us something we need to correct, we can answer him honestly, without excuses, and return to Jesus, trusting in his forgiveness.
exp.1:42:
This verse says that everyone felt a reverent fear, that is, a deep respect and awe before God, not a fear that paralyzes. The word "signs" refers to extraordinary events that pointed to the power of God, and "wonders" are happenings that caused amazement. All of this was taking place through the apostles.

Luke, the author of the book of Acts, recounts what happened after Pentecost. About three thousand had believed and were baptized, and the young church devoted itself to teaching, fellowship, the Lord's Supper, and prayer. The miracles confirmed the apostles' message and stirred respect in the people.

For today: We can cultivate a heart that is amazed before God. Before you pray or read the Bible, take a moment to remember who He is, and respond with humility and gratitude.
exp.2:1:
This verse presents a man who was lame from birth, meaning he had never been able to walk. Others carried him every day and laid him beside the gate of the temple called Beautiful. There he begged for alms, that is, money or help, from those who went in to worship.

The narrator is Luke, the author of Acts. He tells what happened when Peter and John were going up to the temple at the hour of prayer. He first presents this man's need, a man who depended completely on others, to set up the miracle that follows. It is not known with certainty exactly where in the temple that gate stood.

For today: God places us near people with real needs. We can ask ourselves whom we are passing by and, in addition to giving what we can, look at them with attention and compassion.
exp.2:2:
This verse tells that the lame man saw Peter and John when they were about to go into the temple, and he asked them for alms. The word "asked" conveys that he kept on asking, persistently, and alms is money given to the poor out of compassion.

The one speaking in the scene is the narrator, Luke, who recounts an ordinary day of prayer. This man had been lame from birth and depended on the help of those who passed by. Every day he was placed beside the gate called Beautiful. He was waiting for a coin, with no idea of what God would do afterward through the apostles.

Many times we ask God or others for small things, not knowing that He wants to give us something greater. Today we can pray with confidence, but also with openness, ready to receive whatever God considers best. And before someone who suffers, we can truly look at them and help.
exp.2:8:
All the people in the temple saw the man who before could not walk. Now he was walking and praising God.

Here Luke, the author of Acts, tells what happened after Peter and John healed a crippled beggar at the gate of the temple called Beautiful. Luke stresses that the healing was visible to everyone. That is why the people were amazed and gathered together, which gave Peter the opportunity to preach about Jesus.

For today: when God acts in your life, do not keep your thankfulness silent. Your sincere praise can show others that God is still at work and awaken in them questions about Him.
exp.2:9:
They recognized that this was the man who used to sit begging at the gate of the temple called Beautiful. When they saw him walking, they were filled with wonder and amazement, that is, with a mix of surprise and fear over what had happened to him.

This verse is part of Luke's account in Acts. Peter and John had just healed, in the name of Jesus, a man who had been lame from birth. Everyone knew his situation because they saw him every day. That is why his change could not be denied. This sets up the speech Peter gives next, in which he explains that the power comes from Jesus and not from them.

For today: when God works in someone's life, people notice. Let your testimony be visible and humble, and always point to God as the author of the change.
exp.2:17:
It says that God fulfilled what he had announced long before through all his prophets: that his Christ, that is, his Messiah, had to suffer. The word "but" is the meaning of the quoted word, and "suffer" is what it means to endure pain.

Peter speaks in Solomon's Porch, in the temple at Jerusalem, after a lame man was healed in the name of Jesus. Peter explains to the crowd that the death of Jesus, though it was done in ignorance, did not take God by surprise. His goal is to lead them to repentance, as the following verse shows.

For today: when we go through pain we do not understand, we can remember that God is able to work within suffering, as he did on the cross. Let us trust in him, and if we have lived far from God, let us come to him with a repentant heart.
exp.2:24:
Peter's listeners are described as heirs of what the prophets announced and of the promise God made to Abraham: that through his offspring all the families of the earth would be blessed.

Peter speaks in the temple to the Israelites, after God healed a lame man in the name of Jesus. He explains to them that Jesus is the announced prophet and the descendant of Abraham. For this reason he reminds them that the promise belongs to them, and the next verse calls them to turn away from their wickedness.

For today: God's blessing is not only for me, but to be shared with everyone. Today I can ask myself whom I can bless with a word of hope, and whether I need to turn to God in some concrete way.
exp.2:25:
It says God raised up his Son Jesus and sent him first to the Jewish people to bless them. That blessing consists in each person turning away from his wickedness, that is, from his sin.

Peter speaks in the temple in Jerusalem to a crowd, after a lame man was healed in the name of Jesus. He reminds them of the promise made to Abraham: through his descendants all the families of the earth would be blessed. Peter explains that this promise is fulfilled in Jesus and calls his people to turn back to God.

For today: God's blessing is not only receiving good things, but also being transformed. Today you can ask God to show you a habit or attitude you should leave behind, and take a concrete step to change with his help.
exp.3:4:
On the following morning, the rulers, elders, and scribes gathered together in Jerusalem. The verse tells us that the Jewish leaders came together at daybreak the day after. The rulers were the governing authorities, the elders were respected leaders of the people, and the scribes were experts in the Law who taught it. This was the highest court of Israel, commonly known as the Sanhedrin.

Luke, the author of Acts, narrates what happened after a lame man was healed at the temple. Peter and John had proclaimed the risen Jesus and were arrested in the evening. Now the authorities gather to question them. Meanwhile, about five thousand people had believed the message.

For today: when your faith leads you to face pressure or criticism, do not be surprised or remain silent out of fear. God can give you the words and the calm you need, as He gave them to Peter and John.
exp.3:9:
Peter says that everyone must know, including the people of Israel, that this man stands here before them whole through the power of the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth. They crucified Jesus, but God raised him from the dead.

Peter speaks before the Jewish council, the leaders and elders, one day after he and John healed a lame man at the temple. The leaders questioned them about what power they had used to do it. Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, answers with boldness and points to Jesus as the source of that healing.

For today: when God does something good in your life, do not keep the credit for yourself. With humility and without fear, say that it was Jesus who did it, even if others do not want to hear it.
exp.3:10:
This verse says that Jesus is the stone that the builders rejected, but that God made him the main stone of the building. The word "rejected" means thrown out because it was judged to be of no use. The "builders" are the people who were constructing the building. The "cornerstone" is the stone at the corner, the one that holds up and lines up the whole structure.

Peter speaks before the religious leaders of Israel. They have brought him to trial because he healed a sick man in the name of Jesus. Filled with the Holy Spirit, Peter quotes Psalm 118:22 and explains that these same leaders rejected Jesus, but God raised him up and honored him.

For today: even though sometimes the world or people ignore Jesus, he remains the firmest foundation. Today you can build your decisions, your relationships, and your hope on him, without fear of what others think.
exp.3:12:
This verse says that the Jewish leaders saw the boldness of Peter and John. They knew these were men without formal training from the religious schools, unlearned and ignorant in the sense of ordinary people who had not been prepared as teachers. That is why they marveled. And they recognized that these men had been with Jesus. Here, "boldness" means courage and firmness to speak without fear.

Peter and John had healed a lame man, and they were brought before the council, the religious court of Jerusalem. Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, had just declared that salvation is found only in Jesus. The judges did not expect such firmness from Galilean fishermen, and they could not deny the miracle.

For today: you do not need titles or extensive preparation to bear witness to Christ. Spending time with Jesus, in prayer and in his Word, shapes in you a character and a courage that others can notice.
exp.3:13:
This verse says that the Jewish leaders saw the man who had been healed there, standing beside Peter and John. Because his healing was real and visible, they had no argument to offer against it.

Here the account is Luke's, which narrates the trial of Peter and John before the council, the religious court of Jerusalem. They had healed a lame man in the name of Jesus and had been taken into custody because of it. The leaders could not deny the miracle, but they did not want to accept its meaning, and so they met together in private to deliberate.

For today: a life changed by Jesus speaks with power. Although we cannot always win an argument, our sincere testimony and our real change can be hard to reject. Live in such a way that others see Christ in you.
exp.3:15:
The religious leaders ask what they should do with Peter and John. They admit that an evident miracle has been done through them. Everyone in Jerusalem knows it, and they cannot deny it.

The members of the Jewish council are speaking behind closed doors. Peter and John had healed a man who was lame and then proclaimed Jesus. The leaders could not dispute the fact, but the message bothered them. So, instead of believing, they look for a way to silence them.

For today: sometimes the facts are clear, but our pride or our fear keeps us from accepting them. Ask God for a humble heart, willing to recognize his work even when it changes your plans or makes you uncomfortable.
exp.3:16:
They say that the Jewish leaders want to stop the message about Jesus from spreading further among the people. For this reason they propose threatening Peter and John so that they will not speak to anyone in this name, that is, about Jesus. The phrase that the message spread no further means that it would not be passed on or become known more widely.

Those who speak are the members of the council, the Sanhedrin, meeting in private. Peter and John had healed a lame man, and the miracle was so obvious that they could not deny it. Their concern was not whether the event was true, but how to curb the influence of the apostles.

For today: sometimes there will be pressure to silence our faith, whether through mockery or rejection. We can respond as Peter and John did: with respect, but with firmness, asking God for courage to keep speaking of Jesus with love and truth.
exp.3:18:
Peter and John answer the authorities with a direct question: is it right in God's sight to obey you rather than God? They invite the council to judge for themselves, and the answer they expect is clear: God comes first.

Peter and John had healed a man who was lame in the name of Jesus. Because of this they were arrested and brought before the Sanhedrin, the Jewish religious council. The leaders forbade them to speak about Jesus. The apostles did not respond with violence or pride, but with firmness and respect, explaining that they could not keep silent about what they had seen and heard.

For today: respecting authorities is good, but when an order clearly conflicts with what God commands us, we must obey Him. Let us do this with calm, humility and a good witness, without looking down on anyone.
exp.3:20:
This verse tells us that the Jewish leaders threatened Peter and John, but in the end they let them go. The word for "let them go" means that they released them or sent them home. They could not find a way to punish them, because the people were praising God for what had happened.

Peter and John had healed a man who was lame at the temple, and afterward they had spoken about Jesus. The chief priests and the elders arrested them and ordered them not to teach in the name of Jesus. Peter and John answered that they could not keep quiet about what they had seen and heard. The miracle was plain to everyone, and that held back the authorities.

For today: when you are called to defend your faith, do it with respect but with firmness. And do not underestimate the power of a transformed life. Many times, what God does in us speaks louder than any argument.
exp.3:21:
This verse says that the man healed through Peter and John was more than forty years old. Luke, the writer, adds this detail to show that it was not a passing matter. The miracle was a sign of divine power that restored his health.

Here the narrator of the book is speaking. Peter and John had been questioned by the Jewish leaders, who could neither deny the healing nor find a way to punish them, because the people were praising God. Chapter 3 tells that this man had been lame from birth. The forty years emphasize that his case was long-standing and well known, and that the healing was plain to see.

For today: God can work in situations that seem old and beyond help. If you have carried a burden for years, do not stop praying or trusting, and when God helps you, tell of it with gratitude.
exp.3:22:
Peter and John, after being released by the Jewish authorities, returned to their community of believers. There they told everything the chief priests and elders had said to them.

Peter and John had healed a lame man and were brought before the council, which forbade them to speak in the name of Jesus. Luke, the author of Acts, tells us that they were not punished because of the fear of the people, who were praising God. When they returned, the two friends reported to the church, and it responded by praying together.

When you face pressure or fear, do not carry it alone. Share it with your community of faith, and pray together, trusting in God.
exp.3:24:
This verse says that God spoke through King David, who is called "your servant," and asked why the nations raged, that is, stirred up in fury, and why the peoples imagined vain things, meaning useless plans that will come to nothing. The word "nations" refers to the non-Jewish nations or peoples.

Peter and John had just been released by the authorities, who had ordered them not to speak about Jesus. When they told the believers, everyone prayed together. Here they quote Psalm 2 and apply it to what happened to Jesus and to the opposition they were now facing. They begin their prayer by recalling that God is the Creator and is above all things.

Today, when something or someone opposes your faith, remember that no human plan can overcome God. Pray as they did: first by looking at who God is, and then by asking for courage.
exp.3:28:
This verse is part of a prayer. The believers ask God to take notice of the threats made by their opponents. But they do not ask him to remove them. Instead, they ask him to give his servants the courage to announce his word with complete boldness, that is, with firmness and without fear.

Peter and John had just been arrested and threatened by the Jewish leaders for speaking about Jesus (Acts 4:18-21). After being released, they went back to the other believers and prayed together. They remembered that God was in control, even when Herod and Pilate opposed Jesus. After they prayed, the place shook and everyone was filled with the Holy Spirit.

When you face pressure or mockery because of your faith, you can pray as they did: not only asking for the problem to disappear, but asking for courage to remain faithful and to speak with love and clarity.
exp.3:30:
This verse tells us that, after they prayed, the place where the believers were gathered was shaken. All of them were filled with the Holy Spirit and began to speak the word of God with boldness, that is, with courage and without fear.

Peter and John had just been threatened by the Jewish leaders to stop speaking about Jesus. When they returned to the other believers, everyone prayed together. They did not ask that the threats would disappear, but for courage to keep speaking and for God to show His power. The shaking was a sign that God had heard them. Some see it as a visible sign of His presence, but the text gives no further details.

When you face pressure or fear because of your faith, pray with other believers. Ask God for courage rather than comfort, and trust that He will give you strength to speak of Him with simplicity and firmness.
exp.3:32:
This verse says that the apostles testified with great force and boldness that Jesus had risen. The phrase "with great power" is the key expression here, and other translations render it the same way. Also, the phrase about great grace being upon them all means that God's favor rested richly on the whole community. It can be understood as God's kindness working among them, or also as the regard people had for them.

Luke, the author of Acts, reports this after the church prayed, was filled with the Spirit, and began to live together in unity, sharing their possessions. The verse links the preaching of the resurrection with a generous way of life, and what follows shows that no one was in need.

Today we might ask ourselves whether our faith shows in how we live. Proclaiming Jesus with words is important, but grace becomes visible when we help those in need, with simplicity and generosity.
exp.3:33:
It says that in the church in Jerusalem no one was in need. Those who owned land or houses sold them of their own free will and brought the money they received.

Luke, the author of Acts, describes the life of the first believers after Pentecost. They were of one heart and one soul, and their lives gave strength to the apostles' testimony about the resurrection. This sharing was voluntary and responded to concrete needs. The following verse says that the money was distributed according to each person's need.

Today we might ask ourselves: what do I have that I can share with a brother or sister who is in need? Perhaps it does not mean selling a house, but giving time, food, or financial help, with generosity and without showing off.
exp.4:2:
Peter asks Ananias why he let Satan fill his heart to lie to the Holy Ghost. To cheat someone means to keep something for yourself in secret; the land he sold is the field he gave up; the money from the sale is what he brought to the apostles.

Peter speaks in the early church in Jerusalem, where many believers sold their property to help those in need. Ananias and Sapphira sold a piece of land, kept part of the money, and pretended to hand over everything. Their sin was not in keeping a part, since the money was theirs, but in pretending to a full surrender that was not true.

God looks for sincerity more than appearance. We can give little or much, but we must not pretend before God or before others. Today, before you serve or give, ask yourself: "Am I doing this from the heart, or so that people will see me?" Tell God the truth, and He will give you an honest heart.
exp.4:4:
Ananias heard Peter's words, fell to the ground, and died. Great fear came upon everyone who heard about it.

Peter speaks in the early days of the church in Jerusalem. Many believers were selling their possessions to help those in need. Ananias sold a piece of property, but he pretended to hand over all the money when he was actually keeping part of it. Peter tells him that his sin was lying to God, not so much keeping the money, since he was free to give it or not. Scholars agree that the problem was the deceit; the text does not say how to judge Ananias's eternal fate.

For today: God values sincerity. Serve others and give with an honest heart, without pretending to be more than you are, and remember that God sees the heart.
exp.4:5:
What it says: After Ananias fell dead, some young men in the community rose up, wrapped up or took hold of his body, carried him out, and buried him.

Context: Ananias and his wife Sapphira sold a piece of property and gave only part of the money to the apostles, but they claimed it was the whole amount. Peter explained that no one forced them to give, but lying meant deceiving God. Luke tells us the church was filled with great fear. The burial was quick, with no ceremony or words, and the text gives no further details. Some see here a serious judgment meant to protect the purity of the young church.

For today: God values sincerity more than appearances. If we give, serve, or help, let us do it honestly, without pretending so that others will admire us. We can ask God for a clean and simple heart.
exp.4:6:
It says that about three hours passed after the death of Ananias, and then his wife, Sapphira, arrived. She did not know what had happened to her husband.

Luke, the author of Acts, recounts this within the story of the early church. Ananias and Sapphira had sold a piece of property and pretended to give everything to the apostles, but they kept back part of the money. Peter had confronted Ananias for lying. Now Sapphira arrives, and in the following verse Peter gives her the chance to tell the truth.

For today: honesty before God matters more than appearances. If we have kept silent about something or pretended, we can come before God with sincerity, without waiting for others to uncover us.
exp.4:8:
Peter asks Sapphira why she and her husband agreed together to test the Spirit of the Lord, that is, to put him to the test to see whether he would notice her lie. He tells her that the men who have just buried Ananias are at the door and will carry her out too.

Peter speaks in the early days of the church in Jerusalem. Ananias and Sapphira sold a property and pretended to hand over all the money, but they kept back a part. Peter gives both of them the chance to tell the truth, and she insists on the lie. The problem was not giving little, but deceiving in order to appear to give more.

God looks for sincerity more than appearance. Today we can ask ourselves whether, in our giving, our service, or our life of faith, we are trying to impress others. We can ask God to help us be honest, to acknowledge our faults, and not to pretend to be what we are not.
exp.4:9:
She fell down suddenly at Peter's feet. The young men who had buried her husband Ananias shortly before came in, found her dead, carried her out, and buried her beside him. Here "dead" simply means that she had stopped breathing and had died.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells this after Ananias and Sapphira sold a piece of land and pretended to give the whole amount to the church, when in fact they kept part of it for themselves. Peter gives Sapphira the chance to tell the truth, but she keeps up the lie. The text presents it as a deception planned against the Holy Spirit. Then the church is filled with great reverent fear.

God desires honesty in our lives. We do not need to appear to be more than we are. We can give or serve with humility, and if we fail, it is better to admit it honestly than to hide it.
exp.4:20:
They obeyed the angel: at daybreak they went into the temple and kept on teaching. Meanwhile, the high priest and his companions gathered the council and all the elders of Israel. Then they sent for the prisoners from the jail, not knowing that they were no longer there.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells what happened. The apostles had been put in prison for preaching about Jesus. An angel led them out during the night and told them to keep speaking the message of this new life, that is, the message of the gospel. The religious leaders prepare a trial, but God had already acted.

For today: when God gives you a task, carry it out calmly, even when there is opposition. The apostles did not hide; they went back to the most visible place. Trust that God cares for his work and for those who serve him.
exp.4:21:
It says that the officers, that is, the guards or attendants sent by the council, came to the prison to bring the apostles, but did not find them there. So they went back and reported to their superiors. The word "officers" here means assistants or constables, not ministers in the sense of pastors.

The narrator, Luke, tells what happened after an angel of the Lord brought the apostles out of the prison during the night and told them to keep preaching in the temple. While they were already teaching, the high priest and the assembled council sent for them, not knowing that they were no longer in custody.

For today: when the obstacles seem stronger than you are, remember that God can open paths you cannot see. Trust Him and keep obeying what He has asked of you, even when the situation looks closed.
exp.4:22:
The temple officers return with a puzzling report. They say the prison was shut tight, with all safety, and the guards were still standing outside the doors. But when they opened it, they found no one inside.

The ones speaking are the officers, that is, the men sent by the high priest and the council to bring the apostles. The apostles had been put in prison for preaching, and an angel of the Lord had brought them out during the night (Acts 5:19-20). The officers report to the authorities, and the authorities are left confused, not knowing how the whole matter would end.

For today: no closed door or human authority can stop God's plans. When you feel shut in by circumstances, trust that God can open ways you never imagined, and remain faithful in what He has entrusted to you.
exp.4:23:
When they heard about the men who had disappeared from the prison, the religious leaders were perplexed. The high priest is the chief of the priests. The captain of the temple was the head of the temple guard. The phrase "they doubted of them whereunto this would grow" means that they did not know how all this would end, or what was happening.

The apostles had been arrested for preaching about Jesus. The guards reported that the prison was still locked and watched, but empty. Luke, the author of Acts, shows that an angel had led them out (verse 19), although the leaders did not yet know it. Their bewilderment reveals that their plans could not stop the work of God.

For today: when opposition or circumstances seem to control everything, remember that God works even behind closed doors. Trust that his purposes are moving forward, even when you cannot see how.
exp.4:24:
This verse tells that someone came with surprising news for the Jewish leaders. The apostles, whom they had put in prison, were no longer there. Now they were in the temple, teaching the people.

The apostles had been locked up for preaching about Jesus. According to the account, an angel of the Lord had let them out at night and told them to keep teaching. The one speaking here is an informant who reports to the high priest and the other leaders. They are left puzzled, because the doors were still securely shut and the guards were in their places.

For today: when you feel that something is blocking what God has asked you to do, remember that He can open paths you cannot see. Keep being faithful, with patience and trust.
exp.4:25:
This verse says that the captain of the temple went with his guards and brought the apostles before the council, but without using force. They did this because they were afraid the people would stone them. The captain is the one in charge of the temple guard, and the officers are his helpers or guards.

The account is from Luke. The apostles had been put in prison, but an angel led them out at night, and they went back to teaching in the temple. The religious leaders, concerned about their authority, sent for them. Notice that the people respected the apostles, and for that reason the guards acted with care.

For today: sometimes people with power seem more worried about what others think than about what is right. Let us ask God for courage to do what is right regardless of others' opinions, and to treat with respect even those who do not think as we do.
exp.4:28:
Peter and the other apostles answer that they must obey God rather than men.

The apostles stand before the Jewish council, the same court that had earlier forbidden them to teach in the name of Jesus. An angel had brought them out of prison and told them to keep preaching in the temple. That is why the high priest rebukes them, and Peter replies with firmness and without hatred, so that he can keep proclaiming Jesus.

Today, this verse does not give us permission to be rebellious or rude. It invites us to respect authorities in whatever is just, but not to deny our faith or do wrong when we are pressured. Pray, seek guidance in the Bible, and act with humility and courage.
exp.4:29:
This verse says that the God whom our people worshiped from long ago raised Jesus up, the one whom the Jewish leaders put to death by hanging him on a cross. "Raised up" means that God brought him back to life. The "tree" is the cross, and the reference to hanging recalls that, according to Deuteronomy 21:23, a person hanged on a tree was considered under a curse.

Peter and the apostles speak before the Sanhedrin, the Jewish council. They had been jailed and forbidden to teach in the name of Jesus. They answer that they must obey God rather than men, and they present the resurrection as God's answer to the verdict of the leaders.

For today: when what people ask of us clashes with what God has clearly shown, we must obey Him. Let us do so with humility and courage, without hatred, and wishing that others also receive forgiveness and repentance.
exp.4:30:
This verse says that God lifted up Jesus and placed him in the highest position, at his right hand, as Prince and Savior. The word "exalted" means lifted up and honored. The right hand is a picture of power and honor. "Prince" here can be understood as a leader or guide. God did this so that Israel could be given repentance (turning back to God) and forgiveness of sins.

Peter and the apostles are speaking before the Jewish council. They had been arrested for preaching about Jesus, and they had been forbidden to teach. They answer that obeying God comes first. Even to those who put Jesus to death, Peter offers an open door: repentance and forgiveness.

For today: no matter how far you have strayed from God, Jesus offers forgiveness and a new beginning. Today you can turn to him sincerely and receive that grace.
exp.4:34:
Gamaliel speaks to the members of the Jewish council. He says: "Men of Israel, be careful about what you intend to do with these men." The phrase is a warning to pause and think carefully before acting in haste.

The apostles had been arrested for preaching about Jesus. The leaders were so angry that they wanted to kill them. Gamaliel, a respected Pharisee and teacher of the law, asked that the apostles be taken out of the room for a moment. He wanted to speak calmly and put a stop to the violence. He would then give examples of other movements that had failed.

For today: before reacting in anger or judging someone, let us pause. Thinking calmly, listening, and praying help us avoid acting unjustly or opposing what may come from God.
exp.4:36:
Judas of Galilee appeared at the time of the census, that is, the registration of the people for counting them and collecting taxes. Many followed him, but he died, and his followers were scattered and broken up.

The one speaking is Gamaliel, a respected teacher of the law, before the Sanhedrin. The apostles had just been arrested for preaching about Jesus. Gamaliel gives examples of other leaders who failed in order to advise calm. Historians discuss how some of the details of his examples fit together, but the central idea is clear.

For today: do not let yourself be carried away only by what looks popular or noisy, nor reject it in a hurry. Think calmly, pray, compare with the Bible, and watch the fruits over time. Try not to resist God out of pride or fear.
exp.4:40:
They left the presence of the council, meaning the Jewish court, and they did so rejoicing. They were glad because God had counted them worthy to suffer dishonor, that is, shame and mistreatment, for the sake of the Name, which is Jesus.

This is part of Luke's account. The apostles had been arrested for preaching about Jesus. The teacher Gamaliel advised caution, and the council had them beaten and ordered them not to speak in the name of Jesus. Even so, they did not leave discouraged. They saw the suffering as an honor for belonging to Christ, and right away they went on preaching.

For today: when others criticize you or make fun of you for living your faith simply and honestly, do not lose heart. You can ask God to give you a fresh perspective and peace, and to remain faithful with humility and love.
exp.5:1:
The twelve apostles gathered the whole community of believers and told them that it was not right for them to stop teaching the word of God in order to take charge of serving the tables, that is, of distributing the food.

Peter speaks together with the other eleven apostles. The church was growing, and the believers who spoke Greek were complaining that their widows were not receiving the daily help given to the Hebrew widows. The apostles wanted to solve the problem without neglecting their main calling: prayer and teaching.

For today: God distributes different services in his church, and all of them are valuable. Ask yourself what your calling is and how you can serve faithfully without neglecting what is most important. Also learn to share responsibilities, trusting other brothers and sisters so that no one is worn out or left without care.
exp.5:5:
The seven men chosen by the community were brought before the apostles. The apostles prayed and laid their hands on them. "Presented" means that they brought them forward in front of them, and laying on hands was a gesture of blessing and commission.

Luke, the author of Acts, recounts this moment. The Greek-speaking believers complained that their widows were not receiving fair daily care. The apostles did not want to neglect prayer and teaching, so the church chose seven men to serve. Scholars debate whether that role was the origin of the deacons; the text does not call them that.

Serving others is a sacred thing and deserves prayer. If you are asked to help in your church, or if you encourage someone else, do it with prayer, recognizing that God sustains even simple tasks.
exp.5:6:
It says that the message of God kept spreading and that a great many people in Jerusalem came to believe in Jesus. Even a large group of Jewish priests was obedient to the faith, meaning they accepted and followed the gospel. "Obedient" is the word the verse uses for this response.

Luke, the author of Acts, is summarizing what happened after the church solved a problem about caring for the widows. The apostles asked for seven trustworthy men to be chosen to serve, so that they themselves could devote themselves to prayer and teaching. The priests worked in the temple, so their response was remarkable. The Bible gives no further details about them.

For today: when we solve problems with order, humility, and service, the church is free to grow. Ask yourself what simple task you can take on to help others.
exp.5:8:
This verse says that some Jews from a synagogue rose up to argue with Stephen. That synagogue was called the synagogue of the Libertines, who were probably Jews who had been freed from slavery or were descendants of such people. Alongside them were Jews from Cyrene, Alexandria, Cilicia, and Asia. The word used for their arguing means to debate, to dispute with arguments.

Luke, the author of Acts, recounts what happened. Stephen was one of the seven chosen to serve, and God worked miracles through him. As the faith was growing in Jerusalem, opposition arose. Some think it involved several synagogues and others think it was only one; the text does not fully make this clear. What is clear is that they could not answer him, and so they resorted to lies.

For today: when someone opposes your faith, respond with truth, humility, and patience. If you do not have all the answers, do not lose heart; trust that God sustains you, and avoid defending yourself with deceit or anger.
exp.6:2:
God told Abraham to leave his land and his family, and to go to a place that he had not yet shown him. The word "kindred" in the verse means relatives or close family. God asked him to set out first, and the destination would become clear along the way.

The speaker is Stephen, who has been accused before the Jewish council of speaking against the temple and the law. To defend himself, he reviews the history of Israel, beginning with Abraham. In doing so he shows that God acted and revealed himself long before the temple existed, and that God's presence is not tied to one single place.

Today, God sometimes calls us to take a step of faith without giving us the whole plan. We can ask him for the courage to obey what he already shows us, trusting that he will guide the rest of the way.
exp.6:3:
The verse tells how Abraham came out of the land of the Chaldeans and settled in Haran. There his father died, and then God brought him into the land of Canaan, where the hearers of Stephen were now living.

Stephen speaks before the Jewish council, defending himself against false accusations. He reviews the history of Israel to show that God always acted by guiding his people, and that his presence was never tied to one place or one temple. Abraham received the call while he was still in a foreign land. Concerning the timeline between the death of Terah and Abraham's departure, scholars offer different explanations.

For today: Abraham obeyed without seeing the whole destination. When God asks you for a step, take the one you can see, trusting that he knows the entire path.
exp.6:4:
It says that God gave Abraham no property in that land, not even a small piece of ground to set his foot on. But He promised that one day it would belong to him, and to his offspring after him, and He made that promise when Abraham still had no children.

The one speaking is Stephen, before the Jewish council, as he recounts the history of Israel. He wants to show that God works through His promise and His calling, not through what people can see or own. Abraham obeyed and went forward trusting what God had said.

For today: sometimes God promises something and for a long time we see no results. Even so, we can trust His faithfulness and keep obeying with patience, knowing that He keeps His word in His own time.
exp.6:11:
It says that Jacob heard there was grain in Egypt and sent his sons there for the first time, the "fathers" of the Israelites. The "heard" in the verse means that Jacob learned of it. "Sent our fathers" means that he sent his sons to buy food during the famine.

This is part of Stephen's speech before the Jewish council. He is going over the history of Israel and recalls how God looked after Joseph and his family in the middle of the crisis. Stephen shows that God works even in difficult times, though people sometimes do not recognize it right away. In the account in Genesis, the brothers did not yet know who Joseph was.

For today: when we go through scarcity or trials, it is wise to listen, to act with wisdom, and to take the step within our reach. God may be preparing a provision that we cannot yet see.
exp.6:15:
The remains of Jacob and of Israel's forefathers were carried from Egypt to Shechem. There they were placed in a tomb that had been bought with money from the sons of Hamor. The word "carried" in the verse means taken from one place to another.

Stephen is speaking in his defense before the Jewish council. He reminds them of Israel's history to show that God kept his promise even though his people lived far from the promised land. There is a difficulty: Genesis says that Abraham bought a burial place in Hebron, and that Jacob bought a piece of land in Shechem. Scholars explain this in several ways, for example, that Stephen summed up two events into one. There is no single certain answer.

For today: God keeps his promises even when they take a long time. Trust in him and wait with patience.
exp.6:19:
This verse says that Moses was born just when Egypt was persecuting the Hebrew children. The phrase about being pleasing to God can also be understood as being beautiful in God's sight, and the wording allows both meanings. Being brought up means that he was cared for in his father's house for three months, hidden away from danger.

The one speaking is Stephen, before the Jewish council, in his defense. He reviews the history of Israel to show how God worked in the middle of oppression. The three months match the account in Exodus 2, where his parents hid him. Stephen emphasizes that God was caring for Moses even in a time of threat.

For today: even when everything seems against us, God keeps working quietly. You can faithfully care for what He has entrusted to you, without expecting everything to be easy, and trust that He has a purpose.
exp.6:28:
According to the account, when Moses heard these words from that Hebrew man, he fled from Egypt and lived as a stranger in the land of Midian. There he had two sons.

The one speaking is Stephen, in his defense before the Jewish council. He reviews the history of Israel to show that the people often rejected those whom God sent. Moses wanted to help his brothers, but they turned him away. His flight marked the beginning of about forty years of waiting in the desert, before God called him.

For today: when one of our plans fails or someone rejects us, it is not the end. God can use times of waiting and distance to prepare us. Trust that he is still at work, even when you cannot see the way.
exp.6:31:
This verse says that God presents himself to Moses as the same God who revealed himself to his ancestors: Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Moses, filled with fear, did not dare to look. The phrase "fear" here means being frightened or feeling deep reverence, and "did not dare" means he would not venture to look.

These words are part of Stephen's speech before the Jewish council. He reviews the history of Israel and cites Exodus 3, when God spoke from the burning bush. Stephen wants to show that God is not bound to one place, since he revealed himself in the desert, and that he has always been faithful to his people and to his promises.

For today: God is faithful and at the same time holy. We can come to him with confidence, but also with sincere respect. Today, before you pray, pause briefly to remember who God is and to approach him with humility and gratitude.
exp.6:32:
God tells Moses to take off his sandals, because the ground where he is standing is holy ground, that is, a place set apart for God. In that time, the footwear meant here was the sandals worn on the road.

Stephen is speaking before the Jewish council and retells the history of Israel. He recounts how God appeared to Moses in the burning bush, in the desert. The place was not holy in itself, but because of the presence of God. Moses was afraid, and God spoke to him to send him to free his people. Stephen wants to show that God acts and reveals himself also outside the temple.

For today: when we pray or read the Bible, we can pause and approach God with reverence and humility. Taking off our sandals can mean setting aside haste and distractions, so that we can truly listen to him.
exp.6:38:
This verse says that the fathers of Israel did not want to obey Moses. On the contrary, they rejected him, and in their hearts they turned back toward Egypt. They did not return there with their feet, but with their desire: they longed for their former life.

The one speaking is Stephen, defending himself before the Jewish council in Jerusalem. He reminds them that Moses, sent by God, was rejected by his own people. In this way he shows that Israel had a habit of resisting those whom God sent, and the verses that follow illustrate it with the golden calf. So he prepares his accusation against those who had rejected Jesus.

For today: God can speak to us clearly and we can still disobey, because the heart misses what is old. Ask Him to give you a willing heart, and obey today in something specific that you already know He is asking of you.
exp.6:40:
It says that the people of Israel, in the wilderness, made a calf, offered sacrifices to it, and rejoiced in something they had made with their own hands. An image worshiped as a god is what the verse calls an idol.

Stephen speaks before the Jewish council, reviewing the history of Israel. He recalls the episode of the golden calf (Exodus 32), when Moses delayed coming down the mountain. In this way he shows that the people had already rejected those whom God sent, and so he prepares his accusation against his hearers for rejecting Jesus.

For today: we can place our trust and joy in things we ourselves build, such as money, success, or image. Today you can ask yourself what gives you security apart from God, and return to trusting Him.
exp.6:43:
Our fathers, Israel's ancestors, had the tabernacle of witness in the wilderness. That was the sacred tent where God made his presence known among his people. God himself commanded Moses to build it, and asked him to make it according to the pattern he had seen.

Stephen is speaking before the Jewish council, reviewing the history of Israel. Earlier he mentioned the people's idolatry in the wilderness. Now he stresses that, even so, God gave them a place of worship. Many understand that Stephen is preparing his argument that God does not depend on a building, since his presence accompanied a people on the move.

For today: God is not found only in special places. He wants to be near you wherever you are, so seek him with sincerity and obedience, not only in a temple or on a day of worship.
exp.6:48:
God is so great that heaven is like his throne and the earth like the small stool where he rests his feet. For that reason he asks what house human beings could build for him, or what place would be his resting place.

Stephen speaks before the Sanhedrin, accused of speaking against the temple. He quotes the prophet Isaiah (66:1-2). He reminds them that Solomon built the temple, but God is not confined to buildings made by human hands. Then he rebukes his listeners for resisting the Holy Spirit, as their ancestors did.

Today we can remember that God does not depend on a place, and that what matters is a heart ready to listen to him. Before we think about buildings or customs, it is good to ask ourselves whether we are open to what the Spirit says to us.
exp.6:51:
This verse says that the ancestors of the people persecuted all the prophets. They even killed those who announced ahead of time that the Just One would come, that is, Jesus. Now, says Stephen, those who are listening to him have betrayed him and murdered him. The phrase about announcing beforehand means that they warned of it well in advance.

Stephen, a follower of Jesus, is speaking before the Jewish council. They had accused him of speaking against the temple and the law. He reviews the history of Israel and shows that the people often rejected those whom God sent. His words are harsh because he wants them to recognize their resistance to the Holy Spirit. They react with fury.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we are willing to listen to God even when it makes us uncomfortable. Before defending ourselves or getting angry at a correction, it is wise to pray and to examine with humility whether God is speaking to us.
exp.6:56:
What it says: After hearing Stephen, the people listening to him began to shout loudly and covered their ears so they would not hear him anymore. Then they all rushed at him together. The word for "rushed" means to attack with force, and "together" means they did it all in agreement.

Context: Stephen was standing before the Sanhedrin, the Jewish council, accused of speaking against the temple and the law. He had just said that he saw Jesus standing at the right hand of God. To them, this sounded like blasphemy, so they reacted with fury instead of listening. The account goes on to his death, and it mentions Saul, who was present.

For today: Sometimes we cover our ears when a truth makes us uncomfortable. Let us ask God for a humble heart to listen, even to what confronts us. And like Stephen, let us seek to respond with faith and peace, not with anger.
exp.6:57:
This verse tells how they took Stephen outside Jerusalem and stoned him. The witnesses, who were the ones accusing him, laid their outer garments at the feet of a young man named Saul.

Luke, the author of Acts, narrates the death of Stephen, who had just said that he saw Jesus standing at the right hand of God. The council was enraged and condemned him. Here Saul appears for the first time, and he would later become the apostle Paul. The Bible does not say that he threw stones, but it shows that he was present and approved of this (Acts 8:1).

For today: God can use the faithful witness of someone, even in the midst of suffering, to reach lives that seem lost. Let us keep being faithful and pray for those who oppose the faith.
exp.6:58:
This verse tells us that while the people were stoning Stephen, he prayed and said: "Lord Jesus, receive my spirit." To stone someone means to kill them by throwing stones at them. Calling upon God means addressing God in prayer. Here Stephen speaks directly to Jesus.

Stephen had just defended his faith before the Jewish council, and he said that he saw Jesus standing at the right hand of God. The leaders were enraged, dragged him out of the city, and killed him. Among those present was Saul, a young man who would later become the apostle Paul. Stephen's words resemble those of Jesus on the cross, when he committed his spirit to the Father (Luke 23:46).

For today: in our most difficult moments, we can speak to Jesus with confidence, even with a short sentence. He hears and sustains his own, even when everything seems lost.
exp.7:3:
This verse says that the Christians who had to flee from Jerusalem did not stay silent. Wherever they went, they told the message of Jesus. The scattered believers were spread out and dispersed into different places, and the message they carried is the gospel.

Luke, the author of Acts, is narrating what happened after the death of Stephen. Saul was harshly persecuting the church, and many believers left Jerusalem. What seemed like a defeat became an opportunity: the gospel began to spread beyond the city, as the case of Philip in Samaria shows right after.

For today: even in difficult times, such as a forced change, a loss, or a move, God can use us. We can share simply what Jesus has done in us, wherever we are.
exp.7:7:
This verse says that in the city where Philip was preaching there was great joy. The word that refers to this joy names a deep gladness that goes beyond a passing moment of laughter. The phrase that connects this verse to what came before shows that the joy was the result of what had just happened.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells us that Philip came to Samaria after the persecution in Jerusalem. The people listened closely to his message about Christ. They saw signs: people freed from evil spirits and sick people healed. That is why the city was filled with joy. Shortly afterward, Simon, a sorcerer who had previously deceived the people, is mentioned.

Today, the gospel still brings joy when we receive it with attention and faith. This week, listen to God's Word with an open heart and share with someone the good news of what God has done in your life. In this way, others might also rejoice.
exp.7:11:
It says that the Samaritans believed the message Philip preached, which told them about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ. After believing, both men and women were baptized.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells how the gospel came to Samaria. Before this, a man named Simon had amazed everyone with his magic arts, and people followed him. But when Philip preached about Jesus, they stopped focusing their attention on Simon and believed in Christ. Baptism was the public sign of that new faith.

For today: what changes a life is not an impressive person but the message of Jesus. We can ask ourselves whom we are truly following, and share Christ simply, trusting that God works through his word.
exp.7:13:
This verse tells us that the apostles who remained in Jerusalem heard that Samaria had accepted the message of God. Then they sent Peter and John to visit them. The word "Jerusalem" in the verse refers to the city of Jerusalem, and the phrase about receiving the word of God means that the Samaritans believed the message of the gospel.

Here the account is told by Luke. Philip had preached in Samaria, and many believed and were baptized. The Samaritans were a people despised by many Jews, so this was a very big step. The apostles sent Peter and John, probably to accompany, confirm, and support this new work. The verses that follow show that they prayed for the new believers so that they would receive the Holy Spirit.

For today: when God works in places or among people who seem different to us, let us not look at them with suspicion. Let us draw near with support, prayer, and joy, and help new believers grow.
exp.7:14:
Peter and John came to Samaria and prayed for the believers there. They wanted them to receive the Holy Spirit.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells how Philip had preached in Samaria, and many believed and were baptized. The apostles in Jerusalem sent Peter and John to be with these new believers. The following verse explains that the Spirit had not yet fallen on them. Commentators explain this case in different ways, since in Acts the way the Spirit is received varies from one situation to another.

For today: let us pray for one another, especially for those who are just beginning to believe, asking God to fill and strengthen them. We can also welcome and support brothers and sisters from other places, seeking the unity of the church.
exp.7:17:
This verse tells how Simon saw that the Holy Spirit was given when the apostles placed their hands on people. Then he offered them money. The word "laying on" means the act of placing hands on someone, and the word "saw" is the everyday form used today.

The narrator is Luke, the author of Acts. Philip had preached in Samaria, and many believed and were baptized. Later Peter and John came from Jerusalem and prayed for them. Simon, who had practiced magic before, was amazed by what he saw. He wanted to buy that power, as if it were a personal tool. Peter rebuked him firmly.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we seek God for what we can get from Him or for Himself. His gifts cannot be bought, nor are they used to gain prestige or power. They are received with humility and used to serve others.
exp.7:19:
Peter speaks to Simon with great firmness. Peter says that Simon's money should go to ruin along with him, because he thought the gift of God could be bought with money.

Simon was a man from Samaria who had practiced magic and then believed the message preached by Philip. Seeing that the apostles prayed and people received the Holy Spirit, he wanted to buy that power. Peter rebukes him because his heart was not right. Even so, Peter calls him to repent and ask forgiveness. Some debate how genuine his faith was, and the text does not make this clear.

For today: God's grace cannot be bought with money, service, or good works. Examine your motives: do you seek God to receive his gift with humility, or to gain power or advantage? Receive it with gratitude.
exp.7:24:
This verse says that Peter and John, after giving their witness and preaching the word of the Lord in Samaria, returned to Jerusalem. On the way back, they kept sharing the good news about Jesus in many villages of the Samaritans. "Testified" means telling what one has seen and lived. "Gospel" means good news. "Jerusalem" is Jerusalem.

The book of Acts is narrated by Luke. The apostles had gone to Samaria to confirm the work that Philip had begun, and there the encounter with Simon the magician took place. Now, their visit finished, they return, but without ceasing to preach. This shows that the gospel was beginning to cross borders that had once been hard to overcome between Jews and Samaritans.

For today: no special trip is needed to share Christ. As we go from place to place, at work, at home with family, or on our daily path, we can speak simply about what God has done in us.
exp.7:26:
Philip obeys at once: he gets up and goes. On the road he meets an Ethiopian man, a eunuch, a high official of Candace, queen of Ethiopia. He was in charge of all her treasure. He had come to Jerusalem to worship God.

The one telling the story is Luke, the author of Acts. An angel had told Philip to go along the desert road toward Gaza, without explaining why. "Candace" seems to be a title used by the queens of Ethiopia (Nubia), not a personal name. Where and how exactly this man worshiped, the Bible does not detail.

For today: Philip obeyed without knowing the full plan. If you feel God is asking you to take a step, take the one you already understand, and trust that He has prepared someone on the way for that encounter.
exp.7:28:
Here the verse says that the Holy Spirit gave Philip a direct instruction: to go over to the chariot of the Ethiopian and stay by it. The chariot here is a traveling carriage, the vehicle in which the man was riding along the road.

It is the Spirit of God who speaks, and he does so after an angel had already sent Philip to a desert road. There was traveling an important official of Ethiopia, in charge of the queen's treasures, who was returning from worship in Jerusalem and reading the prophet Isaiah. The Spirit arranged this meeting so that someone could explain to him what he was reading.

For today: let us stay attentive to God's guidance and willing to go over to someone who is seeking answers, without waiting until we have everything figured out. Sometimes the first step is simply to come close and listen.
exp.7:32:
