This verse quotes Isaiah 53:7-8 and speaks of someone who suffered humiliation and injustice: he was not given a fair judgment, and his life was taken from the earth. Scholars interpret it in more than one way.

The one speaking is Luke, the author of Acts, who tells how an Ethiopian eunuch, an official of the queen of Ethiopia, was reading this passage from Isaiah in his chariot. He did not understand whom it was about. Philip, guided by God, came near and, starting from this Scripture, proclaimed Jesus to him as the one who suffered in our place.

For today: do not be afraid to approach the Bible with questions. If you do not understand something, ask for help from a mature believer or a faithful teacher, and pray that God will show you Jesus in its pages.
exp.7:33:
Here the eunuch asks Philip about whom the prophet is speaking in the passage he is reading. He wants to know whether Isaiah was speaking about himself or about someone else.

The Ethiopian official speaks, returning in his chariot while reading the book of Isaiah. Philip had come up to him and asked whether he understood what he was reading. He admitted that he needed someone to guide him. His question shows humility and a genuine desire to understand. Philip used that moment to tell him about Jesus.

For today: do not be afraid to ask questions when you read the Bible. Seek the help of people who have experience in the faith, and always have the humility to recognize when you need to learn.
exp.7:36:
Philip tells the eunuch that he may be baptized if he believes with all his heart. The eunuch answers with a simple confession: he believes that Jesus Christ is the Son of God. The word "hinder" in the question before this one means to stand in the way or to oppose.

Philip, an evangelist, had explained to the eunuch, an Ethiopian official, the passage from Isaiah that he was reading, showing him that it spoke of Jesus. Seeing water along the road, the eunuch asked to be baptized. It should be said that this verse does not appear in the oldest Greek manuscripts, and many modern translations omit it or note it separately. Even so, the faith it expresses agrees with what the rest of the New Testament teaches.

Today, the faith God looks for is not perfect knowledge but a sincere trust in Jesus. You can express it simply, as the eunuch did, and live it with joy.
exp.7:37:
This verse tells us that the eunuch ordered the chariot to stop. Then he and Philip went down into the water, and Philip baptized him. Here, "eunuch" referred to a high official of the queen of Ethiopia. The word translated "baptized him" is the one the verse uses for the act itself.

The eunuch had been reading the prophet Isaiah, and Philip explained to him that those words spoke of Jesus. When they saw water, the eunuch asked what would prevent his baptism. Philip told him that believing with all his heart was enough, and the eunuch confessed that Jesus Christ is the Son of God. After being baptized, he went on his way full of joy.

For today: baptism is a simple, public response to faith in Christ. If you have believed, you do not need to complicate this step or delay it without reason. Talk with your pastor or your church, and take this step with joy.
exp.7:39:
After baptizing the eunuch, Philip is said to have been found suddenly in Azotus. Azotus was the ancient Philistine city of Ashdod, near the coast.

It is the narrator, Luke, who tells what happened. Philip had just explained the Scriptures to the Ethiopian eunuch, and the Spirit carried him to another place. Some understand it to have been a miraculous transfer; the text gives no further details. What is clear is that Philip kept preaching along the coast.

For today: when God closes one task, do not keep looking back. Keep serving wherever you are, speaking simply of Jesus to those you meet on your path, in your neighborhood, your work, or your family.
exp.8:1:
Saul asked the high priest for letters of authorization, addressed to the synagogues of Damascus. He wanted that, if he found men or women who followed the Way, he could bring them as prisoners to Jerusalem.

Luke, the author of Acts, describes here how Saul, still an enemy of the church, sought to spread his persecution beyond Jerusalem. The synagogues of Damascus were Jewish communities, and those letters gave him religious backing. A few verses later, Jesus will stop him on the road and completely change his life.

For today: Saul was sincerely convinced he was doing the right thing, and yet he was wrong. We can ask God for humility to examine our convictions in the light of Jesus, and be willing to change course when He shows us the way.
exp.8:8:
This verse says that Saul spent three days in Damascus without being able to see, and that during all that time he neither ate nor drank anything. He was blind and in complete fasting.

The one who narrates is Luke, the author of Acts. Saul, who was persecuting the Christians, had just met Jesus on the road and had been left blind by that light. His companions led him by the hand into the city. Afterward, the Lord tells Ananias that Saul is praying. Many understand that those three days were a time of anguish and reflection, although the text does not explain why he fasted.

There are moments when God stops our life so that we will listen to him. If you are in a difficult pause, do not rush: pray, think, and let God put things in order within you.
exp.8:11:
Saul, who is praying in Damascus, has already had a vision. In it he sees a man named Ananias coming into the house and placing his hand on him so that he may see again.

The one speaking is the Lord, addressing Ananias, a disciple in Damascus. Saul had been left blind after meeting Jesus on the road. God explains to Ananias what He had already shown Saul, so that Ananias may have confidence and obey, even though Saul had persecuted believers, as Ananias himself points out afterward.

For today: God can prepare us and other people at the same time for a task. If He asks us to draw near to someone who frightens us or whom we distrust, we can obey with confidence, knowing that He is already at work in that person.
exp.8:12:
Ananias answers the Lord honestly: he has heard from many people about Saul and about the harm he has done to the saints in Jerusalem. The word "saints" here refers to the believers in Jesus, the people of God.

God has just told Ananias, a disciple in Damascus, to go and pray for Saul so that he may regain his sight. Ananias is afraid, because Saul was known as a persecutor of Christians. This is not rebellious disobedience; it is an honest doubt that he brings to the Lord, and the Lord answers him with patience and explains his plan.

We can bring our fears and questions to God with confidence, without pretending. But we also learn that God can change people who seem impossible to change, and sometimes he invites us to be part of that work.
exp.8:13:
Here Ananias says that Saul, the persecutor, has permission from the chief priests to arrest in Damascus all who call on your name, that is, those who pray to Jesus and believe in him. "Authority" means legal power or permission. To "arrest" means to seize or imprison.

Ananias, a disciple from Damascus, speaks here. In a vision the Lord asks him to go and help Saul, and Ananias is afraid, because he knows this man's reputation. He honestly lays his fear before the Lord. The Lord does not rebuke him, but explains the plan he has for Saul.

For today: you can be honest with God about your fears and doubts when he asks you to do something difficult. Bring them to him in prayer, and then trust that he sees beyond what you see, even in people who seem impossible to change.
exp.8:14:
Here the Lord tells Ananias to go, because Saul is a chosen vessel, that is, a person set apart for a special task. His work will be to carry the name of Jesus before the Gentiles (the non-Jews), before kings, and before the people of Israel.

Ananias was afraid, because Saul had persecuted the believers and had authority to arrest them. Jesus himself speaks and answers that fear: he does not see Saul only for his past, but for what God will do through him. Afterward, Saul is known as Paul.

For today: God can change the life of any person, even someone who seems very far from him. We can obey and treat others with love without confining them to their past, trusting that God knows what he is doing.
exp.8:20:
All who heard Saul in Damascus were amazed. The verse of this verse says that those listening were astonished and could hardly believe what they were seeing.

Saul had been destroying the believers in Jerusalem, and he had come to Damascus to bring them bound to the chief priests. The people remembered this, so they were surprised to hear him now preaching the name of Jesus.

Those speaking here are the listeners, probably Jews from the synagogues. After his encounter with Jesus, Saul was already preaching that Jesus is the Son of God. His change was so great that many could not understand it. As the account continues, some become confused and others want to kill him.

For today: God can transform any person, even someone who seems very far from Him. We should not give up when we pray for others, and if God has changed us, let us live so that our change is seen.
exp.8:21:
Saul, newly converted, grew stronger and stronger in his preaching. The verse notes that the word "but" in the verse is what connects this to what came before, and that "confounded" means he left the Jews of Damascus without an answer. With arguments, he showed them that Jesus is the Christ, that is, the promised Messiah.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells what happened shortly after Saul met Jesus on the road to Damascus. He had once persecuted the believers, and now he was preaching the opposite, which is why people were amazed. His message stirred up so much opposition that the Jews later plotted to kill him.

For today: God can change anyone, and when a person truly believes, they can grow in conviction. We can learn to know our faith well and explain it with firmness and respect, even when some do not accept it.
exp.8:24:
This verse tells that Saul escaped from Damascus at night. His friends, the disciples, took him and let him down through an opening in the city wall inside a basket, which is a large basket made of woven fibers, like those used for carrying things.

Luke, the author of Acts, recounts what happened shortly after Saul met Jesus and began to preach that Jesus is the Messiah. Some Jews in Damascus wanted to kill him and watched the gates day and night. The believers helped him flee by another way.

For today: escaping in time is not always a lack of faith. Sometimes God takes care of us through ordinary people and humble means. Let us learn to accept help and to help others, even when the way seems small or uncomfortable.
exp.8:25:
This verse tells that Saul arrived in Jerusalem and tried to join the disciples. But they were all afraid of him and did not believe that he was truly a follower of Jesus.

The narrator is Luke, the author of Acts. Saul had just escaped from Damascus, where people wanted to kill him. Earlier he had persecuted the believers, so their fear was understandable. Shortly after, Barnabas brought him to the apostles and testified that Saul had seen the Lord and had preached boldly.

For today: when someone changes their life, it is sometimes hard to trust them, and that is normal. We can be prudent, but also willing to be like Barnabas: to draw near, to listen, and to encourage someone who is starting over.
exp.8:30:
This verse says that the churches throughout the whole region, in Judea, Galilee, and Samaria, were at peace. They grew in faith, walking in the fear of the Lord, that is, living with respect and reverence toward God. With the comfort of the Holy Ghost, the number of believers increased.

Luke, the author of Acts, gives here a brief summary. Shortly before, Saul had been persecuted and sent to Tarsus. Many think that this departure helped calm the tensions, although the text does not say so clearly. Afterward, the story returns to Peter and his travels.

For today: a healthy church grows when it combines reverence for God with the help of the Spirit. We can ask him this week to give us comfort and a heart that wants to obey him.
exp.8:31:
Peter was going around visiting the believers in various places, and he also came down to the people who lived in Lydda. The verse's sentence about the word for "saints" is rewritten here: the word is not about perfect people, but about Christians, those set apart for God.

The one who tells this is Luke, the author of Acts. Before this, the church had gone through persecution, but now it had peace and was growing. Peter takes advantage of that time to strengthen the believers. Lydda was in the region of Judea, and there the healing of Aeneas will take place, which shows the power of Jesus working through Peter.

For today: beginning the faith is not enough; we also need to care for our brothers and sisters. We can visit, call, or encourage someone in our church. God often works when we draw near with love and serve.
exp.8:32:
In this verse, Peter, during his travels among the churches, came upon a man named Aeneas in Lydda. He had been lying on a bed for eight years because he was paralyzed, meaning he could not move his body.

The narrator here is Luke, the author of Acts. After a time of peace for the churches, Peter was visiting the believers. Luke introduces Aeneas by name and with specific details to show a real need. Then Peter announces that Jesus Christ heals him, and many in the region believe. The text does not say whether Aeneas was already a believer; the passage does not make this clear.

For today: God takes notice of people with long-lasting suffering, even when others have grown used to seeing them that way. We can draw near to those who have suffered for a long time, offer them attention and prayer, and remember that help comes from Christ, not from ourselves.
exp.8:35:
This verse introduces a woman from the city of Joppa named Tabitha, whose name in Aramaic is rendered in Greek as Dorcas. She was a disciple of Jesus. She is described as being full of good works and almsdeeds, meaning that her life was marked by doing good and generously helping the poor.

Luke, the author of the book of Acts, describes how the church grows after Peter heals Aeneas in Lydda. Now he introduces Tabitha, just before recounting her death and what God would do through Peter. Luke gives us her portrait to show who she was.

For today: no important position is needed to serve God. Tabitha helped with concrete and near-at-hand things. Think of a need you have close by, and help with what you have today.
exp.8:36:
In those days, it says, Tabitha became sick and died. After her body was washed, as was the custom, they laid her in what was an upper room, or upper chamber, inside the house. The phrase about her falling ill simply means that she became sick.

The author, Luke, tells what happened in Joppa, a town near Lydda, where Peter had just healed Aeneas. Tabitha was a disciple known for her good works and for helping the poor. Luke includes her death to prepare what follows: the disciples send for Peter, and the widows weep, showing the clothing she had made for them.

For today: death and grief come even to good and generous people. We can tenderly accompany those who suffer a loss, and serve others with simplicity, knowing that what is done with love leaves a mark that is not forgotten.
exp.8:38:
Peter got up and went with the two men who had come for him. When he arrived, they brought him up to the upper room, where Dorcas's body was. The widows surrounded him, weeping, and showed him the tunics (long garments worn underneath) and the dresses she had made for them while she lived among them.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells what happened in Joppa. Dorcas, also called Tabitha, was a disciple known for her good works. She had died, and the believers sent for Peter, who was nearby in Lydda. The widows gave no speeches; through the clothing they showed the love she had given them.

For today: simple service leaves a mark. We may not do great things, but helping with our hands and with kindness can be remembered and appreciated for a long time. Look at what you can offer today to someone in need.
exp.8:40:
Peter reached out his hand to Tabitha (Dorcas) and helped her to her feet. Then he called the believers, and the widows, and presented her to them alive.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells this miracle in Joppa. Tabitha was a disciple known for her good works, and the widows were weeping over her death. Peter had prayed alone, and God worked through him. The result was that many believed in the Lord. The miracle did not exalt Peter, but drew attention to God.

For today: God can use simple gestures, such as giving a hand to someone, to lift a person up. Think of someone who is down or sad, and offer them concrete help this week, trusting that God is the one who gives true hope.
exp.8:41:
This verse says that the miracle in Joppa became known throughout the whole city, and that many people believed in the Lord. The word "known" here means it was widely talked about and well known. Joppa is the city of Joppa, a port on the Mediterranean Sea.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells what happened after Peter prayed and God restored Tabitha to life, a disciple known for her good works. No one says that Peter performed the miracle by his own power; he prayed first. Luke shows that the news led people to trust in Jesus, not merely to admire Peter.

For today: when God works in your life, do not keep it to yourself. Tell humbly what He has done, and let your testimony and your good works encourage others to know the Lord.
exp.8:42:
Luke, the author of Acts, says that Peter stayed many days in Joppa, a city by the sea. There he lived in the house of a man named Simon, who worked as a tanner, that is, someone who prepared animal hides to make different items. The phrase "a tanner" in the verse above is the word that tells us what Simon did for a living.

Luke closes this account after Peter raised Tabitha (Dorcas) to life and many believed in the Lord. It is a brief detail, but it shows that Peter remained there to keep serving. Some scholars note that the work of a tanner was considered unclean because it involved handling dead animals, so Peter staying with him may prepare what comes next: God breaking down prejudices. However, the text does not explain this directly.

For today: do not despise places or ordinary people. God works in humble homes, and we can open our hearts without prejudice to those whom others ignore.
exp.9:3:
Cornelius looks steadily at the angel and is filled with fear. He asks, "What is it, Lord?" The angel answers that his prayers and his help to the poor have come up before God as a memorial. This means that God has remembered them and taken them into account.

Cornelius was a Roman officer who was not a Jew, but he feared God, prayed, and helped the people. The angel speaks to him to tell him that God has seen his heart. Soon the angel will direct him to send for Peter, who will explain to him the message of salvation in Jesus.

For today: God does not overlook your sincere prayer or your acts of kindness. Keep praying and serving others, and stay attentive to what God may want to show you, with a heart ready to learn more from Him.
exp.9:5:
This verse says that Peter is staying in the house of a man named Simon, who works as a tanner, that is, someone who prepares animal hides. His house is by the sea, close to the water. The angel adds that Peter will tell Cornelius what he ought to do.

An angel of God speaks to Cornelius, a Roman captain who sought God and prayed. The angel gives him clear instructions for finding Peter. God wants to bring the gospel to Cornelius and his household, who were not Jews. That is why God connects him with Peter. Cornelius obeys at once and sends his men.

For today: God often guides us through other people, not only directly. If you are seeking direction, keep your heart open, pray sincerely, and listen humbly to wise believers who know the Word of God.
exp.9:8:
This verse tells us that the next day, while the messengers sent by Cornelius were on their way and drew near to Joppa, Peter went up to the roof of the house to pray. It was around the sixth hour, that is, about noon. The roof was the flat top of the house, a quiet and comfortable place to withdraw for a while.

The account is from Luke, in the book of Acts. An angel had told Cornelius, a Roman soldier who sought God, to send for Peter. While they were traveling, God was already preparing Peter. What follows, the vision of the sheet, will show that the gospel is also for people who are not Jews.

For today: Peter had the habit of setting aside a moment to pray, and there God spoke to him. Find a quiet time and place each day to pray; that way you will be attentive to whatever God wants to show you.
exp.9:11:
This verse describes what Peter saw inside the large sheet that was coming down from heaven: there were all kinds of animals. There were four-legged animals, creatures that crawl, and birds. It was a mixture of animals, and the law of Moses considered some of them unclean to eat.

Peter was in Joppa, hungry and waiting for food, when he had a trance, that is, a vision in which he seemed to be lost in thought. Luke, the author of Acts, tells us that God was preparing his heart for something greater: a visit to the house of Cornelius, a Gentile. Later, Peter understood that the vision was teaching him not to call any human being unholy or unclean (Acts 10:28).

For today: let us ask God to examine the prejudices that separate us from other people. If He accepts them and calls them, we too can draw near with respect and love.
exp.9:15:
This verse says that Peter's vision was repeated three times. After that, the sheet, which was like a large cloth with animals, was taken up again into heaven.

Peter was praying on a rooftop in Joppa, he was hungry, and God showed him this vision. He had said that he had never eaten anything unclean or common, according to Jewish law. The repetition emphasizes that the message was serious. Right away the messengers of Cornelius, a Gentile, arrive, and Peter will understand that God was guiding him to welcome people from other nations.

For today: when God corrects a prejudice of yours, do not hold on to custom. Ask Him for humility to listen, and open yourself to treating with respect and love those who are different from you.
exp.9:20:
Peter goes down from the place where he had been praying, which was the roof of the house, and meets the men whom Cornelius had sent. He tells them that he is the one they are looking for, and he asks them why they have come.

The word "went down" in the verse above expresses the same idea: Peter is coming down from the roof to meet them.

Peter, who had just had the vision of the animals, did not fully understand its meaning. The Holy Spirit had told him not to hesitate to go with these men, who were Gentiles. Peter obeys and receives them openly, although he still does not know the reason for their visit.

For today: when God asks you for something you do not fully understand, take the first step of obedience. Welcome with kindness the people God places in your path, even when they are different from you, and listen before you judge.
exp.9:21:
The men sent by Cornelius explain to Peter why they have come. They say that Cornelius is a centurion, a Roman officer, and they describe him as a righteous man and one who fears God, that is, someone who honored the God of Israel. The Jewish people spoke well of him. A holy angel had told him to invite Peter to his house to hear what he had to say.

The ones speaking are Cornelius's messengers. Peter had just received the vision of the sheet with animals, and the Spirit told him to go with them without hesitation. Now the messengers tell their side of the story. Cornelius was not a Jew, so this encounter would open the door of the gospel to the Gentiles.

For today: God may be preparing people we do not expect. If He places someone in our path, let us not dismiss them because of prejudice. We must be willing to go, to listen, and to share with humility what God has given us.
exp.9:26:
Acts 10:27 tells us that Peter kept talking with Cornelius as they went into the house. There he found many people gathered together. The word "found" in the verse refers to meeting or coming upon them, and "gathered together" means they had come together in one place.

The book of Acts records this after Peter's vision and after Cornelius received his message from God. Cornelius was a Roman officer who was not a Jew. He had gathered his relatives and close friends to hear Peter. Luke, the author, shows that Peter enters a house of non-Jewish people, something very significant in his culture, and finds people waiting to hear the message of God.

Today we can learn to approach other people without prejudice. God often is already preparing hearts before we arrive. Let us ask him for the courage to step out of our comfort zone and share his love with anyone.
exp.9:29:
Cornelius tells Peter what happened four days ago. He says that he was fasting and praying in his house at the ninth hour, which is around three in the afternoon. Suddenly, a man in shining clothing stood before him.

Cornelius was a Roman officer who was not Jewish, but he sought God. Here he answers Peter's question about why he sent for him. He explains that God guided him through a heavenly visit, and that the visitor told him to send for Peter. In this way God opened the door of the gospel to non-Jewish people.

For today: God sees those who seek him with their whole heart. We can pray with perseverance and pay attention to how God guides us, even through other people, without letting prejudice close doors.
exp.9:31:
This verse repeats the instructions the angel gave to Cornelius. It says to send messengers to Joppa to look for a man named Simon, who is also called Peter. Peter was staying in the house of another Simon, a tanner, that is, someone who worked with the hides of animals. That house was by the sea. According to the message, Peter would come and speak to him.

Cornelius, a Roman officer who feared God, tells Peter what he experienced four days earlier. An angel appeared to him while he was praying and showed him where to find Peter. Cornelius wants to explain why he sent for him. This scene prepares the moment when the gospel reaches non-Jewish people.

God knows where we are and can guide others to us. If we are hungry to seek Him, we are not overlooked. We can pray sincerely and be willing to obey when He directs us toward someone, as with Peter and Cornelius.
exp.9:32:
Cornelius tells Peter that he sent for him right away. He thanks him for coming. He says that his whole household is gathered, and that they are ready to hear everything that God has commanded Peter to say. Cornelius was conscious that God was watching them.

Cornelius speaks as a Roman officer who feared God. An angel had told him to call for Peter. Cornelius gathered his relatives and close friends. Peter came into the house of people who were not Jews, something very new for him. This moment opens the door of the gospel to all nations.

For today: approach the Word of God with Cornelius's attitude, with a heart that is ready and attentive. Before you read the Bible or go to church, ask God to speak to you, and get ready to obey what you hear.
exp.9:37:
This verse says that God filled Jesus of Nazareth with the Holy Spirit and with power. Because of this, Jesus went around doing good and healing all who were oppressed by the devil, that is, dominated or harmed by his influence. The phrase "God was with him" means that God was with Jesus and stood by him.

The one speaking is Peter, in the house of Cornelius, a Roman officer who was not a Jew. Peter explains to this family who Jesus is and what he did, reminding them of what was already known throughout Judea. He will then say that he and others were witnesses of his death and resurrection.

Today we can learn that Jesus shows us what the power of God looks like: not for showing off, but for doing good and helping those who suffer. Ask yourself whom you can serve today.
exp.9:38:
This verse says that the apostles saw with their own eyes everything Jesus did in the land of Judea and in Jerusalem. It also says they killed him by hanging him on a tree, that is, they nailed him to a cross. The word "tree" in this verse refers to a wooden beam or trunk.

Here Peter is speaking in the house of Cornelius, a Roman captain. It is the first time a group of non-Jews hears the message about Jesus so directly. Peter explains that he is not passing on rumors, but telling what he saw. Then he announces that God raised Jesus from the dead, and that they were chosen witnesses.

For today: we can share our faith with simplicity and honesty, telling what Jesus has done in our lives, without boasting or pretending to know more than we do.
exp.9:40:
Peter says that the risen Jesus did not appear to all the people, but to witnesses whom God had chosen beforehand. They ate and drank with Him after He rose.

Peter speaks in the house of Cornelius, a Roman officer who was not a Jew. Peter explains the gospel to him and makes clear that the apostles do not tell rumors, but what they saw and lived. That they ate with Jesus shows that His risen body was real and not a vision. What follows is the command to preach the forgiveness of sins through Jesus.

Today we are not eyewitnesses, but we can trust their testimony, which was preserved in the Bible. And we can tell others, simply and honestly, what Jesus has done in our lives.
exp.9:41:
And he commanded us to preach to the people and to testify that this is the one whom God appointed to be the Judge of the living and the dead.

Peter speaks in the house of Cornelius, a Roman officer who was not a Jew. Peter explains to him who Jesus is: he rose from the dead, and the apostles saw him and ate with him. For the first time, the good news is openly announced to non-Jews. Peter connects judgment with the forgiveness that the next verse offers.

For today: since Jesus is both Judge and Savior, we can speak about him with humility and confidence, inviting others to receive his forgiveness, without fear or pride.
exp.9:43:
It says that while Peter was still speaking, the Holy Spirit came upon all who were listening to the message. "Fell" means that he came down with force and in a visible way.

Peter is in the house of Cornelius, a Roman soldier who was not a Jew. Peter had just explained that Jesus is the Judge of the living and the dead and that everyone who believes in Him receives forgiveness of sins. Before he finished, God showed that he was also accepting the Gentiles. The Jewish believers who had come with Peter were astonished.

For today: God gives His Spirit to whoever believes in Jesus, regardless of their origin, culture, or past. Therefore, we too should welcome with joy and without prejudice everyone who trusts in Christ.
exp.9:47:
It says that Peter commanded Cornelius and those with him to be baptized. The baptism was done acknowledging Jesus as Lord. Afterward, they asked Peter to stay on for a few days.

Peter was in the house of Cornelius, a Roman officer who was not a Jew. While Peter was preaching, the Holy Spirit came upon the listeners, and they spoke in tongues and praised God. This convinced Peter and the Jewish believers that God was also accepting the Gentiles. That is why Peter gave the order to baptize them.

For today: God receives all who believe in Jesus, regardless of their origin or their past. We can open our hearts and our tables to those who are different from us, and share life in Christ with them, as Peter and this household did.
exp.10:2:
The believing Jews in Jerusalem confront Peter with a question that sounds like a complaint: how could he dare to go into the homes of uncircumcised men, that is, non-Jews, and eat with them?

Those speaking are the believing Jews who defended circumcision, and they address Peter. He had just visited Cornelius, a Gentile, and those who listened to him received the Spirit. For many Jews, sharing a table with Gentiles was a problem because of their religious customs. Note that they do not dispute that the Gentiles believed, but that Peter lived among them.

Today it invites us to examine our prejudices. Sometimes we place barriers of culture, social class, or custom between ourselves and others whom God also accepts. We can ask ourselves whom we are avoiding, and take a concrete step: invite that person to our table.
exp.10:3:
Instead of getting angry or defending himself harshly, Peter calmly began to explain everything that had happened, step by step. He told them the events in the order in which they took place. What he had experienced in the house of Cornelius is what he was recounting.

Peter had returned to Jerusalem, and some Jewish believers criticized him for entering the home of non-Jewish people and eating with them. For them, this broke very important customs. Peter answers by telling them about his vision in Joppa and how God guided him. In this way he shows that he did not act on his own.

For today: when someone questions us or does not understand what we have done, we can respond with patience, clarity, and humility, telling the facts and showing how God guided us, without attacking anyone.
exp.10:4:
Peter tells what happened to him in the city of Joppa. He was praying, and in a trance he had a vision. He saw something like a great sheet, that is, a large cloth, coming down from heaven, held by its four corners. It came all the way down to where he was.

Peter speaks before the believers in Jerusalem, who criticized him for entering the homes of people who were not Jews and eating with them. He does not defend himself with arguments but instead recounts the events in order, beginning with this vision, to show that God himself had guided him.

For today: when someone questions a decision you have made, explain calmly and humbly what God has done, instead of arguing. And stay open to God tearing down your prejudices toward other people.
exp.10:5:
Peter tells how, as he looked carefully into the large sheet that was coming down from heaven, he saw every kind of animal: the four-footed creatures of the earth, the wild beasts, the reptiles, and the birds of the air.

Peter speaks in Jerusalem before Jewish believers who were criticizing him for having entered the house of Cornelius, a man who was not Jewish, and for having eaten with him. To explain himself, he recounts step by step the vision God gave him in Joppa. Many understand that this mixture of animals had to do with the Jewish laws about clean and unclean foods, and with the opening of the gospel to all peoples.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we have prejudices that keep us from drawing near to certain people. God invites us to watch closely what He is doing, and to receive with love those whom He also loves.
exp.10:8:
A voice from heaven spoke to Peter a second time. The voice taught him that what God has declared clean, Peter must not treat as unclean, meaning as impure or unworthy.

Peter is telling the believers in Jerusalem about what he experienced in Joppa. They had criticized him for entering the homes of Gentiles. He explains his vision: God showed him that he should no longer reject anyone because of their background. Soon after, the men sent by Cornelius arrived, and Peter understood that the vision also applied to people.

For today: before you reject or judge someone because of their culture, their past, or their origin, ask yourself whether God has already received them. Ask Him for a humble heart, willing to love as He loves.
exp.10:11:
This verse says that the Holy Spirit told Peter to go with the men sent from Caesarea, without doubting, that is, without letting doubts hold him back. Peter also mentions that six believing brothers went with him, and that together they entered the house of a man. In this older version, the word rendered "man" means a man, and the phrase about going with them means going along with them.

Peter is speaking before the apostles and the brothers in Jerusalem. Some of them were criticizing him for entering the house of non-Jewish people and eating with them. Peter explains step by step what happened: his vision, the arrival of the men sent, and the guidance of the Spirit. That man was Cornelius.

For today: when God clearly shows you a step of obedience, do not delay it because of prejudice or fear. Ask Him for direction, compare it with the Bible, and move forward with humility and confidence.
exp.10:12:
He told us how he had seen an angel standing in his house, who said to him, Send men to Joppa and call for Simon, whose other name is Peter.

Here Peter is speaking in Jerusalem. Some Jewish believers were criticizing him for having entered the house of Gentiles and eaten with them. Peter explains to them step by step that he did not act on his own, but that God directed everything, including this message from the angel to Cornelius.

For today: God can prepare encounters that we did not plan. If He opens a door for us to share His love with someone different from us, let us ask for humility to obey without prejudice, and have patience to calmly explain what God has done.
exp.10:13:
This verse says that the angel told Cornelius that Peter would bring him words for salvation, not only for himself but for all his household. "Household" means his family and the people who lived with him. The phrase about being saved refers to receiving the forgiveness and life that God offers.

Here Peter is speaking. He is explaining to the believers in Jerusalem why he went into the home of Cornelius, a man who was not a Jew. Some criticized him for it. Peter recounts what God did to show that it was God who opened that door.

For today: salvation comes through the message of Jesus, and someone has to carry it. Think of a person close to you and ask God for an opportunity to share with them, with respect and simplicity, what Christ has done for you.
exp.10:14:
Peter tells how, as soon as he began to speak in Cornelius's house, the Holy Spirit came down on these non-Jewish people, just as it had come on the first Jewish believers. The phrase "At the beginning" refers to Pentecost, when the Spirit first came to the disciples. "Fell" describes a clear and sudden arrival.

Peter is speaking before the believers in Jerusalem, who criticized him for going into the house of Gentiles and eating with them. He explains step by step what happened. His argument is that God himself accepted Cornelius and his family, and so there was no reason to reject them.

For today: God is not limited to our prejudices or to our groups. If God receives someone through faith in Jesus, we too must welcome them with joy. Today, think of a person you have looked at with distance and ask God for a more open heart.
exp.10:15:
Peter tells how, when he saw the Holy Spirit fall on the Gentiles, he remembered what Jesus had said. John baptized with water, as a sign of repentance. But Jesus promised that his followers would be baptized with the Holy Spirit, that is, filled and immersed in the presence and power of God.

Peter speaks before the believers in Jerusalem, who criticized him for having entered the house of Cornelius, a Gentile. He explains what happened to show that God himself accepted those believers, and so he recalls the promise of Jesus.

For today: when we doubt whom God accepts, let us return to the Word of Jesus and to what God does. He gives his Spirit to everyone who believes in Christ, without favoritism.
exp.10:16:
Peter says that if God gave the Gentiles the same gift of the Holy Spirit that he gave the Jewish believers, then he had no right to oppose it. The sentence that explained the word meaning to hinder or put obstacles in the way has been removed, and the quoted old spelling has been dropped.

Peter speaks before the believers in Jerusalem, who were criticizing him for having entered the house of Cornelius, a Gentile, and eaten with him. Peter tells them step by step what happened. His argument is simple: God himself accepted those Gentiles, and that settled the question. The brothers calmed down and praised God.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we put up barriers where God has already opened the door. Before judging someone by their origin, culture, or past, it is wise to look and see whether God is at work in their life, and to receive them with humility and joy.
exp.10:18:
These believers had fled Jerusalem when Stephen was killed, and this verse tells us they went as far as Phoenicia, Cyprus, and Antioch. "Scattered" means spread out, and "persecution" means the suffering they faced. In those places they shared the message about Jesus, but only with Jews.

Luke, the author of Acts, describes how persecution carried the gospel further. Just before this, Peter explained that God had also granted repentance to the Gentiles. Even so, these believers were still speaking only with Jews. The verses that follow show that some began to speak to Greeks in Antioch as well, and many believed.

God can use painful moments to extend his message. Perhaps you are going through a difficult situation today: ask him to show you who you can speak to about Jesus, even people outside your usual circle.
exp.10:19:
This verse tells us that some believers from Cyprus and Cyrene arrived in Antioch and began speaking to the Greeks. They were sharing the good news about the Lord Jesus. The men of Cyprus were from the island of Cyprus, and the men of Cyrene were from Cyrene, a city in the north of Africa. "Greeks" here most likely refers to people who were not Jews.

Luke, the author of Acts, is narrating. After the death of Stephen, many believers scattered and spoke only to Jews. These men took a new step and shared the gospel with non-Jews. Some scholars note that the early Greek text has variations in this word, but the context points to Gentiles.

For today: you do not need a special position to share about Jesus. Ask God for courage to speak to those whom others pass by.
exp.10:20:
This verse says that God was supporting the believers who were speaking about Jesus in Antioch. "The hand of the Lord" is a way of speaking about God's power and help. Many people believed and turned to the Lord, that is, they turned to God to follow Jesus.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells how the church grew. After the death of Stephen, the Christians were scattered because of the persecution. Some men from Cyprus and Cyrene also brought the good news to the Greeks, that is, to people who were not Jewish. In this way an important church was born in Antioch, which Barnabas later went to visit.

For today: God can use even difficult moments to spread his message. We can speak of Jesus simply to those around us, trusting that it is God who touches hearts and gives the fruit.
exp.10:22:
Barnabas came to Antioch and saw the grace of God, that is, the favor and work of God in the lives of those people. He was glad and encouraged everyone to stay steady, with the sincere decision of their hearts to follow the Lord.

The one speaking is Luke, the author of Acts, who tells what happened. The church in Jerusalem sent Barnabas after hearing that many in Antioch, a distant city, had come to believe in the Lord. Luke describes him as a good man, full of the Holy Spirit and of faith.

For today: when you see that God is at work in someone's life, rejoice from the heart instead of comparing or doubting. Then encourage that person with simple words to stay firm in the Lord. A message, a prayer, or a visit can sustain a new believer.
exp.10:26:
In those days, Barnabas and Saul were teaching in Antioch, and a group of prophets came down from Jerusalem to that city. The phrase "came down" is used because Jerusalem was in a higher place, and "prophets" were believers who spoke a message that God gave them.

The narrator is Luke, the author of the book of Acts. He tells how the church in Antioch, made up largely of believers who were not Jews, was growing. The arrival of these prophets shows the connection between the mother church in Jerusalem and the new church. It sets the stage for Agabus's message about the famine and the help that would be sent.

For today: God still joins his people together with bonds of love and service. Value brothers and sisters from other churches or places, receive what God gives them to build you up, and also look for ways to serve them yourself.
exp.11:1:
King Herod had James, the brother of John, killed with the sword. This James was one of the twelve apostles, and he is the first of them whose death the Bible records.

The one who tells this is Luke, the author of Acts. He reports that Herod, probably Herod Agrippa I, began to mistreat some members of the church. According to the verse that follows, Herod saw that James's death pleased the Jews, and for that reason he also arrested Peter. Luke does not explain in detail why James died, but he shows that faith in Jesus was already facing real opposition.

For today: the life of faith does not always end the way we hope, and God does not promise to spare us from all suffering. We can follow Christ faithfully and, even in the face of painful losses, trust that God remains good and sustains his people.
exp.11:2:
This verse says that Herod saw that killing James had pleased the Jews, and so he decided to seize Peter as well. "Pleased" means that it had won them over. "Seize" means to arrest. The "unleavened bread" refers to bread made without yeast, so this was taking place during the Feast of Unleavened Bread, alongside the Passover.

Luke, the author of the book of Acts, tells the story. Herod, probably Herod Agrippa I, had already persecuted the church. According to the text, he acted to win the favor of the Jews. He was a ruler who sought approval, not justice.

For today: be careful about living to win people's applause. That can lead to unjust decisions. And if you find yourself in a difficult situation, remember that the church responded by praying without ceasing for Peter. Prayer is still a simple and real path.
exp.11:3:
The verse tells that Herod arrested Peter and put him in prison. He placed him under the watch of four quaternions, that is, four groups of four soldiers (sixteen in total), who probably took turns during the day and the night. Herod intended to bring him out before the people after the Passover, perhaps to try him or condemn him in public.

Here the speaker is Luke, the narrator of Acts. Herod (Agrippa I) had just killed James and, seeing that this pleased the Jews, wanted to do the same with Peter. It was the feast of unleavened bread, and he waited for it to end.

For today: when problems seem bigger than our strength, the text that follows shows that the church prayed without ceasing. We can bring our fears and the fears of others to God, trusting that he works even when everything seems closed.
exp.11:6:
In the middle of the night, an angel of God appeared in the prison, and a light shone in the place. The angel struck Peter on the side to wake him and told him to get up quickly. The word for quickly here means fast, without delay. At that very moment, the chains fell off his hands.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells this story. King Herod had already killed James and had Peter in custody, intending to bring him before the people the next day. Peter was under heavy guard, chained between two soldiers. Meanwhile, the church was praying earnestly for him. God answered in a way no one expected.

For today: when a situation seems closed and without a way out, keep praying. God can act when we least expect it. Peter was sleeping in peace, and that invites us to trust God even in moments of danger or distress.
exp.11:10:
Peter was in prison, and an angel brought him out without his realizing what was happening. He thought it was a dream or a vision. Here, "came to himself" means that he came to his senses and understood what was really happening. Then he recognized that God had delivered him from Herod and from everything the Jewish people had expected to happen to him.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells of this moment. Herod had ordered James put to death and had imprisoned Peter. The church was praying for him. Peter speaks here to himself, now outside, and says it with amazement, because until that moment he was not sure it was real.

For today: sometimes God works in ways we do not understand at the time. You can keep praying and taking steps of obedience even when you do not yet see clearly. Later, looking back, you will be able to recognize his help and give thanks for it.
exp.11:12:
Peter has just come out of prison and arrives at the house of Mary, where believers are gathered together. He knocks at the door of the gate, which was the outer entrance of the house. A young servant girl named Rhoda, who was probably a servant or a young member of the household, comes to listen to who is knocking. The phrase in the verse about her coming to listen means that she drew near with care before opening.

This is Luke's account in Acts. Peter had been imprisoned by Herod, and the church was praying for him. An angel brought him out of the prison during the night. When Peter arrives, the people who were praying for his release do not yet imagine that he is at the door. Luke mentions the name of Rhoda, and we know nothing more about her.

For today: God can answer our prayers in ways that surprise us, even when we find them hard to believe. Let us keep praying with faith, and receive with humility and joy what He does.
exp.11:13:
This verse tells how Rhoda, the servant girl who answered the door, recognized Peter's voice. She was so overjoyed that she forgot to open the gate (a small door or wicket set into the larger gate). She ran back inside and reported that Peter was standing outside.

Luke narrates this moment after an angel had led Peter out of prison. Herod had locked him up, and the church was praying for him at the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark. No one expected the answer to come so quickly, so they did not believe Rhoda. Some think the people's remark about the angel reflects a belief of that time, but the text does not explain it.

Often we pray with sincere faith, yet we find it hard to believe when God answers. Let us learn from Rhoda: let us receive God's answers with joy and keep praying with confidence, even when they seem surprising.
exp.11:16:
Peter, now free, makes a signal with his hand for them to be quiet, because everyone was speaking at once, amazed. He tells them how the Lord brought him out of prison. He asks them to let James and the brothers know. Then he leaves for another place.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells that Herod had put Peter in prison, and the church was praying for him. When Peter arrives at the house, they find it hard to believe it is really him. This James is probably the brother of the Lord, a leader in Jerusalem, though the text does not make this clear. The text does not say where Peter went; the Bible does not explain it, and it is better not to make it up.

When God answers our prayers, let us not keep it to ourselves. Telling what He has done encourages others to trust in Him. And if His answer sometimes surprises us, as it surprised them, God remains faithful.
exp.11:18:
Herod ordered a search for Peter, but he could not find him. Then he examined the guards and ordered that they be taken away, that is, that they be punished, probably with death. After that he went from Judea to Caesarea and stayed there.

Here the narrator, Luke, is speaking. Peter had been set free by an angel after Herod had imprisoned him in order to please certain Jewish leaders. Herod did not recognize the hand of God and took out his anger on the guards. The text does not explain in detail what happened to them, but the wording suggests a severe penalty. Soon after, Luke tells of Herod's end.

For today: the powerful can make plans and build prisons, but they do not have the final word. We can trust that God cares for his people, and we should also treat with justice and humility those who depend on us.
exp.11:19:
This verse tells that Herod was very angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon, two cities on the coast. They came together in agreement and went to ask him for peace. First they won over Blastus, the king's chamberlain, that is, the officer in charge of his room or his personal service. This is usually understood to mean they convinced or won him over, perhaps with gifts. They needed peace because their food came from the king's lands.

The narrator is Luke, the author of Acts. He has just told of Peter's escape from prison and the anger of Herod. Luke shows the power of this king, on whom other peoples depended. He prepares the next scene, where Herod accepts being hailed as a god. The exact cause of the anger is not explained.

For today: All human power is limited and temporary. We should not place our security in those who have influence, but in God, and we should treat with humility those who depend on us.
exp.12:2:
The church in Antioch, after fasting and praying, laid their hands on Barnabas and Saul and sent them away; that is, they sent them off or let them go. Laying on hands is a gesture of blessing and support.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells what happened in Antioch. While the leaders were serving the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit called for Barnabas and Saul to be set apart for a special work. The church did not act lightly: it sought God, and then it sent them. The verses that follow say they were sent out by the Holy Spirit.

For today: before making important decisions, such as a ministry, a change in life, or a service, seek God in prayer and, if you can, together with other believers. And when someone is sent out to serve, support them with your prayers and your encouragement.
exp.12:5:
This verse tells that Barnabas and Saul traveled through the whole island of Cyprus, from one end to the other, until they reached the city of Paphos. There they met a Jew named Bar-jesus, who practiced sorcery and pretended to be a prophet, though he was a false one. "Sorcerer" here refers to someone who used magic or divination.

It is part of Luke's account of the first missionary journey. The church in Antioch sent them out, guided by the Holy Spirit. Luke narrates the events as an observer; there is no speech here. It prepares the encounter with the proconsul and shows that the message of the gospel would soon face spiritual opposition.

For today: not every voice that sounds religious comes from God. Compare what you hear with the Bible, and ask the Holy Spirit for wisdom to distinguish truth from deception.
exp.12:8:
It says that Saul, who was also called Paul, was filled with the Holy Ghost and fixed his gaze on Elymas. The phrase about setting his eyes on him means that he looked at him intently, with attention and firmness. It is the moment just before Paul speaks.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells that Elymas, a sorcerer, opposed Barnabas and Saul. He wanted the proconsul Sergius Paulus not to believe. Here the account joins the two names of Saul; the Bible does not explain why from this point on he is called Paul. Paul speaks with firmness, guided by the Spirit.

When someone hinders others from knowing God, there is no need to respond with fear or anger. We can ask the Holy Ghost for wisdom, courage and clarity, and speak with truth and with love.
exp.12:9:
Paul speaks with great firmness to Elymas, the sorcerer. He tells him that he is full of deceit and wickedness, that he is a child of the devil and an enemy of all that is right. Then he asks him whether he will not stop twisting the straight paths of the Lord. To twist or turn aside the straight paths means to bend or divert them; deceit means lies or fraud.

Paul was in Cyprus with Barnabas. The proconsul Sergius Paulus wanted to hear the word of God, but Elymas opposed him so that he would not believe. Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, did not speak out of personal anger, but to defend the truth and the way of God. Afterward Elymas was blinded for a time, and the proconsul believed.

For today: we must not use lies or influence to draw others away from God. Instead, let us ask the Spirit to give us courage and wisdom to speak the truth clearly, and with love toward people.
exp.12:11:
This verse says that the proconsul, a Roman governor, saw that the sorcerer Elymas was struck blind by Paul's word. Seeing this, he believed. "Astonished" means amazed, deeply impressed. His amazement was not only at the miracle, but at the teaching of the Lord, that is, the teaching about Jesus.

Paul speaks in Cyprus, in the city of Paphos. The proconsul Sergius Paulus wanted to hear the word of God, but Elymas opposed him to turn him away from the faith. Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, confronted him, and the temporary blindness confirmed the message. The text does not describe how the proconsul's faith developed afterward.

For today: miracles can awaken attention, but what sustains faith is the teaching of Jesus. Let us ask God for an open heart to hear his word with humility, even when it surprises or confronts us.
exp.12:13:
Paul and his companions left Perga and arrived at Antioch in Pisidia, a city in Asia Minor (not the Antioch in Syria). On the Sabbath they went into the synagogue and sat down. The verse of "sat down" is not needed here, since the verse already says it plainly. The phrase about leaving Perga means that they continued their journey from there.

Luke, the author of Acts, narrates the first missionary journey of Paul and Barnabas. Shortly before, John Mark had left them and returned to Jerusalem. Even so, they continued. Going first to the synagogue was a natural way to find Jews and God-fearing people who already knew the Scriptures. Sitting down quietly sets the scene: soon they will be invited to speak.

For today: when someone withdraws or things become difficult, one can keep going faithfully. And often God opens doors when we simply arrive, sit down, and stay attentive to the opportunity.
exp.12:18:
God defeated seven peoples who lived in Canaan and gave that land to Israel as an inheritance. The phrase about dividing the land by lot means that the land was divided by casting lots, that is, by a drawing, so that each tribe received its share. The idea of destroying refers to clearing those nations out of the way.

The apostle Paul is speaking in the synagogue in Antioch of Pisidia. He summarizes the history of Israel to show that God has always kept his promises. This review prepares the announcement that Jesus is the promised Savior. There is debate about how to understand the conquest, but the text emphasizes that the land was a gift from God, not an achievement of Israel.

For today: God keeps what he promises, even when it takes time. You can trust that what he has told you in his Word will be fulfilled in his time. Give thanks today for what you have received as his gift, instead of thinking that you achieved everything on your own.
exp.12:20:
Paul recalls that the people of Israel asked for a king, and God gave them Saul. Saul was the son of Kish and a man of the tribe of Benjamin. Saul reigned forty years, according to Paul. The Old Testament does not clearly explain that number, and scholars explain it in different ways.

Paul is speaking in the synagogue at Antioch in Pisidia. He reviews the history of Israel to show that God guided every step. That account leads him to David and, finally, to Jesus, the promised Savior.

For today: sometimes we ask for things that seem good to us, but God keeps working even when our choices are not the best. We can trust that his plan moves forward, and we should ask him for wisdom before demanding what we want.
exp.12:27:
This verse says that the leaders of Jerusalem found no crime in Jesus that deserved death. Even so, they asked Pilate, the Roman governor, to have him put to death.

The apostle Paul speaks in the synagogue of Antioch in Pisidia, on a Sabbath. He explains to Jews and to people who feared God that the condemnation of Jesus was no surprise: without knowing it, they fulfilled what the prophets had announced. In this way Paul prepares the announcement that God raised him from the dead.

For today: Jesus was innocent and died because of human injustice, but God used that for our salvation. When you face injustice, trust that God can work even there, and ask him to help you not to be carried away by envy or by the pressure of the crowd.
exp.12:29:
This verse says that God raised Jesus after his death. "God raised him from the dead" means that he brought him back to life. The word "But" here marks a contrast: people killed him and laid him in the tomb, but God did something greater.

Paul is speaking in the synagogue in Antioch of Pisidia. He tells Jews and Gentiles who feared God how Jesus fulfilled what the Scriptures had foretold. After Jesus' death and burial, Paul presents the resurrection as the center of the good news, and he mentions the witnesses who saw Jesus alive for many days.

For today: the resurrection reminds us that no situation is beyond God's reach. When something seems lost or without a way out, we can trust that God can still act. That hope encourages us to keep trusting and obeying.
exp.12:30:
This verse says that Jesus, after rising, was seen for many days by those who had traveled with him from Galilee to Jerusalem. The phrase "was seen" is plain modern wording, and "witnesses" refers to people who saw something and can tell others about it. Now they bear their testimony to the people.

Here Paul is speaking in the synagogue at Antioch of Pisidia. He is explaining to Jews and to people who feared God that the death and resurrection of Jesus fulfilled what had been announced in the Scriptures. To support this, he points out that it is not just his opinion: many people saw Jesus alive.

For today: our faith does not rest on a vague idea, but on a testimony that was passed on with firmness. You can read the accounts in the Gospels with confidence and, when you speak about Jesus, do so simply, telling what you have seen him do in your life.
exp.12:34:
This verse says that God promised that his Holy One would not see corruption. Corruption here refers to the decay of the body after death. The Holy One is the Messiah, God's chosen one. The phrase comes from Psalm 16:10.

The speaker is the apostle Paul, in the synagogue of Antioch of Pisidia. He explains to Jews and to people who feared God that Jesus is the fulfillment of the promises made to Israel. Paul points out that David died and his body decayed, so this word points to Jesus, whom God raised up.

For today: if Jesus overcame death, our hope is not an illusion. When you face loss or fear of death, rest in the fact that God keeps what he promises and has the last word.
exp.12:38:
This verse says that the law of Moses could not declare a person righteous before God, but that through Jesus everyone who believes is justified, meaning declared free of guilt and accepted by God. The word "justified" is the key term here.

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, in the synagogue at Antioch of Pisidia, on a Sabbath. He explains the history of Israel and arrives at Jesus, whom God raised from the dead. His message is that the forgiveness of sins is now offered through Christ. Then he warns them not to dismiss this good news.

For today: you do not have to earn forgiveness through your own efforts or carry the weight of your past guilt. Trust in Jesus, receive forgiveness as a gift, and live thankfully, doing good out of love and not out of fear.
exp.12:40:
It says that God warns those who scorn his message. He asks them to look carefully, because they will be amazed and terrified. Those who scorn something are those who look down on it; to be left stunned, without knowing what to say, and to vanish or perish, are the outcomes he warns of. God says that he is doing a work in their days so great that they would not believe it, even if someone explained it to them.

The apostle Paul speaks in the synagogue of Antioch in Pisidia. He quotes the prophet Habakkuk (1:5) and applies it to the work of Christ: forgiveness and justification for everyone who believes, something the law of Moses could not give. His warning is so that they do not reject this good news. Afterward, many Gentiles and Jews wanted to hear more.

For today: let us not harden our hearts out of habit or pride. If God speaks to us through his Word, let us listen with humility and trust in Christ, even when his work surprises us.
exp.12:42:
When the meeting in the synagogue had ended, many of the Jews and also many outsiders who had converted to Judaism followed Paul and Barnabas. As they talked with them, they urged them to continue in the grace of God, that is, to keep trusting in the undeserved favor that God was offering them.

This takes place in Antioch of Pisidia. Paul had just preached that Jesus is the promised Savior and that forgiveness comes through Him. Many of the listeners were deeply moved and wanted to hear more. Luke, the author of Acts, shows here the warm initial welcome, before others opposed the message, as the following verses make clear.

For today: when someone shows interest in God, come alongside them after the meeting with a personal conversation, and encourage them to stand firm in grace, not in their own efforts.
exp.12:44:
The verse tells how some of the Jews in Antioch of Pisidia saw a huge crowd gathered to hear Paul. They were filled with envy and anger, not with a healthy love for God. That is why they opposed what Paul taught, contradicted him, and spoke against him and his message with abusive words.

The one writing is Luke, narrating the journey of Paul and Barnabas. The previous Sabbath, Paul had preached about Jesus in the synagogue. Many were interested, and a week later nearly the whole city came. Some Jewish leaders felt they were losing their place and influence.

For today: when God blesses others, we can feel envy without even realizing it. Let us ask him for a heart that rejoices to see his work grow, even when it does not happen through us.
exp.12:45:
Paul and Barnabas speak out boldly (the phrase that means speaking with frankness and without fear). They say that the word of God had to be spoken first to the Jews. But since they reject it, they themselves judge that they are unworthy of eternal life. For this reason, the apostles turn to the Gentiles, that is, to the non-Jews. The phrase "it was necessary" means that it had to happen.

This takes place in Antioch of Pisidia. Almost the whole city came to hear them, and several Jews, filled with envy and jealousy at the sight of the crowd, contradicted and insulted Paul. The apostles quote what God had said: to be a light for the nations. In this way the message is opened to everyone.

For today: do not lose heart when someone rejects the message of God. Keep speaking with respect and courage, and give thanks that the good news is for everyone.
exp.12:46:
Paul and Barnabas quote a command of God: the Lord had set his servant as a light for the Gentiles, that is, those who are not Jews. That light would carry salvation to the farthest corner of the earth. The word "salvation" here carries the sense of being saved.

They speak in Antioch of Pisidia. Some Jews, full of jealousy, opposed them and spoke against Paul. For this reason the apostles turned to the Gentiles. They quote a prophecy from Isaiah 49:6, which many understand as first applied to the Servant of the Lord and then to those who carry his message.

For today: God wants his light to reach everyone, without exception. We can ask ourselves who near us needs to hear about Christ, and share with kindness and courage what God has done in us.
exp.12:49:
This verse tells that some Jews in Antioch of Pisidia stirred up devout and respected women, and the leading men of the city. "Stirred up" means that they urged them on or incited them against someone. In this way they brought about a persecution against Paul and Barnabas and drove them out of their region, that is, out of their territory.

The one telling the story is Luke, the author of Acts. Paul had preached, and many Gentiles had believed with joy. Some Jews reacted with jealousy and opposition, and used their social influence to remove the apostles. Even so, the word kept spreading throughout the whole region.

For today: rejection does not always mean that we are outside God's will. We can continue with peace and joy, like the disciples in the next verse, trusting that God is still at work even in opposition.
exp.12:51:
This verse says that the disciples lived filled with joy and with the Holy Ghost. "Joy" means a deep gladness that does not depend on circumstances. "Filled" indicates that this joy and the presence of the Spirit marked their whole lives.

Luke, the author of Acts, recounts this in Antioch of Pisidia. Paul and Barnabas had just been driven out by persecution, and they went on to Iconium, shaking the dust off their feet, a gesture of farewell showing that they no longer held themselves responsible for the rejection. The disciples are the believers who remained in the city. Even without their teachers and in the midst of opposition, they were not defeated.

For today: Christian joy does not depend on everything turning out well. When you face difficulties, ask God to fill you with his Spirit, and thank him for what he has already given you.
exp.13:0:
This verse tells us that Paul and Barnabas arrived in Iconium and went together into the synagogue of the Jews. They spoke with such clarity and conviction that a great multitude believed, both Jews and Greeks.

Luke, the author of Acts, recounts the missionary journey of Paul and Barnabas. They were coming from Antioch of Pisidia, from which they had been driven out. Even so, in Iconium they continued their custom of going first to the synagogue, where the Scriptures were already known. The following verses show that some rejected the message and stirred up opposition, but the apostles stayed there a long time.

For today: do not lose heart if you are rejected in one place. Keep sharing the truth with clarity and love, trusting that God will do his work in the hearts that are ready to receive it.
exp.13:4:
This verse tells of a violent movement against Paul and Barnabas in Iconium. The first phrase is about rushing forward with force, like an attack. The second word means to insult or shame someone in public. Jews, non-Jews, and their rulers joined together to mistreat them and stone them.

Luke, the author of Acts, recounts what happened in Iconium. Paul and Barnabas had been preaching there for a long time, and God was confirming their message with signs. The city was divided, and the opposition grew until it became a plan of violence. When they found out, they fled to Lystra and Derbe, and there they continued preaching the gospel.

For today: faithfully serving God does not always bring applause, and sometimes it brings rejection. But fleeing from danger is neither cowardice nor disobedience. Paul and Barnabas acted with wisdom, and they did not stop proclaiming Christ somewhere else. If you face opposition, seek prudence and keep trusting the Lord.
exp.13:12:
It says that the priest of the temple of Jupiter, whose shrine stood at the entrance of the city, brought bulls and garlands (wreaths of flowers) to the gates. He wanted to offer a sacrifice along with the people, to honor Paul and Barnabas as if they were gods.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells what happened in Lystra. Paul had just healed a man who had been lame from birth. The people, speaking their own language, Lycaonian, thought the gods had come down. They called Barnabas Jupiter and Paul Mercury. The Greek names of these gods were Zeus and Hermes; the Bible uses the Roman names.

When God works through us, we must not accept the glory that belongs to Him alone. Paul and Barnabas refused the worship and pointed to the living God. May our service always point to Jesus, not to ourselves.
exp.13:13:
This verse tells how Barnabas and Paul heard that the people of Lystra were planning to offer sacrifices to them. Then they tore their clothes, which was a way of showing grief and refusal, and rushed out into the crowd, shouting. The word "crowd" refers to the large group of people, and "shouting" means they cried out loudly so they would be heard.

Paul had just healed a man who had been crippled from birth. The people believed they were gods: they called Barnabas Jupiter and Paul Mercury, because Paul was the one who did the speaking. A priest brought bulls and garlands to sacrifice to them. The apostles reacted with urgency so that no one would give them the glory that belongs only to God.

Today, when someone praises us for something good we have done, we can respond with humility and point to God. Everything we accomplish is his grace, and we should not accept honors that belong to him.
exp.13:16:
He says that God has never stopped giving signs of who he is. He does this through good things: the rain that falls from heaven and the seasons that bring a harvest. With these he fills people's hearts with food and gladness. The phrase "filling" is the one that appears in the verse, and "food" is the word the verse uses for nourishment.

Paul and Barnabas are speaking in Lystra. They had just healed a man who was lame from birth, and the people wanted to offer them sacrifices, thinking they were gods. They tear their clothes, stop the crowd, and explain that they are only men. They speak to them of the living God, the maker of all things, so that they will not worship creatures but the one who gives rain and bread.

Today, when you eat, see rain falling, or enjoy a good harvest, pause and give thanks to God. The simple things of each day are his gifts, and they invite us to trust him.
exp.13:17:
Pablo and Bernabé, with these words, managed with great difficulty to calm the people of Lystra. The crowd wanted to offer sacrifices to them, as if they were gods.

Paul and Barnabas had just healed a man who had been lame from birth. The people, who worshiped many gods, thought that Zeus and Hermes had come down to earth. The apostles refused the worship and explained that there is one living God, Creator, who makes himself known through his goodness: the rain, the harvests, and joy. Shortly afterward, the people's opinion changed completely.

When God uses us to bless others, we must refuse the applause and point to Christ. All good things come from Him, and He alone deserves the glory.
exp.13:20:
This verse tells that Paul and Barnabas preached the gospel in Derbe and taught many people. Afterward they returned to Lystra, to Iconium, and to Antioch of Pisidia.

The one who tells the story is Luke, the author of Acts. Paul had just been stoned in Lystra and left for dead, and then he went on to Derbe. What is striking is that he went back to the same cities where he had been persecuted. According to the context that follows, he did this to strengthen the disciples and to appoint elders who would care for the churches.

For today: it is not enough to proclaim the gospel; we also need to accompany those who believe. Think of someone new in the faith and look for ways to encourage them, pray with them, or teach them, even when it is costly.
exp.13:23:
This verse tells that Paul and Barnabas, on their way back from their first journey, crossed the region of Pisidia and came to Pamphylia. The name "Pamphylia" is the old spelling of this region, a area on the southern coast of what is today Turkey. It is a brief, simple detail along the way.

The narrator is Luke, the author of Acts. Paul and Barnabas had already strengthened the new believers, appointed elders in the churches, and entrusted everything to the Lord. Now they are heading back to Antioch in Syria, the city from which they had been sent out. Luke shows that the mission advanced step by step, from place to place.

For today: God's work is often carried out faithfully along the way, not only in the great moments. Keep serving and caring for others in ordinary daily life, and entrust the results to the Lord.
exp.13:24:
This verse tells us that Paul and Barnabas preached God's message in Perga, a city in the region of Pamphylia. Then they went down to Attalia, a port on the coast. "Went down" indicates that they left the inland area and headed toward the sea. "The word" refers to the message of the gospel.

The author, Luke, recounts the end of the first missionary journey. Paul and Barnabas had already appointed elders in the new churches and were returning to Antioch in Syria. When they passed through Perga again, they preached there, something the account does not mention them doing before. Attalia was their point of departure by ship.

Even while they were heading home, they did not stop sharing God's message. We can ask him to help us speak about Jesus simply in the everyday places we pass through: at work, on the bus, or in our neighborhood.
exp.13:25:
This verse tells how Paul and Barnabas sailed from Attalia to Antioch in Syria. There, some time earlier, the church had commended them to the grace of God, that is, had entrusted them to God's care and favor. Now they were returning because they had finished the work of that journey.

Luke, the author of Acts, narrates the end of the first missionary journey. The church in Antioch had sent them out with prayer and fasting (Acts 13:1-3). That is why they were coming back to report to those who had supported them. Luke shows that the work was not due to their own merit, but to the grace of God.

For today: no one serves alone. If God gives you a task, place it in his hands and let your church accompany you with prayer. When you finish, share it with gratitude, giving God the credit.
exp.13:27:
This verse says that Paul and Barnabas stayed in Antioch for a considerable time, living alongside the disciples, that is, the believers of that church. The word "there" refers to Antioch of Syria, and "long time" does not say how many months or years it was.

Here the narrator of the book, Luke, is speaking. Paul and Barnabas had just finished their first missionary journey. They had told the church that God had opened a door of faith to the Gentiles, that is, to those who were not Jews. Antioch was the church that had sent them out, so they returned to their spiritual home to rest and share.

For today: after serving and working, we need to return to the community. Seek out your church or your brothers and sisters in the faith, tell them what God has done, and receive encouragement to keep going forward.
exp.14:0:
This verse tells how some men came down from Judea to Antioch and were teaching the brothers that, unless they were circumcised according to the custom that Moses left, they could not be saved. "Custom" means a practice or ceremony, and being circumcised is a physical sign that God commanded for Abraham and his descendants.
