The one speaking here is Luke, who is telling the story. These teachers came from Judea and wanted believers who were not Jews to also keep the law of Moses. This caused a strong argument with Paul and Barnabas, and so the church sent them to Jerusalem to consult the apostles and elders.

Today we can remember that salvation comes through God's grace by faith in Jesus, not by adding human requirements. When disagreements arise, it is good to resolve them with humility, listening together to the Word and to the leaders of the church.
exp.14:1:
Next, the verse says that when some teachers from Judea taught that circumcision was necessary for salvation, Paul and Barnabas strongly opposed them. There was a very sharp argument and debate. For this reason the church decided to send them to Jerusalem, with some other brothers, to take up the matter with the apostles and the elders.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells the event. The church in Antioch faced a serious question: did non-Jewish believers have to keep the law of Moses in order to be saved? Paul and Barnabas maintained that salvation did not depend on circumcision. The issue was so important that they sought an answer together with the leaders of the mother church.

For today: when a serious disagreement about the faith arises, let us not let it grow into quarrels, nor ignore it. Let us bring it before the church with humility and order, seeking the truth in the Word of God.
exp.14:2:
What it says: Paul and Barnabas leave Antioch, and the church sends them off, accompanying them part of the way. On the road to Jerusalem they pass through Phoenicia and Samaria. There they tell how the Gentiles, that is, the non-Jews, had turned to God. This brought great joy to the brothers and sisters.

Context: Luke, the author of Acts, narrates the journey. Some people from Judea were saying that without circumcision there was no salvation, and this caused a strong dispute. That is why Paul and Barnabas go up to Jerusalem to consult the apostles and elders. As they travel, the churches along the way rejoice at the news.

For today: When there are disagreements in the church, let us not stop sharing what God is doing. Telling stories of conversion encourages others and reminds us that salvation is the work of God, not of human requirements.
exp.14:3:
Paul and Barnabas arrived in Jerusalem, and the whole community welcomed them: the church, the apostles, and the elders. They reported everything God had done through them.

Luke tells this story. Paul and Barnabas had been sent from Antioch because of a serious dispute: some insisted that non-Jewish believers had to be circumcised in order to be saved. Along the way they had already brought joy to many brothers and sisters with their account. Now they present the same report before the leaders, and the next verse shows that not everyone agreed.

For today: when there are disagreements in the church, let us begin by listening with respect and humbly recounting what God is doing, instead of fighting over opinions. Recognizing God's work helps us seek the truth together.
exp.14:9:
Peter is questioning those who wanted to require the non-Jewish believers to keep the law of Moses. Testing God means putting His patience to the test, as if defying what He has already done. The neck is the back of the neck, and the yoke is a heavy burden, like the one carried by oxen. Peter says that neither their ancestors nor they themselves were able to bear that law.

Peter speaks at the council in Jerusalem. Some Jewish believers were saying that Gentiles had to be circumcised in order to be saved. Peter reminds them that God had already given the Holy Spirit to the Gentiles without requiring that condition. So, to impose further requirements on them was to go against what God Himself had shown.

For today: let us not add human rules to what God gives freely. We can encourage others to grow in obedience, but without making them feel they earn salvation by their efforts. We are saved by the grace of Jesus, and from there we live in gratitude.
exp.14:11:
This verse says that all the people who were gathered kept silence. After the words of Peter, they listened to Barnabas and Paul, who told them about the great miracles and wonders that God had done through them among the Gentiles, that is, among those who were not Jews.

This happens at the council of Jerusalem. Some were teaching that non-Jewish believers had to be circumcised in order to be saved. Peter had just said that salvation is by the grace of Jesus. Now Barnabas and Paul do not argue with theories, but tell what God has done. Then James would speak to give his judgment.

For today: before debating, let us learn to be silent and listen to how God is working in other people, even when they are different from us. Let us always compare what we hear with Scripture.
exp.14:13:
James says that Simon (that is, Peter) explained how God, from the beginning, visited the Gentiles, meaning that he drew near to them with care and favor. His purpose was to form among them a people who would bear his name. "Gentiles" are the people who were not Jews.

We are at the Council of Jerusalem. The question under discussion was whether non-Jewish believers had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses in order to be saved. After hearing Peter, Barnabas, and Paul, James, a leader of the church in Jerusalem, concludes that God himself had taken the initiative. He then supports this idea with the Scriptures of the prophets.

Today we can remember that God is the one who calls and gathers his people. Therefore we should receive with respect and affection those whom he brings to faith, without placing on them burdens that God did not ask for.
exp.14:14:
It says that what Peter has just told agrees with what the prophets had already written. This verse says "agree" means they are in harmony, going in the same direction. "As it is written" announces that a passage of Scripture is about to be quoted. James does not present a new idea, but shows that God's plan had already been announced.

James, the leader of the church in Jerusalem, is speaking during an important meeting. The question under discussion was whether non-Jewish believers had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses in order to be saved. After hearing Peter, Paul and Barnabas, James supports their accounts with Scripture. The quotation that follows seems to come from Amos 9, and scholars interpret it in several ways.

For today: when disagreement arises, listen humbly to the experiences of others, but place the Bible as the final measure. Let it confirm what we believe or correct it.
exp.14:19:
It says that believers who are not Jews should not be burdened with the whole law of Moses, but they are asked to keep away from four things: what is polluted by idols (such as meat offered to them), sexual immorality, what is strangled (animals that were dead without their blood drained), and blood.

James, the leader of the church in Jerusalem, speaks at a meeting with the apostles and elders. Some were demanding that Gentiles be circumcised in order to be saved. James proposes not to trouble them with that, but to take care of living together with Jewish believers. Scholars explain the exact reason for these four things in several different ways.

For today: salvation is by grace, not by added rules. Even so, love leads us to give up what harms our faith or wounds other brothers and sisters.
exp.14:25:
This verse says that Barnabas and Paul are men who have risked their lives for the sake of Jesus Christ. "Have risked their lives" means that they put themselves in danger of death, without looking after themselves, out of love for the name of Jesus.

The apostles and the elders of Jerusalem are speaking, in a letter addressed to the believers who were not Jews in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia. Some had come saying that they must be circumcised to be saved, and this caused confusion. The church supports Barnabas and Paul as trustworthy messengers, and their story of sacrifice gives weight to their testimony.

For today: let us value and listen to those who serve Christ with dedication and humility, not to those who only create doubts. And let us ask ourselves: am I willing to sacrifice something, even my comfort, for Jesus?
exp.14:32:
This verse tells us that Judas and Silas stayed in Antioch for a while. Afterward, the brothers there sent them off and let them go back to Jerusalem, where the apostles were. They were sent away in peace, meaning with good wishes and without any conflict.

Luke, the author of Acts, is describing what happened after the Council of Jerusalem. The leaders of the church had decided that non-Jewish believers did not have to keep the law of Moses in order to be saved. Judas and Silas carried that letter to Antioch and encouraged the brothers with their words. Their mission ended well.

Today we can learn to carry out what is entrusted to us with care and faithfulness, and to finish our tasks leaving peace and encouragement in others.
exp.14:33:
The verse says that it seemed good to Silas to remain in Antioch. The phrase "it seemed good" means that he decided, gladly and with good judgment, to stay there. An important detail: this verse does not appear in the oldest manuscripts, and many modern translations leave it out or place it in a footnote. Even so, it is found in this version.

Silas and Judas had brought the letter from the council in Jerusalem to Antioch and encouraged the believers with many words. When Judas returned to Jerusalem, Silas stayed. This prepares what follows: later Paul will choose him as his companion on the journey (Acts 15:40).

For today: serving where God places us, even in a place that seems ordinary, can be the preparation for what He has ahead. Staying faithfully is also a way of obeying.
exp.15:2:
Paul wanted to take Timothy along as a traveling companion. Before doing so, he circumcised him, that is, he performed the cut that marked Jewish males as part of God's people. He did this because of the Jews in that region, since everyone knew that Timothy's father was a Greek, that is, not a Jew.

Luke, the narrator of Acts, tells this right after the council in Jerusalem, where it was decided that non-Jews did not need to be circumcised to be saved. Timothy had a Jewish mother and a good reputation among the brothers and sisters. Paul did not circumcise him in order to save him, but so that the Jews would be willing to listen to them. Some scholars see this as pastoral wisdom.

For today: we can set aside our own preferences, without changing the gospel, so as not to place unnecessary obstacles in the way of those who need to hear it.
exp.15:4:
This verse sums up what happened to the churches that Paul and Silas visited. In addition, they grew in number every day, that is, more people kept joining them continually.

Here Luke, the author of Acts, speaks as the narrator. After telling how Paul and Silas carried the decisions of the council of Jerusalem to the cities, Luke offers this summary. Those decisions helped Jewish and non-Jewish believers live together in unity. Luke thus shows that clear teaching and unity went hand in hand with growth.

A healthy church needs both things: deep roots and open doors. Today we can seek both: studying the Bible to strengthen our faith, and welcoming with warmth those who come new.
exp.15:13:
This verse tells us that Lydia, a woman who sold purple cloth and came from the city of Thyatira, was listening to Paul. She was one who worshipped God, that is, someone who honored the God of Israel and prayed to him. The text says that the Lord opened her heart so that she paid attention to the words of Paul. To give heed means that she listened with real interest.

The one telling the story is Luke, who traveled with Paul. They were in Philippi, a Roman city in Macedonia. Since it was the Sabbath, they went out by the river, where some women gathered to pray, and Paul spoke to them about the gospel. Afterward Lydia was baptized along with her household, and she welcomed them into her home.

For today: when you share your faith, remember that only God can open the heart. You speak with love and simplicity, and you trust that He is at work. Ask Him also to open your own heart so that you listen to His Word with attention.
exp.15:14:
Lydia was baptized along with her household. Afterward she asked Paul and his companions to stay at her home. She said, "If you have judged me to be faithful to the Lord, come into my house and stay there." She insisted so strongly that she won them over.

The one speaking is Lydia, a seller of purple cloth, who already worshiped God. The text says the Lord opened her heart to listen to Paul's message. In Philippi, her baptism marks the beginning of Christian faith in that city, and her home becomes a place of welcome for the missionaries. The text does not say how many people made up her household.

Today we can show our faith through concrete actions. Opening our home, sharing a meal, or helping someone can be a simple way to thank God and support those who serve.
exp.15:15:
It says that Paul and his companions were on their way to the place of prayer, in Philippi, when they met a young slave girl. She had a spirit of divination, that is, a spirit that gave her power to tell the future. Her masters made a lot of money from what she said.

Luke, the author of Acts, recounts this as a witness, since he speaks in the first person as one who was there. It comes right after the conversion of Lydia, and it shows that the gospel was advancing in Philippi and running up against dark powers and the interests of money. This young woman was being exploited by other people.

For today: God cares about the people whom others use for profit. Let us ask for wisdom to discern what does harm, and for compassion to help those who are trapped.
exp.15:16:
A young slave girl, controlled by a spirit of divination, kept following Paul and his companions, crying out that they were servants of the most high God and that they proclaimed the way of salvation. "Salvation" here means the same thing as the word "salvation" in the verse. A spirit of divination is the meaning of the phrase here.

This happens in Philippi. The one speaking is the girl, used by her owners to make money. Her words were true, but they came from a dark source. So Paul, after several days, did not accept that support and freed her in the name of Jesus. Some think her testimony confused people or mixed the gospel with fortune-telling.

For today: not everything that sounds true comes from God. Let us listen with discernment, and take care that the message of Christ is presented with purity and without mixture. Let us also remember that Jesus has the power to free people.
exp.15:22:
This verse tells us that Paul and Silas received many blows, strong strokes with rods. Afterward they were thrown into prison. The magistrates, or city officials, ordered the jailer to guard them carefully, so that they would not escape.

Luke, the author of Acts, narrates what happened in Philippi. Some men accused Paul and Silas of teaching customs that the Romans could not accept. The crowd became riotous and the authorities acted without a trial. Later, the text shows that they were Roman citizens, so that treatment was unjust.

For today: sometimes we suffer injustice even when we have done good. This passage reminds us that pain does not mean God has abandoned us. Like Paul and Silas, who soon prayed and sang, we can bring our suffering to God and keep trusting him.
exp.15:23:
He says that the jailer, having received the order to guard Paul and Silas securely, put them in the innermost part of the prison. He also fastened their feet in the stocks, a wooden device with holes where the feet of prisoners were secured, and which could leave them very uncomfortable and in pain.

This is part of the account of Paul and Silas in Philippi. They had been beaten with rods by order of the magistrates, after the crowd rose up against them. The jailer was only carrying out the order to watch them with great care. The narrator is Luke, the author of Acts.

For today: sometimes we find ourselves in dark and painful places, without fault and with no way out in sight. The next verse shows that Paul and Silas prayed and sang right there. When you feel shut in by your circumstances, you can pray and praise God, trusting that He is present with you.
exp.15:26:
This verse tells how the jailer woke up after the earthquake and saw the prison doors standing open. He drew his sword and was about to kill himself, because he presumed the prisoners had escaped.

The one speaking here is the narrator, Luke. Paul and Silas were prisoners in Philippi, and at midnight they were singing hymns to God. After the earthquake, the jailer knew that if the prisoners escaped, he could pay with his own life. Many scholars think Roman law was very harsh toward guards, although the text does not explain this. His despair is seen in this moment.

For today: when someone is in despair, a timely word can save their life. Paul shouted right away, and that changed everything. Let us be attentive to those who suffer in silence and speak to them with love.
exp.15:29:
This verse tells how the jailer of Philippi brought Paul and Silas out of the cell and asked them an urgent question. "Sirs" was a respectful way of addressing them. "What must I do" is the question at the heart of the verse, and "to be saved" means to be rescued or delivered.

The one speaking is the jailer. Paul and Silas were prisoners, and an earthquake had opened the doors. The jailer was about to take his own life because he believed the prisoners had escaped, but Paul stopped him. Amazed and trembling, he realized he was in the presence of something greater than himself. It is not fully clear what he understood by being "saved" at that moment, but their answer points to faith in Jesus.

Today, there is no need to wait until everything falls apart before asking this question. If you feel your need of God, ask him sincerely and listen to what his Word says.
exp.15:30:
Paul and Silas told the jailer to put his trust in the Lord Jesus Christ, and that he would be saved, he and his household. "Household" means his whole family and those who lived with him. "Saved" means rescued, forgiven, and received by God.

Paul and Silas were imprisoned in Philippi. An earthquake opened the prison, and the jailer, trembling and afraid, asked them what he had to do to be saved. They answered him plainly. Then they explained the word of the Lord to him and to all his household, and all of them were baptized. It can be understood that the promise is offered to the whole family, but each one needed to hear and believe.

Today, salvation is not earned through effort or merit. It is received by trusting in Jesus. And if you have a family, you can share God's word with them in love, just as Paul and Silas did.
exp.15:31:
This verse says that Paul and Silas spoke God's message to the jailer. They also spoke it to everyone who lived in his house. "The word of the Lord" means the message about Jesus.

Paul and Silas were imprisoned in Philippi. During the night there was an earthquake and the doors of the prison opened. The jailer, frightened, asked how to be saved. They told him to believe in Jesus, and then they explained that message to him in more detail. After that, he and his family were baptized and rejoiced that they had believed.

When someone shows interest in God, it is not enough to give them a short phrase. We can take the time to patiently explain what the Bible says, and share it with their family as well, with kindness and without pressure.
exp.15:32:
This verse tells that the jailer took Paul and Silas at midnight, that very same hour, and washed the wounds left by the beatings. Afterward, he and his whole family were baptized right away. The wounds left by the blows of the whip or rods are the marks the beating left on their bodies.

Paul and Silas were prisoners in Philippi, unjustly beaten. That night an earthquake opened the doors, and the jailer, frightened, asked how to be saved. They told him about Jesus, and he and his household heard and believed. His kind treatment of the prisoners shows a changed heart.

For today: true faith shows itself in concrete acts of love. If Jesus has touched your life, look today for someone you can serve or relieve, even someone you were harsh with before, and do it with humility and joy.
exp.15:33:
What it says: After being baptized, the jailer took Paul and Silas to his house and set a meal before them, that is, he gave them food. He was very glad because he and his whole household had believed in God. The phrase "rejoiced" means he was filled with great joy.

Context: Luke tells this in Philippi. Paul and Silas had been imprisoned unjustly. That night there was an earthquake, and the jailer, about to take his own life, heard the message of salvation. His change is seen right away: he tended their wounds and cared for them in his home.

For today: True faith is often shown in concrete acts of kindness and gratitude. This week, offer a meal or an act of service to someone, and share with joy what God has done in your life.
exp.15:34:
When morning came, the magistrates of Philippi sent officers with an order: release Paul and Silas. The officers were men who carried out the orders of the authorities. The magistrates were the judges or rulers of the city.

The magistrates had ordered Paul and Silas to be beaten and imprisoned the day before. During the night there was an earthquake, and the jailer and his family believed in God. The Bible does not explain why the magistrates changed their minds; some think it was because of the earthquake, but this is a supposition. Afterward Paul insisted that his rights as a Roman citizen be respected.

For today: God works even in darkness, when we see no way out. We can trust that he knows how and when to open a path, and in the meantime remain faithful, as Paul and Silas did.
exp.15:37:
The officers were the attendants who carried out the orders of the magistrates. They went back and told the magistrates what Paul had said. When they heard that Paul and Silas were Roman citizens, the magistrates were frightened.

In Philippi, Paul and Silas had been beaten and thrown into prison without a trial. This was forbidden for Roman citizens. Paul did not speak up earlier, and the Bible does not explain why; some believe he wanted to use this moment to protect the new believers. This is an interpretation, not something the text states.

For today: there are times to be silent and times to stand up for what is right with firmness and without violence. We can ask God for wisdom to know when to speak, and do so with respect, seeking the good of others.
exp.15:39:
Acts 16:40 tells us that Paul and Silas, after leaving the prison, did not leave Philippi right away. First they went to Lydia's house, where the believers used to gather. There they saw the other Christians, and they comforted them, meaning they encouraged and strengthened them. Then they departed from the city.

Luke, the author of Acts, reports this after Paul and Silas had been beaten and imprisoned unjustly. The magistrates became afraid when they learned that the two were Roman citizens, and they asked them to leave. Lydia had already welcomed Paul earlier (Acts 16:14-15), so her house was a meeting place for the young church.

Although they had just suffered, they used their last moments to encourage others. Today we can do the same: even in difficult times, we can seek out someone in our community and offer a word of encouragement.
exp.16:1:
It says that Paul, as was his custom, went to the synagogue in Thessalonica and for three Sabbaths reasoned and debated with the Jews from the Scriptures. "Reasoned" does not mean fighting, but discussing ideas and making a case with arguments.

Luke, the author of Acts, narrates the journey of Paul and Silas after they left Philippi. Thessalonica had a synagogue, and Paul usually began there because he found people who already knew the Old Testament Scriptures. With them he explained that the Messiah had to suffer and rise again, and that this Messiah was Jesus. Some understand that the three Sabbaths were all the time he spent there, although the text does not fully make this clear.

For today: sharing the faith with patience. Paul relied not on pressure but on the Bible, dialogue, and perseverance. We can speak about Jesus with respect, good reasons, and a willingness to listen.
exp.16:4:
This verse tells how some Jews who did not believe in Jesus were filled with envy when they saw many people joining Paul and Silas. So they gathered some men who were idle loafers from the marketplace, without any trade, and formed a mob that stirred up the city. They attacked the house of Jason, looking to bring out Paul and Silas and hand them over to the crowd.

The one telling the story is Luke, the author of Acts. This takes place in Thessalonica. Paul had taught in the synagogue that the Christ had to suffer and rise again, and that Jesus was that Christ. Some Jews, many Greeks, and several influential women believed. The text points to envy as the motive for the opposition.

For today: the success of others in the faith can awaken envy in our hearts. Let us ask God for humility to rejoice when others come to know Jesus, and not to join forces against them.
exp.16:5:
This verse tells that the attackers did not find Paul and Silas at the house of Jason. So they dragged Jason and some other brothers before the city's rulers, shouting that these men who have turned the world upside down had also come to Thessalonica.

The phrase about turning the world upside down, as the accusation was made, means that they stir up trouble and overturn good order. The city rulers were the local authorities of the city.

Some Jews who did not believe spoke against them, moved by jealousy when they saw many people receiving Paul's message. They gathered idle and wicked men to stir up a mob. When they did not find the apostles, they took Jason, who had hosted them, and accused him in their place.

For today: following Jesus can bring misunderstanding and unjust accusations. Even so, we can remain faithful with calm, without repaying evil with evil. And we can be encouraged to accompany and support brothers and sisters who suffer for their faith, like Jason, who bravely gave shelter.
exp.16:6:
What it says: The accusers say that Jason welcomed Paul and Silas into his home. They charge them with going against the orders of the emperor, because, according to them, they proclaim that there is another king, Jesus. Here "welcomed" means that Jason took them in as guests, and "decrees" are the laws or orders of Caesar.

Context: The ones speaking are the Jews who were jealous, together with some men of the city whom they gathered, in the city of Thessalonica. They did not find Paul and Silas, so they dragged Jason before the city authorities. The accusation was political, not religious, meant to frighten the rulers. The Christians spoke of the kingdom of God, but they were not seeking to overthrow Rome.

For today: Following Jesus as King can bring misunderstanding and opposition. Even so, we can live with respect and honesty, and show hospitality and courage like Jason, even when it costs us something.
exp.16:10:
It says that the Jews of Berea were more noble than those of Thessalonica. The word "noble" here speaks of an open and good-natured attitude, not of social class. They received the message with all readiness of mind, that is, with great willingness and eagerness. Furthermore, searching the scriptures means examining them carefully, and they did so every day to check whether what Paul was saying was true.

The one telling the story is Luke, the author of Acts. Paul and Silas had left Thessalonica by night because of the opposition that arose there. On arriving in Berea they went to the synagogue, as was their custom. Luke praises the Bereans because they neither accepted everything without thinking nor rejected it out of prejudice. For this reason many believed.

For today: when you hear a teaching, whether from a preacher, a book, or online, receive it with respect, but compare it with the Bible. Read with humility and perseverance, asking God to guide you.
exp.16:13:
When danger arose in Berea, the brothers acted quickly and sent Paul out of the city. The word "but" appears in the verse, and "immediately" is the sense of the next phrase, so these are simply the verse's meaning. They sent him away toward the coast; it is not certain whether he traveled by sea or only took that direction. Silas and Timothy stayed behind to care for the new believers.

Luke, the author of Acts, is recounting Paul's journey. The Jews from Thessalonica came to Berea and stirred up the crowds, as they had done before. For that reason the believers protected Paul, while other companions continued strengthening the young church.

For today: serving God does not always mean staying and facing everything. Sometimes it is wise to step away from danger and trust that others will carry on the work. God cares for both people and his message.
exp.16:27:
This verse says that we depend on God for everything. We live, move, and exist because of him. Paul adds that some of the Greek poets said we are God's offspring, that is, his children or descendants. "Offspring" means family or origin.

Paul is speaking in Athens, before philosophers and people who worshiped many idols. He wants to show them that the true God does not live in temples made by human hands. He quotes poets they knew, probably Greek authors such as Aratus, although scholars debate exactly whom he is quoting. He does not say that those poets had the whole truth, but uses their words as a point of contact to call them to repentance.

Today we can remember that every breath and every day is a gift from God. This invites us to give him thanks, to seek him with our whole heart, and not to place our trust in things we make ourselves, such as money or success.
exp.16:30:
This verse says that God has already set a day on which he will judge the whole world with justice. He will do it through a man he has chosen, and God gave proof to everyone: he raised him from the dead.

Paul speaks in Athens, before philosophers, at the Areopagus. He explains to them that God is not an image of gold or stone, and he calls them to change the way they think. He ends by speaking about Jesus and his resurrection. Some mocked, and others wanted to hear more. The Bible does not say here who the man is, but the Christian context understands that it is Jesus.

For today: the resurrection of Christ invites us to take God seriously and not to leave for later the decision to turn back to him. We can trust that his judgment will be just.
exp.16:33:
After Paul's speech in Athens, this verse tells that some people believed and joined him. Dionysius, who was from the Areopagus (the council of the city's leaders), is named, along with a woman called Damaris. Others were also there.

Luke, the author of Acts, reports what happened when Paul spoke to the Athenian philosophers. When he mentioned the resurrection, some mocked him and others put the subject off for later. Even so, there were those who believed. The Bible gives no further details about Dionysius and Damaris; any other stories about them are uncertain.

For today: do not lose heart if only a few respond when you share your faith. God can work in a few hearts, and that has great value. Speak with love and trust that He makes the seed grow.
exp.17:2:
This verse says that Paul stayed to live with Aquila and Priscilla because they had the same trade as he did. They worked together making tents. The word that says he stayed as a guest is not one I can give here, but the sense is that he lodged with them, and the word for trade means the work by which a person earns a living. The word for tents can refer to tents for camping, though some think it also included working with leather or other materials.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells this as part of Paul's journey. Paul had just left Athens and arrived in Corinth, where he met this Jewish couple who had left Rome because of an order from the emperor Claudius. Working with them gave him lodging and support while he proclaimed the gospel, as seen in the verses that follow.

For today: ordinary, everyday work does not get in the way of serving God. It can be the place where we make friends, help others, and bear witness through our lives.
exp.17:4:
This verse tells us that when Silas and Timothy arrived from Macedonia, Paul was pressed in his spirit. Pressed means urged on, driven forward with strength. Some manuscripts say he was completely devoted to preaching. So Paul was earnestly declaring to the Jews that Jesus was the Christ, that is, the promised Messiah.

The narrator is Luke, the author of Acts. Paul is in Corinth, where he worked making tents with Aquila and Priscilla to support himself. With the arrival of his companions, who probably brought help, he was able to devote himself fully to preaching. Many understand that the gift from the brothers in Macedonia freed up his time for the ministry.

For today: when God places a conviction in our hearts, it is worth giving it real time and energy. We can also support those who serve, since our help opens room for them to do more.
exp.17:6:
This verse tells that Paul left the synagogue in Corinth and went to the house of a man named Justus. He was one who worshipped God, that is, a non-Jew who worshipped the God of Israel. His house was right next to the synagogue.

Here the narrator, Luke, speaks. Paul had just been rejected by many Jews who opposed him and insulted him. Then he announced that he would turn to the Gentiles. Afterward, Crispus, the leader of the synagogue, believed with his whole household. The Bible does not say whether Justus owned the house or only lent it, and his full name is not known for certain.

For today: when one door closes, God often opens another nearby. If you are rejected, do not stay stuck in regret; look for where you can keep serving, even in a simple house, with love and courage.
exp.17:7:
This verse tells us that Crispus, the leader of the synagogue, believed in the Lord together with his whole household. In addition, many people from Corinth were listening to the message, believing, and being baptized. The word meaning the person in charge of the synagogue is the one who oversaw it.

Paul was preaching in Corinth. The Jews who opposed him insulted him, so he told them that he had already done his duty and would turn to the Gentiles. He went to the house of Justus, which was next to the synagogue. Luke, the author, shows that, even with rejection, the gospel kept bearing fruit, including among religious leaders.

God can work in difficult places. Do not lose heart if some people reject your testimony; keep speaking about Jesus with love and trust that God opens hearts, sometimes where you least expect it.
exp.17:8:
This verse tells that one night the Lord appeared to Paul in a vision and said to him: "Do not be afraid, but keep speaking and do not keep quiet."

Paul was in Corinth. There some Jews opposed him, and he had withdrawn from the synagogue to teach in the house of Justus. Although many believed, Paul probably felt fear, and the Lord himself encouraged him. He promised him his company and said that he had many of his people in that city. Because of this, Paul stayed there for a year and a half.

When sharing your faith frightens you, remember that God does not ask you to do it alone. You can speak with kindness and with courage, trusting that He is with you and that He is at work in the hearts of those who listen.
exp.17:11:
This verse tells how, while Gallio was the Roman governor of Achaia, a group of Jews agreed together to attack Paul. The governor of a Roman province was called here by a term that the verse above does not use, so the reader should simply understand that Gallio was the governor in charge of the province. A tribunal was the place where people were judged, so they brought him before the governor to accuse him.

Here the narrator, Luke, speaks. Paul had been in Corinth for more than a year, teaching the Word. Shortly before, the Lord had promised him that he would be with him and that no one would be able to harm him. The opposition came, but God's promise still stood. According to the text that follows, they accused him of teaching a way of honoring God that was contrary to the law.

For today: when you face opposition because of your faith, remember that God is with you. Remain faithful, trusting that he cares for you, even in difficult moments.
exp.17:13:
Paul was about to begin speaking in his own defense, but Gallio, the governor, spoke first. He told the Jews that if the matter were a real injustice or a serious crime, it would be reasonable for him to hear them out according to the law.

The Jews of Corinth brought their charges against Paul before Gallio, the Roman proconsul of Achaia, accusing him of teaching a way of worshiping God that went against the law. Gallio judged the case as a judge would: he saw no crime against Rome, only an internal dispute about religion. That is why he chose not to get involved.

For today: not every disagreement about faith is settled with accusations or pressure. Let us seek to speak the truth calmly, distinguishing what harms others from what are simply differences of belief, and trust that God cares for his work.
exp.17:14:
Gallio tells the Jews that if the matter is about disputes over words, names, and their own law, they should settle it themselves. He says he does not want to be a judge of such things.

Gallio was the Roman governor of Achaia, in Corinth. The Jews had brought Paul before him, accusing him of teaching people to worship God in a way contrary to the law. Gallio saw no crime against Rome, only an internal religious debate. For that reason he refused to get involved and sent them away from the court. His decision also left Paul free to keep preaching in Corinth.

For today: not every disagreement deserves a fight. Before entering an argument, ask yourself whether it is truly essential or only a dispute over words. And when something does matter, seek to resolve it with humility, prayer, and Scripture, not with accusations.
exp.17:15:
It says that Gallio, the Roman governor of Achaia, ordered the Jewish accusers to leave his judgment seat. The judgment seat was the place where cases were tried. With this he closed the matter and refused to take up the case.

The Jews of Corinth had brought Paul before Gallio, accusing him of teaching a way of worshiping God that was contrary to the law. Gallio saw that this was not a crime against Rome, but a dispute about their religion. For that reason he refused to be a judge. So Paul was protected and was able to remain in Corinth for some more days.

For today: God can care for his people even through authorities who do not know him. In the face of opposition, we can keep serving with calm and trust that he watches over our path.
exp.17:18:
Paul arrives in Ephesus, a great city in Asia Minor. There he leaves Priscilla and Aquila, who had come with him. Then he goes alone into the synagogue, the meeting place of the Jews, and reasoned with them. That word does not mean to fight but to converse and reason, explaining and debating the Scriptures with arguments.

The one who tells the story is Luke, the author of Acts. Paul is coming from Corinth, on his way to Jerusalem. In Ephesus he makes a brief stop. His custom was to begin in the synagogues, where the Old Testament was already known. The verses that follow say they asked him to stay longer, but he promised to return, if God wills.

For today: we can speak about our faith with respect, giving reasons and listening, even when time is short. A sincere conversation can leave a seed that God causes to grow later.
exp.17:22:
This verse says that Paul spent some time in Antioch of Syria and then set out again on a journey. He went through the region of Galatia and Phrygia, moving from city to city in order, in what is today Turkey. The word that the verse renders as "strengthening" means to make firm and steady. His aim was to encourage all the believers to stand firm in the faith.

Here the narrator, Luke, summarizes the start of Paul's third missionary journey. Paul had already preached in these regions before, and now he was returning to visit the groups of believers he had left behind. Luke gives no details about what Paul said in each place; he only shows his care for them. Afterward the account turns to Ephesus, where Apollos appears.

For today: faith needs continual care. Think of someone who recently began to believe, or who is tired, and seek them out this week to encourage them with a visit, a phone call, or a prayer.
exp.17:23:
This verse introduces a new person: Apollos, a Jew born in Alexandria, who came to Ephesus. He is described as an eloquent man, meaning he spoke very well, and as mighty in the scriptures, meaning he knew the sacred texts of the Old Testament very well. Ephesus is a major city in Asia Minor.

Here the narrator is Luke, the author of Acts. While telling of Paul's travels, he introduces Apollos, who will become an important teacher. The following verses say that he taught with fervor, but knew only the baptism of John. Priscilla and Aquila heard him and explained to him more fully the way of God.

For today: even if you have good gifts and much knowledge, stay humble and willing to learn. Apollos was not offended when he was corrected with love; he grew and became more useful.
exp.18:3:
Paul explains that John the Baptist baptized the people as a sign that they repented of their sins. But John also told them that they should believe on the one who would come after him, and that one was Jesus, the Christ (which means the anointed one, the Messiah).

Paul is in Ephesus and meets some disciples who knew only John's baptism. They had not even heard of the Holy Ghost. Paul makes clear to them that John's message pointed to Jesus. Then they believed and were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.

For today: repentance is a good beginning, but faith in Jesus is the center. Ask yourself whether your faith rests on knowing Christ himself, and not only on traditions or good customs.
exp.18:5:
This verse tells that Paul laid his hands on some believers in Ephesus, and the Holy Ghost came on them. Then they spoke with tongues, that is, in languages they had not learned, and prophesied, or in other words, they spoke messages from God.

Laid his hands upon them means that he placed his hands on them, as a gesture of blessing and prayer.

Luke, the author of Acts, reports that these twelve men knew only the baptism of John. Paul explained to them that John pointed toward Jesus, and they believed and were baptized. Then they received the Spirit. Christians interpret in different ways whether this episode is a pattern for everyone or a unique sign at a moment of transition.

Today we can remember that following Jesus is not only knowing something about Him, but truly receiving Him. Ask God to let His Spirit guide you and give you power to live and serve with faith.
exp.18:6:
This verse says that there were about twelve men in all. "About twelve" means an approximate number, not an exact one. It refers to the disciples in Ephesus who have just been baptized and have received the Holy Spirit.

The author is Luke, who tells the story in the book of Acts. Paul had found these believers in Ephesus, who knew only the baptism of John. After hearing the message about Jesus, they were baptized in his name. Luke gives the number to show that it was a real and small group. Some think the number twelve recalls the twelve tribes of Israel, but the text does not say so, so this is only one possible interpretation.

For today: God works through small groups and simple beginnings. Do not look down on a small group of believers or on your own step of faith; God can use them for something great in his time.
exp.18:11:
This verse tells how people would take the cloths used to wipe away sweat and the work aprons that had touched Paul's body, and bring them to the sick. Then the diseases would leave and the evil spirits would go out.

Luke, the author of Acts, reports this during Paul's two years in Ephesus. He says that God was doing extraordinary wonders, that is, remarkable miracles. The power did not come from the objects or from Paul, but from God. The account that follows, with the sons of Sceva, shows that using the name of Jesus as a magic formula does not work.

For today: trust that God is still the one who heals and sets free, and do not place your faith in objects or in people. Come to Him with humility, and look to Jesus, not to the instruments He may use.
exp.18:16:
This verse tells us that what happened to the sons of Sceva became known throughout the city of Ephesus, both to Jews and to Greeks. The people there were struck with a deep, serious sense of awe. The name of Jesus was held in high honor.

Luke, the author of Acts, reports what happened after some wandering Jewish exorcists tried to use the name of Jesus without really knowing him. The evil spirit overpowered them. Ephesus was a city deeply involved in magic, and this event showed that the power of Jesus is not a formula to be used lightly.

For today: repeating religious words is not enough; a real relationship with Jesus is needed. Let us live with reverence, so that his name is honored by the way we live.
exp.18:23:
This verse introduces Demetrius, a silversmith from Ephesus. He made silver shrines of Diana, that is, small replicas of her temple or of her image. Lucas, the author of Acts, is the one telling the story. Paul had been in Ephesus for some time, and the message about Christ was spreading. Lucas presents Demetrius as the source of the disturbance. According to the verses that follow, he feared losing his business because Paul was saying that gods made by human hands are not gods.

For today: it is worth examining how money influences our decisions. Let us ask God for honesty, so that when the truth makes us uncomfortable, we do not reject it merely to protect our comfort or our profits.
exp.18:25:
What it says: Demetrius speaks to the silversmiths and tells them that they themselves see and hear what Paul is doing. According to him, Paul has persuaded many people, not only in Ephesus but in almost all of Asia (a region of the Roman Empire, today part of Turkey), that gods made by human hands are not gods.

Context: The speaker is Demetrius, a silversmith who made small silver shrines of Diana, a goddess greatly honored in Ephesus. His business brought good profits to many craftsmen. As Paul preached the gospel, people were abandoning their idols and sales were falling. Demetrius mixes his religious concern with his financial interest, and so he stirs up the anger of his fellow workers.

For today: It is worth asking ourselves whether something, such as money or success, weighs more heavily on our hearts than the truth. Let us ask God to give us honesty to follow it even when it costs us.
exp.18:26:
Here Demetrius, a silversmith of Ephesus, warns his fellow craftsmen that their business is in danger. He says they could come to shame, that the temple of Diana could be looked down on as worthless, and that her magnificence, or greatness, could begin to be destroyed, even though all Asia and the world honored her.

Demetrius speaks to the craftsmen who made objects for the worship of Diana. Paul had preached that idols made by human hands are not gods, and many had believed. Demetrius mixes religion with money: his real concern was profit, though he presents it as a defense of the faith. This provoked anger and a great uproar in the city.

For today: let us examine our motives. Sometimes we defend something with religious words when in reality we are protecting our comfort or our wallet. Let us ask God for a sincere heart, willing to obey the truth even when it costs us.
exp.18:27:
What they said: The people who heard Demetrius's speech became extremely angry. They began shouting that Diana, the goddess of Ephesus, was great.

Context: Demetrius, a silversmith who made figures of the temple of Diana, spoke to the craftsmen. He told them that Paul's message was costing them money and the prestige of the temple. Their anger came mainly from concern for their business, although they also defended their religion. Afterward, the city was filled with confusion.

For today: When something touches our wallet or our pride, anger can take over and drive us to act without thinking. Before reacting, it is wise to stop, pray, and ask ourselves whether we are defending the truth or only our own interests.
exp.18:35:
This verse says that since no one can deny what has just been said, it is better for the people to calm down and not act on impulse.

The one speaking is the town clerk of Ephesus, a local official. For nearly two hours the crowd had been shouting for Diana, angry at the preaching of Paul and his companions. The clerk wants to prevent a disturbance that could bring trouble with the Roman authorities. He reminds them that there are courts to settle complaints.

For today: when you feel anger or the pressure of a crowd, stop before you act. Breathe, think, and look for fair ways to resolve the problem, instead of being carried away by the emotion of the moment.
exp.18:39:
This verse says there was a danger that they would be accused of sedition, that is, of stirring up a riot against the authorities, because of what had happened that day. And there was no valid reason to justify that uproar.

The speaker is the town clerk of Ephesus, a local official. The crowd had been shouting in the theater for hours, angry because Paul's message was hurting the business of the silversmiths who made images of Diana. This official feared that Rome would punish the city for the disorder, so he calmed everyone down and sent them home.

For today: when tensions run high, there is no need to shout louder. A calm word, spoken with good sense and respect for fair and lawful channels, can defuse a conflict. Before reacting as a group, let us ask ourselves whether we have clear reasons for what we are doing.
exp.19:0:
He says that, when the uproar had ended, Paul gathered the disciples, encouraged them with his words, embraced them, and took his leave of them to travel to Macedonia. The word for uproar refers to a public disturbance or riot. To encourage means to cheer on, advise, and strengthen.

The one who narrates is Luke, the author of Acts. The uproar was the riot in Ephesus, caused by the silversmiths who opposed Paul's message (Acts 19). After that, Paul left the city, but not before strengthening the believers. Then he continued on his way to visit other churches and keep encouraging them.

For today: after a difficult season, do not stay alone thinking only about the problem. Paul used that moment to encourage others with words and affection. Look today for someone who is weary in the faith and give them a word of encouragement or a sincere embrace.
exp.19:4:
This verse says that a group of Paul's companions went ahead and then waited for him in Troas, a port city. The word "these" refers to the men mentioned earlier: Sopater, Aristarchus, Secundus, Gaius, Timothy, Tychicus and Trophimus. "Us" shows that the one telling the story includes himself in the group.

The book of Acts was written by Luke, and here he speaks about himself and Paul. Paul had discovered a plan by the Jews to harm him, so he changed his route and went back through Macedonia. His companions traveled ahead, and Luke and Paul caught up with them later, from Philippi. The texts do not explain in detail why they separated this way; it was a practical decision about the journey.

For today: serving God is almost never done alone. Paul had a team that traveled with him and waited for him. Think about who walks with you in your faith, and seek to be someone who also helps, waits for and supports others.
exp.19:7:
This verse says that in the upper room, where the believers were gathered, there were many lamps lit. The "upper room" was a room on the upper floor of the house. The lamps were oil lamps, and they gave light during the night.

The one who tells the account is Luke, the author of Acts, who was traveling with Paul. The believers in Troas came together on the first day of the week to break bread and listen to Paul, who was leaving the next day and kept speaking until midnight. Luke mentions the lamps as a detail of the place. We do not know for certain why he includes it; some think it explains the heat or the atmosphere, and others think it shows that it was an open meeting with nothing hidden.

For today: value times of gathering and teaching with other believers. It is worth giving them time and attention, and taking care that tiredness or distraction does not overcome us.
exp.19:8:
This verse tells that a young man named Eutychus was sitting in a window. Paul was preaching for a long time, and the young man, overcome by a deep sleep, fell from the third floor. When they lifted him up, they took him for dead.

The one who tells the story is Luke, the author of Acts. The believers in Troas had gathered on the first day of the week to break bread, that is, to share the Lord's Supper. Paul was leaving the next day, so he extended his teaching until midnight. Afterward God used Paul so that the young man came back to life, as the account that follows shows.

For today: value your time with God's Word and try to stay attentive and rested. And if someone falls asleep or fails, treat them with compassion, for God cares for the weak.
exp.19:15:
This verse explains why the ship did not stop at Ephesus. Paul had decided to sail past it so as not to spend time in the province of Asia. He was in a hurry to reach Jerusalem, if it were possible, by the day of Pentecost, a Jewish feast celebrated fifty days after the Passover.

Luke, the author of Acts, recounts this journey, in which he himself was traveling with Paul (which is why the text says "we"). Paul had already spent years of labor in Asia and in other places. The text does not say in detail why he wanted to be in Jerusalem for Pentecost; some think he wanted to deliver the offering and take advantage of the crowd gathered in the city. This is an interpretation.

For today: It is good to have clear goals and to organize our time to meet them, but without losing care for people. Paul still called the elders of Ephesus to bid them farewell.
exp.19:17:
Paul reminds the elders of Ephesus that they themselves saw how he lived among them from the first day he arrived in Asia, and that he was with them the whole time.

Paul is speaking in Miletus, on his way to Jerusalem. Since he was in a hurry and did not want to stop in Asia, he sent for the elders of the church in Ephesus to say goodbye. Before speaking about his work, he appeals to what they themselves witnessed. His example of life backs up his words.

For today: our daily life speaks louder than our speeches. Let us ask God to help us live in such a way that those who know us closely can see consistency between what we believe and what we do.
exp.19:18:
Paul recalls how he served the Lord among the Ephesians: with great humility, without seeking importance for himself. He also did it with many tears, that is, with deep sorrow and affection for the people. In addition, he faced trials caused by the plots of the Jews, which means traps or conspiracies against him.

Paul speaks in Miletus, near the end of his third journey, with the elders of the church of Ephesus, whom he had called to come to him. He is taking leave of them and reminds them of the way he lived and taught among them. We do not know in detail every plot he mentions, but the book of Acts recounts several of the opposition he suffered.

For today: serve God with humility and a tender heart, and do not give up when opposition comes. Serving is not about seeking applause, but about loving people and remaining faithful even when it costs tears.
exp.19:20:
Paul says that he was testifying, that is, speaking with firmness and seriousness, both to Jews and to non-Jews. His message had two parts: repentance before God, which means changing direction and turning back to Him, and faith in our Lord Jesus Christ. The words "to" and "toward" in the verse show the direction of his message, both toward the people and toward God and Christ.

Paul speaks in Miletus with the elders of the church in Ephesus, whom he has called before traveling to Jerusalem. He takes his leave and reminds them how he lived among them: with humility, with tears, and without holding back anything useful. He summarizes his message for them and shows that he knows trials are waiting for him.

For today: the message of the gospel includes turning to God and trusting in Jesus. We can ask ourselves in what area we need to change direction, and take one concrete step of trust in Christ today.
exp.19:22:
Paul says that in every city he passes through, the Holy Spirit warns him that chains and suffering are waiting for him.

Paul speaks to the elders of the church in Ephesus when he says goodbye to them in Miletus. He is heading to Jerusalem, bound in spirit, that is, feeling driven by God, although he does not know exactly what will happen. He knows that suffering awaits him, but he accepts it with courage. For him, what matters most is finishing his task of proclaiming the gospel.

For today: obeying God does not always mean an easy path. We can follow his calling with confidence, even when there are difficulties, because his presence is with us and our lives have a greater purpose.
exp.19:23:
He says that Paul does not count any of the things that might happen to him as important, nor does he hold his life as something he must protect at all costs. The only thing that matters to him is to finish well the race God has set before him, that is, the task God gave him, and to finish it with joy. That task is to proclaim the good news of the grace of God, his love and forgiveness that cannot be earned by merit.

Paul is speaking in Miletus to the elders of the church in Ephesus, and he is saying goodbye to them. He is on his way to Jerusalem, and the Holy Spirit has warned him that imprisonment and suffering await him. Even so, he goes forward. He knows that he will probably not see them again.

For today: ask yourself what God has entrusted to you, in your family, your work, or your church. Ask him to help you not let fear or comfort turn you aside, and to keep going with joy, step by step.
exp.19:24:
Paul tells the church leaders of Ephesus that he is certain none of them will see him again. He had gone among them preaching the kingdom of God, that is, God's rule and salvation through Jesus.

Paul speaks at Miletus, where he called the Ephesian elders before going on to Jerusalem. He knew through the Spirit that imprisonment and suffering awaited him. His farewell is serious and tender. Some think his certainty was a conviction of the moment; later, the New Testament does not fully make clear whether he visited them again.

For today: live and serve with sincerity, as if every opportunity to speak of Jesus or to love someone were precious. Do not put off until later what God places on your heart to do today.
exp.19:27:
Paul tells the church leaders to take care first of themselves and then of the whole flock, that is, the congregation. God himself, through his Spirit, made them overseers, a word that means supervisors or caretakers. To feed the church means to nourish it and shepherd it, the way a shepherd cares for his sheep. The church belongs to the Lord, who purchased it with his own blood. Some scholars debate whether the final phrase refers to the blood of God or to the blood of his Son; the general sense points to the sacrifice of Christ.

Paul bids farewell to the elders of Ephesus, knowing that he will not see them again. He warns them because false teachers will come, both from outside and from within.

If you take care of others, in the family, the church, or the workplace, remember that they are precious to God. Care for your own spiritual life too, so that you can serve them well.
exp.19:28:
Paul says that, after he leaves, grievous wolves will come in among them, meaning dangerous and greedy people who will attack the believers. The flock is the congregation, the church. Not sparing the flock means they will show no mercy and will do harm. Take heed to yourselves means take care of yourselves.

Paul is saying goodbye to the elders of the church in Ephesus, who had gathered in Miletus. He knows he will not see them again, and he reminds them that he taught them the whole counsel of God. He calls them to care for the church as shepherds. He then makes clear that the danger would come from outside and also from within.

Today we can care for our church by knowing the Bible well, so that we can tell what is true from what is false. Leaders should watch over their own hearts and protect with love those whom God has entrusted to them.
exp.19:30:
This verse says that the leaders of Ephesus must be alert and awake. Watch means to keep guard and not be careless. To warn means to advise with both kindness and firmness. Paul reminds them that for about three years he cared for them day and night, and that he did it with tears, that is, with sincere love.

Paul speaks in Miletus to the elders (pastors) of the church in Ephesus, and he says farewell because he will not see them again. He warns them that dangers will come from outside, savage wolves, and also from within, from people who will teach twisted things to draw followers. His example of devotion is the basis of his call.

For today: take care of your faith and the faith of your family or your church. Compare what you hear with the Bible, and if you must correct someone, do it with humility, truth and love, not with harshness.
exp.19:31:
Paul tells the elders of Ephesus that he is leaving them in the hands of God and of his word, which speaks of his grace (his love and favor, which we do not deserve). God is able to continue building up their lives, strengthening and growing them, and to give them an inheritance together with all who are set apart for God.

Paul says goodbye to the leaders of Ephesus, knowing that he may not see them again. He has just warned them that false teachers will come, even from among themselves. So instead of trusting in himself, he entrusts them to God and to his word.

For today: when you face confusion or doubtful teaching, do not depend on people alone. Read the Bible regularly and pray, trusting that God sustains you and makes you grow.
exp.19:36:
All the elders of Ephesus wept hard. They threw their arms around Paul's neck and kissed him again and again. Weeping is shedding tears, and to fall on someone's neck is to give a tight, affectionate embrace. Kissing was a common way of saying goodbye among friends and brothers in that culture.

Paul is heading to Jerusalem and saying farewell to the leaders of the church in Ephesus, whom he called from Miletus. He has just prayed on his knees with them. He had told them they would not see his face again, and that is why the sorrow is so deep. Luke, the author of Acts, shows the real bond between Paul and them.

For today: do not hide your affection for your brothers and sisters in the faith. Tell someone in your church how much you appreciate them, and say goodbye to people with prayer and gratitude, without assuming there will be another chance.
exp.20:10:
Agabo arrives at Caesarea, takes Paul's belt (a sash that was tied around the waist) and uses it to bind his own feet and hands. Then he says that the Holy Spirit declares that the Jews of Jerusalem will bind the owner of this belt in the same way and hand him over to the Gentiles, that is, to people who are not Jews. "Jerusalem" is Jerusalem.

Agabo is a prophet who had also earlier announced a great famine (Acts 11:28). He uses a visible action, as the prophets of the Old Testament did, so that the message will be impressed on the mind. Paul was on his way to Jerusalem, and his friends, hearing this, begged him not to go up. Paul answers that he is ready to be bound and even to die for Jesus.

God sometimes warns us of difficulties, not so that we will run away, but so that we will face what is coming with open eyes and with faith. We can obey with courage, trusting that He goes with us.
exp.20:12:
Paul tells his friends to stop weeping, because their tears are breaking his heart. He declares that he is not only ready to be bound, but also ready to die in Jerusalem for the name of Jesus.

Paul is in Caesarea, on his way to Jerusalem. The prophet Agabus has just given a warning through a sign, saying that Paul would be bound and handed over to the Gentiles. Paul's friends, out of love, beg him not to go up. Paul understands the warning, but he believes he must go on. Some think his decision was guided by the Spirit, and others believe it may have been his own resolve. The Bible does not make this entirely clear.

Today we can love those who advise us with tears, yet follow what we believe God is asking of us, with humility and prayer. Serving Christ can cost us, and it is worth thinking carefully before we decide.
exp.20:22:
Here James and the elders of Jerusalem ask Paul to do something specific. They tell him that there are four men in the church who have taken a vow, that is, a special promise made to God. It is likely that this is the Nazirite vow, although the text does not spell it out in full.

Paul had just arrived in Jerusalem. The leaders tell him that many Jewish believers had heard false rumors: that he was teaching people to abandon the law of Moses. To calm the situation, they propose that he join these men and pay their expenses. In this way everyone would see that he too lived in keeping with his Jewish heritage.

For today: sometimes we can yield in matters that do not affect the gospel, out of love and to avoid stumbling blocks. But let us do it with wisdom, without changing the truth of Christ.
exp.20:23:
Here Paul is asked to join four men who had taken a vow. He must purify himself with them and pay the costs of their offerings, so that they can have their heads shaved, that is, complete the vow by cutting their hair. In this way everyone would see that the rumors about Paul were false and that he too lived by the law.

The one speaking is James, with the elders of the church in Jerusalem. Many Jewish believers had heard that Paul taught people to abandon Moses. They wanted to avoid a conflict. Some scholars see here pastoral prudence; others, a gesture that Paul accepted out of love, though it was not required of him.

For today: sometimes love asks us to yield in secondary matters, without denying the gospel, so as not to become a stumbling block to others and to keep the peace.
exp.20:27:
What it says: Some Jews from Asia cry out, calling on the people for help. They accuse Paul of teaching everywhere against the people of Israel, against the law of Moses, and against the temple. They also say that he brought Gentiles (people who are not Jewish) into the temple and defiled it, that is, made it ceremonially unclean.

Context: Paul had arrived in Jerusalem and, on the advice of the elders, took part in a purification rite to show that he respected the law. The ones shouting are Jews from Asia who had known him before. The next verse makes clear that they had seen Trophimus, a Gentile from Ephesus, with Paul in the city, and only assumed that he had taken him into the temple. The accusation was based on an assumption, not on a fact.

For today: Before repeating an accusation, it is wise to check the facts. Assumptions and prejudices can harm an innocent person and stir up crowds.
exp.20:31:
It says that the tribune, a Roman military commander, immediately took soldiers and centurions (officers who commanded about a hundred soldiers each) and ran down toward the crowd. When the people saw the soldiers coming, they stopped beating Paul. The verse's wording "beating" here means striking or hitting.

This is a scene narrated by Luke. Paul had gone to the temple in Jerusalem, and some Jews falsely accused him and stirred up a riot. They wanted to kill him. The Roman garrison was nearby, in the Antonia fortress, and the tribune acted to restore order, not necessarily to defend Paul.

For today: God can use unexpected situations and people to protect us. We can trust his care, even when we do not understand how he is working, and give thanks for the help that comes to us.
exp.20:34:
This verse tells us that Paul reached the steps, the stairs leading up to the Antonia fortress in Jerusalem. There the soldiers had to carry him, because the crowd was so furious and violent that they could have harmed him.

Here Luke, the narrator of the book of Acts, is speaking. Paul had been accused in the temple, and the crowd wanted to kill him. The Roman tribune stepped in to stop the uproar, although he still did not understand what was happening. Without knowing it, the soldiers ended up protecting Paul.

For today: God can care for us even through unexpected means, sometimes through people who do not know him. When we face injustice or rejection, we can keep our calm and trust that God is still at work, even in the middle of the chaos.
exp.20:39:
The Roman commander gave Paul permission to speak. Paul stood on the steps, raised his hand to ask for attention, and the crowd fell into a great silence. Then he spoke to them in the Hebrew language, which was probably Aramaic, the common language of the Jews in that region. The steps are the stairs that led up to the fortress.

Paul had just been arrested in Jerusalem, because a mob attacked him in the temple, believing he had defiled it. The commander mistook him for an Egyptian rebel. Paul made clear who he was and asked to speak. Speaking in the language of the people showed respect and helped them listen to him.

For today: even in the midst of pressure, we can speak with calm and respect. When we share our faith, it helps to use language the other person understands and to show closeness before defending our ideas.
exp.21:1:
When they heard that he was speaking to them in the Aramaic language, they became even quieter. The crowd had already been silent, but now they listened with even greater attention. Then Paul began his defense.

Paul had just been arrested in Jerusalem after a disturbance in the temple. An angry crowd wanted to kill him. He asked the Roman commander for permission to speak to them. Many believe the language here was Aramaic, the common language of the Jews of that time, though some think it may have been Hebrew. By using their language, Paul showed them respect and closeness.

When we want to be heard, it helps to speak with respect and in a language the other person understands. A kind and warm manner can lower tension and open a space to share our faith.
exp.21:2:
Paul says that he is a Jew by birth, born in Tarsus, a city in Cilicia. He clarifies that he was raised in Jerusalem, the city where he now speaks, and that he was a student of Gamaliel, a highly respected teacher. He learned the law of his ancestors with great care and was zealous for God, just as his hearers were that day.

Paul is speaking before the angry crowd in the temple of Jerusalem, who accused him of teaching against the people and the law. He uses the Hebrew language to win their attention. With these words he seeks to build common ground before he tells how Jesus changed his life.

For today: when you share your faith, begin with what you have in common with the other person. Listen, respect their story, and speak with simplicity and sincerity, without losing the truth you want to communicate.
exp.21:3:
Here Paul says he persecuted "this way" to the point of death, that is, the followers of Jesus, with such force that he wanted them killed. He would arrest them and throw them into prison, whether they were men or women. Paul's word for arresting means seizing and taking them, and his phrase for handing them over means delivering them into the hands of the authorities.

Paul speaks in Jerusalem before an agitated Jewish crowd that had just seized him in the temple. He speaks in Hebrew to win their attention. He tells them his background to show that he was as zealous as they are. In this way he prepares the account of how Jesus met him on the road to Damascus and changed his life.

For today: God can transform any person, even someone who seems to be his enemy today. And if you have changed, your past, told with humility, can help others understand the grace of God.
exp.21:4:
Here Paul says that the high priest and all the elders of the Sanhedrin can confirm what he is telling. They gave him letters of authorization, addressed to the Jewish believers in Damascus, so that he could arrest the followers of Jesus and bring them as prisoners to Jerusalem to be punished.

Paul is speaking in Jerusalem, before an angry crowd that accuses him in the temple. He tells them his story to show that he was as zealous as they were and that he pursued the Christians with all his strength. His change did not come from carelessness, but from an encounter with Jesus.

For today: God can transform anyone, even someone who opposes Him. Pray for those who today seem far from faith, and remember that your own testimony can help others.
exp.21:5:
He says that Paul was on his way and was already near Damascus, at about noon. Suddenly, a very strong light from heaven surrounded him on every side.

The phrase about noon refers to midday, when the sun is at its highest. The word "suddenly" in the verse above captures the same sense of an unexpected moment.

Paul speaks in Jerusalem, before an angry crowd that accused him in the temple. He tells them his story, and reminds them that he himself once persecuted the believers with letters of authority. He wants them to understand that his change was not his own idea, but something God did. That light was the beginning of his encounter with Jesus.

For today: God can interrupt our path, even when we are walking with complete confidence in the wrong direction. If you sense that God is getting your attention, do not harden yourself; listen with humility. His light does not seek to shame you, but to lead you to Jesus.
exp.21:14:
It says that Paul will have a mission: to tell all people what he has seen and heard. It will not be a mission based on hearsay, but on his own experience of meeting Jesus. The word "his" refers to God, and a "witness" is someone who speaks about what they know firsthand.

Here Paul is speaking in Jerusalem before an angry crowd. He tells how Jesus met him on the road to Damascus. These words were spoken to him by Ananias, a believer from there, who explained that God had chosen him. Paul recalls this to show that his change of life and his calling came from God, not from himself.

For today: you do not need to be an expert in theology to speak about Jesus. You can simply tell what God has done in your life, with humility and respect, and let Him do the rest.
exp.21:17:
Paul tells that, while he was praying in the temple, he saw the Lord Jesus speaking to him. Jesus told him to make haste and get out of Jerusalem quickly, because the people there would not receive what Paul bore witness to about Christ. The word "quickly" in the verse means without delay, right away.

Paul is speaking before an angry crowd in Jerusalem, after he was arrested in the temple. He recounts his conversion and his calling. This vision took place after his conversion, when he had returned to Jerusalem. Later, Paul answers that they knew his past as a persecutor, but the Lord sent him to the Gentiles.

For today: sometimes God leads us to leave a place where there is no openness, even when it hurts. Obeying is not giving up, but trusting that He has another place for us to serve.
exp.21:18:
Paul answers the Lord and tells him that the Jews in Jerusalem know his past. He himself imprisoned and beat, that is, struck, those who believed in Jesus in the synagogues.

Paul speaks before the crowd in Jerusalem, and recounts what he experienced in the temple after his conversion. Jesus ordered him to leave the city. Paul objects sincerely: he thought his history as a persecutor would make his change believable. Some understand that he was thus trying to persuade the Lord; others, that it was a human argument. The Lord, in any case, sends him to the Gentiles.

For today: God can use our past, even the part that shames us, but He decides how and where we serve. We can speak to Him frankly and then obey.
exp.21:22:
This verse describes the reaction of the crowd in Jerusalem. They shouted in fury, and they threw off or flung their cloaks and tossed dust into the air. These were gestures of anger and total rejection, as if they could no longer hold back their outrage.

Paul was speaking to the people in the temple, telling of his conversion and his calling. They listened calmly until he said that God was sending him to the Gentiles, that is, to non-Jews. That idea seemed unbearable to them. Commentators explain the gesture of the clothes and the dust in various ways, but all agree that it showed uncontrolled rage.

For today: when a truth makes us uncomfortable, it is easy to react with fury instead of listening. Let us ask God for a humble heart, one that examines what it hears before rejecting it.
exp.21:23:
It says the tribune, the Roman military commander in Jerusalem, ordered Paul to be taken into the barracks, called the castle. There he wanted to question him under the lash, that is, with whipping, to find out why the crowd was shouting so loudly against him. To be examined means to be questioned. To cry out means to shout.

Paul had just given his testimony to the Jews in the temple, and they became furious when he spoke of being sent to the Gentiles. The tribune did not understand the reason for the uproar, so he used the Roman method of getting information by force. Paul would soon respond by saying he was a Roman citizen, which stopped the punishment.

For today: when people become angry without our understanding why, we can keep calm, speak the truth, and trust that God cares for us, even in unjust situations.
exp.21:25:
What it says: The centurion, a Roman officer in charge of one hundred soldiers, heard what Paul had asked. So he went to inform the tribune, who was the military commander. He told him with concern: "Take care what you are doing. This man is a Roman citizen."

Context: Paul was in Jerusalem, and a crowd had rejected him with violence. The tribune wanted to question him under the lash to find out the cause of the disturbance. Paul, already bound, asked whether it was lawful to scourge a Roman without a trial. The centurion understood that there could be a serious legal problem.

For today: Paul did not respond with anger or despair, but with calm and wisdom. He used a legitimate right to stop unjust treatment. We can defend what is right with respect and composure, without losing self-control.
exp.21:27:
