The tribune, a Roman military commander, admitted that he had paid a large sum of money to obtain Roman citizenship. He had paid a great sum for his citizenship. Paul answered calmly that he had not bought it, but that he was a citizen by birth, that is, since he was born.

Paul had been arrested in Jerusalem and was about to be whipped to make him confess. When he said he was a Roman citizen, the centurion warned the tribune, because Roman law protected citizens from that kind of treatment without a trial. Some believe that Tarsus, his city, or his family, gave him that right, but the Bible gives no further details.

Paul wisely used what was within his reach to protect himself and to continue carrying out his mission. God can also use your situation, your rights, or your resources to care for you and to serve others, without arrogance and with calm.
exp.21:28:
They quickly withdrew from him those who were about to examine him with scourging. Even the tribune, a Roman officer in command of about a thousand soldiers, was frightened when he learned that Paul was a Roman citizen, because he had had him bound.

Paul had been arrested in Jerusalem after a disturbance in the temple. When they were about to whip him, he asked whether it was lawful to do so to a Roman citizen without a trial. Roman law protected citizens from that kind of treatment, and the tribune could be punished for failing to respect it. Luke, the author of Acts, tells how Paul calmly made use of his legal rights.

For today: using lawful rights and resources wisely is not a lack of faith. We can ask for fair treatment with respect and calm, trusting that God cares for us.
exp.21:29:
This verse says that on the next day the Roman commander wanted to know for certain what the Jews were accusing Paul of. For that reason he freed him from his chains, gathered the chief priests and all their council (the Sanhedrin), and set Paul before them. The chief priests are the leaders of the priests.

The narrator is Luke. The commander had ordered Paul bound without knowing that he was a Roman citizen. When he found out, he was afraid, because binding or beating a citizen without a trial was a serious matter. Now he seeks to clear up the case in a lawful way. What follows is Paul's speech before the council.

For today: before judging or accusing someone, let us seek the truth calmly and justly. And if we are the ones accused, we can trust that God can use even unjust situations to open doors for us and to bear witness to our faith.
exp.22:4:
Paul responds to those who rebuked him for insulting the high priest. He says he did not know it was him, and he cites the law of Moses: you must not speak evil of the ruler of your people. "Speak evil" here means to speak badly of someone with contempt or a desire to harm them. "Ruler" means a person in authority or a governing leader.

Paul is before the Jewish council. The high priest had ordered him struck on the mouth, and Paul reacted with anger. Why he said he did not know who he was can be explained in several ways: perhaps he could not see well, perhaps he did not recognize him, or perhaps he spoke with some irony. The Bible does not make this clear.

For today: even when an authority treats us unjustly, we can defend the truth without losing respect. If we get it wrong when we speak, it is good to acknowledge it with humility and correct ourselves.
exp.22:9:
It says that the argument between the Jews became so violent that the tribune, that is, the Roman commander, was afraid Paul would be torn to pieces by the crowd. So he ordered the soldiers to go down, to take Paul out from among them by force, and to bring him into the castle, the Roman barracks.

The narrator is Luke. Paul was standing before the Sanhedrin, and he had said that they were judging him for his hope in the resurrection. That divided the Sadducees and the Pharisees. The tribune only wanted to protect a Roman citizen and keep order. Then, that same night, the Lord encouraged Paul.

For today: God can take care of us in unexpected ways, even through people who do not know him. When you face conflicts or dangers, trust that God is still guiding your path.
exp.22:10:
That night the Lord appeared to Paul and encouraged him. Paul was told to take heart, and the verse gives the sense of the words without quoting them. The Lord reminded him that just as he had testified about Jesus in Jerusalem, so he must also bear witness in Rome.

The Lord, that is, Jesus, speaks to Paul, who was being held in the Roman fortress. That day Paul had spoken before the Jewish council, and the conflict between Pharisees and Sadducees became so violent that the commander removed him for his safety. Paul was in danger and perhaps afraid. Shortly afterward, more than forty men swore to kill him. The Lord's word came just before that threat.

For today: when you feel surrounded by problems, remember that God has not forgotten you. He has a purpose for your life and walks with you in the midst of trials.
exp.22:12:
This verse says that more than forty men took part in the conspiracy, that is, in a secret plan made together. They bound themselves with a solemn oath to kill Paul, and they put themselves under a curse if they failed to carry it out.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells this as the narrator. Paul was a prisoner in Jerusalem, and some Jews who opposed his message wanted to kill him. Just before this, the Lord had told Paul to take courage, because he would also bear witness in Rome. So the human plot stands in contrast with God's purpose.

For today: when there are people or plans against you, remember that nothing can stop what God has decided to do. Trust in Him, do what is right, and do not answer with evil.
exp.22:15:
Acts 23:16 says that Paul's sister's son heard of the plot against him. He went to the castle, which was the Roman barracks in Jerusalem, and told Paul. The word "plot" means secret schemes to harm someone, and "told" means to inform or let someone know.

Paul was a prisoner in Jerusalem. More than forty men had sworn not to eat until they had killed him, and they would ask the commander to bring Paul back before the council. The one telling the story is Luke, the author of Acts. The Bible does not say how the young man found out or how old he was; it simply calls him a young man. God used a family member to protect Paul.

For today: God can use ordinary people, even young ones, to care for others. If you know of a danger that threatens someone, do not stay silent; act with courage and wisdom, and trust that God can use your obedience.
exp.22:16:
Paul calls one of the centurions, a Roman officer in charge of about a hundred soldiers, and asks him to take this young man to the chief captain, the commander of the fortress. He explains that the young man has a certain thing to tell him, that is, an important piece of news to pass on.

Paul is a prisoner in Jerusalem. More than forty men had sworn to kill him with the help of the council. His nephew, the son of his sister, learned of the plot and told him. Paul does not stay silent or act alone: he uses the legal means available to him to protect his life.

Trusting God does not mean doing nothing. We can pray and, at the same time, act wisely, seeking responsible help and listening to those who warn us of danger.
exp.22:17:
He says that the centurion, whom Paul had called, took the young man and brought him before the tribune. He explained that Paul, who was a prisoner, asked him to bring this young man, because he had something important to tell him.

The speaker is the centurion, a Roman officer who carries out Paul's request. Paul is being held in the fortress in Jerusalem. His nephew learned of a plot by some Jews to harm him, and Paul, instead of keeping silent, sought the lawful way for the warning to reach the proper authority.

For today: when we face danger, trusting God does not keep us from acting wisely. Paul prayed and trusted, but he also used the means he had at his disposal. We can ask the right people for help without ceasing to rest in God's care.
exp.22:18:
Here the tribune, who is the Roman commander in Jerusalem, takes the young man by the hand and leads him to one side, in private. There he asks him calmly what he wants to tell him. The act of taking him by the hand shows kind treatment, meant to give him confidence.

The one speaking is Claudius Lysias, the tribune. Paul was under guard, and this young man, whom the Bible presents as Paul's nephew, had learned of a plot to kill him. Lysias withdraws with him apart so that no one can hear and the secret is not ruined. In this way the young man can speak without fear.

For today: when someone comes with a serious concern, it is worth listening to them calmly and in private, without rushing or judging. Patient listening can help save a life or prevent great harm.
exp.22:19:
Here the nephew of Paul speaks to the tribune, the Roman military commander. He tells him that the Jews have agreed together to ask him to bring Paul down to the council, the Sanhedrin, tomorrow. They will say they want to examine him more closely, to look into the matter with more detail.

The young man speaks because he has discovered a secret plan. As the verses that follow explain, the real purpose was to kill Paul along the way. The request sounded lawful, but it hid an ambush. The tribune listens carefully and acts to protect Paul.

For today: not everything that sounds right is sincere. Ask God for discernment and wisdom. Also, when you learn of a real danger, speak to the right person, as this young man did. God can use a brave action, even one that seems small, to care for someone.
exp.22:21:
Here the Roman commander Claudius Lysias lets the young man go, who was Paul's nephew. The commander tells him to keep quiet: no one must know that he told him about the plot against Paul.

The young man had just revealed that more than forty men were planning to kill Paul in an ambush. The commander was the Roman military leader in Jerusalem, and he had Paul in custody. He asks for silence so that the conspirators would not find out, and to protect both the young man and the transfer of Paul that he was arranging right away.

For today: God often looks after his people through sensible people and wise decisions. We can pray with confidence, but also act with prudence, and know when it is wise to keep silent in order to protect others.
exp.22:22:
In this verse, the commander called two centurions and ordered them to get two hundred soldiers, seventy horsemen, and two hundred spearmen ready. They were to be prepared at the third hour of the night, that is, around nine o'clock, and set out for Caesarea.

The one speaking is Claudius Lysias, the Roman commander in Jerusalem. He had just learned from Paul's nephew that more than forty men had sworn to kill Paul. For this reason he decided to take him out of the city in secret and under strong protection. Some scholars see in this the care of God, who uses a pagan authority to guard his servant. The number of soldiers shows how serious the danger appeared.

For today: God often takes care of us through ordinary means, such as a person, a warning, or an authority. Trust in him, and also act with wisdom and gratitude toward the help he gives you.
exp.22:26:
Claudius Lysias tells us that the Jews had seized Paul and were about to kill him. He says that he came with the soldiers and rescued him, because he learned that Paul was a Roman citizen.

He is speaking as a Roman commander in Jerusalem. He writes to Felix, the governor, to explain why he is sending Paul to him as a prisoner. According to Acts 21 and 22, Lysias rescued Paul before he knew that Paul was a Roman, and he learned it only afterward. Many understand that in the letter he shaped the account somewhat to look good before his superior.

Today it reminds us that people often tell things in their own favor. Let us ask God for honesty to tell the whole truth, even when it does not make us look better.
exp.22:28:
This verse says that, when he looked into the case, the Roman commander found that Paul was being accused over matters of Jewish law, that is, religious disputes particular to them. In his view, Paul had not committed any offense deserving death or imprisonment.

The one who speaks is Claudius Lysias, the Roman commander in Jerusalem. He writes a letter to the governor Felix to explain why he is sending Paul to him. Lysias had rescued Paul from a mob and brought him before the Jewish council to understand the problem. His account is favorable to Paul, and some think it highlights his good conduct.

For today: not every conflict is a moral failing. Sometimes we are accused because we defend our faith, and we can keep a clear conscience and trust God, even when others misunderstand us.
exp.22:31:
This verse says that the next day, the foot soldiers who had taken Paul from Jerusalem returned to their barracks, and the horsemen continued with him toward Caesarea. The castle was the Roman garrison in Jerusalem, next to the temple. The mounted soldiers completed the escort.

The one who narrates is Luke, the author of Acts. A Roman commander, Claudius Lysias, had sent Paul at night with a large escort, because more than forty Jews were plotting to kill him. Upon reaching Antipatris, the greater danger had already passed, so part of the troop could return. Luke does not explain this detail in his own words, so it is a reasonable inference.

For today: God often cares for us through very ordinary means, such as people, prudent decisions, and authorities. We can ask for his protection and also give thanks for the concrete help he places in our path, without despising it for being simple.
exp.23:6:
This verse tells how the army officer Lysias, a Roman military officer, intervened and took Paul out of the hands of his accusers with great force. The verse of the word "chief captain" in the verse above would be a commander of the Roman army, but since the verse reads "chief captain," the wording here is simply translated as: "Lysias, the chief captain, was a commander of the Roman army."

Tertullus, the lawyer for the Jewish leaders, speaks before the governor Felix. He accuses Paul and presents what happened in a way that favors his side. According to the account in Acts 21 and 22, Lysias rescued Paul from a crowd that was beating him in the temple. Here it is told as though Lysias had acted wrongly. Some ancient manuscripts include these words and others do not, and scholars debate this.

For today: when someone tells the facts to suit their own interest, let us not answer in kind. Let us try to speak the truth and trust that God knows the whole story.
exp.23:9:
Paul receives a signal from the governor Felix to speak. Then he answers that he knows Felix has been a judge over this nation for many years, and for that reason he feels encouraged to defend himself.

Paul is held prisoner in Caesarea. The high priest Ananias and a lawyer named Tertullus accused him before Felix of causing disturbances. Now it is Paul's turn to respond. He begins with respect, without flattery, by mentioning the governor's experience. Historians do not fully agree on the exact length of Felix's time in office, so "many years" is understood in a general sense.

We can defend our faith and our conduct with respect, clarity, and a good spirit, without returning attack for attack. When we are unjustly accused, speaking with calm and with facts reflects the peace that God gives.
exp.23:10:
Paul tells the governor Felix that he himself can check something simple: it has been less than twelve days since he went up to Jerusalem to worship God. The word "went up" is used because Jerusalem sits on high ground, and "worship" shows the reason for his trip.

Paul is on trial before Felix in Caesarea. The lawyer Tertullus, together with Jewish leaders, accuses him of causing disturbances. Paul answers with respect and begins with verifiable facts: the dates and his purpose. He wants to show that he had neither the time nor the intention to stir up a riot. The exact details of the days have been explained in several ways, but the central idea is clear.

For today: when you are accused unjustly, answer with calm, truth, and clear facts. An honest life and a clear conscience can speak more powerfully than the loudest defense.
exp.23:12:
Paul says that his accusers cannot prove with evidence the things they now charge against him. This is not a mere denial: he is telling them that if they accuse him, they must produce real evidence. The verse's wording sounds like the language of a courtroom.

Paul speaks before the governor Felix, in Caesarea. Some Jewish leaders, with a lawyer named Tertullus, were accusing him of causing disturbances and of desecrating the temple. Paul answers calmly, recalling the facts: he arrived only a few days earlier, and no one saw him provoking fights or stirring up the crowds.

For today: when someone accuses us unjustly, we can respond with composure and with the truth, without shouting or seeking revenge. An honest and consistent life is the best support we have, and we can rest in the knowledge that God knows the truth even when others do not recognize it.
exp.23:13:
Paul says that he does admit something: he serves the God of his ancestors by following what his accusers call "the Way," which they label a sect, a group set apart. Paul explains that he believes everything that is written in the law and in the prophets, and that he worships the God of his fathers in keeping with that Way.

Paul speaks before the governor Felix in Caesarea. The high priest and a lawyer named Tertullus were accusing him of stirring up trouble. Paul replies that he did not argue with anyone or incite a crowd, and that his faith does not break away from Israel. "The Way" was an early name for the followers of Jesus.

For today: let us not be afraid that others will judge us or put labels on us. What matters is to live with sincerity a faith that is grounded in the Word of God. We can explain calmly and respectfully what we believe, without fighting or letting anger carry us away.
exp.23:15:
That is why Paul says he works hard at always keeping a clear conscience, because of his hope in the resurrection. A conscience with no guilt is one that does not accuse him of anything wrong. He wants to live this way before God and also before people.

Paul speaks before the governor Felix, in Caesarea. Some Jews were accusing him of stirring up trouble and teaching something false. He defends himself by saying that he follows the God of Israel, believes what is written in the Scriptures, and lives with sincerity. His hope in a future resurrection guides how he behaves every day.

For today: believing in God should show in how we treat others. This week you can check whether you need to ask forgiveness, give something back, or correct a lie. In this way you seek to keep your conscience clear before God and before people.
exp.23:16:
Paul says that, after many years away, he returned to Jerusalem to bring help to his people and to present offerings. The word for help here refers to money given to those in need, and the word for people refers to the Jewish nation. The offerings were the sacrifices or gifts brought to the temple.

Paul speaks before the governor Felix, defending himself against the accusations of the Jews. He wants to show that he did not come to cause trouble, but to do good and to fulfill his faith. Many understand that this help relates to the collection he gathered among the churches, although this passage gives no further details.

For today: our conduct speaks for us. When we live with generosity and a clear conscience, we have an honest defense against criticism. Ask yourself: whom can I help today with my time or my resources?
exp.23:18:
Paul says that the Jews from Asia, who were the first to bring charges against him, should have come before the governor Felix themselves to make their accusation in person, if they really had anything against him. To appear before an authority and to formally bring a charge are what the text means here, so the verse of those terms is given through the verse itself.

Paul speaks in his own defense before Felix, in Caesarea. Some Jews from Jerusalem were accusing him of causing disturbances. Paul explains that he was in the temple, already purified, bringing offerings, with no crowd stirred up. The ones who started the uproar were Jews from Asia, but they were not even there to support their charge. Paul asks for a fair trial, with witnesses present.

Today we can learn to act with integrity and to seek the truth calmly. If someone accuses us, let us answer with respect and clarity, without seeking revenge. And let us not speak badly of others without having proof or being willing to stand up and show ourselves.
exp.23:19:
Paul tells the governor Felix that if his accusers believe he did something wrong, they should say so themselves. He is referring to the time he stood before the council, that is, the Sanhedrin, the religious court of the Jews in Jerusalem.

Paul is speaking in his own defense before Felix, in Caesarea. Some Jewish leaders accuse him of stirring up trouble. He answers that they did not find him arguing or causing a disturbance, and that the witnesses who accused him in Asia were not even there. Now he calls on those present to be witnesses: if there is a real fault, let them point it out.

For today: live in such a way that our conduct speaks for us. A clear conscience and an honest life allow us to answer with calm and truth when someone accuses us unjustly.
exp.23:24:
Paul speaks before Felix, the Roman governor, on three subjects: righteousness (living in an upright way), self-control (mastering one's desires), and the judgment to come (that God will judge everyone). Felix becomes frightened and cuts the conversation short: "Go your way for now; when I have a convenient time, I will call for you."

Paul is a prisoner in Caesarea, accused by Jewish leaders. Felix and his wife Drusilla hear him speak about faith in Jesus Christ. Many understand that Paul spoke on these subjects because Felix's life was not upright, but the text does not give details. Afterward, Felix calls for him several times, though he was also hoping to receive money. In the end, he leaves him in prison for two years.

When the Word of God makes us uncomfortable, it is tempting to say "for now." It is better to respond today with humility, asking God to correct us and change us. Putting off a decision is also a decision.
exp.23:25:
He hoped that Paul would give him money so that he would let him go. For that reason he sent for him often and talked with him. The verse is that the money was simply money, and the freeing was simply letting him go free.

The narrator, Luke, tells what happened in Caesarea, where Paul was held prisoner without a clear charge. Felix had heard Paul speak about righteousness, self-control, and the judgment to come, and he became afraid. Even so, he did not decide to believe. The conversations continued, but with a selfish purpose: the bribe. This kept Paul imprisoned for two more years.

We can hear the Word of God and even feel fear, but if the heart is still tied to money or to convenience, we do not change. Today is a good time to ask ourselves: do I obey what God shows me, or do I put it off for my own interests?
exp.24:5:
This verse tells that Festus, the new Roman governor, stayed in Jerusalem for about eight or ten days. Then he went back down to Caesarea, and the next day he sat on the judgment seat, the place where cases were heard, and ordered that Paul be brought in.

Luke, the author of Acts, recounts what happened after Festus took up his office. Paul had been held as a prisoner in Caesarea for two years. The Jewish leaders wanted to bring charges against him, and Festus decided to hear the case in a formal trial rather than let it slide.

For today: Festus heard the case in an orderly and open way, giving Paul the chance to answer. We can imitate that attitude: before judging someone, let us listen with patience and seek the truth. And if we find ourselves waiting in an unjust situation, let us remember that God is still at work.
exp.24:6:
When Paul arrived at the court in Caesarea, the Jews who had come down from Jerusalem surrounded him. They brought many serious accusations against him, but they had no proof.

Luke, the author of Acts, reports that Festus, the new Roman governor, had already arrived in Caesarea. The Jewish leaders wanted Paul to be tried in Jerusalem. Paul had been in custody for about two years, and now he again faced accusations with no basis. Paul responds right away by defending his innocence.

Today, we are sometimes unjustly accused or spoken about falsely without evidence. Paul shows us that we can respond with calm, with the truth, and with a clear conscience. And when we cannot control what others say, we can trust that God knows the truth and sustains us.
exp.24:8:
Festus, the Roman governor, wanted to keep on good terms with the Jews. So he asks Paul whether he would be willing to go up to Jerusalem to be judged there, with Festus present.

Paul had been held in prison in Caesarea for more than two years. The Jewish leaders accused him of serious things, but they could not prove anything. Festus was new in his position and wanted to maintain peace with the Jewish leaders. Some think Paul did not trust that such a trial would be fair, since there had earlier been plans to kill him on the road. That is why, in what follows, he appeals to Caesar.

For today: when we want to please everyone, we may end up giving way on what is right. Let us ask God for courage and wisdom to do what is right, even when it does not make us look good to everyone.
exp.24:9:
Paul answers Festus that he is already standing before the judgment seat of the Roman emperor, which is the proper place for him to be judged. He states that he has done no wrong to the Jews, and that Festus knows this well. The word "wrong" here means an unjust harm or injury done to someone.

Paul is held prisoner in Caesarea. The Jews accuse him without proof, and Festus, wanting to win their favor, proposes to send him to Jerusalem. Paul knows that there he is in danger, so he defends his innocence and claims his right as a Roman citizen. Soon he will appeal to Caesar.

For today: defending the truth calmly and clearly is valid. Paul does not turn violent or hide himself; he uses the just means he has within reach. We can trust God while acting with wisdom and honesty in the face of injustice.
exp.24:13:
Verse 14 tells us that King Agrippa and Bernice stayed in Caesarea for several days, visiting Festus, the Roman governor. During that visit, Festus explained Paul's case to Agrippa. He told him that there was a man whom Felix, the previous governor, had left in prison. Being "left in prison" means that Paul remained in jail without his case being resolved.

Here the narrator, Luke, speaks, and then Festus. Paul had already appealed to Caesar, and Festus was not sure what to write about him. Agrippa knew Jewish customs, so Festus seeks his help in understanding the accusation.

For today: when a situation has gone unresolved for a long time, remember that God can use it for something greater. Paul was in prison, yet his words reached rulers. Stay faithful where you are.
exp.24:14:
Here Festus tells King Agrippa what happened when he arrived in Jerusalem. The chief priests and the leaders of the Jewish people came to him and asked that Paul be condemned.

The one speaking is Festus, the Roman governor. Paul had been in custody for some time, since the days of Felix, and Agrippa and Bernice were visiting Caesarea. Festus sums up the case in his own way, and the account shows that the pressure against Paul came from influential religious leaders. Festus then says he answered with the principle of Roman law: no one is condemned without first facing his accusers.

For today: let us not judge anyone only by what their accusers say. Before forming an opinion or condemning, let us listen calmly to the person and seek the truth with justice.
exp.24:18:
What the verse says: Festus tells that Paul's accusers had only disputes with him about their own religion, which here means their faith, and about a certain Jesus who had died. Paul, on the other hand, insisted that this Jesus was alive.

Context: Festus, the Roman governor, is speaking before King Agrippa. He explains Paul's case, which he inherited from the previous governor. Festus expected serious charges, but he found only religious debates among the Jews. For that reason he did not know how to judge him. Some think that his choice of words shows a Roman outlook, one that did not understand Paul's faith.

For today: For Paul, the resurrection of Jesus was the center of everything. Even those who did not understand it could see that this was the main point. Ask yourself whether the people who know you know that Jesus is alive, and whether that shapes the way you live.
exp.24:19:
Festus explains that he did not know how to investigate such a complicated, religious matter. For that reason he asked Paul whether he would be willing to go to Jerusalem to be judged there.

Festus was at a loss, unsure what to do. The questions concerned religious matters about Jesus, who had risen from the dead.

Festus, the Roman governor, is speaking before King Agrippa. He explains how he handled the case of Paul, who was in prison. Festus did not understand the Jewish disputes, and what especially caught his attention was that they spoke of a dead Jesus whom Paul said was alive. Some believe his proposal also aimed to please the Jews, though the text does not say so here.

Today, when some part of the faith is beyond you or you do not understand it, do not ignore it or brush it aside. Ask sincerely, seek answers, and keep listening to Jesus.
exp.24:21:
Agrippa tells Festus that he would like to hear Paul for himself. Festus replies that Agrippa will hear him the next day. Here the wording is simple: Agrippa asks to hear the man, and Festus agrees to arrange it for the following day.

Festus was the Roman governor, and he had just explained to his visitor, King Agrippa, the case of Paul. Paul was in custody and had appealed to Caesar, so Festus needed to have something clear to write about him. Agrippa knew Jewish customs well, which is why his interest makes sense. Jesus had already said that Paul would carry his name before kings (Acts 9:15), and here we can see that promise moving forward.

God can open unexpected doors so that his message reaches those who hold authority. Even in difficult situations, such as injustice or a long wait, we can stay alert and be ready to bear witness with respect and sincerity when someone is willing to listen.
exp.24:22:
This verse describes the grand scene of the following day. Agrippa and Bernice arrive with great pomp and display, that is, with splendor and luxury. They enter the hall of hearing together with the military tribunes (senior officers) and the leading men of the city. Then, at Festus's command, they bring in Paul.

The author, Luke, recounts how Paul, held prisoner in Caesarea, had already appealed to Caesar. Festus, the Roman governor, takes advantage of King Agrippa's visit to have him heard, so that he will have something clear to write. Luke contrasts the splendor of the powerful with Paul, a prisoner. Jesus had announced that his followers would appear before kings (Acts 9:15).

For today: do not let yourself be impressed by power or by appearances. God can use your faithfulness, even when you feel small, to bear witness before very influential people.
exp.24:26:
He says it seems unreasonable to Festus, that is, without sense, to send a prisoner to the emperor without stating the charges against him. A "prisoner" is someone held in custody, and the "charges" are the accusations or grounds against him. For Festus, sending someone off without a clear explanation would be a mistake.

Festus, the Roman governor, is speaking before King Agrippa and other guests. Paul had appealed to Caesar, so he had to go to Rome. But Festus found no crime deserving death and did not know what to write in the report. So he presents the case to Agrippa, hoping that by examining it, Agrippa will help him put something clear in writing.

For today: before judging or deciding about someone, let us seek to understand the facts well. Listening, asking questions, and being fair prevents unjust accusations. It also reminds us that God can use even imperfect human processes to carry out his plans.
exp.25:1:
Paul begins his defense with courtesy. He tells King Agrippa that he considers himself fortunate and happy to be able to answer today before him for all the accusations the Jews have made against him. He means that he is glad to present his case with reasons.

Paul is in prison in Caesarea. The governors Felix and Festus had already judged him, but now he speaks before King Agrippa II, who knew Jewish customs well. Festus had asked for help because he did not know what charges to write to the emperor. Paul sees this hearing as an opportunity, not only as a problem.

For today: even in unjust or difficult situations, we can respond with respect, calm, and gratitude. If someone listens to us, that may be a door for speaking honestly about what we believe.
exp.25:2:
Paul tells King Agrippa that he knows very well the customs and religious debates of the Jews. For that reason, he asks the king to listen to him patiently.

Paul is in prison and speaks before Agrippa II, the governor Festus, and other officials in Caesarea. The Jews accuse him of preaching about Jesus. Agrippa had been raised as a Jew and knew these matters well, so Paul saw an opportunity to explain his faith clearly. His request for patience suggests that he wants to speak calmly and without rushing.

For today: when you have to explain your faith or defend your position, do it with respect. Acknowledge what the other person knows, speak with humility, and ask to be heard calmly, without arguing.
exp.25:11:
Paul says that he was busy persecuting Christians as he was on his way to Damascus. He carried authority, that is, official power, and a commission, or formal assignment, given to him by the chief priests, the leading religious officials of Jerusalem.

Paul speaks before King Agrippa, and he does so as one on trial, defending his faith. Earlier he describes how violently he treated the believers. This verse is the bridge to his account of meeting Jesus on the road. He wants to show that his change did not come from his own idea, but from a divine intervention when he was at his most opposed to Christ.

For today: sometimes we can feel very sure of ourselves and active in something, with the backing of others, and still be mistaken. Let us ask God for humility to listen to his voice and correct our course.
exp.25:13:
Paul tells how he and his companions fell to the ground because of the light from heaven. Then he heard a voice speaking to him in Hebrew, or Aramaic, the common language of the Jews of that time. The voice asked him why he was persecuting it. Then he adds a saying: "it is hard for you to kick against the goads," like an ox that kicks at the sharpened stick of the farmer and only hurts itself.

Paul speaks before King Agrippa and recounts his encounter with Jesus on the road to Damascus. Before this, he had been persecuting the believers with the authority of the priests. Jesus identifies himself with his people: to persecute them was to persecute him.

Resisting God is painful and useless. If you feel restlessness about something God is showing you, do not harden your heart. Listen to it with humility, because his call seeks your good and your purpose.
exp.25:15:
Jesus tells Paul to rise and stand on his feet. He explains that he appeared to him for a purpose: to make him a servant who serves and a witness who tells what he has seen and lived. Paul was to speak about what he had already seen of Jesus and about what Jesus would continue to show him.

Here Paul speaks before King Agrippa, recounting how his life changed on the road to Damascus. Before, he persecuted Christians. Jesus stops him, but not to condemn him: he calls him and gives him a new mission. The verses that follow say that he would send him to both Jews and Gentiles.

For today: God does not only forgive us, he also gives us a purpose. Your story with Jesus, even if it is simple, can be your testimony. Tell it honestly to someone this week.
exp.25:17:
This verse describes the mission Jesus gave to Paul: to open people's eyes so they turn from darkness to light, and from the control of Satan to God. In this way they could receive forgiveness of their sins and a place among those set apart for God, who are made holy through faith in Jesus.

Paul is speaking before King Agrippa and tells how he met Jesus on the road to Damascus. The words of the verse are the ones Jesus spoke to him in that vision. Paul explains why he now proclaims the message to both Jews and non-Jews, and why he could not disobey that calling.

For today: no one changes their life only through pressure or arguments; God is the one who opens our eyes. We can speak about Jesus with kindness and simplicity, and pray that God will bring light to those we care about.
exp.25:19:
Paul tells how, since Jesus called him, he preached to everyone: first in Damascus and Jerusalem, then throughout all Judea, and also among the non-Jews. His message was that people should repent, that is, change their direction, and turn to God. He also said that their lives should show that change through works that fit such a turn of heart.

Paul speaks before King Agrippa while he is a prisoner. He explains that he obeyed the vision of the risen Jesus. Because he preached this, his Jewish opponents tried to kill him in the temple.

For today: repenting is not only feeling sorry. Ask yourself what concrete change God is asking of you, such as asking forgiveness, giving up a bad habit, or correcting an injustice, and take a real step in that direction today.
exp.25:20:
This verse says that the Jews seized Paul in the temple and tried to kill him, and that this happened because he had preached that everyone, Jews and non-Jews alike, should repent and turn to God. The verb "tried" here means that they attempted to kill him. The word "seized" refers to taking hold of him.

Paul speaks before King Agrippa and the governor Festus while he is a prisoner in Caesarea. He recounts how Jesus appeared to him and how, from that time on, he obeyed. What happened in the temple in Jerusalem (Acts 21) was the origin of his arrest. Paul defends himself, but above all he wants Agrippa to come to know Christ.

For today: obeying God can bring opposition, even from religious people. When that happens, do not lose heart. Like Paul, continue with humility, trusting in God's help, and seek for your words and your testimony to point to Jesus.
exp.25:21:
Paul says that God has helped and sustained him, and so he has remained faithful to this day. He speaks of Jesus to everyone, to the humble and to the important, and he makes clear that he teaches nothing new: only what Moses and the prophets had already said would come.

Paul is in prison and is defending himself before King Agrippa and the governor Festus. He recounts that the Jews tried to kill him in the temple for preaching that people should turn back to God. He insists that his message agrees with the Scriptures. Shortly afterward, Festus declares him out of his mind.

For today: when you feel tired of following Christ or of speaking about your faith, remember that persevering does not depend only on your own strength. Ask God for help every day, and share your faith with humility and respect, without distinguishing whom you share it with.
exp.25:22:
He says that, as the prophets and Moses had foretold, the Messiah had to suffer and die. He also says that he would be the first to rise from the dead, and that in this way he would bring God's light both to the Jewish people and to those who were not Jews. "Suffer" means to endure pain and hardship, and "Gentiles" are the nations that were not Jewish.

Paul speaks while a prisoner before King Agrippa and the governor Festus. The Jews had attacked him in the temple, and he explains that his message is not new but agrees with the Scriptures. That is why Festus, when he hears him speak of resurrection, reacts by saying he is out of his mind.

For today: do not be discouraged if the message of Jesus seems strange to others. Christ suffered and rose again, and that hope is light for everyone. Share it with respect, clarity, and gentleness, even when not everyone understands it.
exp.25:25:
Paul says that King Agrippa knows these things well, and that is why he speaks to him without fear. He is sure that Agrippa is not unaware of any of this, because it did not happen in a hidden corner, that is, in secret or in some concealed place, but in full view of everyone.

Paul is in custody and is making his defense before the governor Festus and King Agrippa. Festus has just told him he is out of his mind. Paul answers that he speaks words of truth and soberness. He addresses Agrippa because this king knew the Jewish customs and the events connected with Jesus, which were public in that region.

Our faith is not based on hidden ideas or private mysteries. We can speak about the gospel with respect and confidence, and also with honesty, inviting others to think, ask questions, and examine sincerely what we believe.
exp.25:28:
Paul says that he would ask God, whether in a short time or a long time, that not only King Agrippa but all who were listening to him that day would become like him, that is, believers in Jesus. He makes only one exception: the chains he is wearing.

Paul is a prisoner, and he defends himself before King Agrippa, the governor Festus, and other guests. Agrippa had just said that Paul was almost persuading him to become a Christian. Some understand that statement as sincere and others as irony; the text does not make it clear. Paul answers with kindness and without resentment. Afterward, those present conclude that he does not deserve death or prison.

Paul, even in chains, was not thinking about his freedom but about others coming to know Christ. We can ask God to give us a kind and courageous heart to share our faith, without anger or pride, even in difficult situations.
exp.25:29:
When Paul had finished speaking, King Agrippa rose to his feet, and so did the governor, Bernice, and those who had been sitting with them. This was the signal that the hearing was over.

Paul was a prisoner, defending his faith before King Agrippa and the governor Festus. He had just told how Jesus called him and had invited everyone to believe. Agrippa answered with a remark that can be understood in several ways: as mockery, as sincerity, or as evasion. The text does not make it clear. Afterward, as they withdrew, they agreed that Paul did not deserve prison or death.

For today: when we share our faith, we do not control the response. We can speak with clarity and love, and leave it to God to do his work in each person's heart.
exp.26:2:
This verse says that the next day the ship arrived at Sidon. There Julius, the Roman centurion in charge of Paul, treated him with kindness, that is, with courtesy and consideration. He allowed him to go and see his friends so that they would look after him, in other words, care for him and give him what he needed.

The one speaking is Luke, the author of Acts, who travels with Paul and tells the story in the first person (we). Paul is a prisoner and is heading to Rome to be judged before Caesar. The friends were probably believers from Sidon. The text does not say why Julius was so kind; some think he respected Paul, but that is only a possibility.

For today: God can use the kindness of others and the support of friends in difficult times. Accept help with humility, and be someone who treats those who suffer with kindness.
exp.26:3:
This verse says that the ship left from Sidon and sailed under the lee of Cyprus, that is, it passed along the sheltered side of the island, the side protected from the wind. They did this because the winds were blowing against them. Setting sail means departing.

The one speaking is Luke, who writes in the first person ("we sailed") because he travels with Paul. Paul is going to Rome as a prisoner, under the guard of the centurion Julius. In this part of the journey the sea was already becoming difficult, and that more sheltered route helped them move forward with less risk. Luke simply tells how the voyage went.

For today: sometimes life carries us along with contrary winds that we cannot change. Even so, we can look for the wisest path, keep moving forward with patience, and trust that God is with us, as He was with Paul on that journey.
exp.26:4:
This verse says that the ship continued its course across the sea that borders the coasts of Cilicia and Pamphylia, regions in the south of modern Turkey, and arrived at Myra, a city of Lycia.

Luke, the author of Acts, is the one speaking, and he travels with Paul. Paul is a prisoner heading to Rome to be judged before Caesar. The winds were against them, so the journey was slow and followed protected routes close to the coast. Myra was an important port where they would later change ships. Luke records each stage of the journey with care.

God does not always remove contrary winds, but he does accompany his people at every stretch of the road. When your progress is slow or difficult, do not think that God has forgotten you. Remain faithful and serve those around you, as Paul did throughout this journey.
exp.26:6:
This verse tells that the ship moved slowly for many days. They barely managed to reach the area opposite Cnidus, a city on the coast of Asia Minor, because the wind would not let them keep a straight course. So they changed their route and sailed in the shelter of the island of Crete, near Cape Salmone.

The one telling the story is Luke, who travels with Paul, a prisoner, on the way to Rome. The centurion had transferred them to a ship from Alexandria. The contrary wind makes the voyage difficult and prepares what comes afterward: a dangerous sailing and Paul's warning. The details of the route show that the account is that of an eyewitness present on the journey.

Today, when things move slowly and everything seems to be against us, let us remember that delays do not mean God has left us. Keep going with patience, adjust your course with wisdom, and trust that God works even on difficult roads.
exp.26:8:
It says that a good deal of time had already passed in the voyage, and that sailing had become dangerous because the fast was already over. That fast is the Jewish Day of Atonement, which falls in late September or October, when the season of storms in the Mediterranean was beginning. That is why Paul was giving warnings, that is, he was speaking up seriously about what could happen.

The one telling the story is Luke, who travels with Paul. Paul is a prisoner on his way to Rome, and the ship is held up at Fair Havens, on the island of Crete. Paul warns of the danger before the crew decides to continue. Commentators debate whether his warning was only the experience of a traveler or also guidance from God; the text does not make that clear here.

Today we can learn to listen to wise advice, even when it comes from someone with no official position or authority. Before deciding, it is good to stop and think carefully about the risks.
exp.26:11:
As the harbor where they were (Fair Havens) was not suitable for spending the winter, the majority decided to keep sailing. They wanted to reach Phoenix, another harbor in Crete, and stay there until the stormy season had passed. The description of how that harbor faced is understood in several ways, and it is not known with certainty which one is correct.

Luke recounts Paul's journey as a prisoner toward Rome. Paul had already warned that the voyage would bring great losses, but the centurion put more trust in the pilot and in the owner of the ship. The decision was made for convenience and by majority.

For today: before deciding, do not be guided only by what is most comfortable or by what the majority thinks. Ask God for wisdom and listen humbly to prudent counsel.
exp.26:15:
This verse says that the ship passed by the side of a small island called Clauda that was sheltered from the wind. The lee side is the part of the island where the wind blows less. There, with much effort, they managed to bring aboard the lifeboat, the small boat that the ship was towing behind it.

The writer is Luke, who travels with Paul as a prisoner on the way to Rome. He speaks of "we" because he himself was on the ship. A violent storm, called Euroclydon, had caught them. Luke describes in detail how hard it was to secure the boat, since without it they might lose a possible way of escape. The name of the wind and some nautical details are understood in different ways, but the scene is clear: real danger.

For today: in storms, the Bible does not ask us to pretend that everything is fine. Calmly do what is within your reach, like those sailors, and at the same time trust that God is still caring for you, even when the road is hard.
exp.26:16:
When they had hoisted the small boat aboard, the sailors used helps, that is, ropes passed under the hull and around the ship so that it would not break apart under the force of the waves. They feared running onto the Syrtis, dangerous sandbanks near the coast of North Africa. For that reason they lowered the sail, or the sail gear (some think it refers to a different rigging), and let the wind carry them.

The one who tells the story is Luke, who was traveling with Paul, a prisoner bound for Rome. He recounts in detail what they did to survive in the middle of a violent storm.

For today: when a storm comes, do what sensibly lies within your reach, without sitting idle. But do not place all your hope in your own efforts, because later in this same chapter God sustains Paul with his promise.
exp.26:17:
This verse says the storm was so violent that it battered and shook everyone on the ship. That is why, the next day, they began throwing parts of the cargo into the sea, making the ship lighter so it could better withstand the waves.

The one telling this is Luke, who was traveling with Paul as a prisoner bound for Rome. He writes "we" because he was on the ship. After days of violent wind, the crew had already tried to secure the vessel and feared running aground on sandbanks. Now they were taking desperate measures to save their lives.

For today: in the storms of life, sometimes we have to let go of burdens that weigh us down, even when it costs us. And while we do it, we can trust that God is still caring for us, as he did for Paul on this voyage.
exp.26:18:
This verse tells that on the third day of the storm, those aboard the ship, including the narrator, threw overboard with their own hands the ship's tackling. That word refers to the equipment and gear of the ship, such as ropes, sails, or heavy fittings. Some scholars think of the great mast or its rigging, but the text does not specify.

The speaker is Luke, the author of Acts, who was traveling with Paul, who was being taken as a prisoner toward Rome. Luke describes how a violent tempest had them close to being wrecked. They had already lightened the cargo the day before. Now, in desperation, they were casting away even what was needed to sail.

For today: in crises we sometimes must let go of valuable things to save what matters most. Ask God for wisdom to know what to let go, and trust that He continues to care for you even when you lose something.
exp.26:26:
When the fourteenth night came, they were still being tossed about in the sea of Adria. Around midnight, the sailors sensed that they were getting close to land. The word "sensed" means they noticed it or felt it, without being certain. They probably heard the sound of the waves breaking against the shore.

The one telling the story is Luke, who was traveling with Paul. Paul was a prisoner on his way to Rome. Earlier, an angel had assured him that no one would die, even though the ship would be lost at an island. Now, just as God had said, signs begin to appear that the land is near.

When everything seems dark and long, God keeps fulfilling what he promised, even when we cannot yet see it. Trust his word and act with wisdom while you wait for the dawn.
exp.26:27:
They lowered a weighted line called a sounding line to measure how deep the sea was. First they found twenty fathoms, and a little later fifteen. A fathom is an old unit of depth, a little under two meters. In other words, the bottom was getting shallower and the land was getting closer.

This is part of the account of Paul's voyage to Rome as a prisoner. The narrator is Luke, who was on the ship. They had spent fourteen nights in a violent storm, and the sailors suspected that land was near. They took soundings to confirm it. This matches what God had announced through Paul: they would run aground on an island.

For today: God can promise us something and still want us to do our part wisely. The sailors measured, stayed alert, and acted with care. Trusting God does not cancel responsible effort; it gives us peace while we make it.
exp.26:29:
Acts 27:30 tells us that some sailors tried to escape from the ship in the middle of the storm. They lowered the boat, which was a small rescue boat, and pretended they were going to drop anchors from the front of the ship, that is, the forward part of the vessel. In reality, they wanted to save themselves and leave the others behind.

Luke, the author of Acts, narrates Paul's voyage as a prisoner on the way to Rome. They had been in the storm for days and were close to land, but it was night and they were afraid of crashing against the rocks. The sailors knew how to handle the ship, so their escape put everyone in danger. Paul noticed this and warned the centurion.

For today: when others depend on us, integrity is tested in difficulty. Let us ask God for courage not to abandon our responsibilities, and to speak the truth clearly, as Paul did, when someone is at risk.
exp.26:30:
Paul warns the centurion and the soldiers that, if the sailors leave the ship, they will not be able to be saved.

Paul is traveling as a prisoner toward Rome in the middle of a violent storm. Earlier, an angel had assured him that no one would die (vv. 22-24). The sailors pretend to lower anchors, but in reality they want to escape in the small boat. Paul realizes this and gives the warning. The soldiers cut the ropes of the boat, and so the group stays together, with those who knew how to handle the ship.

God makes promises, but he often expects us to act wisely and to use the means he gives us. Trusting God does not remove the responsibility to care for what we have, to listen to counsel, and to remain united in difficulties.
exp.26:31:
The Roman soldiers cut the ropes that held the small boat of the ship, and let it fall into the sea. The ropes are called ropes, and the phrase about letting it go means they let it drift away.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells of the storm that battered the ship carrying Paul, a prisoner, toward Rome. The sailors wanted to escape in the boat, but Paul warned the centurion that without them no one could be saved, because God had promised that everyone would live. The soldiers obeyed and removed that way of escape.

For today: trusting God's promises does not mean doing nothing. It also means acting with good judgment and staying where God has placed us, without looking for easy ways out.
exp.26:32:
It says that at dawn Paul urged everyone on the ship to eat. He reminds them that they had been waiting for fourteen days in anxiety and had barely eaten. Paul is a prisoner traveling toward Rome in the middle of a huge storm. The sailors wanted to escape in the lifeboat, but Paul warned that everyone had to stay on board in order to be saved, and the soldiers cut the ropes. Now, before a possible shipwreck, Paul encourages them to regain their strength, trusting in the promise God had given him that no one would die.

For today: when you are worn out by worry, look after your body and your spirit with calm. Trusting God does not mean neglecting yourself; you can rest, eat, and give thanks, as Paul did, while you wait for his help.
exp.26:34:
Paul tells everyone on the ship to eat. Then he takes the bread, gives thanks to God in front of everyone, breaks it, and begins to eat. "Gave thanks" means he prayed to express gratitude.

Paul is being taken as a prisoner to Rome, and the ship has been trapped in a violent storm for days. Nearly two weeks of fear and exhaustion have left the passengers discouraged and without strength. Earlier, an angel had assured Paul that no one would die. So he sets the example with calm, and the others regain their courage and eat as well.

For today: in the middle of pressure, thank God for what you have, even if it is little. Your calm trust, shown simply, can encourage others who are tired or afraid.
exp.26:38:
At daybreak the sailors did not recognize the coastline. But they saw a bay with a beach, and decided to try to run the ship in there. A bay or inlet is what is meant here; the beach is the shore; and running the ship aground means making it strike the land on the shore.

Luke, the author of Acts, recounts Paul's journey as a prisoner toward Rome. They had been days in a terrible storm, and God had already promised Paul that no one would die (Acts 27:22-24). The sailors had already lightened the ship by throwing out the grain, and now they were looking for a place where they could be saved.

For today: when we cannot see the way clearly, we can take the next sensible step with what we can see, trusting God's promises. He can keep his word even in the midst of disorder, and sometimes the path to safety includes losses and difficult places.
exp.26:39:
The sailors cut the anchors and let them fall into the sea. They also loosened the lashings that held the steering oars (the "rudders" were large oars used to steer the ship). Then they raised the mainsail (or, according to others, a small sail at the bow; this is not entirely certain) and headed toward the beach.

Here the narrator, Luke, who was traveling with Paul, speaks. After fourteen days of storm, morning comes and they see a bay with a beach. The crew decides to let go of everything that slows them down and try to run the ship aground there, because there was no other way out. Shortly afterward the ship runs aground, just as God had announced through Paul.

For today: sometimes God leads us to let go of what holds us back, even when it costs us, so that we can move toward the salvation He promises. Ask yourself what "anchor" you need to cut today, and trust that God guides even in the middle of the storm.
exp.26:40:
This verse tells that the ship struck a place where two currents of water met, and was stuck fast. The word "stuck fast" describes being caught and held firm on the bottom. The forepart, the front of the ship, drove into the seabed and would not move. The hinder part, the back of the ship, was broken apart by the force of the waves.

Luke, the author of Acts, recounts Paul's journey as a prisoner toward Rome. After a storm lasting two weeks, the sailors try to reach a shore. Earlier, God had told Paul that no one would die, although the ship would be lost. Here the loss of the ship comes to pass, and then the centurion protects Paul and everyone else.

For today: sometimes God cares for us in the middle of real losses. A promise from God does not always remove the blow, but it holds us up through it. Trust Him when things break.
exp.26:41:
The soldiers planned to kill the prisoners on the ship, because they were afraid that some of them would swim away and escape to the shore. Their plan was a decision made in the moment, and the prisoners were the captives, Paul among them.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells of the shipwreck he sailed through with Paul. The ship ran aground and began to break apart. The soldiers were held responsible for the prisoners, and under Roman law they could pay with their own lives if any escaped. Even so, the centurion wanted to save Paul and stopped the plan.

For today: God can use unexpected people to protect us in the middle of the storm. When everything seems lost, we can trust that he cares for our lives and keeps his promises, and we can also act with compassion toward others in moments of pressure.
exp.26:42:
This verse says that the centurion, who was the Roman officer in charge of the prisoners, wanted to save Paul. That is why he stopped the soldiers' plan to kill the prisoners. He ordered that those who knew how to swim should throw themselves into the water first and reach land.

Luke, the author of Acts, narrates the shipwreck near the island of Malta. The soldiers feared being punished if any prisoner escaped. The centurion, named Julius, had treated Paul well even before the voyage. God had already promised Paul that no one would die (v. 24).

For today: God can care for his people by using even people who do not believe. When you are in a storm, trust that he works in ways you may not see, and be thankful to those who help you.
exp.27:5:
This verse says that the islanders expected to see Paul swell up or suddenly fall down dead from the viper's bite. The word "but" is used here, and "changed their minds" means they changed their opinion. After waiting a long time and seeing that nothing happened to him, they began to say that Paul was a god.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells what happened after the shipwreck on the island of Malta. At first the people thought Paul was a murderer being punished by justice. Then, seeing him unharmed, they thought the opposite. Paul did not defend himself or seek fame; right away, in the verses that follow, he keeps serving and healing others.

For today: people's opinions change quickly, sometimes from contempt to admiration. Let us not live worried about what others say. Rather, let us remain faithful to God and keep serving with humility, as Paul did.
exp.27:8:
After Paul healed Publius's father, the other sick people on the island began coming to him, and they too were healed. The word "came" in the verse means that they approached him or came to seek him out. The island is Malta, according to the beginning of the chapter.

Luke, the author of the book, tells what happened after Paul's shipwreck. The travelers were welcomed by Publius, the leading man of the island. The healing of his father spread from mouth to mouth. Luke shows that God was working through Paul, even though he was a prisoner. The people responded with honor and with provisions for the journey.

For today: God can use our lives in any circumstance, even in difficult times. If we serve with kindness and prayer those who are near us, others can receive help and see the care of God.
exp.27:10:
This verse tells that Paul and his companions, after three months on the island of Malta, boarded a ship that had come from Alexandria and had spent the winter there. The figurehead was the carved figure or emblem on the front of the ship, representing Castor and Pollux, the twin brothers of Greek and Roman mythology, whom sailors would ask for protection. To have spent the winter there means the ship had stayed in that place through the cold season.

The narrator is Luke, the author of Acts, who travels with Paul. After the shipwreck, Paul was treated with kindness on the island, and God used him to heal the sick. Now, with the arrival of spring, the journey to Rome continues, just as God had promised.

For today: God carries out His plans even when there are storms and delays. Trust that He leads you step by step, and while you wait, serve others wherever you are.
exp.27:14:
This verse tells us that the believers in Rome heard that Paul was on his way. So they went out to meet him as far as places called Appii Forum and The Three Taverns, stopping points on the road to Rome. When Paul saw them, he gave thanks to God and took courage, that is, he was encouraged and regained his strength.

Luke, the author of Acts, recounts the journey. Paul was traveling to Rome as a prisoner, after a long voyage by sea and a shipwreck. We do not know in detail who informed the brothers in Rome, but there were already believers there. Paul had written them the letter to the Romans some time before. This welcome encouraged him before he faced his situation as a prisoner.

For today: God often encourages us through other believers. Let us do the same: let us go out to meet someone who is weary or going through a trial, and give thanks to God for those who walk alongside us.
exp.27:15:
It says that when Paul and his companions finally arrived in Rome, the centurion handed the other prisoners over to the prefect of the army, that is, to the captain of the emperor's guard. Paul, however, was allowed to live on his own, although with a soldier who kept watch over him.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells the story of the journey. Paul was arriving in Rome as a prisoner, after appealing to Caesar. The believing brothers had already encouraged him along the way. Some understand that the favorable treatment was due to his good witness and the centurion's report, but the text does not explain this in detail.

God can give us room and peace even in limited situations. Paul did not wait to be free before serving: soon he spoke with the Jewish leaders. Today, even in difficult circumstances, we can keep trusting God and look for opportunities to speak of Him with kindness.
exp.27:22:
Paul, now in Rome, arranged a day with the leading Jewish men of the city. Many came to him where he was staying. There he expounded and testified about the kingdom of God, that is, he explained it and bore witness to it. He tried to persuade them about Jesus, using the law of Moses and the prophets, that is, the Scriptures of the Old Testament. He spoke the whole day, from morning until evening.

Luke tells that Paul was a prisoner in Rome. The leading Jews said they had received no bad reports about him, but they wanted to hear his view, since they knew the Christian movement was rejected everywhere. Paul took the opportunity to show that Jesus fulfills what the Scriptures had announced.

For today: when you speak about your faith, make time to listen and to explain patiently, relying on the Bible. The results do not depend on you.
exp.27:24:
This verse says that the Jews who visited Paul in Rome did not agree among themselves. Some believed and others did not, so they began to leave. Before they went out, Paul spoke one final word to them: the Holy Spirit spoke well, through the prophet Isaiah, to their forefathers. The word "disagree" in the verse above describes the same thing as the group not agreeing with one another; the lodging where Paul stayed is not mentioned in it.

Paul was a prisoner in Rome, but he could receive visitors. For a whole day he explained to them that Jesus fulfills the Law and the Prophets. Since many rejected the message, Paul quoted Isaiah 6 to show that this hardness of heart had already happened earlier in Israel's history.

For today: when you share your faith, do not be discouraged if some believe and others do not. Your task is to speak with clarity and love; the rest is God's work in each heart.
exp.27:27:
Paul tells the Jewish leaders in Rome that, whether they want to or not, they must know that this salvation of God has been sent also to the Gentiles, that is, to those who are not Jews. He adds that they, for their part, will listen.

Paul is a prisoner in Rome, and he has spent a whole day explaining the kingdom of God and Jesus to the Jewish leaders. Some believed and others did not. Before sending them away, he quotes Isaiah's words about a hardened heart. He does not speak with hatred but with sorrow, because salvation was coming first to Israel, and God's plan had always included all the nations.

For today: let us not assume who will respond to the gospel. Let us share the good news with everyone, with love and patience, and let God open hearts.
exp.27:28:
This verse says that after hearing Paul's words, the Jews who were with him in Rome left the place. They went away arguing strongly among themselves. Their argument was intense, so there was no single reaction: the news divided them.

Paul was a prisoner in Rome and had spent an entire day explaining the kingdom of God and Jesus from the Law and the Prophets. Some believed and others did not (v. 24). At the end, Paul quoted Isaiah about a hardened heart and announced that salvation would also go to the Gentiles. Some ancient texts leave out this verse, which is why certain Bibles put it in brackets or in a note.

Today, the message of Jesus sometimes divides people, and that does not always mean someone explained it poorly. We can speak with love and clarity, pray for those who do not respond, and let God work in each heart.
exp.27:29:
This verse says that Paul lived for two full years in a house that he rented himself, and that there he welcomed everyone who came to visit him.

Luke, the author of Acts, closes his book by telling how Paul's journey to Rome ended. Paul was a prisoner, but he was under guard in a house, not in an ordinary jail. He had just spoken with Jewish leaders, and some of them did not accept his message. The verses that follow explain that in that house he preached the kingdom of God and taught about Jesus without anyone stopping him. The Bible does not tell us what happened after those two years.

For today: even when your circumstances are limited, you can open the door of your home and of your life. Welcoming people with kindness and speaking to them about Jesus simply can be your way of serving.
exp.6:22:
He says that when Moses was forty years old, he decided to visit his brothers, the children of Israel. Here "decided" means that a choice formed in his heart to go and see them. "Visit" means going to see how they were doing, with real concern for them.

The speaker is Stephen, in his defense before the Jewish council. He reviews the history of Israel. Moses was raised in the Egyptian palace, with every advantage, but his heart did not forget his people. Stephen shows that God had a plan to deliver them, though the people did not understand it at that time. Some think that this decision came from God, although the text does not say so directly.

For today: even when we have comfort or success, let us not forget those who suffer near us. Let us ask God to put love for them in our hearts, and seek his guidance to help them with patience and wisdom.
exp.1:43:
It says that all the believers in Jesus were together and had everything in common, meaning they shared what they had with one another. Having everything "in common" means that what they had was for the good of everyone, not just for oneself. "The believers" are the people who had received the message of the gospel.

Luke, the author of the book of Acts, describes the life of the first church in Jerusalem, shortly after Pentecost. Thousands of people had come to believe, and many were visitors from far away who needed help. The following verse makes clear that they sold possessions and distributed to each according to need. It was voluntary and born of love, not a command. Some scholars debate how exactly to apply it to other times.

Today we might ask ourselves: what do I have that I can share with a brother or sister in need? Perhaps time, food, money, or companionship. Begin with something concrete this week, with joy and simplicity of heart.
exp.17:20:
As he left Ephesus, Paul said goodbye to the Jews there. He told them he was determined to go on to Jerusalem for the coming feast, and he promised to come back to them if God was willing. Then he set sail from Ephesus.

Paul was speaking during his second missionary journey. The Jews in the synagogue had asked him to stay longer, but he had other plans. The text does not say which feast it was; some think it was Pentecost or Passover, but this is not certain. What it does show is his wish to return to them, and later he does come back to Ephesus.

We can make plans with determination and, at the same time, hold them with humility, saying as Paul did, "if God is willing." In this way we move forward with commitment, while letting God guide our steps and correct our path.
exp.24:12:
After several days had passed, King Agrippa and his sister Bernice arrived at Caesarea to pay their respects to the governor Festus. The phrase "pay their respects" here means offering an official welcome or showing honor to a new authority.

The narrator is Luke, the author of Acts. Paul has just appealed to Caesar, and Festus has decided to send him to Rome. This visit seems casual, but it sets the stage for Paul to speak before another ruler, just as Jesus had announced that he would be a witness before kings (Acts 9:15). Festus discusses the case with Agrippa because he needs help understanding it.

For today: God can use encounters that look like simple courtesies to open unexpected doors. We can trust that he works even in ordinary details, and be ready to give testimony when the opportunity comes.
exp.26:0:
When it was decided that Paul and some other prisoners would travel by ship to Italy, they were handed over to a Roman officer named Julius. A centurion was the commander of about a hundred soldiers. The unit he belonged to, the Imperial Regiment, was probably a Roman military group, though no one knows for certain which one it was.

The one speaking is Luke, the author of Acts, who includes himself in the story when he says "we," because he travels with Paul. Paul was a prisoner because he had appealed to Caesar, and that is why they were taking him to Rome. The verses that follow show that Julius treated him kindly and allowed him to visit his friends.

For today: even when your path does not turn out as you planned, God can care for you and use your testimony. Paul was a prisoner, yet he kept serving and received help from others. Trust God, and let others support you.
exp.5:9:
It says that those who argued with Stephen could not win the debate against him. "Could not stand up to" here means they had no way to answer him or to refute what he said. What he spoke had wisdom and was guided by the Spirit, and his opponents had no answer for him.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells that Stephen was one of the seven men chosen to serve in the church in Jerusalem. Some Jews from several synagogues argued with him. Unable to beat him with arguments, they resorted to lies and to paid witnesses to accuse him. This is what sometimes happens when someone runs out of reasons: they turn to force or deception.

For today: when you speak of your faith, ask God for wisdom and trust his Spirit. You do not need to win arguments; it is enough to be sincere, humble, and faithful to the truth, even when others do not accept it.
exp.8:6:
The men who were traveling with Saul stood there, unable to move, because they were overwhelmed with amazement. They heard the voice, but they did not see anyone. "Speechless" means very astonished, almost frozen in place.

Saul was on his way to Damascus to arrest the followers of Jesus. Suddenly the risen Lord spoke to him. His companions were witnesses that something extraordinary was happening, but they did not receive the message as Saul did. In another passage (Acts 22:9) it says they did not understand the voice; scholars explain this apparent difference in several ways.

For today: God can speak to a person in a very personal way, even when others at their side do not notice. Let us ask for an attentive heart, and let us not judge the one who says they have been touched by God.
exp.3:1:
They say that the temple leaders were greatly disturbed, because Peter and John were teaching the people and proclaiming that in Jesus there is the resurrection of the dead. "Greatly disturbed" here means troubled and upset. Proclaiming "in Jesus" means announcing that, through Jesus and his resurrection, the dead will also rise.

Peter and John had just healed a lame man in the temple, and the people gathered. The priests, the captain of the temple guard, and the Sadducees interrupted them. The Sadducees, according to Acts 23:8, did not believe in the resurrection, so this message confronted them. Furthermore, it bothered them that men without official authority were teaching the people.

For today: do not lose heart if the message of Jesus makes some people uncomfortable. Share it with kindness and firmness, trusting that God can open hearts, as happened with the five thousand who believed.
exp.24:25:
Festus says he has nothing definite to write to the emperor about Paul. So he has brought Paul before everyone, and especially before King Agrippa, so that after this inquiry he will have something to put in his report to the emperor.

Festus, the Roman governor, speaks at a hearing with Agrippa and other leading men. The Jewish leaders wanted Paul put to death, but Festus found no wrongdoing that deserved death. Because Paul had appealed to Caesar, Festus had to send him to Rome with a report, yet he did not know what charge to write. He asks Agrippa for help, since Agrippa knew Jewish customs well.

For today: before judging or speaking about someone, let us look for the facts and listen carefully. Festus admitted he lacked clarity and asked for help; we too can seek wise counsel so that we act justly.
exp.16:31:
This verse tells how people responded when Paul spoke about the resurrection of the dead. Some began to mock him, because the idea seemed absurd to them. Others neither mocked nor believed, but said, "We want to hear you again on this topic," that is, they put off the decision for later.

Paul was in Athens, speaking before philosophers at the Areopagus. He declared that God is the Creator, that God would no longer overlook ignorance, and that Jesus, raised from the dead, will be the judge of the world. For many Greeks, the idea of a raised body sounded ridiculous. Even so, some did believe, such as Dionysius and Damaris.

Today too there are those who mock the gospel and those who postpone it. If God speaks to your heart, do not leave it for tomorrow. Listen honestly and respond today in faith.
exp.20:7:
This verse tells us that the next day, Paul and his companions left and went on to Caesarea. There they stayed at the home of Philip, who is called "the evangelist" and who was "one of the Seven."

Luke, the author of Acts, tells the journey in the first person ("we"), since he was traveling with Paul. Paul was on his way to Jerusalem. "The Seven" are the men chosen in Acts 6 to serve the needy in the church. Philip had proclaimed the gospel in Samaria and in other places, and now he was settling in Caesarea.

For today: open your home with joy to host, encourage, or help other believers. A simple table and a willing heart can strengthen those who are on the road in their service to God.
exp.27:6:
This verse tells us that near the place where they landed there was an estate belonging to Publius, the leading official of the island.
