He welcomed them and cared for them with hospitality for three days. The verse uses the words "estate" and "hospitably" to describe his property and the generous way he treated them.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells the story as a companion of Paul. They had just been shipwrecked on the island of Malta, wet and cold. Paul was a prisoner on his way to Rome. After the incident with the viper, Publius showed hospitality. Later, his father was healed.

Today we can follow Publius's example by offering practical help to someone who arrives in need, whether a neighbor, a migrant, or a stranger. A meal, a place to rest, or a kind word can be a real way of showing the love of God.
exp.23:26:
After two years had passed, Porcius Festus took over from Felix as governor. A successor is the person who takes the place of someone else. Wishing to do the Jews a favor means wanting to make them happy and to win their goodwill. That is why Felix left Paul in prison.

Here the narrator, Luke, is telling us what happened. Paul had spent those two years in prison in Caesarea, though no guilt had ever been proven against him. Felix listened to him but did not decide his case, partly because he hoped to receive money. When he left his post, he chose to please the Jewish leaders rather than to do justice.

For today: when we try to please people, we may stop doing what is right. Let us ask God for the courage to decide with honesty, even if no one applauds us. Paul, though in prison, remained faithful, and God did not abandon him.
exp.9:16:
Peter was puzzling over what the vision he had just seen could mean. At that very moment the men sent by Cornelius found Simon's house and came to the gate. "Puzzling" here means being perplexed, unable to understand. "Approached the gate" simply means they came up to the gate and waited there.

The one telling the story is Luke, the author of Acts. Peter was in Joppa, in the house of Simon the tanner, and had just seen three times a sheet filled with animals, together with the command not to call common what God has cleansed. Meanwhile, God had guided Cornelius, a Roman centurion, to send for Peter.

God sometimes gives us a sign and the verse comes later. If something God shows you is not yet clear, do not be anxious: pray, think calmly, and stay attentive. He usually makes the way clear step by step.
exp.14:31:
It says that Judas and Silas, who themselves were prophets, said much to encourage and strengthen the brothers. "Encourage" means they gave them hope and courage, and "strengthen" means they made them firm in the faith. "Said much" indicates that they spoke at length and generously.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells what happened after the church in Jerusalem decided not to impose the law of Moses on non-Jewish believers. Judas and Silas carried the letter with that decision to Antioch. The believers rejoiced when they read it, and these two men reinforced the message with their teaching. They were prophets, that is, they spoke on behalf of God, although the Bible does not detail here how they did it.

Today we can use our words to encourage and strengthen others. Think of someone who is tired or full of doubts, and give them your time to listen and speak to them with encouragement, drawing on the Word of God.
exp.4:13:
More and more people kept putting their trust in the Lord Jesus. They were not just a few: large numbers of both men and women came to believe. The wording shows that the church kept growing steadily.

The writer is Luke, who tells the story of the first church in Jerusalem. Before this verse, the apostles were performing miracles, and the believers met together in Solomon's Porch, an area of the temple. Some were afraid to join them, but the people respected them. Luke shows that faith kept growing even in the midst of that fear and that admiration.

For today: do not worry about whether your community is small. Live with unity, love, and simple faith, and trust that God is the one who makes his work grow. Your witness can encourage others to believe.
exp.11:22:
The angel of the Lord struck him down immediately, because he did not give glory to God. Herod was eaten by worms and died.

Luke describes this after Herod spoke to the people in his royal clothing, and the crowd shouted that it was the voice of a god and not of a man. Herod accepted the worship that belongs only to God. Earlier he had persecuted the church. Some historians identify him with Agrippa I. The historian Josephus describes his death with different details, though he also connects it to that moment of acclamation.

Today, when someone praises us for an achievement, we can respond with humility and acknowledge that every gift comes from God. In this way we avoid keeping a glory that does not belong to us.
exp.26:10:
Acts 27:11 says that the centurion, the Roman officer in charge of the prisoners, was persuaded by the pilot and the owner of the ship, rather than by Paul's advice. "The owner of the ship" refers to the one who owned the vessel, and "persuaded" means he was won over by their judgment.

Paul was traveling as a prisoner toward Rome. The fast had already passed, probably the Day of Atonement, in early autumn, when sailing had become dangerous. Paul warned of the danger, but the centurion preferred the advice of the experts at sea. Besides, the harbor where they were was not suitable for spending the winter, and that tipped the majority toward continuing on.

For today: listening to experts is wise, but it is not always enough. Before deciding, it is good to also weigh the counsel of faithful and prudent people, even when they are less popular or seem less important.
exp.3:2:
They seized Peter and John and put them in custody. The verse says they were held until the next day because evening had come, so it was too late to hold a trial. The narrator is Luke. Peter and John had just healed a lame man at the temple and were speaking to the people about Jesus. The priests, the captain of the temple guard, and the Sadducees were greatly disturbed. The Sadducees did not believe in the resurrection, and the apostles were proclaiming that Jesus had risen from the dead. Even so, the next verse says that many who heard them believed.

For today: sometimes speaking about our faith brings opposition or discomfort. Even so, God's word keeps bearing fruit, even when things seem to be getting complicated. We can keep speaking with love and trust God.
exp.9:42:
All the prophets of the Old Testament spoke about Jesus. The message is that everyone who believes in him receives forgiveness of their sins. "Through his name" means through who Jesus is and what he has done, not through anything a person has earned.

Peter speaks in the house of Cornelius, a Roman soldier who was not a Jew. Peter explains that Jesus died, rose again, and will be the Judge of the living and the dead. While he is still speaking, the Holy Spirit falls on those listening, and the Jewish believers who came with Peter are amazed that this gift has also been poured out on non-Jewish people.

For today: you do not need to earn forgiveness. If something from your past weighs on you, bring it before God today with faith in Jesus and receive his forgiveness with confidence.
exp.20:32:
What it says: The Roman commander came up and arrested Paul, ordering that he be bound with two chains. "Commander" was an officer of the Roman army, and "arrested" means taken into custody. Then he asked who Paul was and what he had done.

Context: Luke, the author of Acts, recounts what happened in Jerusalem. A crowd, angry because they believed Paul had taught against the people and the temple, was beating him with the intent to kill him. The commander stepped in to stop the disorder, not necessarily to defend Paul. Some see here the fulfillment of Agabus's prophecy about the chains (Acts 21:11).

For today: Sometimes we do what is right and still suffer injustice or confusion. Paul did not defend himself with violence; he trusted that God was still at work even in chains. When things do not turn out as you expect, remain faithful and trust that God can use your situation for his purposes.
exp.6:35:
This verse says that Moses was the one who led Israel out of Egypt. He did it by performing wonders and signs, mighty works that only God could accomplish. These took place in Egypt, at the Red Sea, and for forty years in the wilderness.

Stephen, a follower of Jesus, is speaking before the Jewish council that was accusing him. He reviews the history of Israel. He points out that the people first rejected Moses, but God sent him as their deliverer. Stephen suggests a parallel: Israel also rejected Jesus, whom God sent. Commentators see this intention here, although Stephen develops it further on.

For today: sometimes God works through people whom others despise or do not value. Ask him to give you humility to recognize his work, even when it comes in unexpected ways, and trust that he continues to care for his people at every stage of the journey, even through long wildernesses.
exp.20:16:
This verse says that Paul and his companions arrived in Jerusalem, and that the brothers, that is, the believers there, welcomed them joyfully and with open hearts. "Joyfully" means gladly and warmly.

The one telling the story is Luke, the author of Acts, who was traveling with Paul (which is why the text says "we"). They were coming from the third missionary journey, and Paul wanted to report what God had done among the non-Jewish peoples. Some believers from Caesarea went with them and stayed with Mnason. This warm welcome is important, because soon there would be tension in the city. The text says nothing more about how each person felt.

For today: practice hospitality and a good welcome. A sincere greeting to a brother or sister who arrives tired or from far away, or to someone new in your church, can encourage them greatly and show the love of Christ.
exp.16:7:
This verse says that the crowd and the city officials were greatly disturbed when they heard the accusations against Paul, Silas, and Jason. "Greatly disturbed" here means that they were agitated and deeply upset. The city officials were the local authorities who governed the city.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells what happened after some jealous Jews gathered a mob. Since they did not find Paul and Silas, they dragged Jason, who had housed them, before the authorities. They accused him of acting against Caesar, because the missionaries spoke of Jesus as King. That charge was political, and it frightened the officials, even though Paul was preaching the kingdom of God.

For today: when the truth comes with fear or exaggeration, do not respond with the same uproar. Act with calm, with honesty, and with trust in God, and support those who suffer for doing good.
exp.22:24:
This verse is a transition phrase. It says that someone "wrote the following letter." What comes next is the content of that letter.

The writer is Claudius Lysias, the Roman commander in Jerusalem. He has just learned of a plot by more than forty Jews to kill Paul, so he decides to send him under guard to Caesarea, where the governor Felix was. The letter serves as an official report: it explains who Paul is and why he is being sent. Luke, the author of Acts, includes it in full. Some scholars think Lysias presents the facts in a way that makes himself look good, but the text does not state this with certainty.

For today: God cared for Paul even by using civil authorities. We can trust that He protects His people, sometimes in unexpected ways, and we can also learn to speak the truth clearly in what we write.
exp.4:31:
Peter and the apostles say that they are witnesses of what God did with Jesus: he raised him up and exalted him. They also say that the Holy Spirit is a witness, and that God has given the Spirit to those who obey him.

Peter speaks before the Jewish council, the same body that had forbidden them to teach in the name of Jesus. The apostles answer that they must obey God rather than men. What they report is not an opinion but what they saw. The leaders become angry and consider killing them. Some understand "obey" here to include believing in and following Christ.

For today: if you want to sense the presence of the Spirit, start by obeying God in something specific that you already know he is asking of you. And tell simply what Jesus has done in your life.
exp.22:8:
There is a great uproar in the council. Some of the scribes from the party of the Pharisees stand up and argue sharply. They say, "We find nothing wrong with this man." And they ask, "What if a spirit or an angel has spoken to him?" "Argued sharply" means they were debating with strong feeling. The question they raise suggests they are worried about opposing God if Paul's words really came from him.

Paul stands before the Sanhedrin, accused by the Jews. He has just said that he is being judged for his hope in the resurrection, and this divides the Pharisees and the Sadducees. The ones speaking are Pharisee scribes. They probably defend Paul more because of their dispute with the Sadducees than out of faith in Jesus, although the text does not make this clear.

God can use even human divisions to care for his people. And it reminds us to be humble: before rejecting something, it is wise to ask ourselves whether we might be resisting God.
exp.7:15:
This verse explains that the believers in Samaria had already been baptized into the name of the Lord Jesus, but the Holy Spirit had not yet come upon any of them. The verse says the Spirit had not yet fallen upon them, meaning he had not yet come upon them in a visible way.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells how the good news reached Samaria through Philip. Then the apostles sent Peter and John. Christians have understood in different ways why the Spirit came later. Many think God wanted to show that the Samaritans were accepted in the same church as the Jews, under the guidance of the apostles.

For today: we should not doubt God's love when we do not understand his timing. We can pray for one another, receive with humility those who are different from us, and trust that God completes his work.
exp.2:3:
Acts 3:4 tells us that Peter looked directly at the lame man, as did John, and said, "Look at us!" The phrase "looked directly at him" means looking closely and steadily, without turning one's gaze away.

Peter, along with John, speaks to him as they are going up to the temple to pray. The man, lame from birth, was asking for money every day at the gate called Beautiful. Peter asks him to look at them in order to get his attention, and so prepare him to receive something better than money: healing in the name of Jesus.

For today: Peter and John did not walk past; they stopped and looked at a person whom many ignored. We can ask God to help us truly see those who suffer near us, and to offer them attention, respect, and hope, not only material help.
exp.7:8:
This verse introduces a man named Simon, who had practiced sorcery in the city before. "Sorcery" here refers to doing extraordinary things through hidden arts. The description of him astounding the people shows that he was impressing them with what he did, and the words about him claiming to be someone great mean that he claimed to be a very important person.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells how the gospel reached Samaria through Philip. Before this, Simon had the whole city amazed. Right after Philip preaches and there is healing and joy, Luke introduces Simon to show the contrast between human deception and the true power of God.

For today: let us be careful not to admire someone who presents himself as important or powerful. Instead, let us seek Christ and test what we hear against the Bible. And if we want to serve, let us do it with humility, without seeking fame.
exp.7:4:
Philip went down to a city in Samaria and told the people there about Christ. "Went down" means that he traveled there, moving from higher ground to lower. "Proclaimed" means that he announced good news clearly and openly. His message was not about himself or an idea, but about Christ.

Here the narrator of the book, traditionally attributed to Luke, is speaking. After Stephen died, a strong persecution scattered the believers. Saul was making things very hard. Even so, those who fled kept spreading the word wherever they went. This Philip is the same man who was chosen to serve in Acts 6. The Samaritans were a people with whom the Jews had a long-standing tension.

For today: even in difficult times, God can use our changes and setbacks to bring Christ to others. Let us speak about Jesus simply wherever we are, even with people who are different from us.
exp.15:3:
This verse tells us that Paul and his companions traveled from town to town and delivered to the churches the decisions made in Jerusalem. "Decisions" are the official rulings or instructions handed down, and "elders" are the respected leaders of the church. The people were to obey them.

The one telling this is Luke, the author of Acts. These decisions come from the meeting in Acts 15, where the leaders agreed that non-Jewish believers did not have to be circumcised in order to be saved. The aim was to keep unity between Jewish and non-Jewish believers. Some scholars note that Paul had Timothy circumcised for the sake of his witness before Jews, not as a requirement for salvation.

Today we can value unity and the counsel of the church's leaders. Before imposing our own opinions, it is wise to listen with humility and seek what builds up everyone.
exp.2:7:
This verse tells us that the man who had never been able to walk jumped to his feet and began to walk. He went with Peter and John into the temple courts, walking, leaping, and praising God. "Began to walk" describes his first steps on his own feet, and "praising God" means that he thanked God and celebrated Him.

The writer is Luke, the author of Acts. Peter and John were going up to the temple to pray, and at the gate called Beautiful they found a man who had been lame from birth, asking for money. Peter had no silver or gold to give him, but he healed him in the name of Jesus. The man responded with joy and worship, and his healing drew everyone's attention.

For today: when God helps you or changes something in your life, do not keep it to yourself. Give thanks to God with joy and in a visible way, so that others also see His goodness and draw near to Him.
exp.1:4:
Acts 2:5 says that in Jerusalem there were God-fearing Jews from every nation under heaven. The word "dwelling" means living there or staying there as residents. "God-fearing" describes people who were devoted to God and honored him. "Under heaven" is a way of saying "all over the world."

Here the book's author, Luke, is narrating what happened at Pentecost. After the Holy Spirit filled the disciples, Luke clarifies who was in the city. This sets up what follows: each visitor heard the message in their own language. Some scholars think they were pilgrims passing through for the festival, and others that some had settled there to live; the text allows for both ideas.

For today: God wants his message to reach everyone, regardless of language or country. Ask yourself how you can speak about Jesus clearly and with kindness to someone who comes from another culture.
exp.18:9:
This verse says that Paul kept teaching for two years in Ephesus. During that time, everyone who lived in the province of Asia, both Jews and Greeks alike, heard the word of the Lord. Asia here is not the modern continent but a Roman province in what is now Turkey.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells how Paul left the synagogue when some became stubborn and spoke badly of the Way, that is, the Christian faith. Then he taught every day in the lecture hall of Tyrannus. Luke does not say that Paul traveled through all of Asia; many scholars think people came to Ephesus and then carried the message back to their own cities.

When something closes a door for us, we don't have to stop. Paul changed places, but he did not stop teaching. We can be steady and look for new ways to share our faith wherever God places us.
exp.14:23:
This verse is part of a letter from the church in Jerusalem. It says that some men, who had gone out from among them without their authorization, came to the non-Jewish believers and unsettled them, troubling their minds by what they said. The men taught that the believers had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. The apostles make it clear that they had never sent these men or given any such instruction.

The letter comes from the apostles, the elders, and the whole church of Jerusalem. They write to the believers in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia. There was a serious debate over whether non-Jewish believers had to obey the law of Moses in order to be saved. The letter aims to bring calm and make clear what the apostles really taught.

For today: if someone adds requirements that God never asked for, and that leaves you anxious or doubting, do not hold on to that burden. Seek the clear teaching of the Bible and talk with wise leaders in your church.
exp.16:19:
The Athenians tell Paul that what he teaches sounds strange to them. "For you are bringing some strange notions to our ears" means that he brings them ideas they had never heard before. "and we want to know what they mean" means they want an explanation.

The speakers are Epicurean and Stoic philosophers of Athens. They had heard Paul speak about Jesus and the resurrection, and they brought him to the Areopagus, a place of gathering and debate. The verses that follow say that the Athenians loved to hear something new. It is not known for certain whether this was a formal trial or only an invitation to present his message.

For today: even when the message of Christ seems strange to others, we can explain it calmly and with respect. And when someone asks, we should listen carefully, without mockery.
exp.22:34:
Here Felix, the Roman governor in Caesarea, tells Paul that he will hear his case properly once his accusers arrive. In the meantime, he orders that Paul be kept under guard in Herod's Praetorium. "Arrive" is the word the verse uses for the accusers coming, and "kept under guard" is the wording used for Paul's custody. The Praetorium was an official building, serving as the residence and headquarters of the governor.

The one speaking is Felix, the Roman governor in Caesarea. Paul had been sent there by the tribune Claudius Lysias, because some Jews were plotting to kill him in Jerusalem. Felix read the letter, asked what province Paul was from, and decided to wait for the accusers before judging the case. Paul remained in custody, but protected.

For today: when we must wait without answers, let us remember that God can care for us even in the middle of slow or unjust processes. Let us wait with patience, truth, and trust in Him.
exp.19:6:
On the first day of the week, which is Sunday, the disciples in Troas came together to break bread, which probably refers to eating together and remembering the Lord's supper. Paul was leaving the next day, so he talked to them and kept on speaking until midnight.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells the story of Paul's journey and his companions. They had spent seven days in Troas, and this was their last night there. So Paul made the most of the time. Some see here a sign that Christians met on Sunday, although the text only describes one gathering and gives no command.

For today: value the time with your community of faith and listen to the Word with attention. Prepare yourself to gather, rested and hungry to learn.
exp.6:50:
He calls his listeners "stiff-necked," meaning stubborn, like an ox that refuses to be yoked. Their hearts were "uncircumcised," and their ears were closed. Although they carried the outward sign of belonging to God, their hearts did not obey and their ears did not want to listen. He accuses them of always resisting the Holy Spirit, just as their ancestors did.

Stephen, a follower of Jesus, is speaking before the Sanhedrin, the Jewish council that was judging him. He has just traced the history of Israel, showing how the people rejected those whom God sent, such as Joseph and Moses. Now he applies that history to his listeners, who had handed over Jesus, the Righteous One.

For today: having religion or customs is not enough. We can ask ourselves whether we are willing to listen to God when his Word corrects us, or whether we harden ourselves. Let us ask him for a teachable heart.
exp.26:36:
This verse says there were 276 people on the ship in total. The word "ship" means boat, and "of us" means that everyone is counted: soldiers, sailors, prisoners and passengers.

Luke, the writer of Acts, travels with Paul toward Rome, and here he gives the figure as an eyewitness present. They had been in a strong storm for fourteen days, with little food and great fear. Paul had said that no one would die, and he encouraged them to eat. After Paul gave thanks to God and ate, everyone regained courage. Some ancient manuscripts give a different number, so the exact figure is debated, but most translations follow 276.

For today: God cares for each person, not for an anonymous crowd. In your own storms, give thanks, eat, rest and care for those around you; your calm can encourage others.
exp.2:22:
This verse says that anyone who does not listen to Him will be completely cut off from among his people. The phrase "cut off" means separated from the people of God and no longer counted among them.

Peter is speaking to the Jews in the temple, after he healed a man who was lame. He explains that Jesus is the prophet that Moses foretold in Deuteronomy 18:15-19. Peter quotes that passage with some of the words summarized. The warning shows how serious it is to reject Christ, and Peter uses it to invite them to repent.

For today: listening to Jesus is not only admiring him, but paying attention to his words and obeying them. Today you can read a passage from the Gospels and ask yourself: "What is Jesus asking me to do today?" Then, with his help, try to carry it out.
exp.3:7:
Peter begins to speak before the Jewish authorities. He is "filled with the Holy Spirit," meaning that at that moment he is guided and strengthened by God. The rulers of the people were the leaders in charge, and the elders were respected leaders who were part of the council.

Peter and John had been arrested after healing a lame man at the temple. The authorities questioned them: by what power, or in whose name, had they done this? In other words, by what authority had they acted. Peter, who had earlier denied Jesus out of fear, now speaks with courage. Luke, the author, emphasizes that this strength comes from the Spirit.

When you find yourself needing to speak about your faith in a difficult moment, do not depend only on your own strength. Ask the Holy Spirit for courage and wisdom, and answer with respect and clarity.
exp.5:14:
All the members of the council, called the Sanhedrin, looked intently at Stephen and saw that his face was like the face of an angel. The Sanhedrin is the Jewish court. Their gaze was fixed on him as they watched him closely.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells of this moment. Stephen had been accused by false witnesses of speaking against the temple and the law of Moses. While they judged him, his face looked different. The text does not explain in detail what that appearance was like. Some think it showed peace and the presence of God, but that is an interpretation.

When we face criticism or injustice, God can give us a peace that shows on the outside. We do not have to pretend to be strong. We can ask Him to sustain us, and let our attitude, even in hard times, reflect trust in Him.
exp.16:8:
This verse tells how the trouble in Thessalonica was settled. The authorities collected bond from Jason and the others, that is, a guarantee or bail. With that, they were satisfied and released them.

Luke, the writer of Acts, narrates what happened after an angry crowd looked for Paul and Silas. Since they did not find them, they dragged Jason, who had hosted them, before the rulers. They accused him of supporting another king, Jesus. It is not known exactly what the bond consisted of, and scholars explain it in different ways.

For today: sometimes the wisest path is to calm tempers and move forward without fighting. God cares for his people in the midst of opposition, and the work continues, as seen in Berea.
exp.6:47:
He says that God, the Most High, does not live in houses built by human hands. "Dwell" means live or reside. "Built by human hands" means made by people. Then Stephen quotes the prophet, who is Isaiah (66:1-2), to support what he states.

Stephen speaks before the Jewish council, when he was being accused of speaking against the temple. He reviews the history of Israel: David wanted a place for God, but Solomon built the temple. Stephen makes clear that no building can contain God, who made heaven and earth. Many understand that he was also warning them not to confuse the temple with God himself.

For today: God is not limited to a building or a schedule. You can seek him, pray, and worship him in your home, at work, or on the road. Gathering places help, but what is central is having a humble heart before him.
exp.15:9:
When Paul saw the vision, they got ready right away to leave for Macedonia. They had come to the conclusion that God had called them to preach the good news there. "Got ready to leave" means that they began making plans to set out, and "concluding" means that they reached a firm decision.

The one speaking is the author of the book, Luke. Here he shifts to "we," which suggests that he joined the group at this point. Paul had tried to go to other places, but he was not allowed to. In Troas he received the vision of a man from Macedonia asking for help, and the group took it as God's guidance.

For today: when you feel that God is directing you, do not decide alone. Consult with other believers, as this group did, and then take the step with humility. God often guides us as we walk, not only while we wait.
exp.18:32:
They pulled a man named Alexander out of the crowd, and the Jews pushed him to the front. He motioned for silence, because he wanted to explain himself to the people. Here "to explain himself" means to give an explanation or a defense. "The people" here is the crowd that had gathered.

Luke describes the great uproar in Ephesus, stirred up by the silversmiths who were defending their trade and the goddess Diana. Paul and his companions were in danger. It is not known for certain what Alexander intended to say; perhaps the Jews wanted to distance themselves from the Christians, but the Bible does not make this clear. When the crowd noticed that he was a Jew, they silenced him by shouting for two hours.

For today: in the middle of confusion, not everyone who speaks is heard, and many people move along without knowing why. Before we join a popular opinion, let us stop, ask God for wisdom, and seek the truth calmly.
exp.7:20:
He says Simon has no part or share in this matter. The word "part" speaks of taking part, and "share" of a portion or stake in something. The "ministry" here is the work of the Spirit. Peter gives the reason: his heart is not right before God, that is, it is not sincere or aligned with God.

The apostle Peter is speaking. Simon, a man of Samaria who had practiced magic, had believed and been baptized. But when he saw that the Spirit was given when the apostles laid hands on people, he wanted to buy that power with money. Peter rebukes him sharply, but immediately calls him to repent. Scholars debate whether Simon was truly saved, and the text does not make this clear.

For today: examine your motives when you serve God. Gifts cannot be bought, nor used to gain prestige. Ask him to cleanse your heart.
exp.5:12:
This verse tells us that some men were brought in to give false testimony against Stephen. They said that he never stopped speaking against "this holy place," meaning the temple in Jerusalem, and against the law of Moses.

The one speaking here is the writer, Luke, who narrates the events. Some Jews could not answer Stephen's wisdom, so they paid certain men to lie. With this they stirred up the people and brought him before the council. The verses that follow show that they accused him because of his words about Jesus, the temple, and the customs of Moses.

For today: when someone accuses us unjustly, let us not respond with lies or with bitterness. Stephen remained calm, and his face looked like the face of an angel. We can trust that God knows the truth.
exp.22:0:
Paul looks directly at the members of the Sanhedrin, the council, and calls them "Brothers." He tells them that to this day he has conducted himself before God with a good conscience. The verse uses the phrase "conducted himself," which means he has lived his life in a certain way, and the "Sanhedrin" was the court of the Jewish leaders.

Paul had been arrested in Jerusalem and now has to speak before this court. He speaks with confidence and presents himself as a sincere man who has tried to follow God according to what he understood. His statement provokes a reaction from Ananias, the high priest, who orders that he be struck. Interpreters debate how to understand Paul's sharp reply, but the text shows that his clear conscience did not take away his courage.

Take care of your conscience by listening to God and correcting yourself when you fail. In this way you can face difficult moments with honesty and peace, even when others do not understand you.
exp.24:24:
Festus says that after examining Paul's case, he found that Paul had done nothing deserving of death. Since Paul himself asked to be judged by the emperor, Festus decided to send him to Rome. "The emperor" here is the ruler of Rome, and "appealed" means that Paul asked for his case to be decided by Caesar.

Festus, the Roman governor, speaks before King Agrippa, Bernice, and the leading men of the city. The Jews wanted Paul put to death, but Festus found no clear crime. Now he must write a report to the emperor and seeks Agrippa's help in knowing what to say.

For today: even when we are unjustly accused, we can act with honesty and trust that God works even through unjust processes. Paul did not seek revenge or despair; he continued to bear witness to Christ with firmness and peace.
exp.1:44:
Selling their possessions and goods, the believers shared with anyone who was in need. The verse describes them selling their lands and belongings and giving the money to whoever lacked what they needed. "Possessions" refers to property such as land, and "goods" refers to everything else a person owns.

Luke, the author of Acts, describes how the first Christian community in Jerusalem lived, shortly after Pentecost. Many had come from far away and were far from home. Out of love and unity, the believers shared what they had. It was voluntary help, not a command; the text shows them doing it for those who were in need. Christians have debated how to apply this example today.

For today: ask God whether there is someone near you with a real need, and help that person generously, without expecting anything in return.
exp.14:38:
This verse tells us that Paul and Barnabas had a disagreement so sharp that they decided to part ways. The Berean Standard Bible describes it simply as a disagreement that was so sharp they parted company. Barnabas took Mark with him and sailed for Cyprus.

The narrator is Luke, the author of Acts. Paul and Barnabas were planning to visit the churches again. Barnabas wanted to take Mark, but Paul did not, because Mark had left them during the first journey. The text does not say who was right. Afterward, God continued to use both men: Paul went out with Silas, and Barnabas went with Mark.

Even sincere believers can disagree. When it happens, let us seek not to hurt more than necessary, and trust that God can work through both sides and restore the relationship.
exp.4:15:
It tells us that the news of what was happening in Jerusalem reached the towns around the city. From those towns a large crowd came, bringing the sick and people tormented by unclean spirits, that is, evil spirits. The verse states that all of them were healed. "Crowds gathered" simply means that many people came together as a group.

Luke, the author of Acts, describes how the early church grew. The apostles were doing signs and wonders, and people had so much hope that they laid the sick out in the streets so that the shadow of Peter might fall on them. The text does not say that the shadow healed them; it only says that people were trying it. Shortly after, the religious leaders, moved by jealousy, arrested the apostles.

For today: when you meet someone who is suffering, do not just stand by and watch. Bring them before Jesus with your prayer and with practical help, as those did who carried their sick.
exp.20:2:
After sighting Cyprus, the ship passed south of the island, and the travelers sailed on toward Syria. They landed at Tyre because the vessel was to unload its cargo there. "Sighting" means they saw the island from a distance, and "passing south of it" tells us which side of the island they went by.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells the journey in the first person ("we"). Paul is returning to Jerusalem at the end of his third missionary journey. This detail shows that the stop at Tyre was caused by the ship's cargo, and there Paul found disciples and spent seven days with them.

For today: God can use the detours and pauses along the way, which may seem like simple logistical matters, to put us in contact with brothers and sisters who encourage us. Take advantage of those moments to fellowship, listen, and pray with other believers.
exp.12:33:
God raised Jesus from the dead so that his body would never decay again. He would never die a second time or rot in the grave. The verse quotes Isaiah 55:3, where God says he will give the holy and sure blessings promised to David. Those blessings are the secure promises God made to David.

Paul speaks in the synagogue at Antioch of Pisidia. He explains to Jews and to God-fearing listeners that Jesus' resurrection fulfills the promises made to Israel. If Jesus lives forever, the promises to David stand firm and are open to everyone who believes.

For today: you can trust that God's promises are not defeated or fail. When you feel insecure or tired, remember that Jesus lives, and that his love for you is steady and does not change.
exp.19:34:
Paul reminds them that he always showed them by his example: through hard work, we must help those who are weak. The words "help the weak" mean carrying those who are in need, and this can include people who are ill. And we must remember what the Lord Jesus himself said: "It is more blessed to give than to receive." In other words, there is more happiness in giving than in receiving.

Paul is saying goodbye to the leaders of the church in Ephesus, knowing that he may not see them again. He tells them that he did not desire anyone's silver, gold, or clothing, but worked with his own hands to support himself and his companions. This saying of Jesus does not appear in the four Gospels, so Paul knew it through oral tradition.

Today we can look for a concrete way to give: time, a visit, a meal, or help for someone who needs it. As we do this without expecting anything in return, we discover the joy that Jesus promised.
exp.20:33:
The crowd was so confused that each group was shouting something different. The commander, the Roman military officer in charge, could not learn the truth because of the uproar, so he ordered Paul to be brought into the barracks. The "barracks" in this verse is the Antonia fortress, the Roman garrison beside the temple. The word "uproar" describes noise and disorder. Saying that the commander could not get at the truth means that he could not find out what was really happening.

Paul had arrived in Jerusalem, was accused in the temple, and the people wanted to kill him. The one speaking here is the narrator, Luke. The commander stepped in to restore order. Although he had Paul taken into custody, in practice he rescued him from the mob. Some see here the hand of God caring for Paul, although the text does not say so directly.

Today, when there is much noise and confusion, we should not let ourselves be carried along by the loudest voices. Before we give an opinion or judge someone, let us seek calm and truth. And let us trust that God can care for us even in disorderly situations.
exp.0:6:
Jesus answers his disciples that it is not for them to know times or dates that the Father has fixed by his own authority. The meaning of "it is not for you" is simply "it is not for you to know," and the times or seasons are the appointed occasions God has set, while authority refers to power or rule.

Jesus, already risen, is about to ascend to heaven. The disciples ask him whether at that moment he will restore the kingdom to Israel. He does not deny that God has a plan, but he redirects their attention: not to the dates, but to the mission they will receive with the power of the Holy Spirit.

For today: instead of worrying about guessing the future or the dates of events, we can trust that God is in control and devote ourselves to living and sharing our faith today, with the help of the Spirit.
exp.18:29:
Paul wanted to go before the assembly, but the disciples of Ephesus would not allow him. The phrase "to go before the assembly" refers to going to the crowd gathered there, who at that moment were in the theatre, a large, public place.

The silversmiths of Ephesus, led by Demetrius, had stirred up a commotion because the message of the gospel was hurting their business of small shrines to the goddess Diana. The crowd seized Gaius and Aristarchus, companions of Paul. Paul, concerned for them, wanted to step in. The disciples, and also some friendly officials, asked him not to go, since his life was in danger. The text says nothing more about what Paul was thinking.

Being brave does not always mean rushing into danger. Sometimes God takes care of us through the advice of wise brothers and sisters. Let us learn to listen to those who love us and counsel us with prudence.
exp.11:0:
About that time, King Herod reached out to harm some who belonged to the church. The wording here means he set out to attack and mistreat them. It does not speak of the whole church, but of some of its members.

The one speaking is Luke, the author of Acts, who recounts what happened in the early church. This Herod is usually identified as Herod Agrippa I, grandson of Herod the Great, although the verse here simply says "Herod." The verses that follow show that he wanted to please the Jews. Thus, Luke presents a new wave of persecution against the church, now coming from political power.

For today: when faith faces opposition or injustice, it is not a sign that God has been absent. We can pray for believers who suffer today, support them with care, and remain steadfast, trusting that God is still at work even in difficult times.
exp.8:27:
Acts 9:28 says that Saul stayed with the believers in Jerusalem, moving about freely and speaking boldly in the name of the Lord. The verse shows that he was no longer kept at a distance. He moved among them as one of the group and spoke openly about Jesus.

Context: Luke, the author of Acts, describes what happened after Saul's conversion, when he returned to Jerusalem. The disciples were understandably afraid of him, since he had once persecuted the church. Barnabas, whose name means "son of encouragement" according to Acts 4:36, took Saul's side and told the others about his experience. Because of Barnabas, they accepted him.

For today: God can change a person, but trust is sometimes rebuilt little by little. We can be like Barnabas by reaching out to someone who is struggling to be accepted, and by giving them a chance with patience and love.
exp.12:12:
This verse tells of a journey. After setting sail from Paphos, a city on the island of Cyprus, Paul and his companions sailed to Perga, in the region of Pamphylia, in what is now Turkey. There John, also called Mark, left the group and returned to Jerusalem. The verb "came" in the verse means reaching a place, and "left them" means leaving the group.

This is narrative written by Luke. Earlier, the proconsul Sergius Paulus believed in Cyprus. Now the mission moves on to new regions, and Paul appears as the leader of the group. The text does not explain why John left. Some think it was out of fear, weariness, or disagreement, but that is only a guess.

Even servants of God can falter or step off the path. If you feel tired today or have left something unfinished, God can still give you a new opportunity.
exp.6:13:
Joseph, who by then had power in Egypt, sent for his father Jacob and all his relatives. In all, there were seventy-five people. Relatives means family or kin.

The speaker is Stephen, during his defense before the Jewish council. He is reviewing the history of Israel to show how God cared for his people, even by unexpected paths. Here he recalls that Joseph, rejected by his brothers, ended up saving them. About the number, the account in Genesis speaks of seventy people, and the figure of seventy-five comes from the ancient Greek translation. Scholars explain that difference in several ways.

For today: God can use painful situations, such as rejection or injustice, to prepare others well. Trust that he is still at work even when you do not understand your situation.
exp.4:1:
It says that Ananias kept back some of the money from the sale, and that his wife Sapphira knew about it and agreed. Even so, he brought only a portion and laid it "at the apostles' feet," as if it were the full amount. The phrase "kept back" means he held back money for himself in a deceptive way; "proceeds" is what they received from the sale.

Luke, the narrator, tells this right after many believers were selling their property to help those in need (Acts 4:32-37). Ananias and Sapphira wanted to appear just as generous, but they pretended. Peter later makes clear that no one forced them to give everything: the problem was not what they held back, but the lie.

God does not ask us to appear to be more than we are. We can give with simplicity, according to our heart, without seeking applause or pretending to a devotion that does not exist. Sincerity before God is worth more than an image before others.
exp.14:10:
Peter says that the Jewish believers are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, that is, through his undeserved favor, and not by their own merits. He says the same is true for the Gentiles: "just as they are." The word "on the contrary" here means that Peter is setting this truth against what others were arguing.

This takes place at the council in Jerusalem. Peter speaks before the apostles and the elders, because some were teaching that Gentile believers had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses in order to be saved. Peter recalls that God gave the Spirit to the Gentiles when they believed, and he calls that burden, which no one had been able to carry, a yoke.

For today: do not add requirements to grace, either for yourself or for others. Rest in what Christ has done, and treat with humility those who come from backgrounds different from yours.
exp.14:34:
Paul and Barnabas stayed in Antioch of Syria. The verb in the verse means "remained," so the sense is that they stayed there for a while. While they were there, they taught the word of the Lord and proclaimed the gospel, that is, the good news about Jesus, along with many others who also served.

Luke, the author of Acts, narrates what happened after the Council of Jerusalem. There it was decided that non-Jewish believers did not have to keep the law of Moses in order to be saved. The letters with that decision had already reached Antioch. This time of teaching was a moment of calm before the disagreement between Paul and Barnabas that comes later.

For today: serve faithfully where God has placed you, teaching and sharing the faith without seeking to be the only one in the spotlight. God works through many people who labor together.
exp.1:46:
They were praising God and enjoying the favor of all the people. Each day, the Lord added to their number those who were being saved. Some notes on wording: the phrase "enjoying the favor" means they were well liked and respected by others; the phrase "added to their number" means that the Lord was bringing new people into the group.

This is part of Luke's account in Acts. It describes the life of the first community in Jerusalem, shortly after Pentecost. They shared their possessions, gathered in the temple and in homes, and ate together with joy. Luke shows that the growth did not depend on them alone: it was the Lord who added.

For today: live your faith with joy, generosity, and simplicity in your community, and trust that God is the one who makes his work grow. Your part is to love and serve with sincerity.
exp.13:11:
This verse tells us that the people of Lystra called Barnabas "Zeus" and Paul "Hermes." The reason given is that Paul was the one who spoke. Zeus and Hermes are the Greek names of gods from Greek mythology, and Zeus was the chief of the gods. "Chief speaker" means he was the main spokesman.

The narrator, Luke, explains the crowd's reaction after the healing of a man who had been lame. The people spoke the Lycaonian language and thought the gods had come down in human form. It is commonly understood that Hermes, as the messenger of the gods, was associated with the one who spoke. Barnabas, perhaps because of his presence, was linked with Zeus. The text gives no further details.

For today: when God works through us, let us not receive the applause. Like Paul and Barnabas, let us always point to God and not to ourselves.
exp.8:34:
This verse says that everyone who lived in Lydda and Sharon saw Aeneas healed, and turned to the Lord. Turned to the Lord means that they changed the direction of their lives and their trust to follow Jesus.

Luke, the author of Acts, reports what happened after Peter, in the name of Jesus, healed Aeneas, a man who had been paralyzed for eight years. Lydda was near Joppa, and Sharon was the nearby coastal plain. The text does not say how many people there were, so "everyone" is understood as a large number of people in that region. The healing was a sign that pointed to Jesus, not to Peter.

Today, God can use a visible change in a life to draw others toward Himself. May your way of living, simple and sincere, lead others to look to Jesus.
exp.1:17:
This verse says that God will pour out his Spirit on his menservants and maidservants, meaning all of his servants, men and women alike, and that they will prophesy, that is, speak on God's behalf. The word "Even" stresses that this is true of everyone, not just a few. "Pour out" suggests something given in abundance, not in small measure.

Peter is speaking in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost. Some in the crowd thought the disciples were drunk, and Peter explains that what they are seeing is what the prophet Joel foretold. Luke's wording here, "menservants and maidservants," is the wording Peter uses to show that the Spirit comes to people of both sexes who belong to God. The "last days" are usually understood as the time that began with Christ, though they are interpreted in several ways.

For today: God does not reserve his Spirit for special people. If you are his servant, you can ask him to use you to speak words of encouragement and truth to others.
exp.24:23:
Festus presents Paul before King Agrippa and the prominent men of Caesarea. He says that the whole Jewish community has petitioned him about Paul, both in Jerusalem and here in Caesarea, crying out that Paul should be put to death. "Petitioned" means they have brought their demands to him formally. "All who are present" refers to the men gathered in the room. "He ought not to live any longer" means that, in their view, Paul did not deserve to go on living.

Festus is the Roman governor. Agrippa had wanted to hear Paul, and that is why this formal hearing was arranged. Festus already knows, as he says later, that Paul did nothing deserving of death. Paul had appealed to the emperor, so Festus needs clear information for his report. It is possible that "the whole Jewish community" is an exaggerated way of speaking.

For today: do not let yourself be carried along by the pressure of the crowd. Before judging someone, seek the truth calmly, as Festus did, and stand firm in what is right even when many shout the opposite.
exp.17:26:
He says that Apollos wanted to travel to Achaia, a region of Greece. The brothers in Ephesus encouraged him and wrote to the disciples there, asking them to welcome him. When he arrived, he was a great help to the believers, and they had come to believe through grace, that is, through the favor of God. The verse says he was a great help, meaning he was of real benefit to them.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells how Apollos, an eloquent Jew from Alexandria, had been gently corrected by Priscilla and Aquila. After that, the church in Ephesus backed him with a letter of recommendation. In this way his ministry was accepted in another place. Scholars do not know for certain how far Apollos's knowledge reached before he was instructed.

Today, we can encourage and support those who serve God sincerely. It is also good to accept correction with humility, as Apollos did, because then God can use us to bless others.
exp.3:19:
Peter and John say they cannot stop speaking about what they experienced with Jesus. "Cannot stop speaking" means they cannot keep quiet. "What we have seen and heard" refers to what they witnessed: the life, the teaching, the death and the resurrection of Jesus, and the healing of the lame man.

Peter and John had healed a man at the temple and had spoken about Jesus to the people. The Jewish authorities arrested them and ordered them not to teach in the name of Jesus. They answered with respect, but with firmness: their faithfulness to God came before that order.

For today: you do not need to be a great speaker to talk about Jesus. Share simply what God has done in your life, with kindness and sincerity, even when it makes you afraid or uncomfortable.
exp.26:25:
Paul says that the ship must run aground on some island. The phrase "must" means "it is necessary" or "it will be necessary." The idea that "we will run aground on an island" means they will crash onto an island, that is, they will be wrecked there. This is not a promise of good weather but an honest warning that there will be loss.

Paul speaks in the middle of a violent storm that had already lasted many days. Everyone had lost hope. An angel had told him not to be afraid, that he would stand before Caesar, and that God would give him the lives of all who were sailing with him. Paul encourages the men, but he does not promise them an easy path. God will give them their lives, even though the ship will be lost. Later it becomes known that the island was Malta.

God can promise rescue without promising comfort. When you go through a crisis, trust that God keeps his word, even if the path includes losses. Ask him for strength to keep going with hope.
exp.9:1:
This verse describes Cornelius, a Roman soldier. It says he was devout, meaning devoted and respectful toward God, and that he and all his household were devout and God-fearing. He gave generously to the people, meaning he helped the poor among the Jewish people, and he prayed to God regularly.

The one speaking is Luke, the author of Acts, who introduces Cornelius before telling of his vision. Cornelius was not a Jew, yet he sought God sincerely. Luke wants to show that God was already at work in his heart, and so he prepares the moment when the gospel first reaches non-Jewish people.

For today: sincere faith shows in the home, in regular prayer, and in generosity toward those in need. Today you could pray with more consistency and help someone specific this week.
exp.26:35:
After seeing Paul eat and give thanks, everyone on the ship took heart and also ate. The word "encouraged" means they became more hopeful and confident.

Paul was a prisoner traveling to Rome. They had been in a terrible storm for two weeks, with little food and great fear. Paul told them that God had promised him that no one would die. Then he took bread, gave thanks to God before everyone, and began to eat. His example gave them confidence.

For today: the calm faith of one person can encourage others in difficult moments. When everything seems uncertain, we can give thanks to God, take care of the basics, such as eating and resting, and trust in his promises, thus serving as support for those around us.
exp.20:36:
As the soldiers were about to take Paul into the barracks (the Antonia Tower, next to the temple), he asked the Roman commander, the tribune, if he could say something. Asking "May I say something?" was a polite way of requesting permission. The commander, surprised, replied with a question of his own: "Do you speak Greek?"

Paul had just been seized in the temple by a crowd shouting for his death. The soldiers carried him to protect him from the violence. Paul speaks calmly, and the tribune is surprised that he uses Greek, since he thought Paul was an Egyptian rebel. His next words show that he had mistaken him for someone else.

Even in the midst of chaos, Paul kept his composure and spoke with respect. When we are misunderstood, we can respond with serenity and clarity, trusting that God opens doors for us to bear witness.
exp.21:24:
Paul is stretched out and strapped down, ready to be flogged. Then he calmly asks the centurion standing there whether it is lawful to flog a Roman citizen without a trial. "Lawful" here means permitted by law. "Flog" means to strike with a whip.

Paul is speaking in Jerusalem, after an angry crowd turned against him in the temple. The tribune, who did not understand the uproar, ordered him to be questioned under the lash. Paul uses his Roman citizenship, which protected against that kind of treatment without a trial. The text does not say he was dishonest; he simply uses a legitimate right, and the centurion reacts at once.

We can use the legitimate rights we have with wisdom and respect to prevent unjust harm, without ceasing to trust God. Defending what is right calmly is not a lack of faith, and it can also open the way to continue serving.
exp.27:19:
Paul tells the Jewish leaders of Rome that he invited them so he could see them and speak with them. He explains that he is a prisoner, bound with a chain, because of the hope of Israel. That hope is the promise of a Messiah and of the resurrection, which Paul believes was fulfilled in Jesus. The phrase "I have called to see you" simply means that he invited them to come.

Paul is in Rome, under guard, after appealing to Caesar. A few days after arriving, he gathers the leading men of the Jews to make clear that he has not betrayed his people or committed any crime. He wants them to understand why he is in chains and to be able to tell them the message of Jesus.

For today: even in difficult circumstances, we can hold on to hope and see each situation as an opportunity to speak about that hope with respect and clarity. Paul does not complain or accuse anyone; he humbly explains why he lives as he does.
exp.10:25:
He says that Barnabas and Saul stayed in Antioch for a whole year, meeting with the church and teaching many people. There, for the first time, the followers of Jesus were called "Christians." The phrase "met together" here means that they gathered as one group. "First" means "for the first time."

Luke, the author of Acts, tells how the church grew in Antioch, a great city outside Judea. Barnabas went to look for Saul and brought him back to Antioch to help with the teaching. The text does not say who invented the name "Christians"; it only reports that they were called that, probably by the people of the city.

Today, being a Christian means belonging to Christ and becoming like Him. We can ask ourselves whether our way of speaking and of treating others shows Jesus. We also learn to grow in community, teaching and encouraging one another with perseverance.
exp.15:25:
This verse tells that, suddenly, a strong earthquake shook the foundations of the prison. At once all the doors flew open, and everyone's chains came loose. The chains here are the bonds that held the prisoners, and "came loose" simply means they were no longer fastened.

Luke, the author of Acts, recounts what took place in Philippi. Paul and Silas had been beaten and imprisoned, with their feet in the stocks. At midnight they were praying and singing to God, and the other prisoners were listening. Then the earthquake happens. The text does not explain how it came about; it presents it as an intervention of God in the middle of the night.

For today: Paul and Silas praised God before seeing any way out. When you are in a difficult situation, pray and give thanks to God, even though nothing has changed yet. He can act in ways we do not expect, and your faith can also be a witness to those who observe you.
exp.6:36:
This verse recalls that Moses himself announced that God would raise up another prophet from among the people of Israel, like him. "Your brothers" means the Israelites. The Berean Standard Bible renders the promise as "God will raise up for you a prophet like me," and the command to listen to this prophet means that they should follow him and obey what he says.

The speaker is Stephen, before the Jewish council, while they accuse him. He shows that Israel rejected Moses, even though God had sent him. Christians understand that Stephen is preparing the way to speak of Jesus as that promised prophet (Deuteronomy 18:15), although in this verse he does not yet name him.

For today: listening to God is not only hearing, but obeying. Ask yourself whether there is any word of Jesus that you have been setting aside, and take one simple step today to put it into practice.
exp.18:18:
This verse tells that several people in Ephesus who had practiced magic arts brought their books of spells together and burned them in front of everyone. When the value of the books was calculated, the total came to fifty thousand drachmas. A drachma was roughly the pay for one day's work, so it was an enormous sum.

The one telling the story is Luke, the author of Acts. Ephesus was a city closely tied to occult practices. After the name of Jesus was honored and many believers confessed what they had done, this burning shows genuine repentance, one seen in actions and not only in words.

For today: if there is something in your life that pulls you away from God, do not keep it around "just in case." With God's help, let it go in a clear and concrete way, even when it costs you. Obeying Jesus is worth more than anything we have to give up.
exp.1:16:
This verse says that God promises to pour out his Spirit on all people. Sons and daughters will speak on God's behalf (prophesy), young men will see visions, and older men will dream dreams. The phrase "in the last days" refers to the final period God has prepared; many understand that it began with the coming of Christ.

Peter speaks to the crowd in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost. Some thought the disciples were drunk because they were speaking in other languages. Peter answers that this is the fulfillment of what the prophet Joel announced. Scholars agree that Peter applies it to that moment, though they debate how everything will be completed in the future.

Today you can know that God's Spirit is not only for special people. Pray asking for his guidance, and offer to speak about God with your family and friends, regardless of your age.
exp.19:2:
It says that Paul spent three months in Greece. When he was about to set sail for Syria, some Jews made a plot against him. The word "plot" in this verse refers to a secret scheme to harm someone. For that reason, Paul decided to go back through Macedonia instead of taking the ship.

The one telling the story is Luke, the author of Acts. Paul had just encouraged the churches in Macedonia and then came to Greece, probably to Corinth, although the text does not give the name of the city. The Jews who opposed his message followed him with hostility. Luke tells that Paul changed his route, and the verses that follow show that a group of coworkers was traveling with him.

For today: trusting God does not mean being reckless. Paul acted with wisdom and changed his plan to protect his life and be able to keep serving. Sometimes obeying God includes asking for advice, staying alert, and accepting a change of direction.
exp.10:23:
This verse describes Barnabas with three traits: he was a good man, he was full of the Holy Spirit, and he was full of faith. As a result, a great number of people were brought to the Lord. The key idea here is that those who came to faith were brought into a close relationship with the Lord and joined the community of believers.

The one telling the story is Luke, the author of Acts. The church in Jerusalem sent Barnabas to Antioch when they heard that many there had come to believe. He saw the grace of God, rejoiced, and encouraged everyone to remain firm in the Lord. Luke explains why his work bore fruit: because of his character and his life in the Spirit. Afterward Barnabas went looking for Saul to help him teach.

For today: good character, faith, and dependence on the Spirit matter more than titles. Strive to be someone good and encouraging, who helps others grow in Christ.
exp.3:36:
It says that Barnabas owned a field, sold it, brought the money (the price) and laid it at the apostles' feet. That phrase shows that he handed it over to the leaders of the church so that they could manage it. It was a voluntary offering.

Luke, the author of Acts, describes how the first believers in Jerusalem shared their possessions so that no one went without. He presents Barnabas as a concrete example. He was a Levite, that is, from the tribe of Levi, and he was born in Cyprus. His name means "son of encouragement" (or comfort). Some think the account sets up a contrast with Ananias and Sapphira in the next chapter, although the text does not say this directly.

Today we can ask ourselves what we have that could help others: money, time or talents. Giving simply, without seeking applause, and in an orderly way, through the church or through someone trustworthy, can be a real way of bringing comfort.
exp.20:6:
This verse tells us that the sea voyage from Tyre ended at Ptolemais. There the travelers landed, greeted the brothers, that is, the believers of that place, and stayed with them for a day. The phrase "when we had finished our voyage" simply means that they completed that part of the journey by ship.

The one who is speaking is Luke, the author of Acts, who writes "we" because he was traveling with Paul. They were headed to Jerusalem, and they had just said goodbye to the Christians of Tyre with prayer. Ptolemais was a port on the coast. The text does not say who those brothers were or what they did that day, so it is best not to invent details.

For today: even when we are only passing through, it is worth taking time to greet and spend time with other believers. A brief meeting can encourage and strengthen both the one who arrives and the one who receives them.
exp.19:35:
What it says: When Paul had finished speaking, he knelt down with all of them and prayed. Getting down on his knees was a posture of humility before God. It was not a quick prayer, but a shared moment.

Context: Paul bids farewell to the elders of the church in Ephesus at Miletus, on his way to Jerusalem. He has reminded them of his work, his teaching, and his care for the weak. He told them they would probably not see him again. Before parting, it was most natural for him to pray with them, and then came tears and embraces.

For today: In moments of farewell, of difficult decisions, or of strong emotions, make prayer the first thing you do. Praying with others, aloud if possible, joins hearts together and places the future in God's hands.
exp.15:24:
It says that about midnight Paul and Silas were praying and singing hymns to God, and the other prisoners were listening to them. The sentence opens with a word that marks a moment in time and links it to what came before. In other words, even in the darkness and in pain, they were giving praise to God.

The book of Acts is narrated by Luke. Paul and Silas had been beaten with whips and locked in the innermost part of the prison at Philippi, with their feet fastened in the stocks, a kind of wooden frame that held them immobile. They were imprisoned for proclaiming the gospel. What follows shows that God acted in a surprising way.

For today: when you go through difficult moments, you can come close to God with prayer and gratitude, even when you do not understand what is happening. Your faith can be a quiet witness to those around you, because others are listening too.
exp.10:9:
In Acts 11:10, Peter tells the believers in Jerusalem that the vision happened three times, and then everything was drawn back up into heaven. The sheet with the animals was lifted up again, so the whole scene ended with the vision itself withdrawn.

The speaker is Peter. He is explaining to the believers in Jerusalem why he went into the house of Cornelius, a Gentile, and ate with him. Some of them had criticized him for it. Peter recounts the vision step by step to show that God himself had guided him. The threefold repetition shows that the message was firm and not a passing dream.

For today: when God shows us something that changes our ideas about other people, we should not dismiss it right away. Let us ask for humility to listen, compare what we feel with the Bible, and be willing to draw near in love to those we once looked at with distance.
exp.9:45:
This verse says that Peter and the believing Jews who were with him heard the Gentiles speaking in tongues and exalting God. "Exalting" means praising God with admiration. The "tongues" here are languages or expressions of praise that they had not learned. This was the visible proof that God had received them.

Luke recounts what happened in the house of Cornelius, a Roman soldier who feared God. While Peter was preaching, the Holy Spirit came upon all who were listening. The believing Jews were amazed, because they thought that gift was only for them. That sign led Peter to baptize them.

For today: God does not make a difference between people. If someone trusts in Christ, they are received by Him. Let us open our hearts and our church to those who are different from us, without putting up barriers that God has not put up.
exp.19:37:
This verse says that the elders of Ephesus were deeply grieved, especially because of what Paul had told them: that they would never see his face again. "Especially grieved" means feeling a very deep sorrow. A "ship" is a boat. In the end, they went with him to the ship to see him off.

The one speaking in the account is Luke, the author of Acts, who tells of Paul's farewell. Paul had called the elders of the church in Ephesus to Miletus, on his way to Jerusalem. He warned them that difficult times would come and encouraged them to care for the flock. His remark that they would not see him again reflected his conviction that suffering awaited him, although the text does not tell how everything turned out.

Today we can value those who have taught us the faith. Let us not let farewells pass without expressing affection, gratitude, and prayer for them. An embrace, a phone call, or a few sincere words can leave a lasting mark.
exp.19:21:
Paul says that he is now on his way to Jerusalem, "compelled by the Spirit." That wording is usually understood to mean that he feels driven or committed from within to go, though some readers take it to refer to the Holy Spirit and others to his own settled conviction. He also admits that he does not know what will happen to him there.

Paul is speaking to the elders of the church in Ephesus, gathered at Miletus, as he says goodbye to them. He reminds them of how faithfully he taught them. Although he knows that imprisonment and hardship await him, he presses on because he wants to finish the task the Lord Jesus gave him.

For today: sometimes God calls us to take a step without giving us all the details of what lies ahead. We can obey with humility and trust, knowing that He guides us even when we do not understand what is coming.
exp.3:34:
It says that the believers who sold their property brought the money and laid it "at the apostles' feet for distribution." There the apostles gave it out to anyone according to what they needed.

Luke, the author of Acts, describes how the first church in Jerusalem lived after Pentecost. While the apostles preached the resurrection of Jesus, the community lived with voluntary generosity, so that no one was in need. Laying the money at the apostles' feet shows trust in their leaders. The next verse presents Barnabas as an example of this gesture.

Today we can ask ourselves: what do I have that could help a brother or sister in need? Perhaps it is not selling a house, but sharing food, time, or money, with generosity and in an orderly way, through the church or through trustworthy people.
exp.15:19:
The owners of the young slave girl bring Paul and Silas before the magistrates, the authorities of the city. There they accuse the men of "throwing our city into turmoil," that is, of causing disorder and trouble. They stress that the men are "Jews," as if that alone were enough to make people distrust them.

The owners of the girl are the ones speaking. Paul had just cast a spirit out of her, and they lost the money they made through her. They do not state the real reason for their anger, which was money. They invent a charge of a public nature and take advantage of prejudice against Jews in a Roman colony. Philippi was a Roman colony, and that gives weight to their argument.

Today we can learn that rejection of good often springs from economic or personal interests hidden behind respectable accusations. If we are unjustly accused for doing what is right, we can respond with peace and trust in God, as Paul and Silas did, without repaying evil with evil.
exp.14:16:
This verse says that God will restore the fallen house of David with a purpose: that the rest of humanity may seek the Lord, including all the Gentiles, that is, those who are not Jews. They are people who are called by God's name, meaning they belong to him. The phrase "says the Lord who does these things" means that God is the one who accomplishes it.

James speaks at the council in Jerusalem. There was a debate about whether non-Jewish believers had to keep the law of Moses in order to be saved. James quotes the prophet Amos to show that including the Gentiles was already part of God's plan. Some scholars see the "tabernacle of David" as Christ and his church; others understand it in a different way.

Today, remember that God invites everyone. Treat with respect and welcome those who come to faith, without placing on them burdens that God did not place.
exp.26:19:
This verse tells us that the storm was so strong and lasted so many days that neither the sun nor the stars could be seen. Without them, the sailors could not know where they were or which way they were going. That is why they abandoned all hope of being saved. The word "saved" here means being rescued, that is, coming out of it alive. The storm was described as great, meaning it was a very severe one.

The one speaking is Luke, the author of Acts, who was traveling with Paul and tells what they went through. Paul was a prisoner on his way to Rome, on a ship full of people. They had already thrown the cargo and the ship's gear into the sea to lighten the vessel. After this moment without hope, Paul stands up and encourages everyone with a promise from God.

For today: when you see no way out and lack signs, do not hold only to what you can see. Seek God, ask for his word, and be a voice of encouragement for others in the middle of the storm.
exp.14:36:
This verse says that Barnabas wanted to take John, who was also called Mark, on the new journey to visit the churches. The phrase "also called Mark" tells us that this man had a second name. "Take with them" means taking him along as a travel companion.

Paul had proposed going back to visit the believers in the cities where they had already preached the gospel. Barnabas, whose name means "son of encouragement," wanted to give Mark another chance. Paul did not agree, because Mark had left them earlier in Pamphylia. The text does not explain why Mark left; there are several ideas, but none are certain.

For today: God calls us to be patient and to give second chances. But we can also hold different opinions without ceasing to serve the Lord.
exp.19:13:
He says that Paul met up with his companions at Assos, a port on the coast of Asia Minor. They took him aboard and together went on to Mitylene, a city on the island of Lesbos. "We went on" means that the group kept sailing from there.

The one telling the story is Luke, who was traveling with Paul and writes in the first person ("we"). Paul had walked by land from Troas, while the others went by ship. The text does not explain why he chose to go alone; some think he wanted time by himself to pray or reflect, but that is only a guess. They were heading toward Jerusalem in a hurry.

For today: not everything in the Christian life is done the same way or at the same pace. Paul and his friends took different paths, but they came together and continued united toward the same goal. We can value moments of solitude with God and also the companionship of other believers who walk alongside us.
exp.3:5:
This verse names the religious leaders gathered in Jerusalem: Annas, Caiaphas, John, Alexander, and many others from the high priest's family. "High priest" means the head of the priests. "Priestly family" refers to the family line that the priests came from.

Luke, the author of Acts, lists the members of the council that questioned Peter and John after they healed a crippled man and preached about Jesus. Annas and Caiaphas were already known for their role in the trial of Jesus. About John and Alexander we cannot be certain who they were, since the Bible gives no further details.

For today: opposition can come from people with great power and standing, but that does not stop God's work. If you are called to speak about your faith before influential people, trust that God is with you, as he was with Peter.
exp.3:6:
This verse tells us that the Jewish leaders had Peter and John brought in and began to question them: "By what power or what name did you do this?" The word "power" here means power or authority. The question is asked directly to the two apostles, so the leaders want an answer from them about how the healing happened.

The ones asking are the leaders of the people, the elders, the scribes, and the chief priests, gathered in Jerusalem. Peter and John had just healed a lame man at the temple and had spoken to the crowd about Jesus. The leaders wanted to know where this power came from, and they also wanted to stop what was happening. Peter's answer comes right away.
