For today: if someone asks us why we live the way we do, we can answer with simplicity and courage. There is no need to boast about ourselves; we can humbly say that everything good comes from Jesus.
exp.17:5:
He says that when some Jews opposed Paul and insulted him, he shook out his garments as a sign of rejection. He told them that if they were lost, the responsibility would be theirs, and that he was innocent of it. From that moment he would devote himself to the Gentiles, that is, to those who were not Jews. The word "insulted" in the verse refers to speaking abusively, in this case against Jesus.

Paul is in Corinth. He had been teaching in the synagogue every Sabbath, and when Silas and Timothy arrived he gave himself completely to proclaiming that Jesus is the Christ. Faced with opposition, he uses a gesture familiar in his culture to say that he had already done his duty. Even so, the house of Justus, next to the synagogue, and the faith of Crispus show that the door was not fully closed.

Today, let us speak about Jesus with clarity and love, but without carrying the decision of others. God asks us for faithfulness; it is He who changes hearts.
exp.27:1:
The islanders showed Paul and his companions extraordinary kindness. They built a fire and welcomed everyone there, because it was raining and cold.

Luke, the author of the book, tells the story as someone who was part of the group, since he was traveling with Paul. They had just survived a terrible shipwreck and arrived on the island of Malta, also called Melita, soaked and exhausted. Luke highlights the kindness of these strangers as God's care in the middle of their trial.

Today we can imitate that simple goodness. A practical gesture, such as offering food, warm clothing, or a place to rest, can be a great comfort to someone going through a hard time, even if we do not know them.
exp.12:41:
This verse tells us that as Paul and Barnabas were leaving the synagogue, the people urged them to continue this message on the next Sabbath.

Paul had just preached in Antioch of Pisidia. He had explained that Jesus is the fulfillment of God's promises and that through him there is forgiveness. He ended with a warning taken from the prophets: not to despise the work of God. The people's request shows that the message had stirred a real desire to hear more.

For today: when you hear the Word of God and your heart is stirred, do not let it pass. Ask for more, seek to hear it again, and give it a steady place in your week.
exp.14:21:
This verse says that the apostles, the elders, and the whole church in Jerusalem decided to choose men from among themselves and send them to Antioch together with Paul and Barnabas. The men they chose were Judas, called Barsabbas, and Silas. The phrase "two leaders among the brothers" describes men who were respected and trusted among the believers. The word "decided" shows that they reached their choice by common agreement.

Luke recounts here what happened after the council in Jerusalem. The question under discussion was whether non-Jewish believers should be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. A decision had already been made, and now two messengers were sent with a letter, so that the news would arrive clearly and not only by the word of Paul and Barnabas.

For today: when there are disagreements in the church or in the family, let us seek to decide together, with humility, and communicate decisions clearly and through trustworthy people.
exp.25:12:
Paul tells how, around noon and while he was on the road, he saw a light from heaven brighter than the sun. That light shone around him and his companions.

Paul speaks before King Agrippa while he is in custody, and explains how his life changed. Before, he persecuted Christians with violence. He was on his way to Damascus with permission from the religious leaders when Jesus appeared to him. By saying "about noon," he emphasizes that it was not a dream or something vague, but a real and very clear encounter.

For today: no one is so far away that God cannot reach them. If today you feel lost or guilty about your past, Jesus can find you and give you a new direction.
exp.4:37:
Here the verse says that the Jewish leaders should leave the apostles alone. "Leave these men alone" means "don't get involved with them." "Purpose" means plan or aim, and "endeavor" is their activity. If all of this comes only from people, "it will fail," that is, it will come to an end and disappear on its own.

The speaker is Gamaliel, a highly respected teacher of the law, speaking before the Sanhedrin. The apostles had been arrested for preaching about Jesus, and some wanted to kill them. Gamaliel recalls earlier cases of leaders who failed, and he calls for calm and patience.

For today: before reacting with fear or anger to something we do not understand, it is good to wait and pray. Over time the fruit will be seen. And we should examine our own plans: do they seek to please God, or only ourselves?
exp.22:5:
Paul is standing before the Jewish council, called the Sanhedrin. He notices that some of the members are Sadducees and others are Pharisees, and he calls out: "Brothers, I am a Pharisee, the son of a Pharisee." He says that he is on trial because of his hope in the resurrection of the dead. "Called out" means that he spoke loudly, and "brothers" is a respectful way of addressing his fellow countrymen.

Paul had been arrested in Jerusalem and was now trying to defend himself. The Sadducees denied the resurrection, the angels, and the spirits; the Pharisees believed in all of these. Scholars debate whether Paul wanted to divide them with cunning or whether he was truly pointing to the center of his message. Perhaps both. For him, the resurrection of Jesus was the hope of Israel.

Today we can learn to go to the heart of our faith when we are questioned. In the middle of arguments, it is good to remember what is essential: the hope we have in the risen Christ, and to speak of it with clarity and courage.
exp.24:4:
Festus tells the Jewish leaders who are able to come down with him to Caesarea. There, if Paul has truly done anything wrong, they are to bring formal charges against him. The word "man" in this verse is simply the word for a man, and the word for crime refers to a serious offense. The phrase "bring charges" describes what those who accuse him are to do.

Festus, the new Roman governor, is the one speaking. The Jewish leaders had asked him as a favor to transfer Paul to Jerusalem, but in secret they were preparing an ambush to kill him on the way. Festus does not give in to that request and answers with a legal order: Paul will remain in Caesarea, and whoever has evidence must present it there, before the court.

For today: when someone accuses us, what is right is to seek a clear process, with proof and without gossip. And we should avoid accusing others without evidence. God cares for his people even by using imperfect authorities.
exp.25:8:
Paul explains that, before he came to know Christ, he was convinced that he ought to do all he could to oppose the name of Jesus of Nazareth. He says "I was convinced," meaning he sincerely believed it was his duty. He was not acting out of mere whim, but out of a mistaken conviction.

Paul is speaking before King Agrippa while he defends himself against the accusations of the Jews. He wants to show that he himself was a fierce opponent of the Christians. For this reason his change is not explained by custom or convenience, but by his encounter with the risen Jesus, which he describes next.

We can be very sure of something and still be wrong. Today it is wise to examine our convictions in the light of Christ and his Word, with humility. If God corrects us, we can change without fear, as Paul did.
exp.13:14:
Paul and Barnabas say to the crowd: "Men, why are you doing this?" They make clear that they are only men, human like everyone there. Their message is good news: the people should turn away from these worthless things and turn to the living God. He made heaven and earth and sea and everything in them. The idea of turning from something means changing direction.

In Lystra, Paul had healed a man who could not walk. The crowd thought Paul and Barnabas were gods, and the priest of Jupiter wanted to offer sacrifices to them. The apostles, deeply distressed, tore their clothes and rushed toward the people to stop them. They refused the worship and pointed to the Creator.

For today: let us not seek or accept the glory that belongs to God. When something good happens through us, let us give God the honor and direct others toward Him.
exp.6:17:
It says that in Egypt a new king came to power who did not know Joseph. Here "know" does not only mean having heard his name: it means that he did not acknowledge or value what Joseph had done for Egypt.

Stephen speaks this, before the Jewish council, while he is being accused. He reviews the history of Israel to show how God faithfully worked despite difficulties. This verse marks the turning point: from the welcome given to Joseph we move to the oppression of the people. Scholars do not agree on which king it was, and it is not wise to state a name.

For today: people easily forget the good they have received, but God does not forget. If you find yourself in an environment where no one recognizes your effort, keep trusting that God keeps his promises. And you, strive to be grateful to those who have helped you.
exp.4:12:
It says that, although the people regarded the apostles highly, no one else dared to join them. The verse says "dared," so the verse's word here is the same idea. Even so, the people in general spoke very well of them and held them in high regard. There was distance on one side and admiration on the other.

Luke, the author of Acts, relates what happened after Ananias and Sapphira died for lying to God. That caused great fear in the church. The rest may be unbelievers or, according to some, other members who did not dare to join the apostles in Solomon's porch. Scholars interpret this in different ways. Even so, the people praised them, and many more kept on believing.

For today: live honestly before God, without pretending. A sincere and reverent faith can earn respect, even though some prefer to keep their distance.
exp.19:11:
They brought the boy home alive, and the people were greatly relieved. "Boy" here refers to the young man, and the verse says he was taken home alive.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells what happened in Troas. Eutychus had fallen asleep while Paul preached late into the night, fell from a third-story window, and was picked up dead. Paul went down, embraced him, and said that his life was in him. Then he went on with the meeting. The text does not explain the exact manner of the miracle, but it shows that God restored life and brought great relief to the people.

For today: when we go through times of pain or fear, let us remember that God knows how to comfort his people. We can draw near to those who suffer with our presence, embraces, and prayer, without waiting to have all the answers.
exp.24:17:
This verse says that when Paul's accusers rose to speak, they did not charge him with any of the crimes that Festus had expected. Here "expected" means that he assumed or imagined there would be serious offenses, such as crimes or rebellion.

It is Governor Festus who speaks, telling King Agrippa how he handled Paul's case. He wants to show that he acted fairly, following the Roman custom that the accused face his accusers and be able to defend himself. According to Festus, the problem was not a crime but religious disputes about Jesus, whom Paul said was alive.

For today: before judging someone, let us listen calmly and check the facts. We often assume the worst about others without evidence. We can also trust that God cares for those who suffer unjust accusations because of their faith.
exp.12:26:
The people of Jerusalem and their leaders did not recognize Jesus. They also failed to grasp the words of the prophets, which were read aloud in the synagogue every Sabbath. Without realizing it, by condemning Jesus they fulfilled those very prophecies.

The apostle Paul is speaking in the synagogue in Antioch of Pisidia. He addresses Jews and God-fearing Gentiles. He wants to show them that Jesus is the promised Savior. What happened at the cross was not an unexpected defeat but part of the plan God had announced in the Scriptures.

For today: it is not enough to hear the Bible often; we must listen with humility and an open heart. Ask God to help you understand what you read and to recognize Jesus in its pages.
exp.26:33:
Paul urges everyone on the ship to eat something for your own preservation, meaning to regain their strength and survive. He assures them that not a single hair of their head will be lost. It is a way of saying that no one would die.

Paul speaks as a prisoner headed for Rome, in the middle of a storm that had lasted two weeks. The people were exhausted, frightened, and without any desire to eat. Earlier, an angel had told him that God would save the lives of everyone. So Paul encourages them with confidence, and then sets the example by eating and giving thanks to God.

For today: when we trust God's promises, we should also take care of practical matters. Faith and common sense go together. Eat, rest, and ask for help, and encourage others with your calm example.
exp.13:9:
In a loud voice, Paul tells the man, "Stand up on your feet!" The man jumps up and begins to walk. The loud voice is Paul's command, and walking means the man starts moving on his own two feet.

This happens in Lystra, a city where Paul and Barnabas were preaching. The man had been lame from birth and had never walked. Paul looked at him and saw that he had faith to be healed. The Bible does not explain how he knew. Soon after, the people believed that Paul and Barnabas were gods, and they had to correct them.

For today: God can work in our weakness when we trust in him. But the glory belongs to God, not to the people he uses. If God helps you through someone, thank him and serve with humility.
exp.26:43:
Some of them, who could not swim, were to get to shore by holding on to planks and various parts of the broken ship. In this way, just as God had promised, everyone reached land safely. "The rest" refers to those who could not swim, and "parts of the ship" refers to the remains of the vessel.

Luke, who was traveling with Paul, describes the shipwreck on the way to Rome. The soldiers wanted to kill the prisoners so that none of them could escape, but the centurion wanted to save Paul and stopped them. Earlier, an angel had told Paul that no one would die (Acts 27:22-24). So this verse shows that promise being kept, even in the middle of a storm.

God can keep His promises using simple means, even pieces of a broken ship. When everything seems lost, trust His word and hold on to whatever He places within your reach, even if it seems small.
exp.1:1:
Acts 2:2 says that suddenly a sound like a mighty rushing wind came from heaven and filled the whole house where they were sitting. Note that the text says the sound was "like" a wind, meaning it resembled one, but it does not say it was an ordinary wind.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells what happened on the day of Pentecost, a Jewish festival. Jesus' disciples were gathered together and were waiting for what Jesus had promised them: the coming of the Holy Spirit. This sound was the first sign that God was beginning to fulfill that promise.

For today: God acts in his own time and often surprises us. We can imitate those disciples: pray and wait together, with unity and trust, instead of rushing things on our own.
exp.11:4:
Peter was closely guarded in prison, and the church, for its part, was earnestly praying to God for him, continually and with urgency. The word "guarded" here means kept under custody and watch.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells what happened after King Herod had James put to death and arrested Peter. Herod wanted to please the Jews and planned to bring Peter before the people after the Passover. Four squads of four soldiers guarded him in shifts. Humanly speaking, there was no way out.

For today: when you face something you cannot control, do not stop praying, and make that prayer together with other believers. God can act in ways we do not expect, even though he does not always answer as we ask.
exp.4:16:
He says that the high priest and all his associates, who belonged to the party of the Sadducees, rose up filled with jealousy. Here the word means envy and resentment at what was happening with the apostles, not a healthy eagerness. The high priest is the chief priest of the nation, and the Sadducees were a religious party.

The one telling this is Luke, the author of the book. Earlier he has shown that God was healing very many sick people through the apostles, and that people were coming in from the surrounding towns. The Sadducees, who did not believe in the resurrection, saw that the message of the risen Jesus was gaining strength. So they reacted by arresting the apostles.

For today: examine your heart when someone else is blessed or used by God. If you feel jealousy, bring it before the Lord and ask him to teach you to rejoice in God's work, even when it is not done through you.
exp.18:2:
Paul asks these disciples, "Into what, then, were you baptized?" In other words, "What baptism did you receive?" They answer that they were baptized into John's baptism, the baptism of John the Baptist.

Paul had arrived in Ephesus and found some believers who had not even heard of the Holy Spirit. So he asks them this question: he wanted to understand what they had received and what they knew. Their answer shows that they knew only the message of John, who called people to repentance and pointed to Jesus. Afterward Paul explained to them, and they were baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus.

For today: it is good to ask ourselves, with humility, how much we know about Jesus and his work. If our understanding is lacking, there is no need to be ashamed; we can keep learning with an open heart.
exp.7:16:
What the verse says: Peter and John placed their hands on the believers in Samaria, and they received the Holy Spirit. Laying on hands means putting your hands on someone while you pray for them.

Context: Philip had brought the good news to Samaria, and many believed and were baptized. When the apostles in Jerusalem heard about it, they sent Peter and John. Luke, the author, tells us that the Spirit had not yet come upon them. Not everyone explains this the same way: some see a unique moment to unite the Samaritans with the Jewish church; others think it is a pattern for everyone. The text does not settle the question completely.

For today: God wants us to live in fellowship with his people. Pray for other believers, welcome them with kindness, and remember that the Spirit is a gift from God, not something that is bought or controlled.
exp.18:14:
The verse says that the evil spirit answered the sons of Sceva. It recognized Jesus and Paul, but not them. The words "Jesus I know" and "I know about Paul" show that it knew who they were. The word "But" starts the spirit's reply, and the question "but who are you?" shows that these men had no real authority.

The evil spirit speaks through the man who was possessed. In Ephesus, some traveling exorcists tried to use the name of Jesus as a formula, without knowing him personally. They had seen Paul's miracles and wanted to copy them. The result was a public defeat, and that made the name of Jesus respected.

For today: following Jesus is not repeating words or imitating others. It is knowing him and living in a real relationship with him. Ask yourself whether your faith is your own or only borrowed.
exp.9:22:
This verse tells how Peter welcomed the men sent by Cornelius and invited them to stay as his guests in the house. The next day he got ready and set out with them. Some of the brothers from Joppa went along with him. The verse comments on two words from the verse: the word for "went" simply means he went, and the place name refers to the city of Joppa.

Peter was in Joppa, where God had just shown him the vision of the sheet with animals. The men sent by Cornelius, a centurion who feared God, arrived looking for him. The Spirit had already told him to go with them without hesitation. So Peter takes them in as guests and then sets out. The brothers who accompany him will later serve as witnesses of what happened.

Today we can learn to receive kindly those who are different from us, and not to go alone when God leads us toward something new. Asking other believers to go with us gives support, wisdom, and testimony.
exp.9:24:
This verse says that when Peter arrived at the house of Cornelius, Cornelius came out to meet him. He fell down at Peter's feet to worship him, that is, he bowed low in a sign of deep respect and reverence.

Luke, the author of Acts, recounts the moment. Cornelius was a Roman officer who feared God, and he had received a vision asking him to call for Peter. He had gathered his family and friends to hear him. His gesture shows great respect, although Peter corrects him right away, since only God should receive worship. Some think Cornelius acted out of exaggerated honor; the text says nothing more about his intention.

Today we can respect and value those who guide us in the faith, but without putting them in the place of God. Like Peter, let us be humble when others admire us, and always give God the glory.
exp.9:2:
He had a clear vision, not a confused dream. It happened around the ninth hour, which is about three in the afternoon. An angel of God came to where he was and called him by name: "Cornelius!" The phrase "clear vision" means that he saw it plainly.

Cornelius was a Roman officer, a centurion, who was not a Jew. Even so, he feared God, helped the poor, and prayed regularly. Luke, the author of Acts, tells this to prepare for the moment when the good news reaches non-Jews. According to the next verse, the angel tells him that God has taken notice of his prayers and his generosity.

God sees those who seek him sincerely, even when they seem far away. Today we can keep praying and doing good with steadiness, trusting that God hears us. We can also treat with respect those who are seeking God.
exp.26:14:
What the verse says: A violent storm seized the ship, and the wind pushed it with such force that the crew could not steer into it. The ship was caught up and carried along. So the sailors gave up fighting the wind and let themselves be driven along.

Context: Luke speaks, traveling with Paul, a prisoner bound for Rome. The journey began with a gentle wind that encouraged the crew to continue, but it changed suddenly into a fierce storm. Luke recounts what they experienced, and shows that there were moments when they could no longer control anything.

For today: There are situations we cannot control, no matter how hard we try. When they come, we can stop fighting what is impossible and place everything in God's hands. In this same story, God took care of Paul and of everyone who was with him.
exp.14:40:
This verse says that Paul traveled through the regions of Syria and Cilicia, strengthening the churches that already existed there. "Traveled through" means he journeyed across those lands. "Strengthening" means building up, encouraging, and giving firmness in the faith.

The one who tells this is Luke, the author of Acts. Paul and Barnabas had just separated because of a sharp disagreement over whether to take Mark along. Barnabas went to Cyprus with Mark, and Paul set out with Silas. Although there was pain, the work did not stop: there were now two teams on the way. Syria and Cilicia were near Antioch, and Paul probably knew that area well.

Even after a painful conflict, God can keep using his people. If today you suffer over a difference with someone, do not abandon the service. Seek to encourage others in the faith, with humility and without resentment.
exp.10:28:
So the believers in Antioch, on hearing that a great famine was coming, decided to help the brothers in Judea. Each one gave according to what they could. The word "relief" means help, in this case material help or money. "Decided" means that they made up their minds to do it.

The one who tells the story is Luke, the author of Acts. Agabus, a prophet who came down from Jerusalem, had announced by the Spirit that a great famine would come, which according to the text happened in the time of the emperor Claudius. The believers in Antioch, most of them not Jews, responded with love toward the Jewish Christians in Judea. They sent the help with Barnabas and Saul.

For today: giving does not depend on how much we have, but on a willing heart. Think of someone in need near you and help them with what you can, without comparing yourself to others.
exp.21:10:
He says that Paul was blinded by the brilliance of the light, so he could not find his own way, and his companions led him by the hand into Damascus.

Paul speaks in Jerusalem, before an angry crowd, and tells how he met Jesus on the road to Damascus. He wants to make clear that his change was not his own idea but something God did. His blindness shows that the great persecutor of Christians was left helpless. He arrived in the city not as a leader with authority, but guided by others.

For today: sometimes God stops us and takes away our sense of security to teach us to depend on Him. If you are in a time of confusion or weakness, do not reject it. Accept the help of others and wait for the next step God will show you.
exp.7:6:
This verse tells what happened in Samaria when Philip was preaching. Many people were controlled by unclean spirits, which are evil spirits, and these came out with loud shrieks. In addition, many who were paralyzed (who could not move their bodies) and lame (who could not walk well) were healed.

The one speaking here is Luke, the author of Acts, who is telling the story. Philip had arrived in Samaria, a region that many Jews looked down on, and there he proclaimed Christ. The signs that accompanied his message showed that God was backing that news, and the people listened closely. The result, according to the next verse, was great joy in the city.

For today: God cares for people whom others leave aside. We can carry the message of Christ to those who seem distant, with love and without prejudice, trusting that God knows how to work in their lives.
exp.1:33:
Peter explains that David did not ascend into heaven, meaning that David's words were not speaking about himself. David said: "The Lord said to my Lord, 'Sit at My right hand.'" The right hand is the place of honor and authority.

Peter speaks at Pentecost, before a crowd in Jerusalem. He quotes Psalm 110:1 to show that this passage was not fulfilled in David, who died and was buried, but in Jesus, raised from the dead. In this way Peter teaches that Jesus is the Lord and the promised Messiah, and that he reigns alongside God.

For today: if Jesus lives and reigns, you can entrust your worries to him without fear. When you feel that everything is out of control, remember that Christ is in the place of greatest authority, and hand that matter over to him in prayer.
exp.8:5:
The verse shows Saul trembling and amazed after hearing the voice of Jesus. He asks, "Lord, what do you want me to do?" In other words, he is ready to obey. Jesus tells him to get up, go into the city, and there he will be told what he must do. The word "must" in that answer refers to the path that now belongs to him.

Saul was on his way to Damascus, and until then he had been persecuting the followers of Jesus. Jesus himself spoke to him from heaven and stopped him. The one speaking here is Saul, who would later be known as Paul, and then the Lord answers. His question shows that his heart had changed at the voice of Christ.

For today: when you do not clearly know what the next step is, come to Jesus with humility and a willingness to obey. Sometimes He does not show the whole way at once, but only the step that comes next. Take that step with confidence.
exp.21:8:
The verse says that Paul's companions saw the bright light and were filled with fear, but could not understand the voice speaking to him. "Could not understand" means they did not grasp what was being said. "Were filled with fear" means they were badly frightened.

Paul speaks to a crowd in Jerusalem, after being arrested in the temple. He tells them how he met Jesus on the road to Damascus, when he was persecuting Christians. Some scholars point out that Acts 9:7 says they heard the voice but saw no one; there are several possible explanations, such as that they heard a sound without understanding the words.

Today we can remember that God speaks in a personal way. Two people can be in the same place and experience different things. Do not doubt your encounter with God because others do not perceive it the same way.
exp.12:16:
It says that the God of Israel chose the people's ancestors, made the people grow into a great nation while they lived as foreigners in Egypt, and with uplifted strength led them out of that land. "He made them into a great people" describes God's work of growing them and making them strong. "With an uplifted arm" is an expression that speaks of God's power acting on their behalf.

Paul is speaking in the synagogue at Antioch of Pisidia. The leaders gave him the chance to speak after the reading of the Law and the Prophets. He begins by going over the history of Israel, starting with the choosing and the deliverance from Egypt, to prepare his listeners to understand that Jesus is the fulfillment of that history.

For today: God acts before we deserve it. If you remember how He has sustained and rescued you in other times, you can trust Him now, and speak of His faithfulness to others with gratitude.
exp.14:8:
He says that God made no distinction between the believing Jews (the "we" of the verse) and the Gentiles (the "they" of the verse). He treated them all the same, because he cleansed their hearts through faith. Cleansing means making something clean on the inside.

Peter speaks at the council in Jerusalem. There was a great dispute: some said that Gentiles had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses in order to be saved. Peter reminds them that God himself gave the Holy Spirit to the Gentiles, just as he did to the Jews, without first requiring those conditions. That showed what God thought of them.

For today: God accepts us through faith, not because of our background, culture, or merits. For that reason, let us not place extra conditions on those who come to Christ; let us receive them with the same grace with which we ourselves were received.
exp.21:21:
The crowd in Jerusalem listened to Paul closely until he mentioned being sent to the Gentiles. Then they lifted up their voices and shouted, "Rid the earth of him! He is not fit to live!"

Paul is speaking to the Jews in the temple, defending himself after being arrested. He tells them about his conversion and how Jesus sent him to the non-Jews. That message offended those who thought God's promise was only for their own people.

For today: let us examine whether we listen with an open heart or only while it suits us. God sometimes loves people we did not expect, and we should ask him for humility so that we do not reject his work out of prejudice.
exp.15:36:
Paul replied to the officers that they had beaten him and Silas in public, without a trial, even though they were Roman citizens, and had thrown them into prison. Now the officers want to send them away quietly, and Paul says absolutely not. He insists that the magistrates come themselves and escort them out. The word "publicly" means in front of others, not in secret, and the officers who carried out the magistrates' orders are the ones who dealt with the prisoners.

Paul speaks in Philippi, after spending the night in prison with Silas. They had been beaten and imprisoned without a trial, something Roman law protected citizens from suffering. Paul does not complain out of a desire for revenge. By publicly claiming his right, he makes clear that they were not criminals, and this protected the new believers in Philippi. Interpreters often see it this way, though the text does not state it in so many words.

For today: we can ask for justice with firmness and respect, without aggression, when we seek to protect others and not only ourselves.
exp.17:12:
The Jews bring a charge against Paul before the court. They say that this man is persuading people to worship God in ways that are against the law. "Persuade" means to convince, and "worship God" means to honor and serve him. They do not make clear which law they mean.

The ones speaking are the Jews of Corinth who rejected Paul's message. They bring him before Gallio, the Roman governor of Achaia. They probably wanted Rome to see Paul as a danger. Since Roman law tolerated Judaism, they may have meant that Paul was teaching something illegal. Gallio understood that this was an internal religious dispute and chose not to get involved.

Today, when someone accuses us for following Christ, let us remember that God is still at work. Let us respond with calm and without hatred, and keep serving God with sincerity and respect.
exp.1:26:
He says that God would not abandon the soul of the Holy One to Hades, the place of the dead, and would not let his body see decay, that is, fall apart in the tomb.

Peter speaks at Pentecost, days after Jesus' resurrection. He quotes Psalm 16, written by David, and explains that David was not speaking only of himself, since his tomb was still there and his body had died. Peter understands that the promise was fully fulfilled in Jesus, the Holy One of God, whom God raised up.

For today: if Jesus overcame death, your hope is not fragile. When you face loss, fear, or pain, trust that God does not abandon his own, and live with the peace that the tomb does not have the final word.
exp.20:0:
After saying goodbye to the elders of Ephesus, Paul and his companions sailed directly to the island of Cos. The next day they went on to Rhodes, and from there to Patara, a port on the south coast of what is now Turkey.

The one telling the story is Luke, the author of Acts. That is why the account says "we sailed": he was traveling with Paul. This journey moves toward Jerusalem, and the earlier farewell had been very painful. This verse shows the mission advancing step by step.

For today: following God's will often means moving forward one day at a time, even when the goodbyes are costly. Take the step in front of you and trust that God is guiding you.
exp.18:12:
What it says: Some Jewish men who travelled from town to town casting out evil spirits tried to use the name of Jesus to do the same. "Itinerant exorcists" were men who drove out evil spirits and moved from place to place. "Tried to invoke" means they attempted to call on the name of the Lord Jesus. Notice that they said "Jesus, whom Paul proclaims", as if Jesus belonged to Paul and not to them.

Context: Luke, the narrator of Acts, tells this in Ephesus, after the powerful works that God was doing through Paul. These exorcists saw results and wanted to imitate them, treating the name of Jesus as a useful formula. The next verse shows that it did not go well for them.

For today: Faith in Jesus is not repeating borrowed words or depending on another person's faith. It is knowing him personally. Ask yourself: do I know Jesus, or do I only speak about him the way others do?
exp.0:22:
This verse tells us that the believers proposed two men to take the place of Judas among the apostles. The first was Joseph, called Barsabbas, who was also known as Justus. The second was Matthias. The word for "proposed" here means that they put the two men forward as candidates. The name "Justus" was an additional name given to Joseph, a kind of nickname.

Peter had just explained that the replacement had to be someone who had been with Jesus from the baptism of John until his ascension. In this way he could be a witness of the resurrection. About a hundred and twenty people were gathered together, waiting for what Jesus had promised them. The Bible gives no further details here about Joseph and Matthias.

For today: before deciding something important, let us use good judgment, but also pray and ask God to guide us, as they did in the verse that follows.
exp.18:19:
This verse says that the word of the Lord spread powerfully and prevailed. "Spread" means that it reached more and more people and gained new followers. "Prevailed" means that it won out, that it carried more weight than what stood against it.

Here Luke, the author of Acts, summarizes what happened in Ephesus, a city with a great deal of magic practice. Several believers confessed their sins, and those who had practiced magic and occult arts burned their books, which were worth fifty thousand denarii. A denarius was roughly the pay for one day of work. Luke shows that the word of the Lord visibly transformed lives.

For today: the word of the Lord keeps spreading in us when we let go of what pulls us away from Him. Ask Him to show you something you should give up, and do it with sincerity.
exp.12:0:
This verse introduces the leaders of the church in Antioch. They are called "prophets and teachers," meaning people who spoke for God and taught the faith. Five are named: Barnabas, Simeon (called Niger), Lucius of Cyrene, Manaen (who had been brought up with Herod the tetrarch), and Saul.

Here the author, Luke, describes what that church was like. It was a diverse group, with people from different places and different backgrounds. The verses that follow show that while they were serving the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit called them to send out Barnabas and Saul on a mission. This is the beginning of the missionary journeys.

For today: God can use very different people when they are united in service and prayer. Let us seek his direction together as a community, and be willing to listen and obey.
exp.6:0:
It says that the high priest, here called the chief of the priests, asks Stephen a direct question: "Are these charges true?" He wants to know whether the accusations just brought against him are true.

Stephen is standing before the Sanhedrin, the religious council of Israel. Some witnesses accused him of speaking against the temple and the law of Moses (Acts 6:11-14). The high priest gives him the chance to defend himself, and Stephen responds by going through the history of Israel, beginning with Abraham.

For today: when someone questions us about our faith, we can respond calmly and on the basis of God's Word, without fear and without giving offense. Knowing well what God has done helps us give a serene and faithful answer.
exp.14:5:
This verse says that the apostles and the elders of the church met together to look carefully into an important question. The word "matter" can sound unusual today; here it does not mean money, but a question or problem that needed to be settled. To "look into" it means to study it and weigh it carefully.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells what happened in Jerusalem. Some believers who came from the Pharisee party taught that converted Gentiles had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. This caused great division. That is why the leaders came together, and afterward there was much discussion, as the next verse shows, before Peter spoke.

For today: when serious disagreements arise in the church or in the family, we should not ignore them or settle them by shouting. It is better to meet together, listen with humility, seek God's guidance in his Word, and decide together with patience.
exp.3:35:
This verse introduces a man named Joseph, whom the apostles called Barnabas, a name that means "Son of Encouragement." He was a Levite, from the tribe responsible for service in the temple, and he came from Cyprus.

Luke, the author of Acts, describes how the believers shared their possessions so that no one went without. As a concrete example, he presents Barnabas, who sold a piece of property and gave the money to the apostles. His name will appear later as an important companion of Paul. Some scholars think the nickname describes his character, though the text gives no further detail.

Today we can ask ourselves whom we might encourage this week. A kind word, a visit, or a practical help can be a simple way to be "sons of encouragement."
exp.20:25:
Paul accepts the advice of James and the elders. The next day he takes four men who had made a vow, purifies himself together with them, and enters the temple. There he gives notice to the priests of the date when their purification would be complete, that is, when the offering would be made for each one. The words "shave their heads" refer to the end of that vow.

The leaders of Jerusalem wanted to calm the rumors that Paul taught people to abandon the law of Moses. With this act, Paul showed respect for his Jewish heritage. Commentators discuss whether it was a wise decision or a risk; the text does not judge it. Shortly afterward, the crowd was stirred up by a false accusation.

We may yield in customs and preferences so as not to hinder others, without giving up the truth of the gospel. But it is good to ask for wisdom, because doing good does not always prevent misunderstandings.
exp.20:20:
Some Jewish believers had heard a rumor about Paul: that he was teaching the Jews who lived among the Gentiles to turn away from the law of Moses. According to the rumor, he told them not to circumcise their children or to observe our customs. The phrase "under the impression" tells us this was what they believed, not necessarily what was true, and "our customs" refers to the traditions the Jewish people kept.

Paul has just arrived in Jerusalem and reports what God has done among the Gentiles. James and the elders rejoice, but they warn him that thousands of Jewish believers are zealous for the law and have heard this rumor. Paul's letters show that he did not require Gentiles to be circumcised, but there is no evidence here that he forbade these customs to Jews. The rumor seems to be exaggerated.

Today, before we believe or repeat something about someone, it is wise to ask them directly and seek the truth. A rumor can divide the church, but humility and dialogue help keep the unity.
exp.4:32:
This verse says that the members of the council, on hearing the apostles, were filled with fury. The phrase "enraged" in this verse expresses a very strong anger, the kind that makes a person's whole body tense with rage. That is why they resolved to put the apostles to death.

Peter and the other apostles had been arrested for continuing to preach about Jesus. Before the council, they declared that God raised Jesus and offers forgiveness to Israel. Those words not only defended the apostles, but also pointed to the guilt of the leaders. That is why they reacted with anger instead of repentance. Afterward, Gamaliel stepped in to calm the situation.

When the truth makes us uncomfortable, we can get angry or let God correct us. Let us ask for humility to listen, to recognize our mistakes, and to change, instead of defending ourselves with pride.
exp.25:5:
He says that Paul is on trial because of the hope in the promise that God made to the ancestors of the people of Israel. "Ancestors" is the sense of "fathers" here. The phrase "I stand on trial" means that he is being brought before a court. "Promise" points to what God promised, and from what follows in the passage, it includes the resurrection of the dead.

Paul speaks before King Agrippa and Governor Festus, in Caesarea. Earlier he recalls that he lived as a Pharisee, a very strict group within Judaism. He wants to show that his faith does not break away from Israel, but follows the hope that God gave to his people. The Jews accuse him precisely for proclaiming that hope fulfilled in Jesus.

For today: hope in God's promises can give us firmness when we are misunderstood or criticized. We can ask ourselves which promise of God sustains our lives and speak about it calmly and with respect.
exp.0:11:
This verse tells us that the disciples went back to Jerusalem from the Mount of Olives, which is near the city. The distance is described as a Sabbath day's journey, a measure used at that time that equals the distance people were allowed to walk on the day of rest, roughly one thousand meters.

Luke, the author of Acts, recounts what happened just after Jesus ascended into heaven. Two men dressed in white, commonly understood as angels, had told the disciples to stop looking up to the sky, since Jesus would return. Now they obey and go back to the city, where Jesus had asked them to wait.

For today: after a special moment with God, we do not stay only looking at the sky. We return to everyday life, obey step by step, and seek the company of other believers to pray.
exp.13:18:
It says that some Jews arrived there from Antioch and Iconium, cities where Paul had already preached. They won over the crowds in Lystra, stoned Paul, and dragged him outside the city, presuming he was dead. The word "won over" means they convinced the people.

Luke, the author of Acts, recounts this moment. Shortly before, the people of Lystra had wanted to worship Paul and Barnabas as gods because of a healing. Now the same crowd changes and turns against Paul. Some scholars think Paul was seriously injured; the text only says they presumed he was dead, and then he got up and returned to the city.

For today: do not depend on people's applause, because it changes quickly. Serve God faithfully, even when you are rejected, and trust that he sustains you to keep going forward.
exp.16:16:
What it says: Paul spoke and reasoned with others about his faith. Here "reasoned" does not mean arguing angrily, but discussing and explaining with careful thought. He did this in the synagogue with the Jews and with God-fearing Gentiles, meaning non-Jewish people who worshiped the God of Israel alongside the Jews. He also talked every day in the marketplace with whoever he happened to meet.

Context: Luke, the author of Acts, tells what Paul did while he was waiting for Silas and Timothy in Athens. He was deeply troubled to see the city full of idols. So he did not stay silent. He spoke both with people who knew the Scriptures and with people from the street, and this later led him to speak with the philosophers.

For today: When something troubles you in your surroundings, do not stay silent or shut yourself away. Speak about your faith with respect and clarity, both with those who already believe in God and with your neighbors and coworkers you meet each day.
exp.0:4:
Jesus says that John baptized with water, but that the disciples will be baptized with the Holy Spirit within a few days. The word "indeed" is not needed here, and the phrase "within a few days" matches the wording of your verse.

The one speaking is the risen Jesus, who had appeared to his disciples over forty days. He tells them not to leave Jerusalem and to wait for the promise of the Father. He reminds them of John's baptism to show that something greater is now coming: the Holy Spirit himself would come upon them. Shortly after, the disciples ask about the kingdom of Israel, and Jesus directs them to their mission.

For today: do not depend only on your own strength to serve God. Ask the Holy Spirit to guide you, strengthen you, and give you courage, and learn to wait with confidence for what God has promised.
exp.21:0:
Paul begins his defense with respect: "Brothers and fathers" is a courteous way of addressing his fellow Jews and the senior leaders. "Listen now" asks them to pay attention, and "my defense before you" refers to the verse he is about to present.

Paul has just been arrested in Jerusalem, in the temple, because a furious crowd thought he was speaking against the people and the law. A Roman commander rescued him from being beaten, and from the stairs Paul asks permission to speak. He does so in Hebrew, or in Aramaic according to some scholars, and that is why the people grow calm.

For today: when someone attacks us or misunderstands us, we can respond with respect and patience, looking for common ground. A kind word does not guarantee that we will be heard, but it opens doors to give testimony with clarity.
exp.21:6:
Paul recounts that, when he saw the light from heaven, he fell to the ground and heard a voice calling him by his Hebrew name: "Saul, Saul". The voice asked him why he was persecuting. Repeating the name is a way of calling someone with affection and firmness.

Paul is speaking in Jerusalem, before an angry crowd that was accusing him. He defends his story: he himself had persecuted the believers and had taken Christians from Damascus as prisoners. He tells how Jesus stopped him on the road. Notice that Jesus does not ask why he persecutes a teaching, but "why do you persecute Me?". Paul will later learn that Jesus identifies himself with his people.

Today, this reminds us that God reaches us even when we are going in the wrong direction. It also invites us to treat other believers with respect, for Christ is united with them. If we have done harm, we can respond with humility.
exp.9:6:
When the angel who had spoken to Cornelius had gone, he called two of his servants and a devout soldier from among those who attended him.

Here the account tells that, when the angel left, Cornelius called two of his household servants and a soldier who was close to him. The phrase "had gone" describes the angel's departure. "Devout" means a man who honored God.

Cornelius was a Roman officer in Caesarea, who prayed and helped the poor. An angel had told him to send for Peter in Joppa. Here the account shows that Cornelius obeyed at once, and chose trusted people for that journey. What follows in the book of Acts shows that the gospel would also reach non-Jews.

For today: when you sense that God is guiding you, do not put it off. Take a concrete step of obedience, and seek help from trustworthy people who will walk that path with you.
exp.14:37:
This verse says that Paul thought it best not to take Mark with them. "But" is the plain word here, and "thought it best not" means he saw it as a poor idea. Mark had deserted them in Pamphylia and had not accompanied them in the work.

Paul and Barnabas were planning a second journey to visit the churches. Barnabas wanted to give Mark another chance; according to Colossians 4:10, Mark was Barnabas's cousin. Paul thought Mark could not be trusted because he had left earlier. The Bible does not explain why Mark left; people have suggested several reasons, but none can be known for certain. Both men had sincere reasons, and the disagreement separated them.

For today: good believers sometimes disagree. We can defend what we believe is wise, but with humility, remembering that God can work through both paths. Later Paul spoke well of Mark (2 Timothy 4:11).
exp.16:22:
Paul says that as he walked through Athens and looked closely at the objects of worship there, he found an altar with the inscription "To an Unknown God." He tells them that the God they worship without knowing is the one he has come to proclaim to them. "Objects of worship" refers to the sacred places and things the Athenians honored, and "proclaim" means "to tell you clearly and openly."

Paul speaks before the philosophers and the people of Athens at the Areopagus, a place of public debate. They were always eager for new ideas. Paul does not attack them; he starts from something they already knew in order to present the God who created all things. Historians are not completely certain what that altar was like, but Paul uses it as a point of contact.

For today: when you speak about God with others, listen first and look for common ground. Many people have a spiritual hunger, even when they cannot name it. With respect and kindness, you can help them come to know God.
exp.12:21:
God removed Saul as king and put David in his place. God himself spoke well of David: "I have found David, the son of Jesse, a man after my own heart, who will carry out my will in its entirety." After setting Saul aside, God put David on the throne to rule over them.

The speaker is the apostle Paul, in the synagogue at Antioch in Pisidia. He tells them the story of Israel, from the judges to the kings, to lead them to Jesus, a descendant of David. The phrase blends ideas from passages such as Psalm 89:20 and 1 Samuel 13:14. Being "after God's own heart" speaks of a desire to obey him, not of being perfect, since David also failed.

For today: God values a heart willing to obey. When you fail, return to him with humility and keep seeking to do his will.
exp.19:32:
Paul says that he has not wanted anyone's silver, gold, or clothing. To want something that belongs to someone else with a strong, selfish desire is what this kind of wanting means. With this he affirms that his service had no financial motive behind it.

Paul speaks in Miletus with the elders of the church in Ephesus, before saying goodbye to them. He reminds them how he lived among them and prepares them to care for the church without him. The following lines show that he worked with his own hands to meet his needs and to help others, and in this way he gave an example of generosity.

For today: if you serve in the church or in any work alongside others, examine your motives. Ask yourself whether you do it out of love for God and for people, or to gain something. A heart free of covetousness serves with more sincerity and builds trust.
exp.27:7:
This verse tells us that the father of Publius was lying in bed, sick with a fever and dysentery, a serious intestinal infection. Paul went to see him, prayed, placed his hands on him, and healed him. Placing hands on someone was a common way of asking God for help on their behalf.

Luke, the author of Acts, describes what happened on the island of Malta, where Paul and his companions arrived after a shipwreck. Publius, the leading man of the island, had welcomed them kindly for three days. After the viper bite, people already regarded Paul with respect. Luke shows that the healing came after prayer, and that other sick people on the island were healed as well.

For today: when someone shows us kindness, we can respond with care and with prayer for their needs. Praying for others is a simple way of serving, trusting that God is the one who heals.
exp.22:2:
Paul answers the man who ordered him struck with firmness. He says, "God will strike you, you whitewashed wall!" He calls him a whitewashed wall, meaning someone who looks clean on the outside but is corrupt on the inside. He charges him with sitting there to judge Paul according to the law, yet violating the law himself by commanding that Paul be struck.

Paul is standing before the Jewish council, and has just said that he has a good conscience. The high priest Ananias orders that he be struck on the mouth, and Paul reacts with anger. Afterward he says he did not know that this was the high priest, and he acknowledges that Scripture forbids speaking evil of a ruler of the people. Some think his eyesight was poor or that he did not recognize Ananias; the Bible does not make this clear.

For today: one can defend justice with courage, but must watch the tone and show respect. When we react wrongly, the best thing is to acknowledge it with humility.
exp.18:36:
It says that the men the crowd dragged into the theater, Gaius and Aristarchus, had neither robbed the temple nor spoken against the goddess Diana. Those who rob or defile what is considered holy are the ones guilty of such things, and those who insult the goddess are the ones who blaspheme her. The words "you have brought these men here" mean that the people took these men there by force.

The speaker is the town clerk of Ephesus, the city official. The crowd was stirred up by Demetrius and the silversmiths, who feared losing their business because of Paul's preaching. The clerk wants to calm the tumult and keep Rome from punishing the city for a disturbance without legal grounds. His argument shows that Paul's companions had not committed any crime.

For today: when we are accused, it is wise to live in such a way that the accusations have no basis. And when there is a conflict, let us seek to resolve it with calm, truth and order, not with shouting or violence.
exp.23:23:
After several days, Felix returned with his wife Drusilla, who was Jewish. He sent for Paul and listened to him speak about faith in Christ Jesus. "After several days" means that some time had passed since the earlier hearing. "Sent for Paul" means that he had him brought.

Paul was being held in prison at Caesarea, waiting for a decision. Felix already knew something about Christianity and had left the case pending. Now he wants to hear Paul in private. The text does not say why he did this; perhaps out of curiosity or because of Drusilla's influence. Afterward, the account shows that Paul spoke with clarity and that Felix became frightened, but he did not change.

For today: it is not enough to hear the gospel with interest. If God speaks to your heart, respond with sincerity and do not put it off for later.
exp.14:26:
This verse says that the church in Jerusalem sends Judas and Silas along with the letter. They do not only carry the written message, but will also tell you in person the same things the letter says. The phrase "to tell you in person" conveys the same meaning as "to inform you directly."

The apostles and elders of Jerusalem speak here, after gathering together because of the discussion about whether non-Jewish believers had to keep the law of Moses. They wanted the decision to reach Antioch clearly and through trustworthy witnesses, so as to avoid doubts or misunderstandings. Judas and Silas are called prophets later in the chapter.

For today: when there is a disagreement, try to communicate clearly, with humility, and through people you can trust. A message well explained and spoken with love helps to care for unity.
exp.6:49:
This verse is a question that needs no answer: of course God's hand made all things. It comes from Isaiah 66:2. God reminds us that he is the Creator of heaven and earth, so no human building can contain him. The "footstool" is the stool where the feet rest.

Stephen speaks before the Jewish council while they accuse him of speaking against the temple. He reminds them that God was never limited to one place. Right away he rebukes his listeners for resisting the Holy Spirit, as their ancestors did with the prophets.

For today: do not confine God to a place, a temple, or a routine. He is the Creator, and he is near you at home, at work, and on the road. Today, take a moment to speak to him wherever you are.
exp.15:20:
Here the owners of the fortune-telling slave girl accuse Paul and Silas. They say that the two men are promoting customs that are unlawful for Romans to adopt or practice.

The ones speaking are the masters of the girl from whom Paul had cast out a spirit, and so they lost their business. They do not complain about money. Instead, they use a religious and national-pride argument to get the authorities to act. Philippi was a Roman colony, and this could make the accusation stronger. They also present Paul and Silas only as Jews, to stir up prejudice.

Today, people sometimes hide their personal interests behind causes that sound noble. Let us ask God for honesty to examine our own motives, and let us not be surprised when the good we do provokes unjust opposition.
exp.6:53:
This verse says that, when the members of the Sanhedrin heard Stephen's words, they were enraged. The verse states that they were enraged and gnashed their teeth at him, which describes someone clenching and grinding his teeth in anger, showing open hatred toward him.

Stephen was speaking before the council, and he had been falsely accused. He reviewed the history of Israel and concluded that its leaders, like their ancestors, resisted God and had handed over and killed the Righteous One, that is, Jesus. The truth touched their conscience, but instead of repenting, they hardened themselves.

For today: when a truth makes us uncomfortable, we can choose between getting angry or examining our hearts. Let us ask God for humility to hear correction and change, instead of attacking the person who brings it to us.
exp.4:27:
The high priest rebukes the apostles. He reminds them that they had given them strict orders not to teach in this name, that is, in the name of Jesus. He complains that they have filled Jerusalem with their teaching, and he accuses them of determining to make the leaders responsible for the blood of this man.

The high priest speaks before the council. The apostles had been arrested for continuing to teach and heal. The leaders were upset because the teaching placed their responsibility for Jesus's death in the open. Notice that he does not even say the name of Jesus. He also feared the reaction of the people, as the previous verse shows.

For today: when people press us to be silent about what is true, we can respond with respect and firmness, as Peter did. Following God sometimes costs something, but he gives the courage to do it.
exp.21:26:
The commander came to Paul and asked him plainly, "Tell me, are you a Roman citizen?" Paul answered with a single word: "Yes." The term "chief captain" refers to the commander of the military garrison in Jerusalem.

Paul had been arrested after a disturbance in the temple, and they were about to whip him to question him. Then Paul mentioned his Roman citizenship, which protected him from that kind of treatment without a prior trial. The commander wanted to confirm it himself, because binding a Roman citizen was a serious matter.

For today: Paul did not take advantage of his rights out of pride, but so that he could keep carrying out his mission. We can use the legitimate resources we have wisely and without arrogance, asking God to guide us to serve others better and to be faithful to what he has entrusted to us.
exp.25:18:
This verse says that Paul was not disobedient to the vision he saw from heaven. The word "disobedient" means that he did not turn away or refuse to listen. "So then" in this verse connects what Paul says next with what he has just described. Paul tells King Agrippa that, when Jesus appeared to him and called him, he obeyed.

Paul speaks before King Agrippa while he is a prisoner in Caesarea. He recounts how Jesus appeared to him on the road to Damascus and sent him to the Gentiles to open their eyes. Now he explains that he carried out that mission, and for that reason the Jews wanted to kill him.

For today: when we feel that God asks something clear of us, such as forgiving, serving, or speaking about Christ, we can respond with obedience. Obeying is not always easy, but Paul shows us that it is worth saying "yes" to God.
exp.19:9:
Paul went down from the upper floor, threw himself on the young man Eutychus, and embraced him. Then he said to the crowd, "Do not be alarmed! He is still alive!" The phrase "threw himself on" here means that he stretched himself out over him or bent down over him. The "life" in the verse refers to the young man's life. To be alarmed means to be anxious and to make a commotion.

Paul was in Troas, saying farewell to the believers before his journey, and that is why he preached until very late. Eutychus fell asleep, fell from the third floor, and was picked up dead. Paul speaks to calm the frightened brothers. The text does not explain the method, but the account presents it as a miracle: afterward the young man was brought back alive, and everyone was deeply comforted.

God can bring calm and hope in the midst of pain and confusion. When someone beside you is anxious, do not act in panic: come close, embrace them, be a calm presence, and trust that God is still at work.
exp.14:6:
Peter stood up after a very heated argument and spoke to those present as "brothers." He reminded them that, in the early days, God himself made a choice that the Gentiles (those who were not Jews) would hear the message of the gospel from Peter's own lips and come to believe.

This took place at what is called the Council of Jerusalem. Some Pharisees who had come to faith were saying that the Gentiles had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. The apostles and the elders gathered to settle the matter. Peter speaks as a witness: he refers to what happened in the house of Cornelius (Acts 10), where God acted first.

When there are disagreements in the church, let us not start only from our customs or preferences. Let us look at what God has already done and said, and speak with humility, as brothers.
exp.25:14:
Paul recounts that, when he saw the light from heaven, he asked, "Who are You, Lord?" The voice answered that it was Jesus, whom he was persecuting. The word "Lord" here is a title of respect, and Paul was only beginning to understand who was speaking to him.

Paul speaks before King Agrippa and relates his encounter with Jesus on the road to Damascus. He had once persecuted Christians. Jesus says that persecuting his people is persecuting him, because he is united with those who believe in him. Then he calls Paul to serve as a minister and witness.

For today: Jesus is not indifferent to what others go through because of him. We can treat other believers with care and respect, and also be humble enough to recognize when we are wrong. If God corrects us, he can also give us a new purpose.
exp.25:4:
Paul says that the Jewish people who have known him for a long time can testify, if they are willing, that he lived as a Pharisee, adhering to the strictest group within the Jewish religion. The word "sect" here refers to a group or school of thought within Judaism and carries no negative meaning. "For a long time" points to his whole life, from his early years onward.

Paul is speaking before King Agrippa in Caesarea while he defends himself against the accusations of the Jews. He wants to show that he is neither a stranger nor a traitor to his own people. His entire life had been known to them and lived in faithfulness to the faith of Israel. Therefore, believing in Jesus and in the resurrection was not abandoning God's promise, but seeing it fulfilled.

For today: when you share your faith, your testimony carries weight if your life is known and consistent. Live with integrity and humility, so that others see that following Christ is not a passing fashion, but a sincere path.
exp.27:30:
Paul proclaimed that God reigns and taught about the Lord Jesus Christ. "Boldly and freely" means with courage and without holding back.

This is the last verse of the book of Acts. Luke tells it, recounting that Paul arrived in Rome as a prisoner. Although he was under guard, for two years he lived in a rented house and welcomed everyone who came to visit him. Shortly before, some Jews had not accepted his message and argued among themselves. Luke does not say here what happened to Paul afterward, so it is best not to invent it.

For today: even if your circumstances are limited, you can keep speaking about Jesus with courage. Open your home, be kind to those who come, and share simply what Christ has done in your life.
exp.19:14:
This verse describes, step by step, the sea journey of Paul and his companions. They sailed from Mitylene, and the next day they arrived opposite the island of Chios. The day after that they reached the island of Samos. Then they stayed at Trogyllium (some ancient manuscripts do not include this stop), and the next day they came to Miletus.

The one telling the story is Luke, who travels with Paul and uses "we." Paul was returning toward Jerusalem after his third missionary journey. According to the context, he was hurrying to reach Jerusalem for Pentecost, and for that reason he avoided stopping at Ephesus. From Miletus he sent for the elders of that church.

For today: Paul had a clear goal, yet he still cared for the people he loved. We can plan with order and effort, and also leave room to encourage others along the way.
exp.23:22:
Felix, the governor, ordered the centurion to keep Paul under guard, but to allow him some freedom. The verse of "some freedom" is that Paul was to have some of his restrictions eased. The centurion was also to permit Paul's friends to care for his needs and visit him.

This is Luke's account. Paul had been accused before Felix by Jewish leaders. Felix knew quite a bit about the Way and did not want to decide the case right away, so he postponed it. In the meantime, he gave Paul more humane treatment. Commentators do not fully agree on Felix's motives; the text does not explain them.

For today: even in unjust or uncertain situations, God can give us small reliefs and people who stand with us. Be thankful for those supports, and do not feel ashamed to receive help in difficult times.
exp.6:30:
Moses saw something strange and was amazed. He drew closer to look more carefully, and then he heard the voice of the Lord.

The sentence explaining "marveled at the sight" would be rewritten for a word in the verse: "Marveled" means that he was filled with wonder and admiration. "Came to him" means that a voice reached him from God.

Here Stephen speaks, defending his faith before the Jewish council. He reminds them how God appeared to Moses in the burning bush, when Moses had spent forty years as a foreigner in Midian. Stephen shows that God acts and reveals himself in places and at moments people did not expect, even far from the temple.

God often speaks when we stop and draw near with attention. Moses could have continued on his way, but he drew near. Today we can pause in the middle of our routine, open the Bible, and pray with a heart ready to listen.
exp.4:38:
Acts 5:39 says that if this movement is from God, no one will be able to stop it. It warns that those who oppose it may find themselves fighting against God himself. To stop means to prevent or end something. The phrase "you may even find yourselves" is a warning that the opposition could be discovered to be opposition to God.

Gamaliel, a highly respected teacher of the law, speaks before the Jewish council. The apostles had been arrested for preaching about Jesus, and the leaders wanted to kill them. Gamaliel calls for calm and reminds them of other movements that failed. His advice does not prove that he believed in Jesus; it was a prudent warning. The council listened to him, but still had the apostles flogged.

Today, before rejecting or attacking something, it is wise to stop and examine it humbly in the light of the Bible. And if we serve God, we can rest: his work does not depend on our strength.
exp.1:35:
Peter declares with complete certainty to all the people of Israel that God has made this Jesus, whom they crucified, both Lord and Christ. "Let all Israel know with certainty" means "let everyone clearly understand this." "Christ" means the Messiah, the promised Anointed One.

Peter speaks at Pentecost, in Jerusalem, filled with the Holy Spirit. He has just quoted Psalm 110 to show that Jesus rose and was exalted to the right hand of God. His message confronts the people over the cross, and it leads them to a sincere grief that moves them to ask what they should do. Peter answers them with the call to repent.

For today: acknowledging Jesus as Lord is not merely admiring him, but surrendering our lives to him. If the heart is touched by the truth, we can respond with humility and repentance, knowing that God offers forgiveness.
exp.26:13:
Soon after they set sail, a strong and sudden storm wind struck the ship. The sailors called it a "cyclone," a violent wind known as the Northeaster. The wind came sweeping down across the island, and the storm was the main force that Luke describes here. The exact name and its origin are not fully certain, and it is usually understood as a fierce wind from the northeast.

Luke, who was traveling with Paul, recounts the voyage toward Rome, where Paul was going as a prisoner. A gentle wind from the south led the sailors to believe they could reach Fair Havens, so they set out confidently. But the weather changed all at once. Luke shows how things seemed to be going well and then suddenly became difficult, even though Paul had already warned them of the danger.

For today: do not rely only on favorable circumstances when you make a decision. A gentle breeze does not always confirm that you are on the right course. Before moving forward, listen to wise counsel and pray, and remember that God still cares for you even when an unexpected storm arrives.
exp.12:1:
While the leaders of the church in Antioch were worshiping the Lord and fasting, the Holy Spirit spoke. Here "worshiping" describes serving and honoring God. The Spirit asked that Barnabas and Saul be set apart for a special work to which God had already called them.

The Bible does not say how the Holy Spirit spoke, though it may have been through one of the prophets who were present. This happens in Antioch, a church with leaders from different backgrounds. Then the church prays, fasts, lays hands on them, and sends them out. This is how the first missionary journey begins.

For today: before making important decisions, set aside time to seek God through prayer and worship. Listen for his direction, confirm it together with other believers, and then obey with confidence.
exp.21:9:
Paul recounts that, after seeing the light and hearing Jesus, he asked, "What should I do, Lord?" Jesus told him to get up and go into Damascus, and there he would be told all that he had been appointed to do.

Paul is speaking before an angry crowd in Jerusalem, and he describes how he came to know Jesus on the road to Damascus. Before this, he had been persecuting Christians. His question shows surrender: he went from persecuting to obeying. Jesus does not give him the whole plan at once, but the next step.

For today: when you don't know what to do with your life, don't worry about seeing the whole path. Ask God for direction, and take in faith the step He already shows you. He usually guides step by step, often through other people, as He did through Ananias.
exp.18:21:
He says that Paul sent two of his helpers, Timothy and Erastus, to Macedonia, while he himself stayed in the province of Asia for a time. "Asia" here does not mean the whole continent, but the Roman province whose center was Ephesus, in what is now Turkey. The "helpers" were co-workers who served alongside him in the work.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells how Paul was planning his next journey: to pass through Macedonia and Achaia, then go to Jerusalem and afterward to Rome. Before leaving, he sends Timothy and Erastus ahead, probably to prepare the way. This happens while the word of God was growing in Ephesus, just before the uproar caused by Demetrius.

For today: the work of God is almost never done alone. Paul entrusted important tasks to others and sent them out with support. We can think about whom we might help or encourage with a responsibility, and also serve humbly in whatever is entrusted to us.
exp.16:28:
He says that, if we are God's offspring, it makes no sense to think that the Divine Being is like an image made of gold, silver, or stone. "Offspring" means descendants or family. "The Divine Being" is God himself. "An image formed by man's skill and imagination" describes something people make with their own craft and ideas.

Paul speaks in Athens, at the Areopagus, before philosophers and people who worshiped many idols. So that they would understand him, he quotes Greek poets (it is often linked to Aratus or Cleanthes, though scholars debate which one). He does not say that everyone is a child of God in the sense of salvation, but that all of us come from Him as Creator. Then he calls them to repent.

Today we can ask ourselves what mental images or things we have put in the place of the true God, such as money, success, or an idea of God shaped to our own measure. It is worth knowing him by what he says about himself in the Bible and in Jesus.
exp.6:55:
These words say that Stephen, looking up toward heaven, saw heaven open and Jesus, called "the Son of Man," standing at the right hand of God. "At the right hand of God" means at the right side, the place of honor and authority. The verb "see" is in the present tense: he was seeing it at that very moment.

Stephen stood before the Jewish council, accused of speaking against the temple and the law. After reviewing the history of Israel, he told them that they were resisting the Holy Spirit. Furious, they listened to him with rage. When he declared that he saw Jesus, they took it as blasphemy and stoned him. Here Saul appears for the first time. It is notable that in other passages Jesus is shown seated, but here the verse shows him standing at the right hand of God; some see in that a gesture of support for his witness, though this is an interpretation.

For today: when you face pressure or rejection because of your faith, fix your gaze on Jesus. He knows your situation and is near you.
exp.26:28:
This verse tells us that the sailors feared the ship would crash against rocks or dangerous stretches of the coast, in the middle of the darkness. The rocks mentioned are rough, stony places along the shore. So they dropped four anchors from the back of the ship to slow it down, and they prayed for morning to come.

The narrator is Luke, who travels with Paul, a prisoner, on the way to Rome. They have been caught in a storm for fourteen nights, not knowing where they are. When they take soundings, they notice the water is getting shallower and suspect land is near. Dropping anchors was the prudent thing to do, but shortly afterward some of the sailors try to escape, and Paul warns of the danger.

For today: when everything is dark and we cannot see the way, it is wise to do the sensible thing within our reach and to wait patiently, trusting God. We will not always have answers right away, but the day comes.
exp.24:10:
Paul says that if he has really done anything wrong, anything that deserves death, he does not refuse to die. But if there is no truth to the charges the Jews bring against him, no one has the right to hand him over to them. For this reason he asks to be judged by the emperor: "I appeal to Caesar!" The word "guilty" here means having done something wrong or harmful. "Refuse" means "I do not turn away from."

Paul is a prisoner in Caesarea. Festus, the Roman governor, wants to please the Jews and proposes that Paul go to Jerusalem to be judged. Paul knows he is in danger there, so he uses his right as a Roman citizen to appeal to the emperor. His appeal would take him to Rome.

For today: we can calmly defend what is right, using the lawful means we have, while remaining honest. Paul does not run from the truth or from its consequences, but neither does he accept an injustice in silence.
exp.25:6:
Paul says that the twelve tribes of Israel are hoping to see God's promise fulfilled. Because of this hope, they serve God earnestly, "day and night," that is, with steady, daily devotion. The words "are hoping to see fulfilled" mean that they expect to receive that promise. And it is precisely because of that hope that some Jews accuse him.

Paul speaks before King Agrippa while he defends himself as a prisoner in Caesarea. He explains that he teaches nothing foreign to Israel.
