The promise that God made to the fathers, according to the context, is connected with the resurrection of the dead, and Paul affirms that it is fulfilled in Jesus. Scholars discuss exactly how many Jews of his time understood that promise, but Paul presents it as the central hope of his people.

For today: hope in God is not something occasional. We can cultivate it through prayer and daily faithfulness, even when others do not understand us or reject us.
exp.20:38:
Paul answers the Roman commander that he is a Jew from Tarsus, an important city in Cilicia. He describes it as "a citizen of no ordinary city," meaning a city of real importance, well known and respected. Then he asks permission to speak to the people.

Paul has just been arrested in Jerusalem after a crowd attacked him in the temple. The commander thought he was an Egyptian revolutionary. Paul clarifies who he is, without anger or fear, and takes the opportunity to speak. His main interest is not to defend himself, but that the people listen.

For today: even in the midst of injustice, we can respond with calm and truth. Paul does not let himself be carried away by anger; he uses his difficult moment to bear witness. When we are misunderstood, let us clarify with respect and seek to open a door to share what God has done in us.
exp.18:17:
This verse says that many believers in Ephesus came forward to openly confess what they had been doing. "Confessing and disclosing their deeds" means explaining clearly what they had been practicing, without hiding it. The word "deeds" here refers to actions or conduct, especially those connected with magic.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells what happened after some Jewish exorcists tried to use the name of Jesus without knowing him and failed. This caused fear throughout the city, and the name of Jesus was honored. The believers understood that spiritual power is not a game. So they came forward and, right away, burned their books of magic. The text does not detail how or before whom they confessed.

For today: when God shows us something that draws us away from him, the best thing is to acknowledge it honestly and leave it behind. Confessing frees us from hiding what we do and brings us close to God again. We can start by talking about it with him and with someone we trust.
exp.23:3:
Tértulo tells Félix that he does not want to take up more of his time, and he asks him to listen to a short presentation. "But in order not to delay you any further" means he wants to avoid wasting the governor's time. "I beg your indulgence" is a polite way of asking Félix to be patient and kind as he listens.

Tértulo was a lawyer who spoke on behalf of the Jewish leaders, including the high priest Ananias, to accuse Paul before the governor Felix. Before making the accusation, he praises Felix greatly, and it is likely that he does so to win his favor. Many understand that his flattery was more a strategy than a sincere truth.

For today: it is good to speak with respect and brevity, but always with sincerity. A good tone should not be used to manipulate, but to tell the truth honestly and with love.
exp.16:11:
It says that, because the people of Berea examined the Scriptures with sincerity, many of them believed. Among those who believed were prominent Greek women and men, and quite a few of them. The phrase "quite a few" in the verse means "a good number" or "many."

The one speaking is Luke, who recounts the journey of Paul and Silas. They left Thessalonica by night because of the opposition there. In Berea they preached in the synagogue, and the listeners compared what they heard with the Scriptures of the Old Testament. The verse shows the result: faith grew out of that careful study, and it reached both Jews and Greeks, both women and men.

For today: do not be afraid to examine calmly what you are taught, whether in church, on the radio, or on the internet. Open your Bible every day, with humility and a desire to learn, and ask God to help you understand. In this way your faith is grounded in the Word of God and not only in opinions.
exp.16:23:
Paul says that the true God is the Creator of the world and everything in it. Since he is Lord of heaven and earth, he does not live in temples made by human hands.

Paul speaks before the philosophers of Athens, at the Areopagus, a city full of temples and images. He had seen an altar to an unknown god and uses it as a starting point to present the God they worshiped without knowing him. He does not attack them; he leads them from what they already believe toward the truth.

For today: God is greater than any building, place, or tradition. You can seek him and speak with him anywhere, at home, at work, or on the road. And when you share your faith, as Paul did, begin with what the other person already understands.
exp.0:18:
This verse says that what happened to Judas and the purchase of the field became known to everyone who lived in Jerusalem. So, in their own language, the field was called "Akeldama," which means "Field of Blood." "Lived in Jerusalem" refers to the people who made their homes in the city, and "became known" means the news spread widely.

Peter is speaking to about one hundred and twenty believers gathered before Pentecost. He reminds them what happened to Judas, who betrayed Jesus, to explain why another apostle needs to be chosen. This verse appears to be Luke's added explanation for his readers. Matthew 27 tells the event in a different way, and interpreters explain the connection in various ways.

For today: sin leaves traces that cannot be hidden, and deceit ends badly. Let us serve Christ with sincerity, and if we fail, let us come to Him in repentance.
exp.10:17:
The believing Jewish brothers in Jerusalem, on hearing Peter's account, stopped objecting and praised God. They understood that God had also granted the Gentiles repentance that leads to life.

Peter had just explained why he went into the house of Cornelius, a Gentile. Some of the brothers had criticized him for eating with non-Jews. Peter recounted the vision he had and how the Holy Spirit came upon those listeners, just as upon them at the beginning. That evidence settled the church's doubts.

For today: when God works in people we did not expect, let us set aside our prejudices, listen with humility, and praise him. His grace is broader than our customs.
exp.1:12:
This verse tells us that some of those present were mocking the disciples. They said the disciples were "drunk on new wine." New wine is fresh grape juice which, if it fermented, could make a person drunk. In other words, they were accusing the disciples of being drunk.

It is the day of Pentecost, in Jerusalem. The disciples, filled with the Holy Spirit, were speaking in other languages about the wonders of God. Many visitors from different lands were amazed because they could understand them. But others, perhaps because they did not understand or did not believe, mocked them. Peter answers them right away, saying they are not drunk, since it was only nine in the morning.

Today, when God works in a way we do not understand, we may respond with wonder or with mockery. Let us ask for a humble heart that is ready to listen, rather than judging hastily.
exp.22:1:
This verse tells how the high priest Ananias ordered those standing near Paul to strike him on the mouth. "High priest" refers to the chief priest, and "strike" means "hit."

Paul was before the Jewish council, called the Sanhedrin, and he had just said that he had lived with a good conscience before God. Ananias was probably offended by those words, or wanted to silence him, but the Bible does not explain his exact reason. It was an unjust order, because Paul had not yet been condemned. Paul answered sharply, and later admitted that he did not know that he was the high priest.

For today: when we are treated unjustly, let us ask God for self-control. We can defend the truth with firmness, but without losing respect or humility.
exp.25:16:
This verse says that Jesus promises to rescue Paul from his own people and from the Gentiles, meaning those who were not Jewish. Jesus is sending him to these same people. The idea of rescue means protecting you or bringing you safely out of danger.

Paul speaks before King Agrippa and recounts what he experienced when Jesus appeared to him on the road to Damascus. He is defending himself against accusations and explaining why he preaches. Jesus had called him to be a minister and a witness, and that mission included real risks, but also the promise of protection.

For today: when God calls you to something, he does not promise that there will be no difficulties, but he does promise that you will not go alone. Trust that his care accompanies you as you serve others, even where it seems hard.
exp.7:12:
This verse says that Simon, the sorcerer of Samaria, also believed and was baptized. Afterward he stayed close to Philip, and seeing the signs and great miracles that were taking place, he was astounded. The word "astounded" in the verse means greatly surprised, almost left speechless. The phrase "followed Philip closely" means that he attached himself to him and went along with him.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells how the gospel reached Samaria through Philip. Simon had deceived many people with his magical arts, and everyone followed him. Now he himself is amazed before the power of God. Later the account shows that his heart was not right, for he wanted power for himself. For this reason some believe his faith was shallow, though others think differently.

For today: it is not enough to be amazed at what God does. Let us ask him for a humble heart that seeks Jesus himself, not just impressive experiences.
exp.27:2:
Luke tells us that Paul gathered some dry sticks, or branches, and laid them on the fire to keep it burning. Then a viper, driven out by the heat, fastened itself to his hand. The word "fastened" here means the snake attached itself to him by biting.

This happened after the shipwreck, on the island of Malta, which was called Melita at that time. The islanders, whom Luke calls "barbarians" because they did not speak Greek, showed the shipwrecked travelers great kindness. Paul, although he was a prisoner, did not simply stand by watching but helped with the fire. When the people saw the snake hanging from his hand, they thought it was a punishment, but he suffered no harm.

Even after a crisis, God invites us to serve with humility in small things. And when an unexpected difficulty comes, we can trust that God cares for us.
exp.6:25:
The verse tells us that the next day Moses came upon two Israelites who were fighting. He stepped in and tried to reconcile them. He reminded them that they were brothers and asked them why they were mistreating each other. The phrase "tried to reconcile them" means he was seeking to bring peace between them.

The one speaking is Stephen, in his defense before the Jewish council. He reviews the history of Moses. Stephen points out that Moses thought his people would understand that God was using him to deliver them, but they did not understand and they rejected him. In this way Stephen prepares his accusation: Israel had already rejected the one whom God had sent.

For today: when there are quarrels between brothers and sisters in the faith, let us remember that we are family. Before arguing, let us seek peace with humility and gentleness, even though at times people may not listen to us.
exp.9:27:
Peter speaks to Cornelius and to those gathered in his house. He reminds them that, according to Jewish custom, it was considered wrong for a Jew to associate with or visit a foreigner, that is, someone who was not Jewish. The word "unlawful" here refers to something seen as deeply wrong. Peter's words about calling a person "impure" or "unclean" describe what was considered ritually unfit. But God had shown him that he should not call any man that way.

Peter is a Jew, and he has just seen a vision that God gave him, in which he learned that he should not look down on anyone. For this reason he agreed to enter the house of Cornelius, a Roman officer who was not Jewish. This is a key moment: the gospel opens up to all peoples.

Today, ask God to help you see each person as He sees them. Think of someone you tend to avoid or judge, and take a simple step to approach them with respect and kindness.
exp.2:5:
Peter tells a man in need that he has no money, but that he has something better to give him. "Silver or gold I do not have" means that Peter has no money. Then he commands, in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, that the man get up and walk. Saying "in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth" means that he does this by the power and authority of Jesus, not by his own strength.

Peter and John were going up to the temple to pray. At the gate, a man who had been lame from birth was begging for alms. He expected money, but he received healing. After being raised up, he entered the temple walking and praising God, and the people were amazed.

Sometimes we think we have nothing to offer because we lack money or resources. But God has given us other things: a word of encouragement, prayer, companionship, faith in Christ. Offer today what you do have, and trust that God can work through it.
exp.10:7:
Peter tells what he answered when he heard the voice commanding him to kill and eat. He says, "No, Lord, for nothing impure or unclean has ever entered my mouth." The word "ever" shows that throughout his whole life he had kept those rules. That is why he refuses the command, even though the voice comes from heaven.

Peter speaks before the believers in Jerusalem, who were criticizing him for entering the house of non-Jewish people and eating with them. He explains his vision to them step by step. As a Jew, he had learned from childhood to distinguish between permitted and forbidden foods. Through the vision, God teaches him that he must no longer call impure the Gentiles whom God accepts.

For today: sometimes we defend customs that seem right to us, and we find it hard to see that God works in a different way. Let us ask for humility to listen to his voice and not shut the door on those whom he has already received.
exp.19:19:
Here Paul says that he did not hold back from declaring anything that would help them. He taught them in public, in front of everyone, and also from house to house, going from home to home.

Paul is speaking to the elders of the church in Ephesus, whom he had called to Miletus to say goodbye. He thinks he may not see them again. He reminds them how he lived among them, with humility and devotion, so that they will faithfully care for the flock after he is gone.

For today: let us not keep the faith only for the church building. We can share what God teaches with sincerity and kindness, both in gatherings and in simple conversations at home, without staying silent about what truly helps others grow.
exp.27:3:
The people speaking here are the islanders of Malta, as the account makes clear. They have just seen Paul and his companions survive a shipwreck. These islanders had welcomed them with kindness, but when they saw the creature hanging from Paul's hand, they quickly reached a conclusion. They believed such a misfortune must be punishment for some wrongdoing.

The islanders are called "barbarians" in older translations, but the word here simply describes people who did not speak Greek. It does not mean they were savage. The word "murderer" refers to someone who takes another person's life. The islanders used the word "justice" to mean a force that punishes wrongdoing. They said that Paul had escaped the sea, yet this justice would not allow him to live.

For today: let us not judge someone by what happens to them. Suffering is not always the result of guilt, and God may be at work even in the middle of difficulty.
exp.26:24:
Paul tells the men on the ship to take courage. Here "men" is the word used for the group he is addressing, and "take courage" means take heart and do not lose hope. Paul says that he trusts God and believes that everything will happen just as God told him.

Paul speaks in the middle of a terrible storm, when everyone had lost hope. That night an angel assured him that he would reach Rome before Caesar and that God would save the lives of all who were with him. For this reason Paul speaks with calm and confidence. Shortly afterward, he himself explains that the ship would run aground on an island.

For today: when everything seems confused, we can lean on what God has already promised in his Word. That trust does not deny difficulties, but it allows us to encourage others with calm assurance.
exp.22:27:
This verse says that the Roman commander wanted to understand what Paul was being charged with. For that reason he brought him down to the Sanhedrin, the Jewish religious court. "Charges" means the accusations made against him, and "wanted to understand" shows that he was looking for information before deciding anything.

The one speaking is Claudius Lysias, the Roman commander in Jerusalem. He writes a letter to the governor Felix to explain why he is sending Paul, a prisoner, to Caesarea. In his account he presents himself favorably, and it is possible that he emphasizes what suits him. Even so, the text shows that he investigated the case.

For today: before judging or repeating an accusation against someone, try to find out the facts calmly and fairly. Asking questions and listening helps us avoid being carried along by rumors or by the pressure of the moment.
exp.7:31:
This verse tells us that the Ethiopian official was reading a passage from Isaiah. It speaks of someone led away to be slaughtered like a sheep, and who, like a lamb silent before the one who shears it, did not open his mouth. In this verse, "silent" means quiet, without protest.

Philip approached the chariot of the Ethiopian official, a high-ranking court officer, and heard him reading aloud. He asked whether he understood, and the man admitted that he needed someone to explain it to him. Luke records the text of Isaiah 53 to prepare what follows: Philip will proclaim Jesus to him. In the New Testament, Christians understand this passage as referring to Christ.

For today: do not be afraid to say that you do not understand the Bible. Ask help from someone you trust, and keep reading with humility. God often uses other people to open up the meaning of his Word to us.
exp.4:17:
It says that the Jewish authorities arrested the apostles and put them in the public jail. "Arrested" means to seize or detain by force. "Put them in the public jail" means they were held in a jail open to the public, not a private place.

Here the narrator speaks, Luke, the author of Acts. He tells that many people were coming to Jerusalem so that the apostles would heal their sick. The high priest and the Sadducees, who did not believe in the resurrection, were filled with jealousy and anger when they saw the apostles' influence. That is why they arrested them. Afterward, an angel brought them out of the prison.

Doing good and speaking about Jesus sometimes brings opposition, even from religious people. If you are criticized or made uncomfortable because of your faith, remember that God has not left you alone. Keep going with gentleness and trust, knowing that He cares for His people in the middle of difficulty.
exp.20:37:
The Roman commander asks Paul whether he is the Egyptian who, some time ago, incited a rebellion and led four thousand members of the Assassins into the wilderness. The word "rebellion" means an uprising against authority. The word "Assassins" refers to a violent group of men who attacked people, so the commander is describing a dangerous armed band.

The one speaking is the Roman commander of Jerusalem. He had just rescued Paul from a mob that wanted to kill him in the temple, and since he did not understand the reason for the uproar, he thought Paul was that well-known rebel. The historian Josephus mentions an Egyptian of this kind, although the numbers he gives differ a little from those in this passage. Paul calmly corrects him: he is a Jew from Tarsus.

For today: when you are accused or misunderstood, respond with calm and truth, without shouting or returning the offense. Paul made clear who he was without losing his peace, and that opened the door for him to speak about Christ.
exp.0:20:
This verse begins to explain what kind of man was to take Judas's place among the apostles. Being necessary means it was required or the right thing to do. He had to be someone who had been with the disciples the whole time the Lord Jesus lived and moved among them. The phrase "the whole time the Lord Jesus went in and out among us" simply means he had lived alongside them day by day.

Peter speaks before about one hundred twenty believers gathered in Jerusalem, after Jesus's ascension. He has just cited the Psalms to show that Judas's place should be taken by another. He looks for someone who had seen the whole of Jesus's ministry, so that he could give firm witness to his resurrection.

For today: bearing witness to Jesus requires knowing him closely. Make a habit of spending time with him in prayer and in his Word, so that your faith rests on a real and daily relationship.
exp.18:31:
This verse describes the chaos in the theater of Ephesus. Some were shouting one thing and others another, and the crowd was in turmoil. Most of them did not even know why they had come together. The word "assembly" refers to the people gathered together, and "most of them" refers to the majority.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells of the uproar stirred up by the silversmith Demetrius. He claimed that the gospel threatened his business of making images of the goddess Diana. The crowd rushed to the theater, dragging along some companions of Paul. Paul wanted to go in and defend them, but the disciples and some friendly officials prevented him, to protect him.

Today it is also easy to be swept along by the noise of the crowd, social media, or rumors, without really knowing what is going on. Before we shout, share, or take sides, let us stop to ask, listen, and pray. God invites us to seek the truth with calm and wisdom.
exp.20:15:
Some disciples from Caesarea went along with Paul and his companions on the way to Jerusalem. They took them to stay at the home of Mnason, a Cypriot and an early disciple, meaning someone who had been following Jesus for a long time.

The one telling the account is Luke, who travels with Paul and writes in the first person, using "we." Paul was determined to go to Jerusalem even though he had been warned of dangers. After accepting the Lord's will, they continue on their way. The disciples from Caesarea accompany them and arrange a place for them to stay. We know nothing more about Mnason; the Bible does not tell his story.

For today: hospitality is a simple way of serving. Opening your home, offering help, or accompanying someone in a difficult moment can strengthen others, even when no one notices.
exp.24:0:
This verse tells that Festus, the new Roman governor, arrived in his province and, three days later, traveled from Caesarea up to Jerusalem. The phrase "three days after his arrival in the province" means that he had already taken up his post. The verb "went up" fits because Jerusalem sits high, in the hill country of Judea.

This is a narrative from Luke, the author of Acts. Festus had replaced Felix, who left Paul imprisoned in Caesarea. Upon arriving, Festus went quickly to Jerusalem, the religious and political center of the Jews. The following verses show that their leaders took the opportunity to bring accusations against Paul again, because they wanted to kill him.

For today: although it may sometimes seem that people in power decide everything, God continues to guide history. Paul was in prison, but his life was not outside the hands of God. Trust in Him when everything looks uncertain.
exp.19:33:
Paul reminds the leaders of Ephesus of something they themselves saw: with his own hands he worked to meet his own needs and the needs of his companions. "You yourselves know" means that these are things they know firsthand. "Ministered to my own needs" means that his work provided for him.

Paul is saying farewell to the elders of the church in Ephesus, in the city of Miletus, knowing that he may not see them again. He tells them that he did not covet anyone's silver, gold, or clothing. From what Acts tells us, he worked making tents (Acts 18:3), although here he mentions only his hands.

We can serve with generosity and with integrity in money matters. If we work honestly, avoid greed, and use what we have to help others, our lives back up what we say we believe.
exp.21:13:
Ananias tells Paul that God had appointed him beforehand for three purposes: to know God's will, to see the Righteous One, and to hear God's voice. Here, "appointed beforehand" means chosen or set apart in advance.

The speaker is Paul, who recounts his conversion before the crowd in Jerusalem, and he repeats what Ananias told him, a Jew respected for his devotion to the law. Paul wants to show that his change of life was not his own idea but a calling from God, confirmed by a devout man faithful to the law.

For today: God not only saves us, he also calls us to know him and to serve him. Ask him to show you his will, listen to his voice in the Bible and in prayer, and be ready to share with others what you have seen and heard of him.
exp.18:10:
It says that God was doing extraordinary miracles, beyond the ordinary, using Paul as his instrument. The word "extraordinary" points to the miracles being out of the ordinary and uncommon, and the phrase "through the hands of Paul" shows that Paul was the means, but God was the one at work.

Luke, the author of Acts, reports this in Ephesus. Paul had already been teaching for two years, and some had become hardened and were speaking evil of the Way, that is, the Christian faith. Even so, the word spread throughout all of Asia. These miracles backed up the message, and the verses that follow show that people recognized the power of Jesus, not the power of Paul.

For today: God can use ordinary people and their gifts, but the glory belongs to him. Serve faithfully and humbly, and let God work as he wills.
exp.8:7:
Saul got up from the ground after the voice of the Lord. When he opened his eyes, he could not see a thing. So others took him by the hand and led him into Damascus.

Saul was on his way to Damascus to arrest the followers of Jesus. On the road, the Lord appeared to him and stopped him. Saul asked what he should do, and Jesus told him to go into the city, where he would receive instructions. His companions heard a voice but saw no one. The text does not explain every detail of the blindness; it presents it simply as part of this encounter.

For today: sometimes God stops our plans so that we will depend on him. When we cannot see the way ahead, we can obey the next step, accept help with humility, and wait for his direction.
exp.10:29:
It says that the disciples in Antioch carried out what they had decided: they sent their gifts to the elders of the church in Judea, with Barnabas and Saul carrying them. The "gifts" were money or supplies to help people in need.

The narrator is Luke, the author of Acts. A prophet named Agabus had announced a great famine across the known world, and the believers in Antioch, who were mostly not Jews, wanted to help the brothers and sisters in Judea. Each one gave according to what they could. The elders were the leaders of the Jewish churches. Scholars often see this visit by Saul (Paul) as part of his path toward ministry, although they do not all agree on how it relates to Galatians 2.

For today: do not wait for a crisis to come before you help. Give according to what you have, with confidence and order, and make sure your help reaches those who need it through honest hands.
exp.5:7:
What it says: Stephen was a man full of grace and power. Grace is God's favor and help, and power means strength. Your verse says he was performing great wonders and signs among the people. Those signs and wonders showed the work of God and were happening in front of everyone.

Context: Luke, the author of Acts, describes how the church was growing in Jerusalem. Stephen had just been chosen, along with six others, to care for the widows. Although his task was practical, God was also using him with power. This verse sets up the account of the opposition that would soon come against him.

For today: God can work through any humble service. You do not need a great position to be useful. Serve faithfully in whatever you are given, and depend on God's grace more than on your own strength.
exp.1:22:
Jesus was handed over according to God's set plan and his foreknowledge. Even so, the listeners are held responsible: they took him, and by the hands of lawless men they put him to death by nailing him to the cross. "Set plan" here means God's purpose. "Foreknowledge" refers to God knowing this beforehand.

Peter speaks on the day of Pentecost to Jews gathered in Jerusalem. He reminds them that God endorsed Jesus with miracles, and then confronts them with their guilt. But he does not stop there: he immediately announces that God raised him from the dead. His aim is to lead them to repent and to call on the name of the Lord so that they may be saved.

For today: God can carry out his plan even in the midst of human injustice, but that does not remove our responsibility. We can honestly acknowledge our failures and trust that Christ offers forgiveness and hope.
exp.18:4:
When these men from Ephesus heard what Paul explained about Jesus, they were baptized into his name. "On hearing this" means "after hearing this." Being baptized "into the name of the Lord Jesus" means that they were baptized acknowledging Jesus as Lord and placing their faith in him.

Paul arrived in Ephesus and found some disciples who knew only the baptism of John, a baptism of repentance. Paul made clear to them that John himself pointed toward Jesus, the one who would come after him. Once they understood this, they believed and were baptized. Scholars debate some details of their situation, but the text shows that they received a fuller faith.

For today: a half-hearted or inherited faith is not enough. We can ask ourselves honestly whether we truly know Jesus, and be willing to keep learning and to obey him when God shows us something more.
exp.11:17:
At daybreak, the soldiers who had been guarding the prison were thrown into great commotion. They could not find Peter anywhere. The phrase "no small commotion" means there was considerable confusion and anxiety among them.

The narrator is Luke, the author of Acts. Peter had been imprisoned by Herod Agrippa and kept under watch by soldiers. During the night an angel had led him out of the prison while the believers were praying. By the time the guards discovered he was gone, Peter was already safe, and they could not understand what had happened. The verses that follow show that Herod punished them.

For today: God can work quietly and in unexpected ways, even when everything seems closed off. We can keep praying with confidence, remembering that no human power can stop his purposes.
exp.12:6:
This verse says that Bar-Jesus, the magician, was an attendant of the proconsul Sergius Paulus, a man of intelligence and sound judgment. The proconsul was the Roman governor of the island. He summoned Barnabas and Saul because he wanted to hear the word of God.

Here Luke, the author of Acts, is telling about the first missionary journey. Barnabas and Saul, sent out by the church in Antioch, arrived at Paphos, on the island of Cyprus. The magician had influence over the governor, but the governor, even so, wanted to hear the message directly from the apostles.

For today: Being wise is not only having intelligence, but also being willing to listen. Even when others pull us in another direction, we can humbly seek the word of God and let it speak to us.
exp.20:24:
This verse says that believers who are not Jews do not have to keep the customs of the law of Moses. They were only asked to abstain from food sacrificed to idols, from blood, from the meat of strangled animals (animals that died without being bled), and from sexual immorality. The word "but" introduces the exception, and "decision" means "what was agreed upon."

The ones speaking are James together with the elders of Jerusalem, addressing Paul. They recall the decision of Acts 15 to reassure Jewish believers, who were hearing rumors that Paul taught people to abandon the law. They propose a public gesture of respect for their culture. The texts do not explain every detail of that vow, so it is best not to claim more than they say.

For today: seek unity without demanding that others adopt your customs. Guard what is essential to the faith, and be flexible in what is not essential, out of love for your brothers and sisters.
exp.24:7:
Paul answers the accusations by saying that he has committed no offense against the law of the Jews, against the temple, or against Caesar. "Made his defense" means that he was speaking in his own defense. "Offense" here refers to having done wrong or broken a law.

Paul speaks before Festus, the Roman governor, in Caesarea. Some Jews who had come down from Jerusalem were accusing him of many serious things, but they could not prove them. Paul does not stay silent: he gives a clear and brief defense, covering the three points of the religious and political charge.

For today: when someone accuses us unjustly, we can defend ourselves calmly and truthfully, without insulting or repaying evil with evil. And living with a clear conscience gives us the firmness to speak with tranquility, even when not everyone believes us.
exp.19:1:
Paul traveled through the regions of Macedonia, encouraging the believers with many words, and then he came to Greece. The phrase "after traveling through that area" describes the journey itself, moving from place to place. "Speaking many words of encouragement" refers to his steady effort to build up and strengthen others in their faith.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells of Paul's journey after the uproar in Ephesus. Paul left for Macedonia, visited the churches he had founded, and then arrived in Greece, where he stayed for three months. The text gives no further details about what he said in each place, but it emphasizes that his ministry was to encourage the disciples.

Today we can imitate Paul by seeking out someone who is tired or discouraged and giving them our time. A visit, a phone call, or a few words filled with Scripture can strengthen their faith and their hope.
exp.16:15:
He says that Paul was in Athens waiting for Silas and Timothy. Meanwhile, he was deeply disturbed in his spirit when he saw that the city was full of idols. "Deeply disturbed in his spirit" means that something troubled him at his core and filled him with distress. "Full of idols" means the city was crowded with images and objects of false worship.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells that Paul had left Berea because of persecution. The brothers took him as far as Athens, and he was waiting for his companions. At first he did not intend to preach there, but what he saw moved him to speak: first in the synagogue and then in the marketplace, with philosophers who listened to him with curiosity and mockery.

For today: when we see people searching for meaning in empty things, let us not respond with contempt, but with sincere sorrow and love. That compassion can lead us to converse with respect and to share Jesus with clarity.
exp.0:24:
It says that the apostle who is chosen will take up the service and apostolic task that Judas abandoned. Judas left that position because of his sin, and he went to his rightful place, meaning the destiny that matched what he had done. "Ministry" refers to service or responsibility, and "abandoned" means walked away from or betrayed. As for exactly what "his rightful place" means, Christians have understood it in different ways, and the text does not give more detail.

Peter and about 120 disciples were gathered in Jerusalem after Jesus went up into heaven. They had seen that Judas was no longer among the twelve, and they were looking for someone who had accompanied Jesus from the beginning. So they pray, asking God himself to show whom he chooses.

For today: before making an important decision, pray with humility and ask God to guide you, instead of relying only on your own judgment.
exp.3:17:
Then the Jewish leaders called Peter and John back in and firmly ordered them not to speak or teach at all in the name of Jesus. The command came with authority behind it and a warning of punishment. The word "at all" means in no way whatsoever.

The ones giving the order were members of the Sanhedrin, the religious council of Jerusalem. They had just seen a man who had been lame from birth healed by Peter and John, and they could not deny that it had happened. Unable to answer the miracle itself, they tried to stop the message through threats, so that it would not spread among the people.

For today: there will sometimes be pressure to keep our faith quiet, whether at work, at home, or among friends. This passage invites us to speak of Jesus with respect and courage, without letting fear win. We can ask God for wisdom to know when and how to speak.
exp.24:15:
This verse says that Festus, the Roman governor, told the Jewish leaders that it was not the Roman custom to hand a man over before he had the chance to face his accusers and defend himself against their charges.

Festus is speaking with King Agrippa, who was visiting him in Caesarea. He explains how he handled the case of Paul, who had been kept in prison since the time of Felix. The Jewish leaders were pressing for a guilty verdict, but Festus points to the Roman legal process as the proper way to proceed. Some scholars note that Festus presents himself favorably before the king; even so, the principle he states is sound.

For today: before judging or speaking badly of someone, let us listen to their side. Justice and love for our neighbor ask us to give room to the truth and to the right of a person to defend himself.
exp.4:18:
This verse tells that during the night an angel of the Lord opened the doors of the jail where the apostles were held. He brought them out and spoke to them. The word "but" in the verse marks a contrast with what the authorities had just done, and "brought them out" means he led them outside. The message the angel gives comes in the next verse.

The narrator is Luke, the author of Acts. The religious leaders, driven by zeal (jealousy), had jailed the apostles for preaching about Jesus. In the face of this opposition, God intervenes with an angel. He not only sets them free, but also commands them to keep speaking in the temple. The deliverance has a purpose: to continue the witness.

For today: when you face opposition or feel shut in by circumstances, trust that God can act in unexpected ways. And if He helps you, remember that He does so that you will keep serving Him with courage.
exp.1:31:
This verse states that God raised Jesus from the dead, the same Jesus who was crucified. The apostles say that they saw him alive, and that is why they are "witnesses," meaning people who tell what they saw with their own eyes. The phrase "raised to life" means that God gave him life again.

Peter speaks on the day of Pentecost before a crowd in Jerusalem. He has just quoted King David, who in the Psalms foretold that the Christ would not be left in death and that his body would not see decay. Peter explains that this promise was fulfilled in Jesus. The other apostles were standing beside him and shared that testimony.

Our faith does not rest on an idea, but on a fact that God accomplished. Today you can trust in Jesus with confidence and, when you have the opportunity, share simply what he has done in your life.
exp.15:1:
This verse says that the believers in Lystra and Iconium spoke well of Timothy. "Spoke well of him" means that they recommended him, because they knew his life and his character. "The brothers" refers to other Christians in those cities.

The author is Luke, who tells of Paul's second missionary journey. Paul arrives in Lystra and finds Timothy, a young disciple, the son of a believing Jewish mother and a Greek father. Before inviting him to travel with him, Paul pays attention to what others said about him. Lystra and Iconium were near each other, so many people knew him well.

Today, this verse reminds us that character is formed in everyday life, and that God often uses those who live faithfully among their own people. Take care of your testimony in your church, your family, and your work, even when no one seems to be watching.
exp.6:23:
It says that Moses saw a Hebrew being mistreated by an Egyptian. Moses went to his defense and avenged him by striking down the Egyptian who was oppressing him. "Mistreated" here means treated cruelly or attacked unjustly. "Avenged" means that he took action to set things right for him, though with violence.

Stephen speaks before the Jewish council, reviewing the history of Israel. He tells how Moses wanted to help his people, but did not do it in God's way or in God's time. Stephen points out that the people did not understand that God wanted to free them through him. Exodus 2 tells that Moses killed the Egyptian, and then had to flee.

Today: defending someone who suffers injustice is good, but it must be done with wisdom, not with anger or violence. Before acting, let us ask God for direction and look for ways of helping that reflect his justice and his peace.
exp.3:23:
When the believers heard the report, they all prayed together, speaking aloud to God. Their first words named him as the Creator of heaven, earth, and the sea, and of everything in them. "Sovereign Lord" is the title they use here, and it points to God's authority over all things.

The first disciples are speaking in Jerusalem. Peter and John had just been arrested and questioned by the Jewish authorities for healing a man, and they were ordered to stop speaking about Jesus. When they returned to their own people, they told everything, and the community responded by praying instead of panicking.

For today: when you face opposition or fear, begin your prayer by remembering who God is. If he made everything that exists, no threat is greater than he is. Pray also in the company of other believers.
exp.12:23:
John the Baptist, before Jesus began his work, preached a baptism of repentance to all the people of Israel. The phrase "before the arrival of Jesus" in this verse means "before Jesus arrived," like someone preparing the way for a visitor. Repentance means turning around and returning to God.

The speaker is Paul, in the synagogue at Antioch of Pisidia. He surveys the history of Israel, from David to Jesus, to show that Jesus is the promised Savior. He mentions John because John was well known and respected, and his message prepared the people to receive Christ.

For today: before receiving God's blessings, it is good to examine the heart. Today you can ask God to show you something you need to let go of, and take a concrete step to change.
exp.3:0:
Acts 4:1 tells us that while Peter and John were still speaking to the people, the priests, the captain of the temple guard (the officer in charge of keeping order on the temple grounds), and the Sadducees (an influential religious group that did not believe in the resurrection) came up to them. The phrase "came up to them" means they approached the apostles, and the verse does not say whether they came quietly or suddenly.

The account continues after the healing of a lame man in the temple and Peter's message to the crowd. According to the verses that follow, the leaders were upset because the apostles were teaching the people and announcing that Jesus had risen from the dead. That is why they arrested them.

For today: speaking about Jesus can bring opposition, even from religious people or those in authority. If this happens to you, do not be afraid; stay firm and gentle, trusting that God continues to work through those who bear witness to him.
exp.10:10:
Right after the vision Peter had three times, three men arrived at the house where he was staying. They had been sent from Caesarea to find him. The verse you read says "Just then," which shows that their arrival came at the same moment as the vision's end.

Peter speaks before the believers in Jerusalem, who were criticizing him for entering the house of Gentiles and eating with them. He explains step by step what happened. He stresses that the vision and the arrival of the messengers came together, as a sign that God was directing everything. The three men had come on behalf of Cornelius.

For today: God can arrange circumstances to guide us. It is good to be attentive and willing to obey, even when what He asks breaks our customs or prejudices. Seeing His work, we can explain it with humility to others.
exp.10:6:
Peter tells how, while he was praying, he heard a voice from heaven telling him to get up, kill animals, and eat. Those animals were the ones he had seen in the large sheet: four-footed animals, wild animals, creeping things, and birds. Here, "kill" means to put an animal to death so that it can be eaten.

Peter is speaking to the believers in Jerusalem, who criticized him for going into the house of Cornelius, a Gentile. He explains step by step what God showed him. For a Jew, many of those animals were unclean according to the law, which is why Peter refused. Many understand that the vision was preparing his heart to accept the Gentiles, although the text makes this clear only later.

Today, when God asks us for something that goes against our customs or prejudices, it is wise to listen with humility. Let us pray that He will enlarge our hearts and teach us to welcome everyone as He welcomes them.
exp.20:29:
This verse says that word about Paul spread through all of Jerusalem and that the people crowded together. They seized him and dragged him out of the temple by force. At once the gates were shut. The phrase "stirred up" means that the city was agitated and enraged, and "rushed together" means that the people gathered in a noisy crowd.

Paul had arrived in Jerusalem and was in the temple. Some Jews from Asia accused him of teaching against the people, the law, and the temple, and of bringing Gentiles into the holy place. They based this on an assumption: they had seen Trophimus, an Ephesian, with Paul in the city and thought he had taken him inside. It was a rumor without proof. The shut gates were probably meant to keep the temple from being defiled by violence.

Before reacting to a rumor, it is wise to stop, ask questions, and check the facts. Assumptions and collective fury can lead us to harm innocent people. Let us ask God for prudence and a love of the truth.
exp.3:25:
The verse says that the kings and rulers of the earth took their stand and gathered together against the Lord and against His Anointed One. The picture is of people getting into position, like those preparing for a fight, as they set themselves in opposition to God and to His Anointed One, the Messiah.

The believers in Jerusalem are praying after Peter and John were threatened by the authorities. They quote Psalm 2, written by David, and see that this opposition was fulfilled when Herod, Pilate, and others joined together against Jesus. They recognize that God already knew everything and remained in control.

When you face rejection or pressure for following Jesus, remember that it is not something new or surprising. You can pray with confidence, as they did, knowing that God is still greater than any human power.
exp.4:14:
People brought the sick out into the streets and laid them on cots and mats. They hoped that, as Peter walked by, his shadow would fall on at least some of them. "Cots" are simple beds or stretchers, and "at least" means "at the very least."

Luke, the author of Acts, describes how the church was growing in Jerusalem. The apostles were doing signs and wonders, and many people were coming to believe in the Lord. The text says the people wanted Peter's shadow to fall on the sick, but it does not say clearly whether anyone was healed by it. Later it does mention that everyone who came was healed. The power came from God, not from Peter.

For today: when you are sick or burdened, do not stay silent or alone. Bring your need to God with simple faith, and help others draw near to Him, as these neighbors did when they carried their sick.
exp.20:13:
What it says: Paul's friends urged him not to go to Jerusalem, but he did not change his mind. Then they quieted down and said, "The Lord's will be done."

Context: The speaker is Luke, who was traveling with Paul. In Caesarea, the prophet Agabus had announced that Paul would be bound in Jerusalem. His companions and the believers there, weeping, wanted to prevent it. Paul, however, was determined to obey Christ even if it cost him his freedom or his life. Some understand that the friends were only expressing affection, while others hold that Paul already felt a clear calling.

For today: We may ask for counsel and even plead for those we love, but we also need to learn to let go. When someone has sought God sincerely and is determined to obey him, let us trust that God knows how to guide him.
exp.2:12:
Peter says that the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, the God of Israel's history, has honored his servant Jesus. The people handed Jesus over and rejected him before Pilate, even though Pilate had decided to release him. "Glorified" means honored and exalted. "Rejected" means turned away from. "Release" means set free.

Peter speaks in Solomon's Portico, in the temple, after a lame man has been healed. The people are amazed, and Peter makes clear that the miracle did not come from his own power or piety, but from Jesus. He shows them that the God they worship is the one who honored Jesus.

For today: when God does something good in your life, do not take the credit; point to Jesus. And if you have ever turned away from him, you can always return to him with humility.
exp.26:22:
Paul explains why he can speak with such confidence: just last night an angel of God stood beside him. Paul says God is the one he belongs to, and he serves him, meaning he worships him and obeys him.

Paul is a prisoner on a ship bound for Rome, and a violent storm has been battering the vessel for days. The crew has lost hope, and almost no one has eaten. Paul stands up and encourages them with what God revealed to him: no one will die, although the ship will be lost. The angel's message comes in the following verse.

For today: when fear surrounds you, remember to whom you belong. Paul did not control the storm, but he knew that God had him in his care. Ask God for calm and trust, and then encourage those beside you with simplicity.
exp.1:40:
What it says: Those who embraced Peter's message were baptized. That same day, about three thousand people were added to the believers. "Added to the believers" means they were joined to the group of followers of Jesus. "Embraced his message" means they accepted and welcomed what Peter taught.

Context: It is the day of Pentecost. Peter has just explained that Jesus, whom they crucified, is Lord and Messiah. Many people were deeply moved and asked what they should do. Peter called them to repent and urged them to save themselves from that crooked generation. This verse shows how they responded.

For today: Believing in Jesus is not just hearing, but responding. And it is not lived alone: they joined other believers. If you have embraced the message of God, look for a Christian community where you can grow, learn, and be encouraged in the faith.
exp.14:27:
This verse says that the leaders of the church in Jerusalem, guided by the Holy Spirit, decided not to place on the non-Jewish believers any more weight than was necessary. "It seemed good" means it seemed right and wise to them. "Not to burden you" means not to load you down, and a burden here is a heavy obligation.

Here the apostles and elders gathered at the council of Jerusalem are speaking. Some were teaching that believers of non-Jewish origin had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses in order to be saved. The letter, carried to Antioch by Judas and Silas, aimed to settle that dispute and give a common answer.

For today: let us take care not to add human rules to what God asks. We can encourage others to follow Christ with simplicity, without unnecessary burdens, and seek the Spirit's guidance when there are disagreements.
exp.7:0:
This verse says that Saul was there and approved of Stephen's death. That same day a great persecution broke out against the church in Jerusalem. Everyone except the apostles was scattered throughout Judea and Samaria. "Approved" means that he agreed with what happened, and "scattered" means spread out to different places.

The narrator is Luke, author of the book of Acts. He recounts what happened right after Stephen was stoned for speaking about Jesus. Saul, who would later become the apostle Paul, was still an enemy of the church. This scattering, although painful, caused the message of Jesus to reach new places, as seen in the following chapters. Interpreters often note that the apostles stayed in Jerusalem, though the Bible does not explain in detail why.

Today we can remember that God can use difficult moments to extend his good. When you go through a trial, pray and keep serving with faith wherever you are.
exp.9:18:
This verse says that Peter kept reflecting on the vision he had seen. While he was doing so, the Spirit told him that three men were looking for him. "Reflecting" here means thinking carefully, trying to understand something.

Peter was in Joppa, staying at the house of Simon the tanner. He had seen a sheet with animals that God told him to eat, and he did not understand what it meant. At the same time, messengers sent by Cornelius, a Roman officer who was not a Jew, were arriving. The one speaking is the Holy Spirit, who shortly afterward makes clear that he himself had sent them.

For today: when you do not understand what God is doing, do not worry. Think about it calmly, pray, and stay alert. God often gives us the answer step by step, and many times it comes in the form of a particular person or situation.
exp.20:28:
This verse explains why the Jews from Asia accused Paul. They had previously seen Trophimus the Ephesian with him in the city, and they assumed that Paul had brought him into the temple. The words "had previously seen" and "assumed" show that this was a supposition, not something they had confirmed. Trophimus was a Gentile, that is, not a Jew.

Luke, the narrator of the book, explains the origin of the uproar. Paul was in Jerusalem fulfilling a vow of purification to show respect for Jewish customs. Gentiles were forbidden to go past a certain boundary within the temple. Those who accused him shouted without evidence, and the crowd was stirred up.

For today: before accusing someone, it is wise to verify the facts. A suspicion or an appearance can lead us to judge wrongly and to cause harm. Let us ask God for prudence to speak the truth and not to repeat what we only suppose.
exp.13:1:
It says that the Jews who refused to believe Paul and Barnabas's message stirred up the Gentiles, that is, the non-Jews of Iconium. The phrase "stirred up" means to push or provoke, and the wording about their minds means they poisoned their minds and turned them against the believers, who are called "the brothers."

Luke, the author of Acts, tells what happened in Iconium during Paul and Barnabas's first missionary journey. Many people, both Jews and Greeks, had believed in the synagogue. But those who rejected the message did not stay quiet; they sought allies to oppose them.

For today: do not be surprised if sharing your faith brings rejection or criticism. The apostles did not give up; they stayed a long time, trusting in the Lord. Ask God for courage and peace to remain faithful.
exp.6:39:
This verse says that the people of Israel asked Aaron to make them gods who would go before them. The reason they gave was that they did not know what had happened to Moses, the one who led them out of Egypt. The request is to make gods that would lead the way ahead of them.

Stephen, the first martyr, speaks before the Jewish council. He reminds them of Israel's history to show that their ancestors rejected Moses, the leader God had sent them, and turned to idolatry. Stephen tells this episode of the golden calf (Exodus 32) to point out that the people had already resisted those whom God had sent.

For today: when God seems slow or keeps silent, we are tempted to look for security in things we make ourselves. Instead, we can wait with patience and trust the God who has already shown us his faithfulness.
exp.26:23:
Here an angel of God speaks to Paul in the middle of a terrible storm. He tells him not to be afraid, because he must stand before Caesar, the emperor of Rome. And God has granted him the lives of everyone who sails with him on the ship. The word "must" here reflects the wording of the verse as it stands.

Paul is a prisoner, and he is heading to Rome on a ship. They have gone many days without seeing the sun or the stars, and everyone has lost hope. Paul tells the sailors and soldiers what the angel said to him that night, to encourage them. He trusts that God will keep his word, even though the ship will be lost.

For today: when everything seems lost, God can give you calm and purpose. Trust his promises, and even in your own trial, seek to encourage others with hope and not only think about yourself.
exp.4:7:
Peter asks Sapphira a direct question: is this the price you and your husband got for the land? The word "land" refers to the property that was sold. The amount Peter mentions is not repeated in the text here. She answers yes, confirming that amount.

Peter, the leader of the early church, is the one speaking. Ananias, her husband, had just died after giving part of the money as though it were the whole sum. Peter gives Sapphira the chance to tell the truth, but she keeps up the lie. The problem was not keeping some of the money, but pretending to give everything.

For today: let us be honest with God and with others. When we are given the chance to correct a lie, it is a gift. It is better to tell the truth with humility than to maintain an appearance.
exp.6:18:
The king of Egypt, who was new to the throne, exploited the people of Israel and oppressed them. He forced the parents to abandon their newborn babies so that they would die, in order to keep the people from growing. "Family line" means family or descendants. "The generation was cut off" means that their descendants would be wiped out.

Stephen speaks before the Jewish council while he is on trial. He reviews the history of Israel and shows how God kept his promise to Abraham, even while the people were oppressed. This prepares the account of Moses, whom God used to deliver his people.

For today: even when evil seems strong and the plans of the powerful threaten the weak, God continues to work and to keep his promise. We can trust him in difficult times and stand up for those who are most vulnerable.
exp.8:23:
Saul learned of the plot against him. The phrase in the verse above refers to the schemes or secret traps the people had set. The Jews watched the city gates day and night, waiting to seize him and kill him when he tried to leave.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells this after Saul's conversion. Saul was now preaching that Jesus is the Christ, and this angered the Jews in Damascus, who could not answer his arguments. So they decided to get rid of him. The verses that follow show that the disciples helped him escape at night by lowering him over the wall in a basket.

Following Christ can bring opposition, even from people who are close to us. Even so, God often takes care of us through other believers. Accept the help of your Christian community with humility, and do not be afraid to ask for it when you need it.
exp.8:19:
It says that Saul, right after regaining his sight and being baptized, promptly began to proclaim Jesus in the synagogues, which were the meeting places of the Jews. The phrase "began to proclaim Jesus" means that he declared Jesus to be the promised Messiah. The words "He is the Son of God" express that Jesus has a unique relationship with the Father.

Here the narrator of the book, Luke, is speaking. Saul, who had once persecuted the believers, had met Jesus on the road to Damascus. Afterward he spent several days with the disciples there. The verses that follow show the amazement of the people, for he had come to arrest the Christians and now defended what he had once attacked.

For today: we do not need to wait until we are perfect or know everything before sharing what Jesus has done in us. We can speak simply and sincerely about our experience with Him, starting where we are.
exp.16:9:
As soon as night fell, the believers in Thessalonica sent Paul and Silas away toward Berea. When they arrived there, they went first into the Jewish synagogue.

The phrase "as soon as night had fallen" means it happened right away, that same night. The words "sent away" mean that the believers let them go in order to keep them safe.

The one telling the story is Luke, the author of Acts. In Thessalonica, Paul's preaching stirred up a great uproar, and the city leaders required a security deposit from Jason and other believers. That is why the brothers quickly sent the missionaries out, to avoid more violence. Even so, Paul kept his custom of beginning in the synagogue.

For today: when there is opposition, we do not always have to stay and fight; sometimes it is wise to change places. But let us not stop proclaiming the gospel and looking for new opportunities, trusting in God.
exp.2:10:
While the man clung to Peter and John, all the people were astonished and ran to them in the walkway called Solomon's Colonnade. This verse tells us that the man clung to Peter and John, and the people hurried toward them. They gathered in Solomon's Colonnade, a covered walkway with columns inside the temple area. "Astonished" means very amazed, so surprised that people could hardly find words.

The one telling the story is Luke, the author of Acts. The man everyone knew for begging was now walking, and that caught everyone's attention. This crowd gathered together gives Peter the opportunity to speak, and what he will say next is that the power does not come from them, but from God and from Jesus.

For today: when God does something good in our lives, the people around us take notice. We can use that moment to point to Jesus and not to ourselves.
exp.1:34:
This verse ends a quotation from Psalm 110:1. It says that the Lord speaks to another Lord: "Sit at my right hand, until I make Your enemies a footstool for Your feet." A footstool was a low seat where the feet could rest. The image speaks of total victory and of authority over every enemy.

Peter is preaching at Pentecost. He explains that David did not go up into heaven, so that psalm was not speaking of him, but of Jesus, whom God raised up and exalted. Peter uses it to show that Jesus is Lord and Christ, and that the Spirit poured out is a sign of this. The listeners were deeply moved and asked what they should do.

For today: although evil may sometimes seem strong, Christ already reigns, and his final victory is certain. We can live with hope and obey him with confidence.
exp.1:2:
This verse tells us that the disciples saw something like tongues of fire. These flames separated and came to rest on each one of them. The text says they were like flames of fire, so they looked like fire, yet they are described as a visible sign. "Separated" means they were spread apart, and "came to rest" means they settled on each person.

It is the day of Pentecost, a Jewish festival, and the followers of Jesus were gathered together in unity. Luke, the author of Acts, tells what happened. First there was a sound like a strong wind, and then fire appeared. In the Bible, fire and wind are often linked with the presence of God. The next verse shows that this sign accompanied the coming of the Holy Spirit.

For today: God wants to be close to each one of us, not just a few. You can ask him simply that his Spirit guide you, give you courage, and help you live in unity with other believers.
exp.16:2:
This verse says that Paul was explaining and presenting evidence that the Christ, that is, the Messiah, had to suffer and rise from the dead. He then declared that Jesus, the one he was proclaiming, is that Christ. The Berean Standard Bible uses the words "explaining" and "proving" to describe what Paul was doing, meaning he was setting out the case clearly and backing it with evidence. The phrase "had to suffer" conveys that this was necessary within God's plan.

The one speaking is Luke, the author of Acts, recounting what Paul did in Thessalonica. Paul went to the synagogue, as was his custom, and for three Sabbaths he reasoned with the Jews from the Scriptures. His central point was that the suffering and resurrection of the Messiah had already been foretold in them. Some believed and others became angry.

For today: when you speak about Jesus, rely on the Bible and explain with respect and patience. Some will believe and others will not, but your task is to present clearly who Christ is.
exp.4:39:
This verse says that the council accepted Gamaliel's advice. They called the apostles in and had them flogged, then ordered them not to speak in the name of Jesus, and released them. "At this, they yielded" means they gave way to his counsel, and "ordered" means they gave a command with authority.

The Jewish leaders were angry because the apostles kept preaching about Jesus. Gamaliel, a respected teacher of the law, advised them not to act with violence, and the council listened to him. Even so, they wanted to make their authority clear through punishment and prohibition. The flogging was a physical punishment and also a public humiliation.

Following Christ can bring rejection or mockery, and sometimes even pain. This passage encourages us not to keep silent about our faith out of fear, but to continue with humility and firmness, trusting that God sustains those who are faithful to him.
exp.17:1:
He says that when Paul arrived in Corinth, he found a Jew named Aquila, a native of Pontus, who had recently come from Italy with his wife Priscilla. They had come because the emperor Claudius had ordered all the Jews to leave Rome. Paul went to visit them. The word for "found" suggests a meeting, and the phrase "Paul went to visit them" means that he went looking for them.

Luke, the author of Acts, narrates the beginning of Paul's work in Corinth. Paul was coming from Athens, and in this city he needed a place to stay and a way to support himself. Ancient historians mention an expulsion of Jews from Rome under Claudius, though the exact date is debated. The text does not say here whether Aquila and Priscilla were already believers; that cannot be stated with certainty.

God often cares for us through people and circumstances that seem ordinary. Even what hurts us, such as exile, can prepare valuable encounters. Today, stay alert to those whom God places in your path, and open your heart to friendship and shared work.
exp.27:26:
This verse says that this people's heart has become hard and unfeeling. The idea of a heart that has grown callous means it has become hardened and insensitive. They hardly hear, as if they did not want to listen. Their closing of their eyes means they shut them on purpose. The reason is that they did not want to see, hear, or understand, because that would lead them to turn back to God and be healed.

Paul is a prisoner in Rome and speaks with Jewish leaders, who listen to everything for a whole day. Some believe and others do not, and they leave arguing among themselves. Paul quotes Isaiah 6 to explain that this same hardness had already happened earlier in Israel. Then he announces that the message of salvation will also go to the Gentiles.

For today: examine whether there is anything in the Word that you find hard to listen to. Ask God for a humble and open heart, so that his truth may correct you and heal you.
exp.7:23:
Simon asks Peter and John to pray to the Lord for him. He wants nothing of what Peter warned him about to happen to him. The word "pray" in the verse above is the request Simon makes of them, and "you" in the verse is the plural form addressed to both apostles.

Simon, who had earlier practiced magic in Samaria, had believed and been baptized. Then he offered money to the apostles so that he could receive the power to give the Holy Spirit. Peter rebuked him sharply. His response shows fear of the consequences. The text does not say whether there was genuine repentance, and people have interpreted it in different ways.

For today: it is not enough to fear punishment; God seeks a heart that changes. When someone corrects us with truth, it is wise to examine ourselves with humility, confess our wrong to God, and ask him to transform us, not merely to spare us from the consequences.
exp.9:14:
God speaks to Peter a second time and tells him not to call anything impure that God has made clean. The word "impure" here means unacceptable under Jewish law, and "clean" means that God has made it acceptable.

It is a voice from heaven during a vision. Peter saw a sheet with all kinds of animals, some of them forbidden by the law of Moses. That is why he refused to eat. Right away the messengers of Cornelius, a Gentile, arrived. In this way Peter understood that the vision was also speaking about welcoming people from other nations (Acts 10:28).

For today: do not put up barriers where God has taken them down. Examine whether there are people you reject because of prejudice, culture, or custom, and ask the Lord for a heart willing to receive them with love.
exp.18:13:
This verse introduces seven sons of a man named Sceva, who is described as a Jewish chief priest. They were doing the same thing as the exorcists mentioned before: trying to drive out evil spirits by using the name of Jesus. "Were doing this" refers to that attempt to cast out demons.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells what happened in Ephesus. God was performing extraordinary miracles through Paul, and some traveling exorcists wanted to copy his power. It is not known for certain whether Sceva was an official high priest; there is no other clear historical record of him. What matters is that they used the name of Jesus as a formula, without knowing him personally.

For today: faith in Jesus is not a formula or something borrowed from others. Rather than using religious words, we need to know Christ truly and walk with Him.
exp.15:17:
Paul grew tired of a girl following them and shouting for many days. He turned and spoke directly to the spirit that controlled her. In the name of Jesus Christ he commanded it to come out of her, and it left her at that very moment. The word translated here as "aggravated" means that he was bothered and annoyed. The phrase "spirit of divination" refers to a spirit of fortune-telling.

We are in Philippi. The girl brought her masters profit through her fortune-telling. What she shouted was true, but it came from a source outside of God, and Paul did not want that kind of publicity. Some think he waited several days out of prudence; the text only says he grew aggravated. Her deliverance caused her masters to lose their business, and so the persecution began.

For today: the authority of Jesus is real and sufficient. Also, doing what is right can cost us dearly, but God continues to work in the midst of difficulties.
exp.26:9:
Paul says to those on the ship: "Men, I can see that our voyage will be filled with disaster and great loss, not only to ship and cargo, but to our own lives as well." The word "cargo" means the goods the ship is carrying, and "disaster" here means serious harm or hardship.

Paul is traveling as a prisoner toward Rome. The fast had already passed, which probably refers to the Day of Atonement, at the end of September or in October, when sailing in the Mediterranean became dangerous. Paul warns them sincerely, although the centurion chose to follow the pilot and the owner of the ship. Some scholars think his warning comes from his experience in sea travel; others see it as an inspiration from God. The text does not make this clear.

Today we can learn to listen humbly to wise advice, even when it is not comfortable or popular. Before making an important decision, it is wise to ask God for wisdom and to weigh the risks carefully.
exp.1:38:
Peter says that God's promise belongs to those who were listening to him, to their children, and to those who are far off. It reaches everyone whom God calls to Himself.

Peter speaks in Jerusalem, on the day of Pentecost, to a crowd that felt guilty for having rejected Jesus. They asked what they should do. "Those who are far off" may refer to Jews scattered abroad or, according to many, also to non-Jews. Scholars understand it in several ways, but all see a wide invitation.

For today: no one is too far from God. If you sense that He is calling you, respond with humility and trust. And pray for your children and for those who seem distant, because the promise reaches them too.
exp.2:23:
This verse says that all the prophets, beginning with Samuel and continuing with those who came after him, announced "these days." That is, the times in which Peter and his hearers were living, with the coming of Jesus as the Messiah. The phrase "from Samuel on" marks the start of the line of prophets who came after Moses.

Peter is speaking in the temple in Jerusalem after a lame man was healed in the name of Jesus. The people were amazed, and Peter takes the opportunity to explain that this is no coincidence. He shows them that Jesus is the prophet promised by Moses and that the Scriptures they knew pointed toward him. He wants them to recognize Christ and turn to God.

For today: when you read the Bible, remember that its parts form one story that leads to Jesus. Ask God to help you see him in every page.
exp.7:38:
When Philip and the eunuch came up out of the water after the baptism, the Spirit of the Lord suddenly carried Philip away. The eunuch could no longer see him, but he went on his way full of joy. The phrase "carried Philip away" means he was taken off suddenly, and the eunuch's departure is described with the same kind of wording the verse itself uses.

Here the narrator, Luke, is speaking. Philip had been sent to explain the Scriptures to an Ethiopian official who was reading the prophet Isaiah. The man believed in Jesus and was baptized. Afterward, Philip was taken to another place, Azotus, and continued proclaiming the gospel. The text does not explain exactly how this transfer happened.

For today: true joy comes from knowing Jesus, not from depending on a person. The eunuch went on his way rejoicing even though his teacher was no longer there. We can help others come to know Christ and then trust that God sustains them.
exp.9:44:
This verse says that the Jewish believers who were with Peter were amazed. The word "astounded" means they were very surprised. "The circumcised believers" refers to the Jewish believers. "Gentiles" are people who were not Jewish. What surprised them was that God would also pour out his Holy Spirit on people from other nations.

The account is told by Luke. Peter was in the house of Cornelius, a Roman soldier, and was speaking to them about Jesus. While he preached, the Spirit fell on those who were listening. For the Jewish believers this was unexpected, because they thought the promise was only for them. This led Peter to baptize that family.

For today: let us not place limits where God has not placed them. If someone believes in Jesus, he is received by God, regardless of origin, culture or past. Let us ask God for an open heart to welcome gladly those whom He accepts.
exp.22:6:
As soon as Paul finished speaking, a sharp argument broke out between the Pharisees and the Sadducees, and the assembly was divided into two opposing sides. A "dispute" is a strong disagreement, a clash of opinions.

Paul was standing before the Jewish council, accused by his own countrymen. When he noticed that there were two groups, he declared that he was being judged for believing in the resurrection. The Pharisees believed in it; the Sadducees did not. Some think it was a strategic move, others that he expressed a genuine conviction. The Bible does not make this entirely clear.

For today: sometimes people divide over differences that distract them from what is essential. Before we argue, let us ask what truly matters, and let us not allow rivalries to pull us away from the truth or from loving our neighbor.
exp.9:46:
Peter asks a question that already carries its own answer: can anyone hold back the water to baptize these people? To withhold the water means to keep them from being baptized. Peter points out that they have received the Holy Spirit just as we have, in the same way the Jewish believers did.

Peter is speaking in the house of Cornelius, a Roman who feared God. While Peter was preaching, the Spirit fell on the Gentiles, and the Jewish believers who had come with him were amazed. Peter sees this as a clear sign that God had accepted them, and for that reason he orders that they be baptized.

For today: when God welcomes someone, let us not place barriers that He did not place. Let us receive with joy every person who believes in Jesus, regardless of their origin, culture, or past.
exp.23:4:
What it says: The accusers call Paul "a pestilence," meaning a plague or a harmful man. They also say he is "stirring up dissension among the Jews all over the world," meaning he causes unrest and division among them, and they call him "a ringleader of the sect of the Nazarenes," which means the leader of the group of followers of Jesus of Nazareth.

Context: The speaker is Tertullus, a lawyer hired by the high priest Ananias and the Jewish elders. He begins by flattering the governor Felix and then brings his accusations against Paul before him. He wants Felix to see Paul as a danger to public order. The charges are presented without proof, and Paul answers afterward.

For today: At times we will be labeled as something bad for following Christ. Let us keep an upright conduct, answer with calm and truth, and trust that God knows our heart, even when others slander us.
exp.5:4:
The apostles' proposal pleased the whole group. The original wording says the idea pleased everyone, which means they liked it. So they chose seven men: Stephen, described as a man full of faith and of the Holy Spirit, along with Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas, and Nicolas. Of Nicolas it is said that he came from Antioch and was a convert to Judaism, that is, a non-Jew who had joined the Jewish faith.

The apostles had asked the believers to choose seven men of good reputation to handle a problem in the daily distribution of food to the widows. They wanted to devote themselves to prayer and to the teaching of the word.
