All the names are Greek, and many believe this reflects the Greek-speaking believers, although the text does not state this directly.

For today: the church works best when responsibilities are shared. Serve wherever God places you, and choose those who serve by their character and not by their fame.
exp.18:20:
After these things had happened, Paul made up his mind in the Spirit to go to Jerusalem, passing through Macedonia and Achaia. He said, "After I have been there, I must see Rome as well." The word "must" points to a strong sense of need or purpose. The phrase "in the Spirit" can be understood either as Paul's own settled decision or as guidance from the Holy Spirit, and scholars read it both ways.

The one telling the story is Luke, who is writing the book of Acts. Before this point, the church in Ephesus had seen remarkable growth: people turned away from magic, burned their costly books, and the word of the Lord kept spreading. Now Paul looks ahead and plans the next stage of his work, with Rome already in view.

For today: even after a season of success, Paul does not settle into comfort but keeps looking for the next step. Ask God for direction, make your plans with humility, and stay willing to go wherever he leads you.
exp.24:20:
Here it says that Paul asked to have his case held over for the decision of the emperor, who was Caesar of Rome. To "appeal" meant that he brought his case before a higher authority. Being "held over" meant that he would remain in custody while the matter was pending. The phrase "the decision of the Emperor" means that the emperor would examine his case. That is why Festus ordered that Paul be held until he could be sent to Caesar.

The one speaking is Festus, the Roman governor. He explains the case to King Agrippa, who is visiting him. Festus says that the Jewish accusers were arguing with Paul about their religion and about a certain Jesus who had died, whom Paul claimed was alive. Festus did not know how to handle that matter, and Paul had already appealed to Caesar.

For today: even when circumstances seem closed or unjust, we can act with wisdom and keep trusting God. He can use even a slow process to carry his message further.
exp.11:9:
She says that Peter and the angel passed the first and second guards, that is, the guard posts of the prison. Then they came to the iron gate that led to the city, and it opened by itself. The verse says the gate opened for them by itself, with no one turning the lock. They went out, walked the length of one block, and suddenly the angel left him.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells how God brought Peter out of prison. Herod had put him in jail and planned to bring him to trial, after having killed James. Meanwhile, the church was praying for him. Peter thought he was dreaming until the angel left him alone in the street.

For today: God can open doors that seem impossible, and often He guides us step by step. Keep praying and obeying what He already shows you, even when you cannot see the whole road.
exp.16:29:
It says that God overlooked, or did not punish right away, the times when people lived without knowing him. God bore with those times in patience. But now God commands, that is, announces with authority, that all people, everywhere, must repent. To repent is to change direction and turn back to God.

The apostle Paul speaks in Athens, before philosophers at the Areopagus. The city was full of idols. Paul explains to them that God is the Creator and cannot be reduced to a statue. This message prepares the announcement of judgment and of Jesus' resurrection.

For today: God calls us with patience, not with indifference. Do not leave turning back to him for later. Today you can acknowledge in prayer whatever you have put in God's place and ask him for help to change.
exp.22:29:
This verse is part of the letter that the officer Claudius Lysias writes to the governor Felix. It says that, after he was informed of a plot against Paul, he sent Paul to Felix at once. He also instructed Paul's accusers to present their case against him before Felix. The letter ends with a simple closing wish, which we might put in modern words as "may things go well for you."

Lysias, a Roman officer, wants to explain why he is moving Paul to Caesarea. He had already concluded that Paul had done nothing deserving death or prison, and that the dispute concerned questions of Jewish law. More than forty men had sworn to kill Paul, and that is why he took him out of Jerusalem by night. Some scholars note that Lysias presents himself favorably in his letter, but the text does not say so clearly.

God can use even human authorities to protect his people. We can trust that He cares for us, even when He acts through unexpected ways.
exp.20:35:
This verse says that a large crowd was following Paul and the soldiers, shouting, "Away with him!" The words "Away with him!" are a direct cry for removal. The people were not asking for a trial; they were demanding that he be done away with.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells what happened in Jerusalem, in the temple. Some Jews accused Paul of teaching against the law and the temple, and a riot broke out. The Roman tribune rescued him, but the crowd, furious, kept following behind. The soldiers had to carry him up the steps of the fortress to protect him. It was a cry similar to the one heard against Jesus.

An enraged crowd can drag many people into condemning without understanding or checking anything. Before we repeat an accusation or join in the general outrage, let us stop, listen, and seek the truth. And if we are called to suffer for being faithful, let us remember that God took care of Paul even in the middle of the chaos.
exp.20:14:
After these days in Caesarea, Paul and his companions packed up and went on to Jerusalem. Jerusalem sits on high ground, and people often spoke of going there in this way.

Luke speaks here, for he travels with Paul and tells the story in the first person, saying "we." His friends had begged Paul not to go, because of the warnings about the suffering that awaited him. Paul did not change his mind, and they gave in, saying, "The will of the Lord be done." Now, without further argument, they set out on the way.

For today: when you believe God is calling you to something hard, prepare yourself with calm and obedience. Seek counsel from other believers, but commit the path to God, trusting that He sustains those who obey Him.
exp.6:12:
On the brothers' second visit to Egypt, Joseph revealed his identity to them, and his family became known to Pharaoh.

The speaker is Stephen, speaking before the Jewish council at the time he was being accused. He reviews the history of Israel. He tells how Joseph, whom his brothers had rejected, ended up as their savior. Many see a parallel here with Jesus, who was also rejected by his people, although Stephen develops this more fully later on.

For today: God can use even what was rejected or misunderstood to bring a blessing. If you feel ignored or mistreated today, trust that God is still at work, and try to respond with forgiveness, as Joseph did.
exp.7:27:
The verse tells us that the Ethiopian official was already on his way back to his homeland. He was traveling seated in his chariot, and as he went along, he was reading the prophet Isaiah. "On his return" means that he was heading back. "Chariot" here refers to a vehicle for travel, not an automobile.

The one telling the story is Luke, the author of Acts. Earlier, an angel sent Philip to a desert road, and there he met this man, a high official of the queen of Ethiopia who had gone to worship in Jerusalem. Luke highlights that he was reading the Scriptures, and this prepares the conversation that follows: the Spirit will lead Philip to approach him. Some scholars think the man was reading aloud, which was common in that time.

For today: even if you have a busy job or are traveling, set aside time to read the Bible. If something is hard to understand, ask God to help you and look for someone with whom you can talk it over.
exp.3:27:
Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles, and the people of Israel, when they came together against Jesus, carried out what God's hand and will had decided beforehand would happen. "Hand" speaks of his power, and "will" of his purpose. "Decided beforehand" means settled in advance.

The believers in Jerusalem pray together after Peter and John were threatened by the authorities. They quote Psalm 2 and acknowledge that Jesus' death did not take God by surprise. This does not make the guilty innocent; Christians have debated how God's sovereignty and human responsibility fit together, and the text does not fully explain it.

For today: when you face injustice or opposition, remember that God still rules and can work good even through evil. Pray as they did: ask for courage and trust, not just relief.
exp.27:16:
Paul arrives in Rome and, three days later, calls together the leaders of the Jews in the city. He tells them that he has done nothing against his people or the customs of our fathers. Even so, he was taken prisoner in Jerusalem and handed over to the Romans. He summoned them so that they could meet with him.

Paul speaks as a prisoner, yet with a certain freedom: he lives with a soldier who keeps watch over him. Before rumors can spread, he wants to explain his situation to the Jewish leaders in Rome. He speaks to them with respect, addressing them as "brothers." He seeks to prevent misunderstandings and to open a door for sharing the gospel with them, as the chapter shows afterward.

For today: when you are misunderstood or accused, follow Paul's example. Explain the truth calmly, without bitterness and with respect. Your goal is not to win an argument, but to keep open the way to speak of your faith with love.
exp.20:11:
When we heard this, Paul's companions and the believers from Caesarea pleaded with him not to go up to Jerusalem. This verse tells how they responded after hearing Agabus's prophecy. The phrase "go up" reflects the fact that Jerusalem was built on high ground.

The one speaking is Luke, who travels with Paul and includes himself in the account by saying "we." Agabus had announced that Paul would be bound and handed over to the Gentiles. Out of love, everyone wanted to protect him. Paul, however, was already determined to obey, even if it cost him his life. In the end, they accepted the will of the Lord.

For today: affection for someone can lead us to want to spare them all suffering. Let us learn to accompany others with prayer and respect when they sense a calling from God, and to trust that his will is good even when the path is hard.
exp.11:14:
These believers gathered at home did not believe Rhoda when she said Peter was standing outside. They told her, "You are out of your mind," but she kept insisting it was so. Then they said, "It must be his angel." By this they meant that perhaps it was an angel or a spirit representing Peter. The Bible does not fully explain this idea, and it has been understood in different ways.

Peter was in prison, and the church was praying for him. An angel had brought him out of the prison. Rhoda, full of joy, ran to tell them without opening the door. The others, although they were praying, were surprised to see the answer.

For today: we pray with faith, but sometimes we struggle to believe when God answers. Let us ask God for a simple faith, and receive his answers with humility and joy, even when they come in unexpected ways.
exp.20:8:
Acts 21:9 says that Philip, the evangelist in whose house Paul and his companions stayed, had four unmarried daughters who prophesied. Prophesying here means speaking messages from God to encourage and guide others.

The one telling this is Luke, who travels with Paul and recounts what they experienced in Caesarea. He mentions Philip's daughters as a detail of the household where they were received. The text does not say what they prophesied. Shortly afterward Agabus arrives and announces that Paul would be handed over in Jerusalem. So we see that God was speaking through different people in that church.

For today: God can use any member of his family, young or old, men or women. Ask yourself how you can put your gifts at the service of others, and open your home with hospitality, as Philip did.
exp.11:23:
This verse says that God's message kept moving forward and spread wider and wider. "Continued to spread" means that it kept going out to new places, and "multiply" means that more and more people were receiving it. Here "the word of God" refers to the message of the gospel.

Luke, the author of Acts, is the one telling the story. He has just recounted the death of Herod Agrippa, who accepted being worshiped instead of giving the glory to God. Earlier, Herod had persecuted the church and imprisoned Peter. Luke contrasts these two things: a powerful king falls, but the word of God keeps spreading.

For today: do not lose heart when opposition seems strong. God does not depend on human power to accomplish his work. Keep sharing and living out his word with confidence, and avoid seeking glory for yourself.
exp.9:19:
It says that Peter must get up, go downstairs, and go with the three men who are looking for him, without hesitation. "Without hesitation" means not to hold back or raise objections. The reason is that God himself has sent them. "Go downstairs" refers to coming down from the rooftop where Peter was praying.

The Holy Spirit speaks to Peter, who was in Joppa thinking about the vision of the animals and about what is clean and unclean. The men came on behalf of Cornelius, a Roman officer who was not a Jew. For a Jew, entering the house of a non-Jew was something very delicate. That is why the Spirit makes clear to him that he should not hesitate: God is behind all of this.

For today: when God shows us clearly that he wants us to serve or help someone, let us not allow prejudices or customs to hold us back. Let us pray, listen, and obey with confidence.
exp.1:45:
This verse says that the first believers in Jerusalem met together every day. They gathered in the temple courts and also shared meals in their homes. "Continued to meet daily" means they kept at it steadily, day after day. "With one accord" means they had the same mind and purpose. "Break bread" meant sharing a meal, and many believe it included the Lord's Supper. "Sincerity of heart" means honesty and openness, with no hidden motives.

Luke, the author of Acts, describes how the newly born church lived, shortly after Pentecost. The believers shared their possessions with anyone in need. Because they were close to one another, their faith showed in practical ways. Luke does not give a command but describes what was happening.

For today: open your home or your table to someone from your church this week. Sharing a meal with joy and honesty strengthens fellowship and shows the love of Christ.
exp.12:10:
He says that God himself is going to act against this man: he will be blind for a time and will not be able to see the light of the sun. Immediately mist and darkness came over him, and he groped about, looking for someone to lead him by the hand. The blindness is described as lasting "for a time," which means it would not be permanent.

Paul, filled with the Holy Spirit, is speaking in Cyprus. The man is Elymas, a magician who was trying to turn the proconsul Sergius Paulus away from the faith. Paul confronts him because he was hindering the message of the gospel. The blindness was a sign, and the proconsul believed when he saw it.

For today: God takes the truth seriously and does not overlook those who obstruct it. Examine whether, by your words or attitudes, you help others come close to God or get in their way.
exp.9:13:
Peter answers firmly, "No, Lord!" He says he has never eaten anything impure or unclean. Those are the kinds of food the law of Moses set apart as unfit to eat. What is striking is that he calls the one giving him an order "Lord," yet at the same time tells him no.

Peter is praying on a rooftop in Joppa, he is hungry, and he receives a vision of a sheet full of animals. As a faithful Jew, he had kept the food laws all his life. Later in the chapter it becomes clear that God uses this vision to teach him that he must accept non-Jews, such as Cornelius, without regarding them as unclean.

For today: sometimes our sincere customs make us resist what God wants to do. Let us ask for humility to listen to his voice, even when it makes us uncomfortable, and to welcome those whom he has already accepted.
exp.16:0:
This verse tells that Paul and his companions traveled through the cities of Amphipolis and Apollonia, and came to Thessalonica. There was a Jewish synagogue there, that is, the place where Jewish people gathered to pray and read the Scriptures.

The one telling the story is Luke, the author of the book of Acts. He recounts Paul's second missionary journey. The text does not say that they stopped to preach in Amphipolis or in Apollonia; they only passed through them. They stopped in Thessalonica, an important city, where there was a Jewish synagogue. The verses that follow show that Paul began there, as was his custom, speaking about Jesus from the Scriptures.

For today: look for the places where people are already open to listen. Paul did not wander aimlessly; he went with purpose to where he could share his faith clearly and with respect.
exp.9:33:
Peter begins to speak and says that he now truly understands something important: God does not show favoritism. He has no favorites and does not treat some people better because of where they come from, their race, or their position. Peter's words are spoken with seriousness, as he opens the matter with a solemn statement of what he has come to see.

Peter speaks in the house of Cornelius, a Roman officer who was not a Jew. God had sent an angel to Cornelius, and had shown Peter a vision so that he would not reject non-Jewish people. Cornelius and his household were gathered together, ready to hear what God had commanded Peter to say. That is why this moment marks a change: the message of Jesus is for all peoples.

Today we can examine our hearts and ask whether we look at someone as having less worth because of their country, their skin color, their money, or their culture. If God shows no favoritism, neither should we. Today, treat someone who is different from you with respect and kindness.
exp.6:54:
He says that Stephen, full of the Holy Spirit, looked intently into heaven and saw the glory of God. He also saw Jesus standing at the right hand of God, that is, in the place of honor and authority.

Stephen is being judged before the Sanhedrin. He has just reviewed the history of Israel and accused the leaders of resisting God. They, furious, ground their teeth at him. In that tense moment, God allows him to see Jesus standing. The text does not explain why Jesus is shown standing, although the next verse calls him "Son of Man". Some think the standing position suggests support for Stephen, but that is an interpretation.

When you face opposition or fear, lift your eyes to Jesus in prayer. He continues to reign and is close to his own.
exp.27:25:
This verse records the words that God spoke to the prophet Isaiah, which Paul quotes. It says that the people would keep on hearing but never understanding, and keep on seeing but never truly perceiving. The phrase "Go to this people" points to the people Isaiah was sent to speak to, and the word "perceiving" means grasping what is seen.

Paul is in prison in Rome and explains the message of Jesus to the leading Jews. Some believe and others do not, and they leave divided. Paul quotes Isaiah to show that this hardness of heart had already happened before. Then he says that God's salvation also goes to the Gentiles, that is, to the non-Jews.

For today: hearing the Word is not enough; it must be received with a humble heart. Before reading the Bible, we can ask God to open our understanding and to make us obey what we understand.
exp.16:32:
This verse says that Paul left the gathering in Athens. The phrase "Paul left" means that he withdrew from the place where he had been speaking.

Paul had just spoken before the philosophers at the Areopagus, a place of meeting and debate in Athens. When he announced that God raised Jesus and that there will be a judgment, some mocked him and others asked to hear him again. Luke, the author of Acts, tells that Paul left without quarreling or insisting. The text does not explain his reasons, so it is best not to assume more. But the next verse shows that his message did bear fruit: some people believed.

For today: you do not need to convince everyone. Share what you believe with respect, let God work in each heart, and do not be discouraged by mockery. Some seeds bear fruit even when you do not see it right away.
exp.6:14:
It says that Jacob went down to Egypt, where he and our ancestors died, meaning the twelve sons of Jacob. The phrase "went down" is used because Egypt lies to the south and lower on the map, and "family line" in the previous verse means household or kin.

It is part of Stephen's speech before the Jewish council, when he was accused of speaking against the temple and the law. He reviews the history of Israel to show how God worked with his people, even outside the Promised Land and through people who were rejected, such as Joseph. The texts of Genesis and Exodus mention seventy or seventy-five people, and the difference is usually explained by different ways of counting.

For today: God continues to keep his promises even when we go through difficult or unexpected places. We can trust that he guides our story, even when we cannot see the whole path.
exp.27:0:
Paul and his companions found out, after they had been rescued from the shipwreck, that the island where they had come ashore was called Malta. The phrase "safely ashore" means that they reached land safe and sound. Malta is the name most commonly linked with this island today, though some scholars have suggested other places.

The narrator is Luke, the author of Acts, who was traveling with Paul. Paul was a prisoner on his way to Rome. A violent storm at sea had wrecked the ship, but God had promised that no one would die. This verse opens a new scene: now they are safe, but in an unfamiliar place, and soon they will receive help from the people of the island.

For today: after a crisis, take a moment to acknowledge that God sustained you. And when you arrive at a new and unfamiliar place, trust that He also cares for what comes next.
exp.6:29:
It says that forty years had passed since Moses fled from Egypt. Then an angel appeared to him in the desert, near Mount Sinai, within the flames of a burning bush, a thorny shrub. "After forty years had passed" marks the length of time. "Appeared to him" means that he saw it.

Stephen speaks before the Jewish council, accused of speaking against the temple and the law. He reminds them of their history to show that God acts and reveals himself outside the temple and outside the promised land. Moses had been rejected by his own people, and yet God chose him. According to the account in Exodus, the angel is tied to the very presence of God.

For today: God can call us in unexpected places and times, even after years of silence or failure. Learn to wait with patience and to listen with reverence.
exp.6:59:
Stephen kneels down and cries out in a loud voice, "Lord, do not hold this sin against them." Having said this, he fell asleep, a gentle way of saying that he died. The phrase "hold this sin against them" means to count a wrong as charged to someone's account, to record it against them.

Stephen is a follower of Jesus, falsely accused and stoned by Jewish leaders. His prayer echoes the words of Jesus on the cross, in Luke 23:34. Among those present is Saul, the young man who was watching the cloaks and who would later become the apostle Paul. The text does not say that Stephen knew this.

When someone hurts us, we can pray for that person instead of repaying evil for evil. Forgiving does not deny that an injustice happened. It hands judgment over to God and asks him to change the heart of the one who harmed us. Today you can name someone who hurt you and pray for their good.
exp.7:34:
Luke says that Philip began to speak, and he describes it with the words "opening his mouth," which is an old way of saying he started explaining eagerly. He began with the passage from Isaiah that the official was reading and told him the good news about Jesus. The word "scripture" refers to the text of the prophet Isaiah.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells that Philip met an Ethiopian official who was reading Isaiah 53 in his chariot. The man did not understand whom the prophet was speaking about and asked whether he was speaking about himself or about someone else. Philip took advantage of that sincere question to show him that the passage points to Jesus, as Christians believe.

For today: when someone asks you a question about faith, listen first and start from what that person is already reading or living. Speak of Jesus simply, without pressure and without arguments.
exp.17:3:
Paul spoke in the synagogue every Sabbath, reasoning with the people and trying to persuade both Jews and Greeks. The word "reasoned" here does not mean arguing or fighting. It means discussing, explaining, and giving reasons from the Scriptures. Trying to persuade means he was working to help both Jews and Greeks, that is, non-Jewish people who came to the gathering, come to believe.

Paul is in Corinth. He worked alongside Aquila and Priscilla making tents, and on the Sabbath he used the synagogue gathering to speak about Jesus. Luke, who wrote Acts, shows that Paul supported himself through his own labor while never giving up the work of proclaiming the gospel.

For today: we can share our faith with respect, patience, and clear reasons, without neglecting our work and responsibilities. Speaking of Jesus is not about arguing to win, but about explaining with love so that others can believe.
exp.2:11:
Peter sees the crowd amazed and asks them two questions: why are they so surprised, and why do they stare at him and John as if they had made the lame man walk by their own power or godliness? The words "power" and "godliness" come straight from the verse, and "godliness" refers to their devoted way of life.

Peter is speaking in Solomon's Porch, in the temple, just after the crippled beggar was healed. The crowd rushes toward them, impressed. Peter takes the moment to correct a mistake: he does not want to be admired, but points toward God and toward Jesus, as the next verse shows.

For today: when God does something good through us, let us not take the glory. We can serve with humility and say sincerely, "It was God who did this, not me."
exp.12:36:
This verse says that God raised Jesus from the dead, and that his body did not decay in the tomb. The word "saw" in the verse above is the one used here, and "decay" refers to the breakdown of the body after death.

Paul speaks in the synagogue at Antioch of Pisidia. He quotes Psalm 16 ("you will not let your Holy One see decay") and explains that David could not be the fulfillment, because he died, was buried, and his body decayed. That is why Paul says this promise was fulfilled in Jesus, raised from the dead, and from there he announces the forgiveness of sins.

For today: if Jesus has overcome death, our hope does not rest on our efforts or our good record, but on him. Today you can entrust your failures and your fears to the living Christ, knowing that he offers you forgiveness and true life.
exp.15:35:
The jailer tells Paul that the city's magistrates have sent orders to set them free. The magistrates were the judges or rulers of Philippi. The officers were the officials who carried out their orders. "Set free" means released from prison. The jailer says to them: "Now you may go on your way in peace."

The jailer is the man who, the night before, had believed in God along with his whole household. Paul and Silas had been beaten and thrown into prison without a trial. Now, at dawn, the authorities want to let them go quietly. The jailer, grateful and changed, passes on the message with good intent. Paul will respond afterward by claiming his rights as a Roman citizen.

For today: God can change a heart and open doors in the midst of suffering. When he works, we can respond with gratitude and with peace. We can also act with wisdom and justice, without yielding to injustice, as Paul did.
exp.25:26:
Paul asks King Agrippa a direct question: "Do you believe the prophets?" and then answers it for him: "I know you do." Paul is not expecting a debate; he wants to bring the conversation into the personal.

Paul is in prison and defends his faith before Festus and King Agrippa, who knew the Jewish Scriptures and what had happened with Jesus. Paul had already said that Christ fulfilled what the prophets announced. Now the focus turns to Agrippa's conscience. We do not know what Agrippa felt inside; his response can be understood in several ways.

For today: knowing the Bible or agreeing with it in the mind is not enough. Ask yourself honestly whether you trust God and respond to what He tells you.
exp.26:12:
It says that a gentle south wind began to blow. The sailors thought they had their opportunity, so they weighed anchor and sailed along, hugging the coast of Crete. "Weighed anchor" means they pulled up the anchor to set out; some scholars understand it as the start of the voyage itself.

Luke, who travels with Paul, recounts the voyage toward Rome. Paul had warned that sailing was dangerous, but the centurion trusted the pilot and the owner of the ship more. They wanted to reach Phoenix, a better harbor for spending the winter. That gentle wind seemed to confirm their decision.

For today: a favorable circumstance does not always confirm that a decision is wise. Before moving forward, it is good to pray, listen to prudent counsel, and not let ourselves be guided only by the comfort of the moment.
exp.1:23:
This verse says that God raised Jesus from the dead and freed him from the agony of death, the way a person breaks free from restraints. It says it was impossible for death to keep him in its grip. The verse presents the resurrection as God's action, and it describes Jesus as no longer bound by death.

Peter speaks at Pentecost, just after the Holy Spirit has come. He addresses the Israelites gathered in Jerusalem. He explains that Jesus was handed over according to God's plan, although they bore responsibility for crucifying him. Then he quotes David to show that the resurrection had already been foretold in the Scriptures.

For today: if Christ overcame death, our hope does not depend on circumstances. When you face loss, fear, or pain, remember that God has the final word, and trust in Him.
exp.18:28:
This verse says that the city of Ephesus was thrown into disarray. The people rushed together into the theatre, dragging along Gaius and Aristarchus, two men from Macedonia who were traveling with Paul. The wording "dragging with them" shows that the two men were taken along against their will, pulled through the streets by the crowd.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells what happened after the silversmith Demetrius stirred up the craftsmen. They earned their money making images of Diana, and Paul's message threatened their business and their religion. Angry and looking for someone to blame, they seized Paul's companions, even though Paul himself was not there.

For today: when anger and the crowd pull us along, it is wise to stop and think. Often the pressure of the group, or the fear of losing money or comfort, leads us to treat others badly. Let us ask God for calm and courage to act with justice.
exp.23:8:
In Acts 24:9, the Jews who had come to accuse Paul also joined in and firmly affirmed that everything the lawyer Tertullus had said was true. The phrase "concurred" means they backed the accusation with force, and "charges were true" means the claims against Paul were presented as accurate.

Paul is in Caesarea, before the governor Felix. Tertullus, an orator hired by the high priest and the elders, had just accused Paul. The Jews present back up his speech, although the text shows no proof, only insistence. Afterward Paul will answer calmly.

For today: repeating something with great force does not make it true. Before joining in an accusation, it is wise to ask for the evidence and to listen to the other person. We can also learn from Paul to respond with composure and truth.
exp.14:39:
This verse tells us that Paul chose Silas as his companion for the journey. The brothers and sisters of the church sent them off by commending Paul to the grace of the Lord, that is, asking that the Lord would watch over him and sustain him.

The verse's wording shows that Paul made the choice himself, and the phrase "commended by the brothers" shows that the church gave its blessing to the journey.

The narrator is Luke, the author of the book of Acts. Paul and Barnabas had just parted ways over a disagreement about taking John Mark along, since Mark had left them earlier. Even so, the work went on: Barnabas continued with Mark, and Paul went with Silas. The text does not say that the church took sides; it only says that they blessed Paul.

For today: disagreements between believers can be painful, but God can continue to work through both sides. Let us seek to serve with humility, and let us commend ourselves, and commend others, to the Lord's grace.
exp.18:1:
Paul asks some disciples in Ephesus whether they received the Holy Spirit when they became believers. They answer that they have not even heard that there is a Holy Spirit.

Paul arrives in Ephesus and finds these disciples. From what follows, they knew only the baptism of John, which called people to repentance and pointed to Jesus. Paul asks them the question because he notices that something is missing from their faith. Scholars debate how exactly to understand their condition, but the text shows that they needed to know Jesus more fully.

For today: let us not assume that everyone understands the Christian faith well. We can ask questions kindly, listen, and help others know Jesus and the work of the Holy Spirit better, and also be willing to keep learning ourselves.
exp.8:10:
The Lord tells Ananias to get up and go to a street called Straight. There, at the house of a man named Judas, he is to ask for Saul, a man from Tarsus. The reason is simple: Saul is praying.

Here is the background. Jesus, the Lord, speaks to Ananias, a disciple in Damascus, in a vision. Saul had just met Jesus on the road and had been blind for three days, neither eating nor drinking. Saul had previously persecuted Christians, which is why Ananias will be afraid, as the next verse shows. The Lord gives an exact direction and place.

For today: God sees and knows the people we might consider lost. If someone seems impossible to reach, pray for that person and ask God to show you how to obey him, even when you feel afraid.
exp.17:9:
He says the Lord promises Paul his presence and protection: "I am with you." No one will lay a hand on Paul to harm him or successfully attack him. The reason is that the Lord has many people in Corinth, that is, many people who will respond to the gospel. The word "no one" in the verse means no one at all.

Jesus, the Lord, speaks in a night vision. Paul was in Corinth, where some Jews opposed him, and it is possible that he felt fear. Jesus encourages him: "Do not be afraid, but speak." Afterward Paul stayed there for a year and a half teaching. Interpreters understand "many people" as people who would believe, even though they had not yet believed.

When you serve God and feel fear, remember that his companionship is real. It does not mean there will be no difficulties, but it does mean that he sustains you while you remain faithful.
exp.12:3:
This verse tells how Barnabas and Saul set out from Antioch, sent forth by the Holy Spirit. They went down to the port of Seleucia and from there sailed to the island of Cyprus. The phrase "went down" describes their journey to the port, and "sailed" describes the trip across the water to Cyprus. Cyprus is the island we know by that name today.

Luke, the author of Acts, narrates the beginning of the first missionary journey. The church in Antioch was worshiping and fasting when the Holy Spirit set them apart for a special work. The church prayed, laid hands on them, and sent them away. Cyprus was a logical place to begin, since Barnabas was from there (Acts 4:36).

For today: when God calls us to something, it is wise to seek it in prayer and with the community of faith, and then take the first concrete step of obedience, even when we cannot see the whole road.
exp.7:35:
Here it says that Philip and the eunuch were traveling along the road and came to some water. The eunuch, an official from Ethiopia, said: "Look, here is water! What is there to prevent me from being baptized?"

The eunuch is the one speaking. He had been reading the prophet Isaiah, and Philip had explained to him that the passage was about Jesus. Once he understood the good news, he wanted to respond right away. His question shows a sincere desire to obey.

For today: when you understand who Jesus is, do not delay your response of faith without reason. Ask honestly what is holding you back, and seek counsel in your church.
exp.5:13:
False witnesses accuse Stephen of saying that Jesus of Nazareth will destroy "this place," meaning the temple, and will change the customs, that is, the laws and traditions that Moses handed down to us.

This happens when Stephen is brought before the council, the Jewish court. Some men, angry at his preaching, paid for or arranged false witnesses. What they said had some truth to it, since Jesus had indeed spoken about the temple, but they twisted it to charge Stephen with blasphemy. Interpreters see here an echo of the accusations made against Jesus himself.

For today: when someone accuses us or distorts our words, we should not respond with lies or resentment. Stephen remained at peace, and his face, as the next verse says, looked like the face of an angel. Let us trust that God knows the truth and sustains us.
exp.23:5:
This verse says that Paul "tried" to desecrate the temple. To desecrate it means to defile it, to treat it as an ordinary place and not a holy one. The verse says they "seized" him, meaning they arrested him. The accusers say they were prepared to judge him under their own religious law.

The speaker is Tertullus, the lawyer for the Jewish leaders, addressing the governor Felix in Caesarea. He accuses Paul with strong words to persuade the governor. However, the account in Acts 21 shows that the crowd grabbed him and was trying to kill him, and that the commander rescued him. His version leaves out that detail and presents the facts in his own favor.

For today: not everything that is said with confidence is the complete truth. Before we believe or repeat an accusation, let us look for the facts and listen with fairness. And if we are unjustly accused, Paul reminds us that we can respond with calm and truth.
exp.15:8:
During the night Paul had a vision. In it he saw a man from Macedonia standing before him, pleading with him: "Come over to Macedonia and help us." Macedonia was a region north of Greece, across the Aegean Sea.

Luke, who wrote the book, tells how Paul and his companions had wanted to go to Bithynia, but the Spirit did not allow them to go there. They arrived at Troas, a port by the sea. There God showed them where to go. The next verse says that they concluded God was calling them to take the gospel to Macedonia.

For today: sometimes God changes our plans by closing some doors. We can pray, ask for direction, and stay attentive, also with the counsel of other believers, to discover whom He is sending us to serve. Then, with confidence, we take the step.
exp.9:23:
Luke tells us that Peter and his companions arrived in Caesarea the day after leaving Joppa. Cornelius was already waiting for them and had gathered his relatives and his closest friends. The word "relatives" here can mean people he trusted deeply, not only blood relatives. "The following day" simply means the next day.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells how the gospel reached non-Jews. Cornelius, a Roman officer who feared God, had received a vision that led him to send for Peter. Peter traveled with some brothers from Joppa, who would be witnesses to what was about to happen. Cornelius did not expect merely a visit, but a message from God, and that is why he invited others.

For today: Cornelius did not keep his interest in God to himself, but invited those dear to him to listen. We can do the same: open our homes and call family and friends to share the faith, with expectation and simplicity.
exp.26:7:
The ship moved along the southern coast of the island of Crete with great difficulty until it reached a place called Fair Havens. Moving along the coast means following the shoreline, and the effort was real because the wind was against them. Near that place was the town of Lasea.

The one speaking is Luke, the author of Acts, who travels with Paul. Paul is going as a prisoner toward Rome, under the custody of a centurion. The voyage is being delayed and the weather is getting worse. This place is an important stop before Paul warns of the danger of continuing to sail. Today not everything is known with certainty about Lasea, but the passage places it near that harbor.

For today: there are seasons of life that move slowly and with difficulty. Even so, God cares for us at every stage. Be patient, and when there are signs of danger, listen humbly to good advice.
exp.13:3:
The people of the city of Iconium were divided. One group sided with the Jews who did not believe, and the other group sided with the apostles, Paul and Barnabas. The word "crowd" here refers to the ordinary people of the city.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells what happened in Iconium during Paul and Barnabas's first missionary journey. They had preached the good news, and many believed, but others strongly opposed them. Even so, the apostles stayed a long time, trusting in the Lord, until the opposition turned violent and they had to flee.

For today: the message of Jesus will not always unite everyone; sometimes it divides opinions. We should not be frightened by this. We can keep speaking with love, humility and firmness, trusting that God cares for his word and for us.
exp.0:10:
Two men dressed in white speak to the disciples. They ask why they are standing there looking up at the sky. The men say that this same Jesus, who has been taken from them into heaven, will come back in the same way they saw him go into heaven.

Jesus had just gone up, and a cloud hid him from their sight. The disciples stood there looking up, perhaps amazed or unsure of what to do next. The two men call them back to their task of waiting and getting ready. So the disciples return to Jerusalem and gather in the upper room.

For today: Waiting for Christ's return does not mean standing around staring at the sky and doing nothing. It means living with hope and serving faithfully at the same time. Today you can help someone, pray, or share your faith, trusting that Jesus will keep his promise.
exp.2:18:
It says we should change direction: repent and turn back to God, so that our sins are wiped away. The phrase about "times of refreshing" points to relief, rest, or renewal, like cool water on a hot day. The idea that these times come from the Lord means this relief is given by Him. Some understand it as a blessing already present, and others understand it as also referring to the return of Christ.

Peter speaks in the temple in Jerusalem, after God healed a man who was lame. He addresses the people who had rejected Jesus. He tells them that they acted in ignorance, but that God fulfilled what the prophets had announced. For this reason he invites them to turn to Him.

For today: do not carry your guilt alone. Speak to God today with sincerity, acknowledge what you did wrong, and take a concrete step to change. He offers forgiveness and true rest for the soul.
exp.18:34:
A city official, called the "city clerk" (something like the chief secretary), manages to calm the crowd. He reminds them of what everyone already knows: that Ephesus is the guardian of the temple of the great goddess Artemis (Diana) and of her image, which was believed to have fallen from heaven. The text speaks of the image as having fallen from heaven, but exactly what that image was is not known for certain.

The people were stirred up because Paul's preaching was hurting the business of those who made figures of the goddess. They had been shouting for almost two hours. The city clerk speaks to prevent punishment from the Roman authorities for the disorder.

Today, God can use a calm and sensible voice to put out a conflict. Before reacting in anger or following the crowd, stop, breathe, and speak with calm and truth.
exp.6:7:
He gave Abraham the covenant of circumcision, a sign of his promise. Abraham became the father of Isaac and circumcised him on the eighth day. After that came Jacob, and from Jacob came the twelve patriarchs, the heads of the twelve tribes of Israel.

Stephen speaks before the Jewish council as he defends himself against false accusations. He reviews the history of Israel to show that God was at work among his people long before the temple and the law. Here he highlights that the promise and the covenant came first, and that God carries out his plan step by step, even in the midst of the family envy that continues in verse 9.

God is faithful from generation to generation. Today we can trust that his promises do not depend on our circumstances. Furthermore, it falls to us to pass on the faith to our children and to those who follow us, through words and through daily example.
exp.20:18:
He greeted James and the elders of Jerusalem, and then he reported in detail everything God had done among the non-Jewish peoples (the Gentiles) through his work. The verse's phrase "one by one" means he went through each point in turn, giving the details. The word "ministry" in the verse refers to his service to the Lord.

Luke, who writes the book and travels with Paul, recounts this meeting upon their arrival in Jerusalem. James was a recognized leader of the church there. Paul does not boast of his achievements; he credits the work to God. The leaders respond by glorifying God, though they soon mention a concern: rumors about Paul and the law of Moses.

For today: when you share what you have experienced in your service or in your life of faith, give the credit to God and do so with humility. Telling what God is doing encourages others and leads them to give thanks to Him.
exp.1:20:
This verse says that everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will receive salvation. To "call on" the name of the Lord means to call out to him in faith, and to "be saved" means to be rescued or delivered by God. The promise sets no limits: it covers everyone.

Peter speaks to a crowd in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost. He has just received the Holy Spirit along with the disciples, and the people are amazed. He quotes the prophet Joel to explain what is happening. Then, in the verses that follow, he presents Jesus of Nazareth, crucified and risen, as the one in whom this promise is fulfilled. Many understand that "the Lord" here refers to Jesus.

For today: if you feel far from God or doubt that he hears you, you can call on him simply and sincerely. You do not need perfect words; you only need to trust in Jesus and ask him for his help and his forgiveness.
exp.25:24:
Paul answers Festus respectfully: "I am not insane." He calls him "most excellent Festus," a courteous title for a person in authority. Paul affirms that his words are true and sensible. "Sobriety" here means good judgment, sound sense, and self-control, not a fit of madness.

Paul is defending his faith before Festus, the Roman governor, and before King Agrippa. He has just spoken of Christ, who suffered and rose again. Festus, who was not used to these ideas, interrupts him and thinks that so much study has unbalanced him. Paul is not offended and does not defend himself in anger, but answers with calm and returns to speaking the truth.

For today: sometimes we will be called extreme for believing in Jesus. We can answer as Paul did, with kindness, firmness, and clarity, without fighting, trusting that the truth stands on its own.
exp.5:3:
The apostles say that they will devote themselves to two things: prayer and the ministry of the word. "Devote ourselves" means that they will give their full attention to these, holding to them firmly and without giving up. "Ministry of the word" means the work of preaching and teaching.

The twelve apostles are speaking to the whole community of disciples in Jerusalem. The church had grown a great deal, and a complaint arose because some widows were not receiving the daily help well. The apostles did not look down on that service, but they proposed that seven men of good reputation take charge of it, so that they could keep to their main calling.

For today: every church and every believer needs to recognize their calling and share the tasks. Serving those in need is important, and so is praying and feeding on the Word. Ask yourself what is yours to do, and do not stop praying while you serve.
exp.20:30:
It says that while the crowd was trying to kill Paul, someone reported to the Roman commander that all Jerusalem was in turmoil. The "commander of the Roman regiment" was the officer in charge of about a thousand soldiers, and the "regiment" was that Roman unit. "Turmoil" means agitated and full of disorder.

It is part of Luke's account in Acts. Paul had arrived in Jerusalem, and some Jews from Asia falsely accused him of having brought a Gentile, Trophimus, into the temple. With that suspicion, the people dragged him out to kill him. The report to the commander led the soldiers to arrive quickly and stop the beating.

For today: when emotions boil over, it is easy to judge by suspicion rather than by facts. Before reacting or repeating an accusation, it is wise to check the truth calmly and seek justice, not revenge.
exp.5:10:
Unable to defeat Stephen with arguments, the text says, some men paid or persuaded others to lie. They were to say that Stephen had spoken offensive words against Moses and against God. The phrase "prompted some men" means that they got others to say what they wanted, through bribery or pressure.

The one who writes is Luke, who recounts what happened in the church in Jerusalem. Stephen spoke with wisdom, and members of several synagogues could not answer him. Instead of admitting their mistake, they resorted to lies. They wanted the people and the leaders to see him as an enemy of the law and the temple.

When someone cannot win by the truth, they sometimes turn to slander. Today we can avoid repeating rumors and seek the truth honestly. If we are unjustly accused, we can trust that God sees everything.
exp.12:17:
This verse says that God patiently endured the conduct of the people of Israel for about forty years in the wilderness. The word "endured" means that he showed patience toward them, despite their complaints and their disobedience. "Conduct" refers to the way they behaved. Some ancient manuscripts say "he cared for them, as one carries a child," and it is not known with certainty which reading was the original. In either case, the faithfulness of God is shown.

Paul is speaking in the synagogue at Antioch in Pisidia on a Sabbath. He reviews the history of Israel before Jews and people who feared God. He wants to show that God has always acted in grace, and so lead them to Jesus, the promised Savior.

For today: if God was patient with his people, he is also patient with you in your stumbles. Thank him for his patience, and seek to show that same patience to the difficult people you have near you.
exp.8:0:
This verse introduces Saul, who was still full of hatred toward the followers of Jesus. The words "breathing out murderous threats" mean that his speech and his way of living were marked by constant hostility, like someone who never stops breathing. "Disciples of the Lord" refers to those who believed in Jesus. The "high priest" was the chief religious authority among the Jews, and Saul went to him.

Luke, the author of Acts, is recounting a new beginning in the story here. Saul had approved of the killing of Stephen and was persecuting the church. Now he wants to extend that persecution as far as Damascus. The verses that follow show that he asked for letters of authorization, and that along the way something would change his life completely.

For today: no one is too far from the grace of God. If there is someone who seems impossible to reach, keep praying for that person. And if you yourself carry a hard past, God can transform you.
exp.12:28:
This verse says that, after everything the Scriptures had said about Jesus was carried out, they took him down from the tree and laid him in a tomb. The word "tree" here refers to the cross, and the tomb is the place where his body was placed.

The apostle Paul is speaking in the synagogue at Antioch of Pisidia. He is explaining to Jews and to people who feared God that Jesus' death did not take God by surprise, since the prophets had already spoken of it. With this he prepares the next announcement: God raised him up. Some interpreters see in this those who took him down, such as Joseph of Arimathea, while others read it in a more general way.

For today: even in moments that seem like total failure, God continues to carry out his plan. You can trust that he works even when you do not understand.
exp.12:50:
Paul and Barnabas, after being driven out of Antioch in Pisidia, shook the dust off their feet in protest against those who had rejected them, and went to Iconium. The phrase "stirred up" means that the Jews agitated or provoked others. "Devout" refers to women who were committed and feared God.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells what happened. Shaking off the dust was a gesture Jesus had taught his disciples (Luke 9:5) to show that they had done their duty in proclaiming the message. Some understand it as a sign that the responsibility rested with those who rejected it. It was not revenge, for the disciples went on with joy.

For today: when someone rejects the message, we can do our part with love, let go of the hurt without bitterness, and move forward with joy, trusting that God is still at work.
exp.6:26:
This verse says that when Moses tried to stop a fight between two Hebrews, the man who was abusing his neighbor pushed Moses aside and rejected him. He asked him with contempt who had made him ruler and judge over them. Here "abusing" means doing harm to someone, and the word for pushing him aside means shoving with force.

The speaker is Stephen, before the Jewish council, reviewing the history of Israel. He recounts that Moses thought his people would understand that God would use him to deliver them, but they rejected him. Stephen thus shows a pattern: Israel rejected the deliverer whom God sent. Later he points out that they also rejected Jesus, the Just One.

Today, we sometimes reject the correction or help of the one God places in our path, simply because it makes us uncomfortable. We can humbly ask ourselves: am I listening, or am I defending myself? And if we serve others, let us remember that sometimes rejection does not mean we have failed.
exp.9:30:
This verse says that God heard Cornelius's prayer and did not forget his generosity toward the poor. The gifts he gave to those in need are the verse's "gifts to the poor," and the verse says they have been remembered before God, meaning God has kept them in mind and taken note of them with approval.

Here Cornelius tells Peter what the angel said to him four days earlier, while he was praying. Cornelius was a Roman officer who sought God, though he was not a Jew. God prepared him to receive Peter and to hear the message of the gospel. These words explain why he sent for him.

For today: God sees sincere prayer and also our kindness toward others. Pray with confidence and help someone in need this week. Remember that God draws us near to Jesus by his grace, not by our own merit.
exp.18:0:
This verse tells us that, while Apollos was at Corinth, Paul passed through the interior and came to Ephesus. There he found some disciples. The word "interior" means that Paul traveled through the inland areas, the higher ground away from the coast, though some understand the phrase in another way.

The author is Luke, who narrates Paul's third missionary journey. Earlier, Apollos had been in Ephesus, and Aquila and Priscilla had explained the way of God to him more fully. Now Paul arrives in the city and meets a group that knew little, as the following verses show.

For today: do not assume that someone knows Jesus well just because they call themselves a believer. Ask with respect and kindness, and patiently help them grow in faith.
exp.6:10:
There came a severe famine over all the land of Egypt and Canaan, and great suffering. This verse tells us that a very strong famine swept across all of Egypt and Canaan. There was great suffering, meaning a great deal of hardship and distress. The ancestors of Israel, whom Stephen calls "our fathers," could not find food. Here "food" means something to eat, especially grain.

The one speaking is Stephen, before the Jewish council, as he reviews the history of Israel. He has just said that Joseph's brothers sold him out of envy, but that God was with him and raised him up. Stephen shows that God works even in the middle of crisis, and that the divine plan moved forward even though people acted wrongly.

For today: when times of scarcity or distress come, do not think that God has withdrawn. You can trust that He is still at work, even by ways you do not yet understand, and ask Him for wisdom for the day at hand.
exp.27:17:
Paul says that the Romans questioned him and wanted to set him free, because they found no basis in him for a death sentence. The word "let go" means to release someone from custody, and the phrase "no basis for a death sentence" refers to a charge that could lead to execution.

Paul speaks to the Jewish leaders in Rome, a few days after arriving as a prisoner. He wants to explain why he is in chains. He tells them that he was handed over to the Romans from Jerusalem, and that he was examined by the authorities (such as Felix, Festus, and Agrippa, as the earlier chapters describe). Because the Jewish leaders opposed his release, he had to appeal to Caesar.

When we are falsely accused, we can defend the truth calmly and without bitterness, as Paul did. He did not attack his own people, but explained the facts with respect and kept his focus on the hope of the gospel.
exp.1:41:
They "devoted themselves" to four things: the apostles' teaching, the fellowship (sharing life with one another), the breaking of bread, and prayer. About the "breaking of bread," some think it refers to shared meals, others to the Lord's Supper, and others to both.

Luke, the author of Acts, recounts what happened after Peter preached at Pentecost. About three thousand people believed and were baptized. Now the account shows how that new community of faith lived, freshly born and still without experience.

For today: faith grows through steadiness, not only through emotion. We can choose a simple habit, such as reading the Bible, praying, and meeting with other believers each week, and keep it faithfully.
exp.3:14:
This verse says that the religious leaders ordered Peter and John to leave the room where the council met. The words to note here are "Sanhedrin" and "conferred together": the Sanhedrin was the Jewish governing body, and "conferred together" means they talked with one another in private.

The council had arrested Peter and John for speaking about Jesus and for healing a man. The judges were in a difficult position: they could see the healed man standing there and could not deny what had happened. So they sent the apostles out, in order to discuss among themselves what to do. What follows shows that they were not seeking the truth, but looking for a way to silence them.

For today: when the truth is plain, we can acknowledge it with humility, or resist it out of pride and fear. Let us ask God for a heart willing to accept what He does, even when it troubles us or changes our plans.
exp.9:9:
He became hungry and wanted something to eat. While the meal was being prepared, he fell into a trance, a spiritual experience in which his attention was completely taken up and God spoke to him through a vision.

Luke, the author of Acts, reports that Peter was in Joppa, on the roof of a house, praying around noon. Shortly before, God had prepared Cornelius, a non-Jewish centurion, to look for Peter. The vision that follows, with animals of every kind, would prepare Peter to accept that the gospel was also for non-Jewish people.

God can speak to us in ordinary moments, even when we are hungry or busy. Let us set aside time to pray and stay attentive to his voice, willing to let him correct our prejudices and widen our hearts toward other people.
exp.4:3:
Peter reminds Ananias that no one forced him to sell the property or to give the money. If he kept the property, it belonged to him; and after he sold it, the money was still at his own disposal. So why did he plan this deed in his heart? His sin was not in giving little, but in lying: he deceived not only people, but God.

Peter speaks in the early days of the church in Jerusalem, when believers shared their goods with generosity. Ananias and his wife Sapphira sold a property, but pretended to hand over everything when they actually kept a part. Peter does not condemn the amount, but the deceit and the false appearance.

For today: God values sincerity more than appearances. Serve and give with honesty, without seeking applause. If you give little but with truth, that pleases God more than pretending to a surrender that is not real.
exp.20:3:
We sought out the disciples in Tyre and stayed with them for seven days. Through the Spirit, they kept telling Paul not to go up to Jerusalem. The phrase "sought out" means they searched for them and found them, and Jerusalem is the city itself.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells the story of Paul's journey toward Jerusalem. The ship stopped at Tyre to unload its cargo. Paul was already determined to go (Acts 20:22-23). The believers in Tyre seem to have understood through the Spirit that suffering awaited him, and that is why they urged him not to go. Some scholars think the Spirit showed them the danger and that they drew the conclusion of urging him to stop; others understand it differently.

Today we can learn that the love and concern of fellow believers are valuable, but every important decision should be prayed over with humility, listening to God and to wise fellow believers.
exp.6:41:
He says that God turned away from his people and let them follow their own path: worshiping the stars, "the host of heaven," that is, the sun, the moon, and the stars. Then he quotes a prophet with a question: did they really bring sacrifices and offerings to God during the forty years in the wilderness? "Turned away" means he withdrew his protection from them.

Stephen speaks before the Sanhedrin, reviewing the history of Israel. After the golden calf, he shows that the people already had a habit of rejecting God and their leaders, just as they were now rejecting Jesus. The prophet's question suggests that their offerings were not sincere, because their hearts were set on other gods. Some interpreters debate how exactly that question should be understood.

Today we can ask ourselves: where do I truly give my heart? God does not seek only rituals, but sincere loyalty. It is worth examining what things occupy God's place in our lives.
exp.27:12:
This verse tells part of Paul's journey toward Rome. From Syracuse the ship sailed along the coast until it reached Rhegium, in the south of Italy. After one day, a south wind came up, and on the second day they arrived at Puteoli, an important port in Italy.

The one speaking is Luke, the author of the book, who was traveling with Paul and writes "we arrived." Paul was being taken to Rome as a prisoner to be judged before Caesar, after being shipwrecked on Malta. Luke notes each stop along the way, and so we see that the journey moved forward step by step until it reached its destination.

For today: God carries out His plans little by little, sometimes with delays, storms and waiting. Trust that He leads you step by step, and give thanks for each stretch of the road, even when you cannot yet see the end.
exp.12:43:
This verse tells us that a week later, nearly the whole city gathered to hear the word of the Lord. The phrase "nearly the whole city" shows that it was a very large crowd. "The following Sabbath" refers to the next Jewish day of rest.

The speakers in this passage are Paul, together with Barnabas. The Gentiles, that is, the non-Jews, had asked them to speak to them again about these things. Their eagerness to hear the message drew many people. But, as the account continues, some Jews were filled with jealousy when they saw the crowd and opposed them. Because of this, Paul and Barnabas turned more clearly toward the Gentiles.

For today: When someone shows interest in knowing God, let us not put it off. Let us respond with kindness and patience, and let the Word speak for itself.
exp.6:45:
It says that David, the one Stephen was speaking about, pleased God and found favor in God's sight. David asked to provide a dwelling place for the God of Jacob. "Found favor in the sight of God" means that he received God's favor and approval.

Stephen is speaking, defending his faith before the Jewish council. He goes over the history of Israel: first the tent in the desert, then David with his sincere desire, and after that Solomon, who built the temple. Stephen shows that God has never been confined to a building, as the next verse says. Some scholars see here a criticism of giving too much value to the temple.

For today: we can have good desires to serve God, as David did, but without forgetting that God does not depend on places. Let us seek a life given over to Him, where God is welcome every day, not only in the temple.
exp.2:20:
The verse says that Jesus, whom God sent, must remain in heaven until the time when all things are restored. The word "must" here means that heaven is where he has to stay until that moment comes, so the wording is straightforward. The verse also tells us that the restoration of all things is not a new idea. God announced it long ago through his holy prophets, from the beginning of the world.

Peter is speaking in the temple in Jerusalem, right after a man who had been lame from birth was healed in the name of Jesus. The crowd was amazed, and Peter uses the moment to call them to repent and turn to God. He explains that Jesus will return, and that this matches what Moses and the prophets had said all along. Christians understand the how and the when of this restoration in different ways, but all agree that God will bring it about.

For today, the world is still full of pain and disorder, yet we can live with hope, knowing that God has not abandoned his work. You can answer Peter's call today by repenting and trusting in Christ, and by waiting with patience for the time God has appointed.
exp.4:19:
It says an angel tells the apostles: "Go, stand in the temple courts and tell the people the full message of this new life." "Go" means "go," and "tell" means "tell." "This new life" refers to the new life announced in the gospel, centered on the risen Jesus.

The one speaking is an angel of the Lord, who has just brought the apostles out of the public prison. The religious leaders had locked them up for preaching about Jesus. Instead of sending them into hiding, the angel sends them back to the temple courts, the most visible place. They obey, and by dawn they are already teaching.

For today: God does not call us to be silent when there is opposition, but to keep sharing with simplicity and courage what Christ has done in us. Today you can speak to someone about your hope, with respect and without fear.
exp.19:16:
This verse tells that Paul, while in Miletus, sent a message to Ephesus asking for the elders of the church to come to him. The elders were the leaders who watched over and guided the community of believers. The phrase "sent to Ephesus for" here means that he asked them to come and see him.

The one acting is Paul, who was on his way to Jerusalem and in a hurry to arrive there for Pentecost, if possible. For that reason he decided not to stop in Ephesus, so as not to be delayed in Asia. Nevertheless, he wanted to say farewell to the leaders there. In the verses that follow he speaks to them about the service he gave them with humility and tears.

For today: even when we are busy, it is worth taking time to encourage and strengthen those who care for others in the faith. A sincere meeting, a word of encouragement, or a prayer with them can sustain them more than we imagine.
exp.25:0:
Agrippa gives Paul permission to speak in his own defense. Paul stretches out his hand, a gesture often used at the start of a speech, and begins his defense.

Paul is in prison in Caesarea. Before King Agrippa II and the governor Festus, he must explain what the Jews accuse him of. Festus wanted help to know what to write to the emperor, since Paul had asked to be judged by Caesar. Agrippa knew Jewish customs, and that is why his opinion mattered.

For today: when you have the chance to speak about your faith, do so calmly and with respect, without becoming defensive. Paul does not lose his composure or his courage, and he takes every opportunity to bear witness to Christ with clarity.
exp.9:12:
This verse says that Peter heard a voice telling him: "Get up, Peter, kill and eat!" "Kill" here means to slaughter an animal so that it can be eaten. Peter had just seen a large sheet full of all kinds of animals come down from heaven.

Peter was praying on a rooftop and was hungry, and he fell into a trance, a vision given by God. The voice comes from heaven, and Peter calls it "Lord." Many understand that God used this vision to teach him that he should no longer separate people by considering them unclean, since soon he would be called to visit Cornelius, a Gentile. The text itself makes this clear afterward, in Acts 10:28.

Today, this invites us to examine our prejudices. If God accepts someone, we should not reject them because of their origin or customs. Let us ask God for an open heart to love and welcome everyone.
exp.21:20:
Jesus told Paul, "Go," because He was going to send him far away to the Gentiles, meaning people who were not Jews. The word "far" points to distance, both in location and toward people unlike Paul himself. "I will send you" shows that the mission came from Jesus, not from Paul.

Paul is speaking to a Jewish crowd in Jerusalem and describing how he met Jesus. He had been praying in the temple and argued with the Lord that, because of his past as a persecutor, the Jews would be more likely to listen to him. Jesus did not argue with his reasoning but sent him anyway. When the crowd heard the word "Gentiles," they erupted in anger and demanded his death.

For today: God can use even those who have a shameful past. If He calls you to serve or to draw near to people different from you, do not hide behind your failures; obey with humility and trust that He is with you.
exp.0:8:
He says that Jesus, after speaking with his disciples, was taken up into heaven while they watched him. Then a cloud hid him, and they could no longer see him. The wording in this verse differs from older translations, so a note is needed: the phrase "was taken up" describes him rising as they looked on, and "a cloud hid him from their sight" describes the cloud covering him so they could no longer see.

The one who tells the story is Luke, the author of Acts. Jesus, already risen, had just told his followers not to worry about dates and times, but to wait for the Holy Spirit. With that power they would be witnesses of him, beginning in Jerusalem and reaching the most distant places. His departure marks the start of that mission.

For today: Jesus is not in sight, yet he remains present and keeps his promise. Instead of standing and gazing at the sky out of curiosity or anxiety about the future, we can ask for the Spirit's help and speak of Jesus kindly to those near us.
exp.22:14:
This verse shows the plan of the conspirators. They ask the council (the Sanhedrin) to petition the commander to bring Paul down to them, on the pretext of wanting to examine his case more carefully. The phrase "on the pretext of" means under a false reason, and "examine" means look into closely. They plan to kill Paul on the way.

The speakers are more than forty men who had bound themselves by an oath not to eat or drink until they had killed Paul. They speak with the chief priests and elders, seeking their help. Paul had caused a great disturbance in Jerusalem, and these men wanted to get rid of him through an ambush disguised as a legal procedure. The deception was part of the plan.

For today: wickedness sometimes disguises itself as something respectable. Let us ask for wisdom to discern, and remember that God cares for his own. In this case, he used a young man, Paul's nephew, to frustrate the plot.
exp.15:12:
On the Sabbath, Paul and his companions went outside the city gate and along the river, where people customarily gathered to pray. After sitting down, they began to speak with the women who had come together there.

The one telling the story is Luke, the author of Acts, who describes the journey using "we." Paul had come to Macedonia because of a vision. No synagogue is mentioned here. Some think there were few Jews in the city, but the text does not make this clear. Paul began with a small group of women who were gathered to pray, and there the Lord opened Lydia's heart.

For today: God can work in small and simple gatherings. Do not despise a small prayer group or a humble conversation; something great can begin there.
exp.15:18:
When the girl's owners saw that their hope of making money was gone, they seized Paul and Silas and dragged them before the authorities in the marketplace. The word "seized" simply means they arrested them. Saying "their hope of making money was gone" means their business had come to an end.

This takes place in Philippi. Luke, the narrator, tells how Paul freed a young woman who was controlled by a spirit and who predicted the future. Her owners were getting rich from this. They did not care that she had been freed; they were upset about losing money. That is why they accused the apostles on other grounds, as becomes clear afterward.

For today: let us examine whether money weighs more heavily on our hearts than the good of people. And if we do what is right and things go badly for us, let us remember that God is still at work.
exp.13:7:
This verse introduces a man in the city of Lystra who could not move his feet. The Berean wording says he was "crippled in his feet," so he could not walk properly, and "lame from birth" means he had been this way since he was born. The verse adds that he had never walked, not even once. He was sitting, probably in a public place.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells what happened when Paul and Barnabas arrived in Lystra after fleeing Iconium. There they continued proclaiming the gospel. This man appears as someone who was listening to the message, and in the verses that follow, Paul heals him.

For today: God notices the people others overlook. Let us listen to his Word with attention and faith, even when our situation seems impossible to change.
exp.15:7:
This verse tells that Paul and his companions passed through the region of Mysia and went down to Troas, a port city on the Aegean Sea. "Passed by" here means that they went through the region without stopping to preach, and "went down" indicates that they traveled toward the coast.

Luke, the author of the book, recounts Paul's second missionary journey. The verses before say that the Holy Spirit blocked two paths for them: Asia and Bithynia. It does not explain how He did so. With no open doors, they kept moving forward until they reached Troas, where Paul received the vision that led them to Macedonia.

For today: when you cannot clearly see the direction of your life, do not stand still. Keep taking faithful and simple steps, trusting that God can close doors and open others at the right moment.
exp.26:37:
It says that, after the men had eaten their fill, they lightened the ship by throwing the grain into the sea. The word "lightened" means taking off weight, and "grain" here refers to the grain they carried as cargo. The phrase "throwing the grain into the sea" is what the verse describes.

Luke, who writes the account, tells what happened after fourteen days of storm. Paul had encouraged them to eat, assuring them that no one would die, and they already had better spirits. With renewed strength, they sought to make the ship float better so they could approach the coast. Some think that grain was their valuable cargo and also their provision.

For today: when life gets hard, sometimes we have to let go of burdens that sink us, even valuable things, in order to save what matters most. First receive strength, rest and trust God; then calmly decide what to leave behind.
exp.14:29:
So the men were sent off and went down to Antioch, where they assembled the congregation and delivered the letter. The phrase "sent off" means they had been dispatched with a mission, and "assembled the congregation" means they brought the community of believers together. They are said to have "gone down" because the journey was from Jerusalem, which sits on higher ground.

The context is the debate over whether non-Jewish believers were required to keep the law of Moses. The apostles and elders in Jerusalem decided not to burden them with further demands. Judas and Silas, along with Paul and Barnabas, carried this answer in writing to bring clarity and unity.

For today: when there are disagreements in the church or the family, it is wise to resolve them through dialogue, humility, and clear communication, and to share the conclusions openly with everyone, so that there is peace and not confusion.
exp.13:8:
This man from Lystra was listening to the words of Paul. Paul looked at him intently and saw that he had faith to be healed. The phrase "listening to the words of Paul" indicates that he was paying close attention. The verse's wording, "looked intently at him," shows Paul's steady, careful gaze.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells that Paul and Barnabas were preaching the gospel in Lystra. There was a man there who had been lame from birth and had never walked. The text does not explain how Paul knew he had faith; it only says that Paul saw it as he looked at him. Immediately he healed him, and the people responded with amazement.

For today: faith often grows when we listen carefully to the word of God. Today we can listen with an open heart, trusting that God can work, and be attentive to those who need encouragement and hope.
