exp.22:30:
The soldiers followed their orders and brought Paul by night to Antipatris. The phrase "followed their orders" describes plainly what the verse above says.

Antipatris was a town on the road from Jerusalem to Caesarea.

The one telling the story is Luke. The Roman commander, Claudius Lysias, had learned of a plot by some Jews to kill Paul. For that reason he sent him with a military escort and a letter to the governor Felix. The sentences just before this verse are part of that letter. Traveling by night helped move Paul quickly out of Jerusalem.

For today: God can care for us through ordinary means, such as authorities, plans, or wise decisions. Trust in His protection, but also act with wisdom and gratitude when He opens a safe way.
exp.1:7:
Here the crowd asks in amazement: "How is it that each of us hears them in his own native language?" The phrase "native language" means the language a person grew up speaking. They are surprised because the speakers do not look like people trained to speak so many languages.

The speakers are Jewish visitors and converts who were in Jerusalem during the feast of Pentecost. The Holy Spirit had just come upon the disciples, and they were speaking in other languages. The crowd, coming from many places, recognizes their own languages and cannot understand how this is possible, since the disciples were Galileans.

For today: God wants his message to be understood. We can speak about Jesus with simple, familiar words, lovingly adapting to the person who is listening to us.
exp.16:12:
Some Jews from Thessalonica learned that Paul was also proclaiming the word of God in Berea. So they went there themselves and stirred up the crowds against him. The phrase "incite and agitate the crowds" means that they deliberately set the people into turmoil and unrest.

The one who tells this is Luke, the author of Acts, as he describes Paul's second missionary journey. The people of Berea had just received the message with eagerness and were examining the Scriptures every day. But the opposition Paul had faced in Thessalonica followed him there. For this reason the brothers sent him away, while Silas and Timothy stayed behind.

For today: the truth of God sometimes meets resistance, even when many receive it well. Do not be discouraged when it happens. Follow the example of the Bereans: examine the Scriptures with humility and do not let yourself be carried along by the noise of the crowd.
exp.19:26:
Paul says that he did not hold back and did not leave anything out. The word "shrink back" in the verse means avoiding or dodging something difficult, so Paul is saying he never avoided hard truths. "The whole will of God" means God's plan and purpose, everything He wants us to know in order to be saved and to live in His way.

Paul is speaking to the elders of the church in Ephesus, whom he called to meet him in Miletus to say goodbye. He knows he may not see them again. So he reminds them that he was faithful in teaching, and he warns them that dangerous wolves will come who will want to harm the flock.

Today we can ask God for the courage to read the whole Bible, not only the passages that comfort us or that we like. And whoever teaches others can do so with love, but with honesty, without hiding the uncomfortable parts of the truth.
exp.22:13:
These men went to the chief priests and the elders and told them that they had bound themselves with a solemn oath not to eat anything until they had killed Paul. The phrase "a solemn oath" means that they had sworn a binding promise, and that they would face the consequences if they did not keep it. "Not to eat anything" means that they would go without food until the task was done.

These are Jewish conspirators speaking. Paul was being held in Jerusalem under the protection of the Roman tribune, and they wanted to silence him. They seek the help of the religious leaders to set a trap for him. Later on, Paul's nephew discovers the plan and warns him.

For today: be careful with promises made in moments of anger or fanaticism. A solemn vow is worth nothing if it goes against the will of God. Moreover, God cares for his own even through simple means, like a young man who listened and spoke at the right time.
exp.4:11:
This verse says that many signs and wonders happened among the people through the apostles. "Signs and wonders" are supernatural deeds that showed God's power. The believers gathered together with one accord, meaning they were united and of one mind. They met in Colonnade of Solomon, a covered walkway with columns in the temple in Jerusalem.

The book of Acts was written by Luke as an account of the early steps of the church. This comes after the fear caused by the deaths of Ananias and Sapphira, who lied about their offering. Even so, the church remained united and kept growing, and people looked on them with respect. Some understand that the fear and the miracles come together to show the holiness of God.

Today, we can care for unity and honesty in the church. When believers live sincerely and in harmony, their witness speaks powerfully of God.
exp.27:4:
This verse tells that Paul gathered up the creature that had fastened on his hand and shook it off into the fire. He suffered no ill effects. The phrase "suffered no ill effects" means that he was not hurt and had no injury from the bite.

Paul and his companions had just been shipwrecked and arrived on the island of Malta, where the local people received them with kindness. The one telling the story is Luke, the author of Acts. The islanders thought Paul was a criminal being punished by divine justice, but when they saw that nothing happened to him, they changed their minds. Luke shows that God watched over Paul while he carried out his mission.

For today: when others judge you wrongly because of a difficulty, do not despair or defend yourself in anger. Do as Paul did: continue calmly, trust in God, and let time reveal the truth.
exp.25:27:
Agrippa says to Paul, "Can you persuade me in such a short time to become a Christian?" His words are a question, and the wording of the question makes its tone hard to pin down. Scholars discuss whether Agrippa was sincere, mocking, or simply sidestepping the pressure with a polite reply. The text does not make it clear.

Paul is a prisoner, and he presents his defense before King Agrippa, the governor Festus, and other officials. He tells of his encounter with Jesus and asks Agrippa directly whether he believes the prophets. It is an invitation to respond.

Today we might ask ourselves: do I stay close to believing, but never decide? Being nearly persuaded is not the same as trusting Christ. Paul wished that everyone would believe. Let me not postpone my answer.
exp.6:21:
It says that Moses received a complete education in the wisdom of the Egyptians, that is, in the knowledge and culture of Egypt. The phrase "was powerful in speech and action" means that he had strength and influence both in how he spoke and in what he did.

Stephen speaks before the Jewish council as he reviews the history of Israel. He wants to show how God worked in the life of Moses, preparing him from childhood, even in Pharaoh's palace. Stephen does not say in detail what that teaching was, nor does he explain what his manner of speaking was like; he only summarizes his preparation. There are discussions about how to reconcile this with Exodus 4:10, where Moses says he is slow of speech, and the Bible does not fully clarify it.

For today: God can use your preparation, study and experiences, even those that seem far from his plan, to serve others in his time. Cultivate what you learn and place it in his hands.
exp.3:31:
This verse says that the whole group of believers in Jesus lived united, with one heart and one purpose. No one claimed anything they owned as their own alone, but they shared everything they had.

Luke, the author of Acts, describes the first church in Jerusalem. They had just prayed boldly in the face of threats from the authorities, and God filled them with the Holy Spirit. The verses that follow show that they sold property of their own free will to help those in need, so that no one went without.

For today: ask yourself whether your heart is joined to the hearts of your brothers and sisters in the faith. One practical way is to look at what you have (time, money, food, help) and share it with someone in your church who needs it this week.
exp.1:30:
Peter says that David, foreseeing what was to come, spoke about the resurrection of the Christ. The word translated "Hades" refers to the place of the dead, not necessarily a place of punishment. Here the point is that Christ was not abandoned to the realm of the dead, and his body did not decay. In other words, Jesus did not stay in death, and his body was not destroyed.

Peter is speaking to the Jews gathered in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost. He quotes Psalm 16:10. He reminds them that David died and his tomb was still there, so his words pointed to someone greater: Jesus, the promised Christ from David's descendants, whom God raised up.

For today: the resurrection of Jesus is a fact we can trust, not just a comforting idea. If Christ overcame death, we can face our losses and fears with hope, and trust that God keeps what he promises.
exp.9:17:
The men sent by Cornelius had already arrived at the gate of the house where Peter was staying. They called out to ask if a man named Simon, also called Peter, was staying there. The word "staying" simply means that he was living or resting there for a time. "Called Peter" points to the additional name by which he was known.

Luke, the author of Acts, shows how God brings two stories together at the same time. Peter was in Joppa, puzzled by a vision of animals that God had shown him three times. At the same moment, God had guided Cornelius, a Roman soldier who feared God, to send messengers to find him. The timing lines up in a remarkable way.

For today: God may be preparing the way before we understand what He is asking of us. When something in your life confuses you, do not rush; pray, wait attentively, and watch for the doors He opens, for the answer is often already knocking at your door.
exp.8:37:
This verse tells us that Lydda and Joppa were neighboring towns. The disciples in Joppa learned that Peter was in Lydda, and they sent two men to him with an urgent request: "Come to us without delay." Today we say Joppa and Lydda.

The one telling the story is Luke, the author of Acts. Tabitha, a woman much loved for her kindness, had just died. The believers in Joppa, sad but hopeful, learned that Peter was nearby, since he had just healed Aeneas in Lydda. So they called for him in haste. The Bible does not say exactly what they expected from him.

For today: when we go through difficult moments, we do not have to face them alone. We can seek out brothers and sisters in the faith, ask for their help, and pray together, trusting that God hears and can act.
exp.13:6:
This verse says that Paul and Barnabas, after fleeing from Iconium, continued to proclaim the good news about Jesus in Lystra and Derbe. The phrase "the good news" is what the text calls the message they carried. The word "there" refers to those cities in the region of Lycaonia and the land nearby.

The one telling the story is Luke, the author of Acts. In Iconium, some Jews and Gentiles, together with their rulers, planned to mistreat them and stone them. When the apostles found out, they left. Luke shows that fleeing from danger did not silence them. They only changed places, but not their mission.

For today: when you face opposition, mockery, or closed doors, you do not have to give up. God may be asking you to change your place or your approach, but not to stop sharing your faith with love and simplicity. Ask God in prayer where you can speak about Jesus today, even if it is with just one person.
exp.1:24:
This verse quotes King David, who said that he kept the Lord always before him. "At my right hand" means that God was at his side as help and protection. That is why David says he will not be shaken, that is, he will not fall or stumble.

Here Peter speaks, on the day of Pentecost, to the people of Jerusalem. He quotes Psalm 16 to explain that Jesus, whom they killed, rose again. Peter understands that David, in that psalm, was speaking prophetically of Christ, who always trusted in the Father, even in the face of death. Christians often read it this way, although it also reflects David's own confidence.

For today: if we keep God at the center of our attention each day, through prayer and the Word, we will have steadiness when trials come. We do not depend on our own strength, but on the fact that He is at our side.
exp.25:23:
While Paul was still speaking in his own defense, Festus broke in loudly and told him he was insane. In his view, Paul's great learning was driving him to madness. The phrase "great learning" refers to the many writings or books Paul had studied.

Paul is standing before the governor Festus and King Agrippa. He has just told of his encounter with Jesus and that Christ suffered and rose again. For Festus, a Roman, talk of resurrection sounded absurd. Paul answers with respect and calm, saying that he speaks words of truth and sober sense.

If you speak about your faith, someone may take it for exaggeration or madness. You can follow Paul's example: answer with respect, composure and sincerity, without quarreling or being ashamed of what you believe.
exp.13:15:
In past generations, God let all nations go their own way, this verse tells us. "Past generations" refers to the times long before. "Nations" are the peoples who were not Jewish. "Let go" means that God allowed them to live by their own paths, without forcing them to obey him.

Paul and Barnabas are in Lystra. They had just healed a man who could not walk, and the crowd believed they were gods and wanted to offer them sacrifices. Paul is speaking to people who did not know the Scriptures, and he explains that there is one living God. Interpreters debate whether "let go" implies judgment or patience. What is clear is that God was not absent, since the next verse says he did not leave himself without witness, showing his kindness.

For today: God continues to show his kindness to everyone, even to those who do not know him. When we speak of him with others, we can begin with what they already see: the rain, the bread, the joy. And we should always direct the glory to God, not to ourselves.
exp.18:38:
The verse says that if anyone wants to take a matter further, it must be settled in a legal assembly, meaning an official meeting with the authority to decide it. "Seeking" here means asking for a hearing or bringing a complaint. A "legal assembly" is a gathering recognized by law, not a noisy crowd.

The speaker is the town clerk of Ephesus, a city official. An angry mob was shouting in support of the goddess Diana (Artemis) because of Paul's preaching. The clerk calms the people, reminds them that Gaius and Aristarchus have neither robbed temples nor insulted the goddess, and directs them to use the proper legal channels. He fears that Rome may punish the city for the disorder.

For today: when we have a complaint or a conflict, let us seek fair and orderly ways to address it instead of being carried along by the anger of the group. Calm and dialogue protect people and help us find the truth.
exp.14:17:
This verse says that God has known all his works for ages. The phrase "for ages" is a way of saying from long ago, from before time began. Nothing God does takes him by surprise.

Here James is speaking at the council in Jerusalem. The question being debated was whether non-Jewish believers in Jesus had to keep the law of Moses. James quotes the prophet Amos to show that including the Gentiles was not a new plan, but something God had already announced. He then gives his judgment: they should not be burdened with more weight.

For today: when your life or the church seems to be changing without direction, remember that God sees the whole picture. You can trust his plan and welcome with love those whom he calls.
exp.17:17:
It says that Paul remained in Corinth for quite some time before saying goodbye to the brothers, and then he sailed for Syria. Priscilla and Aquila sailed with him. In Cenchrea, the nearby port, he had his head shaved to keep a vow he had made. Having his head shaved means that his hair was cut very short.

This is part of Luke's account of Paul's travels. After the uproar before Gallio, Paul did not flee, but stayed for a time and then left calmly. The text does not say clearly who made the vow: it could be Paul or Aquila. Many think it was Paul, but that is not certain. The reason for the vow is not explained; it was probably a vow of dedication to God.

For today: God can guide our decisions with calm and faithfulness. If we make a promise to God, let us keep it sincerely, without seeking to look good in front of others.
exp.4:35:
Here it is told that, some time ago, a man named Theudas rose up, claiming to be somebody important. About four hundred men joined him. But he was killed, all his followers were dispersed, and it all came to nothing. The phrase "it all came to nothing" means that the movement fell apart.

Gamaliel, a Pharisee held in high regard and a teacher of the law, speaks before the Jewish council. He wants to keep them from killing the apostles, so he gives examples of leaders who failed. Historians debate exactly who this Theudas was, because Josephus mentions one with a different date, and there is no certainty.

Today we can learn to be patient and prudent before condemning something. Instead of reacting with fear or anger, it is wise to wait, pray, and observe the fruits with humility, trusting that God makes clear what comes from Him.
exp.16:25:
He says God made all of humanity from one man, that is, from one common origin, a single human being. He also says God set in advance the times of history and the boundaries of the lands where the peoples live. God is in control of everything.

Paul speaks in Athens, before philosophers at the Areopagus. They worshiped many gods and idols. Paul explains to them that there is one Creator, who has no need of temples or anything from us. He tells them that we all come from him and that we should seek him. Some scholars see here a reference to Adam, although the text does not name him.

For today: all human beings have the same worth before God, regardless of their country, skin color, or language. Today you can treat with respect and kindness anyone who is different from you, remembering that God also created them and loves them.
exp.0:16:
It says that Judas was part of the group of the twelve apostles. "He was one of our number" means that the others counted him among themselves. "Shared in this ministry" means that he was given a share, an assigned place, in this ministry, that is, in the service of an apostle. Here the word "shared" does not speak of chance, but of a portion received.

Peter speaks before about one hundred twenty believers gathered in Jerusalem, shortly after Jesus went up to heaven. He is going to propose that someone take the place of Judas. Before that, he reminds them that Judas was truly one of them, and that his betrayal did not take God by surprise, since the Scripture had already foretold it.

For today: being close to the things of God is not the same as having a faithful heart. We can serve, attend, and be part of a group, but it is wise to examine our hearts with humility and ask God to keep us faithful to Christ.
exp.6:42:
God says that Israel carried a portable tent for Molech and the star of their god Rephan, idols they had made themselves to worship. For this reason God would send them into exile, far beyond Babylon.

Stephen speaks before the Jewish council, accused of speaking against the temple and the law. He quotes the prophet Amos (5:25-27) to show that Israel rebelled against God from the wilderness onward. The prophet said "Damascus"; Stephen says "Babylon," perhaps to point ahead to the exile the people later lived through. About Rephan, scholars are not certain of his exact origin.

Today we can ask ourselves what things take the place of God in our hearts, even while we continue with religious practices. Let us ask Him to help us worship Him alone.
exp.8:4:
Saul asks who is speaking to him, and the answer comes back that it is Jesus, whom he is persecuting. The verse adds that it is hard for him to "kick against the goads." The goad was a pointed stick used to guide oxen. If the animal kicked against it, it only hurt itself more.

Saul was on his way to Damascus to arrest the believers. The risen Jesus speaks to him out of the light. By saying "you are persecuting me," he shows that he is united with his people and suffers with them. With that statement, the Lord makes Saul see that resisting God only harms him. Some think Saul already felt an inner restlessness, but the text does not say so.

Today we can ask ourselves: where am I resisting God? Fighting against his direction wears us down. It is better to answer with humility, as Saul did: "Lord, what do you want me to do?"
exp.20:4:
After those seven days in Tyre were over, Paul and his companions set out again. All the disciples, together with their wives and children, went with them as far as the edge of the city. There, on the beach, they knelt down together and prayed with them. The phrase "when our time there had ended" simply means that the days of their stay had come to an end.

The one telling the story is Luke, who travels with Paul and writes in the first person. Paul was heading toward Jerusalem and had stopped in Tyre while the ship unloaded its cargo. The believers there urged him, through the Spirit, not to go up to Jerusalem. This can be understood in several ways, but Paul continued on his way, and they did not abandon him: they sent him off with affection and prayer.

For today: even when we sometimes disagree with the decisions of other believers, we can still love them and support them. Before a difficult parting, praying together, even with the children present, is a beautiful expression of faith.
exp.24:1:
This verse tells that when Festus arrived in Jerusalem, the chief priests and the leading men among the Jews presented their case against Paul to him. The chief priests are the top priests, and "urged" means they pressed their request on Festus again and again.

Luke, the author of Acts, reports what happened with the new Roman governor. Paul had been held in prison in Caesarea for two years. These leaders still held a grudge against him and, according to the following verse, wanted him brought to Jerusalem so they could kill him on the way. Festus did not agree, and they were left with their plan thwarted.

For today: a grudge held for years can become an obsession that leads us to do harm. Let us ask God to heal our hearts and help us forgive, instead of seeking revenge.
exp.24:16:
When Paul's accusers arrived in Caesarea, Festus did not delay. The next day he took his seat on the judgment seat, the place where sentences were pronounced, and ordered that Paul be brought in. The words "I did not delay" describe how quickly he acted. Here, "ordered" means that he gave the command for Paul to be brought in.

Festus, the Roman governor, is speaking before King Agrippa and Bernice. He explains how he handled Paul's case. He wants to show that he acted with order and fairness, following the Roman custom that the accused face his accusers and be able to defend himself. This is his account of events, told with some intention of making himself look good.

For today: justice requires patience and listening to both sides. Before judging anyone, let us give them the chance to speak and to explain themselves. In this way we honor the truth and the person.
exp.16:17:
What it says: Paul was in Athens and talked with people in public. Some Epicurean and Stoic philosophers began to debate with him. Some of them asked what this babbler was trying to say. The word "babbler" is a mocking term; the sense is someone who picks up scraps of ideas, like a bird pecking at seeds. Others said he seemed to be advocating foreign gods, because he was proclaiming Jesus and the good news of the resurrection.

Context: Luke, the author of Acts, reports what happened. Paul had been distressed to see the city full of idols, which is why he spoke every day in the marketplace. The Epicureans sought calm pleasure, and the Stoics valued self-control and duty. Perhaps they confused "resurrection" with the name of a goddess, though some scholars debate this.

For today: When we speak about Jesus, we may be misunderstood or mocked. Even so, we can keep going with respect and clarity, speaking with people where they live and work.
exp.6:20:
This verse says Moses was "set outside," that is, exposed or left to die. According to Exodus 2, he was placed in a basket by the river. Then Pharaoh's daughter took him and brought him up as her own son. The verse's phrase "took him" means that she adopted him and took responsibility for him.

The speaker is Stephen, before the Jewish council, in his defense. He reviews the history of Israel to show how God worked in the midst of oppression. He highlights that God cared for Moses, the future deliverer, even using a princess from the people who oppressed Israel.

For today: God can care for us and carry out his plans even in hard and unexpected circumstances. When everything seems uncertain, we can trust that he is still at work, sometimes through people we would never have imagined.
exp.8:9:
In Damascus there was a follower of Jesus named Ananias. The Lord spoke to him in a vision, meaning a special experience in which God makes something known, and called him by name. Ananias answered, "Here I am, Lord." This shows a readiness to obey.

The one speaking is the Lord Jesus. Saul, who had been persecuting the Christians, had just been struck blind after meeting Jesus on the road. He was in Damascus, unable to see, and for three days he neither ate nor drank. God is preparing Ananias to help him. Later Ananias will have doubts, but the text shows that God was already at work in both of them.

Today we can learn to have an attentive heart. Before we understand everything God asks, we can say to him, "Here I am, Lord." That attitude prepares us to serve him and help others.
exp.2:4:
This verse says that the lame man gave his full attention to Peter and John. "So the man gave them his attention" shows that he kept looking at them closely, and "expecting to receive something from them" means he thought they would give him money.

It is Luke's account of the early days of the church. Peter and John were going up to the temple to pray, and this man, lame from birth, was asking for money at the gate. Peter asked him to look at them so as to get his attention. The man expected money, but he would receive something far greater.

For today: we often ask God for something small, and He wants to give us more than we imagine. We can pray with confidence, but also with openness, willing to receive what God knows we truly need.
exp.11:7:
The angel gives Peter simple instructions. "Get dressed and put on your sandals" means putting on what you need so you are ready to move. Then he tells him to wrap his cloak around himself and follow him. Peter obeys one step at a time.

The angel of the Lord speaks to Peter, who was imprisoned by Herod's order, and sets him free in a miraculous way. Although the chains had already fallen off, Peter still had to get ready and act. Afterward, the text says he thought it was a vision, so he kept going while trusting without understanding everything.

For today: when God opens a door for you, he sometimes asks you to take small steps of obedience. Trust and move forward, even if you don't yet understand everything.
exp.10:1:
When Peter returned to Jerusalem, some believers took issue with him and confronted him. The verse describes them taking issue with him in a forceful way. "The circumcised believers" were Jewish believers who considered it important to keep the customs of their people, such as circumcision.

Peter had just visited the house of Cornelius, a man who was not Jewish, and the members of his household had believed in Jesus. The brothers in Jerusalem heard about it and became concerned, for many Jews considered entering the homes of non-Jews and eating with them to be a very sensitive matter. The words that follow show that their complaint was about this sharing of life together. Peter responds by explaining everything calmly.

For today: when something troubles us or we do not understand what God is doing, it is wise to ask questions and listen calmly, without judging right away. And if we are called to explain, let us do so with humility and clarity.
exp.5:11:
They stirred up the people, the elders, and the scribes. Then they confronted Stephen, seized him, and brought him before the Sanhedrin, the Jewish court. The verse describes a sudden, forceful action in which they grabbed him and took him away against his will.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells what happened to Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Spirit. His opponents could not answer his wisdom, so they resorted to lies and to inciting the crowd. They wanted to silence him with a serious religious accusation.

For today: when someone cannot win with arguments, they sometimes turn to pressure, gossip, or lies. If this happens to us, let us seek to respond with truth, calm, and trust in God, without repaying evil with evil.
exp.22:20:
Here the reader is warned of a plot against Paul. More than forty men are waiting to ambush him. They have bound themselves with an oath not to eat or drink until they have killed him. They are ready now, waiting only for the commander's consent. "Waiting to ambush" means they are lying in wait, watching for him so they can attack by surprise.

The one speaking is Paul's young nephew, speaking to the Roman commander. The Jewish leaders wanted to use a supposed new hearing as a trick to ambush Paul on the road. The young man found out and gave warning in time. The text does not say how he learned of it.

For today: when you know of a danger or an injustice, act with caution and warn those who can help. Trusting God does not remove our responsibility to use wisdom and courage to protect others.
exp.7:30:
This verse says that the Ethiopian man, when Philip asked him whether he understood what he was reading, answered humbly: "How can I, unless someone guides me?" Then he invited Philip to come up and sit beside him. The phrase "How can I" and the word "invited" carry the sense of his humility and eagerness to learn.

The speaker is the Ethiopian official, a high officer of the queen of Ethiopia, who was returning from Jerusalem and reading the prophet Isaiah. He recognizes that he needs help to understand. God had already sent Philip by the Spirit, and the passage he was reading spoke of a suffering servant. Philip would use it to proclaim Jesus to him.

For today: do not be ashamed to admit that you do not understand something in the Bible. Ask for help from a teacher, a pastor, or a friend with more experience, and pray that God will guide you. Learning together brings us closer to Christ.
exp.14:18:
James says that the Gentiles, meaning the non-Jews who are turning to God, should not be bothered or burdened with unnecessary demands. "Trouble" here means disturbing, bothering, or pressing people with extra requirements. "It is my judgment" simply means "this is my conclusion."

This happens at the council in Jerusalem. Some Jewish believers taught that Gentiles had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses in order to be saved. After hearing Peter, Barnabas, and Paul, James points to the words of the prophet Amos, who foretold that the Gentiles would also seek the Lord. From this he draws his conclusion: God is receiving them, so no obstacles should be placed in their way.

Today, let us not place human requirements on anyone who comes to God. We can encourage new believers to grow in obedience and love, but without adding burdens that God has not asked for regarding salvation, which is by grace.
exp.21:7:
Paul recounts that, when he saw the light and heard the voice, he asked, "Who are You, Lord?" The answer was clear: "I am Jesus of Nazareth, whom you are persecuting." Here "Lord" is a term of respect, since Paul did not yet know who was speaking to him.

Paul speaks in Jerusalem before an angry crowd and explains how his life changed. He had been persecuting Christians, believing he was serving God. Jesus says that persecuting his people is persecuting him, because he is deeply united with those who believe in him.

For today: we can be sincere and still be mistaken. It is wise to ask God with humility, "Who are You, Lord?", and to be willing to listen and change course. Moreover, Jesus is concerned with how we treat his followers.
exp.22:32:
The horsemen came to Caesarea with Paul. There they handed the letter to the governor, who was Felix, and presented Paul to him.

The one who tells the story is Luke, the author of Acts. A group of Jews had made a plot to kill Paul in Jerusalem. For this reason the Roman commander Claudius Lysias sent him by night, under a strong escort, to Caesarea, where the governor was, together with a letter explaining the case.

For today: God took care of Paul through very ordinary means, such as soldiers, roads, and official documents. We can trust that He also cares for us in the midst of difficult situations, even when He does so in simple ways that we barely notice. In the meantime, we continue faithfully doing what is ours to do.
exp.2:14:
The verse says that the people Peter is speaking to killed Jesus, and it calls him "the Author of life." That phrase points to the source of life, the one from whom life comes. But God raised him from the dead, and the apostles say they are witnesses of this fact, meaning they saw him alive and can testify to it.

Peter speaks in Solomon's Porch, in the temple at Jerusalem, after he healed a lame man. The crowd was amazed, and Peter explains that the healing did not come from his own power, but from Jesus. He speaks firmly about their responsibility, but he quickly offers forgiveness, saying that they acted in ignorance and inviting them to turn to God.

For today: Jesus is not just a figure from the past; he is alive and is the source of life. We can come to him with our failures, trusting that his call always brings hope and new life.
exp.12:25:
It says the message of salvation was sent to the listeners. "Brothers" is a respectful way of addressing the people he is speaking to. "Children of Abraham" are the Jews, descendants of Abraham. "You Gentiles who fear God" were people from other nations who respected and worshiped the God of Israel. "Salvation" here means salvation.

Paul speaks in the synagogue of Antioch of Pisidia, on a Sabbath. He has just recalled the history of Israel and the testimony of John the Baptist about Jesus. Now he addresses both Jews and Gentiles who feared God, and tells them that the good news is for them, before explaining the death and resurrection of Jesus.

For today: do not assume you already know the message of Jesus just because you have heard it many times. Receive it as a word addressed personally to you, and respond with faith and gratitude.
exp.12:35:
This verse says that David, after serving God's purpose in his own generation, died. The phrase "fell asleep" is a gentle way of speaking about death. "Was buried with his fathers" means he was laid to rest like his ancestors. "Saw decay" means that his body decayed in the tomb.

Paul is preaching in the synagogue at Antioch of Pisidia. He quotes the Psalms to show that the promise of not seeing decay was not fulfilled in David, who died and whose body decayed. It was fulfilled in Jesus, whom God raised.

For today: David reminds us that our life is brief, but it can have purpose. Let us serve God faithfully in the time we are given, trusting that Christ, who overcame death, is our true hope.
exp.10:24:
It says that Barnabas left Antioch and went to Tarsus to look for Saul. When he found him, he brought him back with him to Antioch. In this wording, "went" means that he traveled away, and "found" means that, after locating him, he took him along to Antioch.

Here the narrator is Luke, the author of Acts. Barnabas had been sent by the church in Jerusalem to Antioch, where many people believed in Jesus. Seeing that the work was growing, he sought help. Saul, who would later be called Paul, was from Tarsus. The text does not explain all of Barnabas's reasons, but it shows that he thought of someone who could help teach the new believers.

For today: serving God does not mean doing everything alone. We can encourage others and make room for them to use their gifts. Who could you invite today to serve alongside you?
exp.12:32:
Paul says that God has fulfilled the promise made to Israel's ancestors, and that he has fulfilled it for their children, that is, for us, by raising Jesus up. He quotes Psalm 2: "You are My Son; today I have become Your Father." In this quotation, the words about "today" speak of God publicly declaring Jesus to be his Son.

Paul preaches in the synagogue at Antioch of Pisidia. He summarizes the history of Israel and explains that Jesus is the promised one people have been waiting for. For him, the resurrection is the public sign that God stands behind Jesus. Some scholars understand the "today" as the resurrection itself; others understand it as Jesus' exaltation in general.

For today: God keeps what he promises, even when it takes a long time. Trust his faithfulness when you are waiting for an answer, and rest in the fact that Jesus lives.
exp.7:9:
All the people of Samaria, from the least important to the most important, listened closely to Simon. They said his words were "the divine power called the Great Power." Here "power" means strength, that is, they saw him as someone with a special divine power.

The one speaking here is Luke, the author of Acts, who tells what was happening in Samaria. Simon had practiced magic and deceived the people by pretending to be a great figure. That is why they followed him. Luke tells this to show the contrast with Philip, whose message about Jesus brought true joy and led many to be baptized.

For today: let us not follow someone merely because they impress us or are famous. Let us compare what they say and do with what the Bible teaches about Jesus. True power brings glory to God, not to a person.
exp.16:24:
He says that God does not need anything from human beings. The phrases "served by human hands" and "as if He needed anything" mean that God is not served with human works as if something were lacking to Him. On the contrary, God is the one who gives everyone life, breath, and everything else.

Paul speaks in Athens before philosophers and people who worshiped many gods. He has just mentioned an altar to an unknown god and uses it as his starting point. He explains to them that the true God, creator of all things, does not live in temples or depend on offerings or idols, as many in that culture thought.

For today: remember that every breath is a gift from God. Instead of serving him in order to repay him or to earn his favor, you can live with gratitude and trust, serving him because he has already given you everything.
exp.14:4:
Verse 5 tells us that some believers who had previously been Pharisees, a very strict religious group, stood up and declared that Gentile believers must be circumcised and required to obey the law of Moses. The word "party" in this verse refers to a group or faction, and "must" carries the sense of necessity.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells us that Paul and Barnabas arrived in Jerusalem and joyfully reported how God was saving people from other nations. Then this objection arose. These men believed in Jesus, but they thought that salvation also required following Jewish customs. This disagreement led to the gathering of the apostles and elders.

We can thank God for what He does in others, even when it does not match our customs. Before adding rules to faith, let us ask whether they truly come from God or only from our tradition.
exp.13:26:
When Paul and Barnabas came back to Antioch in Syria, they gathered the whole church together and reported all that God had done through them. They also told how He had opened the door of faith to the Gentiles, meaning people who were not Jews. The word "reported" here carries the sense of telling in detail what happened.

The narrator is Luke, the author of Acts. Paul and Barnabas had just finished their first missionary journey. They had been sent out from that same church, and now they gave an account to it. Their report did not center on their own accomplishments but on what God had done. The "door of faith" shows that the good news was reaching all peoples.

For today: when God works in your life, share it with your church or your family. Telling what He has done encourages others and gives glory to God, not to yourself.
exp.12:4:
This verse tells us that Barnabas and Saul arrived at Salamis, a city on the island of Cyprus. There they proclaimed the word of God in the Jewish synagogues. "Proclaimed" means that they made the message known. John was with them as their helper, serving alongside them in the work.

Luke, the author of the book of Acts, narrates the beginning of the first missionary journey. The church in Antioch had sent them out after fasting and praying, and the text says that the Holy Spirit sent them. It is notable that they began in the synagogues, where the Scriptures were already known. This John is usually understood to be John Mark, although the verse only says "John."

For today: God uses both those who proclaim and those who help. Serve where you are, even if your task seems small, and do it faithfully.
exp.6:8:
It says that the sons of Jacob, here called patriarchs, were jealous of their brother Joseph and sold him as a slave into Egypt. "Because the patriarchs were jealous" means that their jealousy of Joseph was the reason they acted. "But God was with him" means that God was with Joseph, accompanying him and watching over him.

Here Stephen, a follower of Jesus, speaks before the Jewish council that was accusing him. He reviews the history of Israel to show that the people often rejected those whom God sent. Joseph was rejected by his brothers, but God later used him to save them. Many see here a comparison with Jesus, although Stephen develops this further on.

For today: when someone rejects you or treats you unfairly, remember that God can be with you and work for good, even in the middle of pain. And if you feel jealous, ask God to heal your heart.
exp.9:36:
Peter tells his listeners that they themselves know what has happened throughout Judea, beginning in Galilee with the baptism that John proclaimed. The news about Jesus was spread widely, and people passed it along from one to another.

Peter is speaking in the house of Cornelius, a Roman officer who was not a Jew. God had guided him there so that Peter could tell him the good news. Peter reminds them of public events about Jesus, and then goes on to explain who He is and what His work means for all peoples.

For today: when you talk about Jesus, you don't need to start with complicated words. You can simply tell what He did and what He has done in your life. God uses clear and sincere testimonies to draw others close to Him.
exp.22:23:
It says that mounts were to be prepared so that Paul could ride and be taken safely to Governor Felix. "Prepare" means to get ready or arrange; "mounts" are animals for riding; "safely" means securely and unharmed; "governor" here is the Roman ruler of the province.

Claudius Lysias, the Roman tribune, speaks. He had found out that more than forty Jews had sworn to kill Paul. So he decides to take Paul out of Jerusalem by night, with a large escort, and send him to Caesarea, where Felix was. Lysias acted out of duty and to protect a Roman citizen. The Bible does not say he did it out of faith, but the account shows how God took care of Paul.

God can use unexpected means, even authorities who do not know Him, to keep His own safe. Trust in His care, and also be wise: make use of the help and protection that He places within your reach.
exp.14:12:
He says that, after Barnabas and Paul had finished speaking, James stood up to address the group. The words "Brothers, listen to me" are a direct request for attention, and they show James asking the others to hear him out before he gives his view.

We are at the Council of Jerusalem. The church was debating whether non-Jewish believers had to keep the law of Moses in order to be saved. Peter, Barnabas and Paul had already shared what God had done among the Gentiles. James, who according to the text held an important role in the church in Jerusalem, now speaks to help the group reach a conclusion, relying on the Scriptures.

For today: before giving your opinion in a disagreement, let us learn to be quiet and listen. Then let us compare what we have heard with what the Bible says, seeking unity with humility.
exp.11:11:
Luke, the narrator of Acts, is describing what happened next. After Peter was freed from prison, he took time to think over what had just happened to him and then went to the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark. The phrase "when he had realized this" means that he paused to understand what had taken place. Many people had gathered there and were praying.

Here Luke is speaking as the narrator of the book of Acts. Herod had killed James and had Peter put in prison. An angel led Peter out, and now Peter is seeking out the believers. It is notable that many people were praying in that very house, although the verse does not say in detail what they were praying for; the context suggests it was for Peter.

For today: when God helps us, it is good to stop, reflect, and give thanks. Praying together is also valuable, because we are not alone, and we can support one another in hard times.
exp.0:1:
This verse says that Jesus gave instructions to the apostles he had chosen, and that he did so through the Holy Spirit, up until the day he was taken up to heaven. "Taken up to heaven" means that he was lifted up and went to heaven. The instructions were the teaching and direction he gave his chosen followers.

The one speaking is Luke, the traditional writer of this book, addressing Theophilus. He picks up what he told in his first book, the Gospel, and prepares the account of what comes next. He wants to show that Jesus' work did not end, but continues in his apostles through the power of the Spirit.

For today: Jesus did not leave his followers without direction. We can seek his guidance in his Word and ask the Holy Spirit to help us follow it, rather than depending only on our own strength or ideas.
exp.6:46:
It was Solomon, David's son, who built the temple in Jerusalem. David had wanted to find a dwelling place for God, but it was his son who carried out the work. "It was Solomon who built the house for Him" means that Solomon built a place of worship for God.

Stephen, speaking before the Jewish council, is reviewing the history of Israel. First he recalls the tabernacle, the tent where God met with his people, and then the temple. But the next verse makes his point clear: God does not live shut up in buildings made by human hands. Stephen probably wanted to show that God is not bound to one place.

For today: value the places where you gather to worship, but remember that God is with you everywhere. Seek him in your home, at your work, and on your way, not only in the temple.
exp.8:22:
This verse says that a considerable amount of time passed after Saul's conversion, and that some Jews in Damascus conspired to kill him. The word "conspired" means they secretly made a plan together. The phrase about the many days does not say how long it was. In Galatians 1:17-18, Paul mentions a trip to Arabia and then three years before he went up to Jerusalem, though scholars debate how those details fit together.

Luke, the author of Acts, is narrating what happened in Damascus. Saul had changed from persecutor to preacher, and with arguments he demonstrated that Jesus is the Christ. His former companions felt confused and threatened, and they responded with violence.

For today: following Jesus can bring rejection, even from people close to us. We should not be surprised or keep silent out of fear. We can keep speaking with truth and love, and trust that God cares for us, as he cared for Saul through other believers.
exp.7:1:
This verse tells us that some God-fearing men, that is, people who honored God, buried Stephen and mourned deeply for him. "Buried Stephen" means they took charge of his burial, and "mourned deeply" speaks of a deep and sincere grief.

The book of Acts was written by Luke, and here he describes what happened right after Stephen was stoned. A severe persecution of the church in Jerusalem was beginning. Even so, these men did not hide their sorrow or their affection for Stephen. Some think they were devout Jews and others that they were believers; the text does not make this clear.

For today: there is no need to pretend strength when someone dies. Weeping is a healthy and human response. Let us stand with those who suffer through presence, concrete help and affection, and remember that God continues to work even in the midst of sorrow.
exp.8:3:
This verse tells how Saul fell to the ground after seeing a bright light from heaven. Then he heard a voice calling his name twice and asking him why he was persecuting Me. The phrase about falling means that he fell down to the ground.

Saul was on his way to Damascus with official letters to arrest the believers in Jesus and bring them as prisoners to Jerusalem. The one speaking is Jesus, as the next verse makes clear. Notice that the words are "why do you persecute Me?" and not "why are you persecuting my followers." Jesus identifies himself so closely with his people that what is done to them, he feels as done to himself.

For today: God cares about how we treat others, especially those who believe. Also, no one is so far away that Christ cannot reach him and change him. If today you feel you have gone wrong, he can also speak to you and give you a new direction.
exp.8:28:
This verse tells us that Paul, newly converted, spoke about Jesus in Jerusalem with courage and without fear. The word "talked" means he spoke openly, and "debated" means he argued and reasoned with them. The "Grecian Jews" were Jews who spoke Greek, not Jews from Judea. "Tried to kill him" means they were looking for a way to take his life.

Luke, the author of Acts, narrates what happened after Barnabas presented Paul to the apostles. Paul had persecuted the church, so now he had to show that his change was real. The Greek-speaking Jews probably saw him as a traitor. That is why the brothers took him down to Caesarea and sent him off to Tarsus, to protect him.

Speaking about Jesus with courage can bring rejection, but it can be done with humility and firmness. Ask God for courage and wisdom to share your faith with love, and leave the result in his hands.
exp.9:34:
This verse says that God welcomes people from every nation who fear him and do what is right. "Fear" here does not mean being afraid, but respecting and honoring God. Doing what is right means living uprightly. "Welcomes" means he receives them gladly.

The apostle Peter is speaking in the house of Cornelius, a Roman officer who was not a Jew but was seeking God. Peter had believed that the gospel was only for the Jews. God showed him otherwise, and now he acknowledges it. With these words he introduces his message about Jesus, the Lord of all. Some debate whether it speaks of salvation without Christ; the context shows that Cornelius still needed to hear about Jesus.

Today we can set aside prejudice. God looks at the sincere heart, not at a person's origin or culture. Treat everyone with respect and share with them the message of Jesus.
exp.14:24:
This verse says that the leaders of Jerusalem, having reached full agreement, decided to choose some men and send them to the believers in Antioch along with Barnabas and Paul, whom they call "beloved." The phrase "we all agreed" means that the group shared one mind on the matter.

The church in Jerusalem speaks through the apostles, the elders, and the brothers. They write a letter to non-Jewish believers, because some had taught that they had to be circumcised and keep the law in order to be saved. The leaders make it clear that they did not send those teachers. They send messengers to give assurance and to confirm in person what was written.

For today: when confusion or disagreement arises, let us seek to resolve it together, with humility, with clarity, and with love. Let us send messages that bring peace, not messages that unsettle others.
exp.1:29:
This verse says that David was a prophet, and that he knew God had promised him with an oath that one of his descendants would be the Christ (the Messiah) and would sit on his throne. The reference to a descendant points to a member of David's own family line. The verse begins with "But," which marks a contrast with what Peter has just said.

Peter speaks to the crowd in Jerusalem on the day of Pentecost. He quotes Psalm 16 and explains that David was not speaking about himself, since his tomb was still there. David was looking forward to the promised Messiah, and Peter affirms that this promise was fulfilled in Jesus, who was raised from the dead.

For today: God keeps what He promises, even when centuries pass. When waiting wears you down, remember that He is faithful, and trust His word with patience.
exp.13:22:
Paul and Barnabas appointed elders for the believers in each church, meaning mature leaders who would look after the community. The word "appointed" points to the act of choosing and placing these leaders in their role. Then they prayed and fasted, that is, they went without food for a time to seek God earnestly. In the end, they entrusted those believers to the Lord, placing them into his care, the One in whom those new believers had come to trust.

Luke, the author of Acts, recounts this during the first missionary journey. Paul and Barnabas were returning through Lystra, Iconium and Antioch, cities where they had faced opposition. Before moving on, they wanted to leave the new believers with steady guidance. The verse does not explain how the elders were chosen.

For today: when you have to make decisions about who will lead or care for others, do it with prayer, and entrust to God the people you cannot always accompany.
exp.23:14:
Paul says that he has the same hope in God that his accusers hold, namely that there will be a resurrection of both the righteous and the wicked. The phrase "there will be" conveys that the resurrection is certain to take place.

Paul is speaking before the governor Felix in Caesarea. The Jews accused him of causing trouble and of belonging to a group they called a "sect," the followers of Jesus, whom they called "the Way." Paul answers that he serves the same God as his fathers and believes everything written in the law and the prophets. His hope in the resurrection was not new, and that is why he presents it as something that connects him to his own people. The Bible speaks of the resurrection in passages such as Daniel 12:2.

For today: living with the certainty that we will all give an account to God encourages us to act with honesty and to take care of our conscience, as Paul says in the next verse.
exp.11:15:
Peter kept on knocking without giving up. When they finally opened the door and saw him standing there, they were astounded. "Kept on knocking" means he continued insisting. "Were astounded" means they were enormously surprised, not that they were afraid.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells how an angel had just brought Peter out of prison, where Herod had him locked up. Peter came to the house of Mary, the mother of John Mark, where the believers were praying for him. The servant girl Rhoda was so overjoyed that she ran to tell them without opening the door. They did not believe her, even though they had been asking for exactly this miracle.

God can answer our prayers in ways that surprise us, even when our faith is weak. Let us keep praying with perseverance and receive his answer with joy, even when it comes in an unexpected way.
exp.0:15:
Peter addresses the believers as "brothers," meaning fellow brothers and sisters in the faith. He says that the Scripture had to be fulfilled, that what the Holy Spirit foretold through the mouth of David about Judas had to come true. Judas becoming a "guide" for those who arrested Jesus means that he was the one who led them to Him. "Had to be fulfilled" means that it was bound to happen.

Peter speaks in Jerusalem, after the ascension of Jesus, before about one hundred and twenty disciples who were gathered together. He wants to explain Judas's betrayal and prepare the choosing of a replacement among the apostles. Scholars often connect this with psalms of David, such as Psalm 41 and Psalm 109, although the text does not quote one in this verse.

For today: even painful events, such as a betrayal, did not take God by surprise. We can trust that He remains in control and find comfort in His Word when something hurts us.
exp.6:52:
It says the people received God's law "ordained by angels," meaning it was given with angels taking part, but they did not keep it. "Keep" here means to observe, to obey. Many understand this to refer to a Jewish tradition that angels were present at Sinai; the Bible also hints at this in Galatians 3:19 and Hebrews 2:2.

Stephen, full of the Spirit, speaks before the Jewish council that was accusing him. After reviewing the history of Israel, he shows them that they are repeating the rejection of their ancestors: earlier they killed the prophets, and now they have killed the Just One, Jesus. His point is that having the law is not enough if it is not obeyed. They reacted with fury.

For today: knowing the Bible or having a good religious tradition is not enough. Ask God for a humble heart, willing to obey what you already know He asks of you.
exp.20:1:
At Patara, Paul's group found a ship that was crossing over to Phoenicia. They boarded it and set sail. The words "finding" and "crossing over" mean that they came upon a ship making the crossing to that region, the coast of what is today Lebanon. "Set sail" means that they left the port.

The one telling the story is Luke, the author of Acts, who was traveling with Paul; that is why he says "we boarded it." Paul was heading back toward Jerusalem at the end of his third missionary journey. Changing ships at Patara was practical: that vessel followed a longer and more direct route to Phoenicia, and so they kept moving forward on their way.

For today: following God's will often means taking concrete and simple steps, such as looking for transportation, planning the way, and moving ahead with steady perseverance. We can pray and, at the same time, diligently do what is within our reach.
exp.3:26:
In Jerusalem, they really did gather together against Jesus, God's holy servant, whom God anointed, meaning he chose him and set him apart for his work. Herod, Pilate, the Gentiles (the non-Jews), and the people of Israel all joined in opposing him. "Conspired" means that they made their plans together, working in agreement with one another.

The believers are praying after Peter and John were threatened by the authorities. They quote Psalm 2 and see in it a fulfillment of what happened to Jesus. They remember that, although many opposed him, God still held control. That gives them encouragement in the face of their own pressure.

For today: when you feel opposition or fear for following Jesus, do as they did. Remember that God still reigns, and ask him for courage to speak and live your faith with love and confidence.
exp.0:19:
Peter says that the Scriptures had already spoken of this moment. He quotes two phrases from the Psalms: that the place of Judas be deserted and that no one live in it, and that another take his position. The word used there means "office" or "position of responsibility," in this case the position of apostle.

Peter speaks before about one hundred twenty believers in Jerusalem, after Jesus's ascension. Judas had betrayed the Lord and died in a tragic way. Peter uses passages from the Psalms (69:25 and 109:8) that speak of enemies of the righteous man, and applies them to Judas. In this way he explains why a replacement must be chosen from among those who had accompanied Jesus.

For today: even falls and failures do not frustrate God's plan. If we fail, we can return to Him, and He continues to work through those who are willing to serve Him faithfully.
exp.26:5:
There, in Myra, a port in Lycia, the centurion found an Alexandrian ship sailing for Italy, and he put us on board. An Alexandrian ship was a vessel from Alexandria, in Egypt. The centurion was the Roman officer in charge of the prisoners.

Luke speaks here, the one who recounts the voyage, using "we" and "us." Paul is a prisoner, traveling toward Rome to be tried before Caesar. The centurion, called Julius in verse 1, makes the decision to change ships. Many believe it was a grain freighter, but the text does not say so.

God sometimes guides us by paths we did not choose. Paul did not choose the ship, but his life remained in God's hands. When changes seem uncomfortable or beyond your control, remain faithful where you are and trust that God is still at work.
exp.5:0:
When this verse was written, the believers in Jerusalem were growing in number, and a complaint arose. The Grecian Jews were Jewish believers who spoke Greek and had come from other places; the Hebraic Jews were believers from the area who spoke Aramaic. The first group said their widows were being overlooked. The complaint was a grumbling, a quiet kind of protest, and the problem concerned the daily distribution of food.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells the story like a historian. The widows depended on this help, because in that time many had no one else to support them. It was probably an oversight caused by the rapid growth, although the text does not explain the exact cause. The apostles respond to the problem in the verses that follow.

For today: when a church grows, oversights can appear. Let us hear complaints with humility and look for fair solutions, caring especially for the most vulnerable.
exp.25:31:
Agrippa tells Festus that Paul could have been released if he had not appealed to Caesar. The word translated "released" means set free, and "appealed" means that Paul asked for his case to be judged by the emperor in Rome.

Paul had just spoken before King Agrippa II, the governor Festus, and Bernice. After hearing him, those present concluded that he had done nothing deserving death or prison. However, Paul had already appealed to Caesar (Acts 25:11), and that step could not easily be undone. Some believe God used this to bring Paul to Rome, as he had promised (Acts 23:11).

For today: sometimes our decisions lead us down paths we did not expect. We can trust that God works even in circumstances that seem like an obstacle, and remain faithful wherever we are.
exp.14:20:
The verse says that Moses has been proclaimed from ancient times in every city, and that his law is read aloud in the synagogues, the places where Jews gathered, on every Sabbath. The word "proclaimed" in the verse means that someone announces the law and teaches it.

James is speaking at the council in Jerusalem. The question being debated was whether believers who were not Jews had to be circumcised and keep the whole law. James proposes asking them only for what is essential: to stay away from idolatry, sexual immorality, what has been strangled, and blood. This verse is usually understood in several ways: that Moses is already well known and taught, or that Jews would be respected if these few rules were kept. Scholars do not fully agree.

For today: let us look for agreements that do not place unnecessary burdens on others, and let us care for the customs of others with love.
exp.18:30:
Some of Paul's friends who were officials of the province of Asia sent word to him, begging him not to venture into the theatre. These were important people in the region, and they pleaded earnestly with him, because the crowd there had broken into an uproar.

This is part of Luke's account of the trouble in Ephesus. The silversmiths, alarmed that the gospel was hurting their business of making shrines to the goddess Diana, stirred up a disturbance. Paul wanted to speak to the people, but the disciples and these friends tried to keep him safe. The text does not say whether these officials were believers; it only says that they were Paul's friends.

For today: sometimes courage does not mean rushing into danger, but listening to the advice of wise people who care about us. Let us ask God for humility to receive such a warning.
exp.16:18:
They took hold of Paul and brought him to the Areopagus, where they asked him, "May we know what this new teaching is that you are presenting?" The word "took" here means they took him along with them, not necessarily by force. They wanted him to explain this new teaching, that is, the new message he was proclaiming.

Some philosophers and curious people in Athens were talking. Paul had been preaching about Jesus and the resurrection in the marketplace. Some called him a babbler, and others thought he was announcing foreign gods. The Areopagus was a place or council of the city where such matters were heard; scholars do not fully agree on whether it was a formal trial or only a meeting to hear him. What we do see is that their curiosity was great.

For today: when someone asks about your faith, even out of simple curiosity, take the opportunity. Answer with respect, clarity and simplicity, as Paul did, and let God do his work in the heart.
exp.0:14:
In those days, a few days after Jesus went up into heaven, Peter stood up among the brothers, a gathering of about a hundred and twenty. Here "brothers" means fellow believers, and the gathered group is the people who had come together.

Peter speaks in the middle of a group that had been praying together with one heart, waiting for what Jesus had promised. One apostle was missing, because Judas was no longer among them. Peter takes the floor to explain that what happened with Judas did not take God by surprise, and that the Scripture had foretold it. Afterward, someone will be chosen to take his place.

For today: God uses imperfect people, like Peter, who had failed, to guide his people. Even when a situation hurts us or confuses us, we can gather with other believers, pray together, and look to the Scripture for the direction we need.
exp.12:47:
When the Gentiles heard this, they rejoiced and honored the word of the Lord, as Paul and Barnabas had preached it. All who were appointed to eternal life believed. The word "appointed" can also be understood as "inclined" or "destined."

Paul and Barnabas were in Antioch of Pisidia. Some Jews rejected the message, so the apostles turned to the Gentiles, quoting the prophecy that God would make them a light for the nations. Christians understand that phrase in different ways: some see God's choosing before all things, others see people with open hearts. The text does not settle the question completely.

For today: when you hear the word of God, receive it with joy and thankfulness, and do not take it for granted. And if someone rejects it, do not be discouraged; keep sharing it with love.
exp.19:29:
It says that, even from among the church's own members, some will rise up and distort the truth. Their aim is not to serve Christ but to draw followers to themselves. "Drawing disciples after them" means that people follow them and not the Lord.

Paul speaks to the elders of Ephesus in his farewell, near Miletus. He knows he will not see them again and wants to prepare them. Earlier he spoke of fierce wolves that would come from outside; now he warns that the danger can also arise from within. So he asks them to keep watch and remember his example of care and tears.

For today: do not follow a teacher just because he speaks well or has many followers. Compare what he teaches with the Bible, and if you are a leader, make sure people are drawn to Christ and not to you.
exp.6:6:
God told Abraham that he would punish the nation that enslaved his descendants. Afterward, they would come out free and worship him in this place. "Punish" means that God would carry out justice against those who held them in slavery. "Enslaves" refers to people being placed under the control of another.

These words are spoken by Stephen when he defends himself before the Jewish council. He reviews the history of Israel and cites what God promised Abraham (Genesis 15:13-14). Stephen wants to show that God guides his plan across the centuries, even in times of suffering. Some understand "this place" as the promised land; others think it points to the worship of God in general, since Stephen speaks of the temple later on.

When you go through a hard season, remember that God has not forgotten you. He sees, he brings justice, and he keeps his promises in his own time. Trust him and keep worshiping him.
exp.1:39:
Peter keeps speaking to the crowd at Pentecost. He says he testified to them and urged them with many other words. His central appeal was to be saved, that is, to get yourselves out of harm's way. The word "corrupt" describes something twisted or spoiled, and "generation" refers to the people of that time.

Peter has just preached to a crowd in Jerusalem. He told them they had rejected Jesus, whom God made Lord and Christ. Many were moved and asked what they should do. Peter does not condemn them outright; he invites them to repent and to turn away from the path of that generation that rejected the Messiah. The result was that about three thousand joined the believers.

Today, following Jesus involves concrete decisions. It is not enough to admire him; it is about turning to him and turning away from what harms the soul. Seek a community of believers that can help you persevere.
exp.20:5:
This verse describes a very heartfelt farewell. Paul and his companions said their goodbyes to the believers of Tyre, went aboard the ship, and the others returned to their homes. "Having found the disciples" means that they searched for them and found them. "Ship" is the vessel in which they continued their journey.

The one who narrates is Luke, who travels with Paul and writes "we." Paul was heading toward Jerusalem. The disciples in Tyre, through the Spirit, were urging him not to go up, perhaps because of the dangers that awaited him. It is debated how to understand this, since Paul continued his journey, convinced of his calling. Even so, everyone sent him off with affection, kneeling and praying on the beach.

Today we can learn to send off with love and prayer those who walk a difficult path, even when we do not always fully understand it. An embrace, a prayer, and words of encouragement strengthen others.
exp.15:11:
This verse tells that Paul and his companions arrived at Philippi, a leading city in that district of Macedonia. Philippi was a Roman colony, a city whose citizens enjoyed special privileges. The verse calls it "the leading city," and some think this means the principal city or the first one they entered, but this is not known for certain. They stayed there several days.

The one telling the story is Luke, the author of Acts, who was traveling with Paul (which is why the account speaks of "we"). After a vision, the group believed that God was calling them to bring the gospel to Macedonia. This verse is part of the journey and prepares the meeting with Lydia.

For today: when you sense that God is guiding you, take the step with obedience, even if the place is new. And afterward, be patient: sometimes God works in the "several days" of waiting and routine.
exp.16:20:
This verse is an explanation added by the author, Luke. It says that all the Athenians and the foreigners who lived there spent their time doing nothing more than hearing and sharing new ideas. "Foreigners" refers to the outsiders who lived in the city or were passing through it. The phrase that describes how they spent their time means that they occupied themselves with, or devoted their time to, this activity.

Paul was in Athens, a city famous for its debates and its philosophers. They took him to the Areopagus, a place of gatherings and judgments, because they were intrigued by his message about Jesus and the resurrection. Luke explains this custom so that their curiosity makes sense. Scholars are not sure whether it was a formal trial or simply an invitation to explain his ideas.

We can have a great deal of curiosity about what is new and still not let the truth change us. Let us ask God for a heart that listens with humility and obeys.
exp.6:16:
It says that as the time drew near for God to fulfill His promise to Abraham, the people of Israel increased greatly in number in Egypt. The verse's "increased greatly in number" means they became very numerous.

Stephen, a follower of Jesus, is speaking before the Jewish council that has accused him. He reviews the history of Israel to show that God has always acted faithfully, even when His people were far from the promised land. Here he summarizes the years in Egypt before Moses appeared. Stephen wants his hearers to see that God is not bound to a single place.

For today: God keeps His promises even when many years pass and circumstances seem against them. We can wait with patience and confidence, knowing that He works quietly, even in difficult times.
exp.17:24:
This verse says that Apollos had been taught in the way of the Lord, meaning he had been instructed in the faith in Jesus. He was "fervent in spirit," which means he had an enthusiastic heart full of passion. He spoke and taught accurately about Jesus. But he knew only the baptism of John, which shows that his knowledge was incomplete.

Luke, the narrator of Acts, presents Apollos here as a Jew from Alexandria, skilled in the Scriptures. His teaching was sincere, but he lacked a full understanding of all that God had done in Christ. Interpreters explain in various ways what exactly he was missing, and the text does not spell it out. That is why Priscilla and Aquila later helped him.

For today: a person can have great zeal and still need to learn more. Let us be humble enough to receive correction and teaching from other believers.
exp.25:30:
After listening to Paul, King Agrippa, the governor Festus, Bernice, and the others left the room and talked among themselves. They agreed that Paul had done nothing that deserved death or imprisonment. The phrase "nothing that deserves" means "not worthy of" the punishment. "On their way out" means they spoke to one another as they left the room.

Paul had just told his story before Agrippa and Festus, and explained his faith in Jesus. He was being held in Caesarea because of accusations from the Jewish leaders. The ones speaking here are the authorities who had heard him. Even so, since Paul had appealed to Caesar, he remained in custody, as the next verse explains.

For today: living with integrity and speaking with respect can leave a clear witness, even when circumstances do not change or seem unfair.
exp.3:8:
Peter tells the Jewish leaders that today they are questioning him about a kind service done for a man who was lame. They want to know how he was healed.

Peter speaks filled with the Holy Spirit before the council of rulers and elders of Jerusalem. He and John had healed a lame man at the temple, and the leaders arrested them. Peter points out, with a touch of irony, that they are being questioned about doing good, and in this way he prepares his answer: the man was healed by the name of Jesus.

For today: when you are questioned about your faith or for doing good, do not shrink back or seek the credit. Answer with calm and simplicity, pointing to Jesus as the source of all good.
exp.19:5:
After the Feast of Unleavened Bread, which is the Jewish Passover, Paul and his group sailed from Philippi by ship. Five days later they rejoined their companions in Troas, where they stayed for seven days.

The one telling the story is Luke, the author of Acts, who includes himself in the account with the word "we." Paul was travelling back through Macedonia and Asia with several companions, and some of them had gone ahead to wait for him in Troas. Luke carefully records the days and places, which shows that the journey was real and well remembered.

For today: Paul did not travel alone but was accompanied by brothers and sisters from several places. Seek out other believers to serve and move forward together, and give time to being with them, not only to getting tasks done.
exp.14:35:
Some time later, Paul suggested to Barnabas that they go back and check on the believers in every town where they had shared the word of the Lord, to see how they were getting along. He wanted to visit the fellow believers and find out how they were doing.

Paul says this after the Council of Jerusalem, where it was decided that non-Jewish believers were not required to follow the law of Moses. That good news had already been shared in Antioch. Now Paul thinks of the churches that began during his first missionary journey and wants to encourage them. His concern is caring for people, not only starting new work: he wants to look after them.

For today: it is not enough to bring someone to faith; we also need to stay with them afterward. Think of a person you could call, visit, or encourage this week, and kindly ask how they are doing.
exp.3:11:
This verse says that only Jesus can save us. Here, salvation does not refer only to being physically well, but to being rescued from sin and reconciled with God. To be "saved" means to be rescued or delivered. Peter declares that there is no other name under heaven given to human beings by which they can receive that salvation.

Peter speaks before the religious leaders of Jerusalem, who had called him to explain by what power he had healed a lame man. Filled with the Holy Spirit, he answers boldly that it was by the name of Jesus, whom they crucified and whom God raised up. The leaders are astonished that uneducated men should speak with such confidence.

For today: we can rest in the knowledge that our salvation does not depend on our merits, but on Christ. And, like Peter, we can speak of Jesus with humility and without fear, for he himself is hope for all.
exp.18:37:
Here the city clerk tells the crowd that if Demetrius and his fellow craftsmen have a complaint against anyone, the courts are open and proconsuls are available, so the matter should be brought there. The phrase "the courts are open" means that the legal system is available for hearing complaints, and "proconsuls are available" refers to the Roman governors who held authority over the province. "Let them bring charges against one another there" means that the complaint should be made formally before those officials.
