The speaker is the city clerk of Ephesus, a high-ranking city official. Demetrius, a silversmith, had stirred up a riot because Paul's preaching threatened his business of making silver shrines of the goddess Diana. The clerk wants to calm the uproar before Rome punishes the city.

For today: when we face a conflict, let us avoid reacting in anger or under the pressure of the crowd. Let us seek the orderly, just, and peaceful way to resolve it.
exp.17:10:
This verse says that Paul stayed in the city of Corinth for a year and a half. There he devoted himself to teaching the people the word of God. To "stayed" means that he remained to live in that place for a long time, without hurrying to move on to the next part of his journey.

The one who tells this is Luke, the author of the book of Acts. Earlier, the Lord had spoken to Paul in a vision at night and told him not to be afraid, to keep speaking and not to be silent, because God was with him. Because of this, Paul stayed on with confidence. Later, some Jews would bring accusations against him before the proconsul Gallio.

For today: when God calls you to serve in a place, do not lose heart if the work requires patience and time. Remain steadfast, teaching and sharing his word, trusting that he is with you.
exp.6:33:
God says he has truly seen the suffering of his people in Egypt. He repeats "I have seen" to stress that he is not indifferent to it. He also heard their groaning, that is, their cry of pain. That is why he says "I have come down," meaning he has decided to step in and rescue them. Then he calls Moses: "Now come," and says he will send him back to Egypt.

Here Stephen speaks, defending his faith before the Jewish council and going over the history of Israel. He quotes what God said to Moses at the burning bush, in Exodus 3. Stephen shows that Moses, whom the people rejected at first, was the very one God sent to deliver them.

God sees and hears those who suffer, and often he acts through people willing to obey him. We can bring our pain to him with confidence, and also ask him whom he might use to help today.
exp.2:16:
Peter calls the people "brothers" and tells them that they acted in ignorance when they turned against Jesus, just as their leaders did. He uses the word "leaders" for the rulers or authorities who were involved. "Ignorance" here means that they did not truly understand who Jesus was, though their guilt does not disappear.

Peter is speaking in the temple, after God healed a lame man in the name of Jesus. He takes advantage of the amazed crowd to proclaim Jesus. First he confronts them firmly, but now he speaks to them with tenderness and opens a door for them. Soon he will call them to repent and turn back to God.

For today: when someone has failed us or does not understand the faith, we can speak to them with truth and with compassion, without humiliating them. And if we ourselves have gone wrong, there is always a way back to God.
exp.6:37:
This verse says that Moses was in the assembly of the people of Israel in the wilderness, and that the angel who spoke to him on Mount Sinai was with him there, along with their ancestors. Moses received living words from God to pass on to the people. The word "assembly" here means the gathering of the people.

Stephen, a follower of Jesus, is speaking before the Jewish council that was accusing him. He reviews the history of Israel to show that God had given his word through Moses, but that the people often rejected it. With this he prepares his accusation: his listeners were repeating that same resistance.

For today: the Word of God is not only a set of rules; it is words that give life. Today you can read it with a heart ready to obey, and not only to admire it or argue about it.
exp.6:9:
This verse says that God rescued Joseph from all his troubles. He granted Joseph favor and wisdom before Pharaoh, king of Egypt, and Pharaoh appointed him ruler over Egypt and all his household. The word "troubles" refers to hardships and distress; "favor" here means goodwill and a warm reception; "rescued" means that God brought him out of trouble and saved him.

Here Stephen, speaking before the Jewish council, reviews the history of Israel. He recounts that Joseph's brothers sold him out of jealousy, but God was with him. Stephen shows that God works even when his people reject the one he sends. In this way he prepares his accusation: they too rejected Jesus.

For today: even if you go through injustice or long trials, God has not forgotten you. He can give you wisdom and sustain you in hard times. Trust that his presence with you is worth more than any position or comfort, and keep doing what is right while you wait.
exp.9:39:
This verse says that God raised Jesus up on the third day and caused him to be seen. The word "raised" means that God brought him back from death. The phrase "caused him to be seen" means that Jesus showed himself clearly and really, not in secret or as a doubtful vision.

Here Peter is speaking in the house of Cornelius, a Roman officer who was not a Jew. Peter explains to him who Jesus is: the one anointed by God, who went about doing good and healing. Then he says that the disciples were chosen witnesses of his death and of his resurrection, and that they ate and drank with him.

For today: our faith does not rest on an idea, but on a fact that trustworthy witnesses announced. Today you can trust that Jesus lives, and share that hope simply, by telling what he has done in your life.
exp.9:28:
Peter tells Cornelius and those gathered in his house that he came without objection, because they had invited him. Then he asks why they sent for him. The question "why have you sent for me?" is a direct request to hear their reason.

Peter, a Jew, speaks in the house of Cornelius, a Roman officer who was not a Jew. Earlier, God had shown Peter in a vision that he should not call anyone common or unclean. That is why Peter goes in, even though his custom discouraged it. Now he wants to know the reason for the invitation, and Cornelius will begin to tell it.

Today, when God guides us to draw near to someone different from ourselves, we can obey with humility. We can also listen to their story before assuming things, letting God tear down our prejudices.
exp.27:9:
It says that the people of the island of Malta treated Paul and his companions with great kindness, honoring them in many ways. "Honored" here means showing appreciation and respect. When the group was ready to leave, the islanders supplied what they needed for the voyage.

The one telling the story is Luke, who traveled with Paul and writes in the first person ("us"). After the shipwreck, Paul prayed and healed the father of Publius and other sick people on the island. The people responded with gratitude. Luke does not say that Paul asked for anything; the text only tells us that they gave.

For today: God often cares for his servants through grateful people. If you receive help, accept it with humility. And if someone has served or blessed you, don't stop at words: help them in a concrete way, with generosity and without expecting anything in return.
exp.11:20:
This verse describes a special day in Caesarea. King Herod put on his royal robes, sat on his throne, which was the place of authority, and addressed the people. The phrase "addressed the people" here means speaking publicly to a group in a solemn tone.

The narrator is Luke, the author of Acts. Herod Agrippa I was angry with the people of Tyre and Sidon, who depended on food from his land. They sought peace through Blastus, an official of the king. This speech was the occasion for them to flatter him. The historian Josephus tells the episode with other details, such as a shining robe, but here the center is that Herod accepted praise that belongs only to God.

For today: when we receive praise or achievements, let us remember that everything comes from God. We can give thanks simply and return the glory to Him, instead of seeking applause for ourselves.
exp.24:3:
Festus replies that Paul is being held in Caesarea and that he himself is going there soon. "Being held" means that Paul was kept in custody, under watch.

Festus had just arrived as the new governor of the province. The Jewish leaders asked him as a favor to bring Paul to Jerusalem, but their real intention was to kill him with an ambush on the way. Festus did not agree to their request. The texts do not say whether he suspected the plan; they only say that he kept Paul in Caesarea and invited them to present their accusations there.

God can care for us by using ordinary circumstances, such as an administrative decision, to deliver us from dangers we do not even see. We can trust that he works even in everyday matters.
exp.27:23:
This verse says that, after hearing Paul, some were convinced by what he said, but others refused to believe. The wording of the verse itself shows that the reaction was split: some accepted the message and some turned it down.

The one speaking here is Luke, who tells what happened in Rome. Paul was a prisoner, but he welcomed into his home the leaders of the Jews. All day long he explained to them that Jesus is the Messiah, using the law of Moses and the prophets. Some were persuaded, others refused, and this caused division among them.

For today: not everyone will respond the same way when we share our faith. Our task is to speak with clarity, with love and with patience, and to let God touch each heart. We should not be discouraged if some refuse to believe, nor stop sharing what God has done in us.
exp.23:1:
Here it says that when Paul had been called in before the governor, Tertullus opened the prosecution. But before making the accusation, he spoke flattering words to Felix: he said that because of him they enjoyed a lasting peace, and that his foresight had brought improvements to this nation.

Tertullus was an orator, something like a lawyer, whom the Jewish leaders, together with the high priest Ananias, brought to accuse Paul in Caesarea. His praise was meant to win the governor's favor. Historians do not agree on how much peace there really was under Felix, so his words sound more like flattery than truth.

For today: let us be wary of pretty words that serve hidden interests. Let us speak with sincerity, and may our praise never be a tool for manipulating others.
exp.12:15:
Paul stands up, motions with his hand, and begins to speak. He addresses two groups: "Men of Israel," meaning the Jewish people present, and "you Gentiles who fear God," meaning non-Jewish people who respected the God of Israel and attended the synagogue. He calls out to them to listen.

Paul and his companions arrived at Antioch in Pisidia and went into the synagogue on the Sabbath. After the reading of the law and the prophets, the leaders offered them the chance to speak if they had a word to encourage the people. Paul accepts the invitation and begins a message that reviews the history of Israel in order to arrive at Jesus.

Before speaking, Paul asked for attention and spoke in a way that made everyone feel included. Today we can imitate him: when we share our faith, let us first listen to people, speak with respect and clarity, and give each person a place in the conversation.
exp.17:21:
This verse tells us that Paul arrived by ship at the port of Caesarea. From there he went up to Jerusalem, greeted the church, and then went down to Antioch. "Landed" means that he came to shore at a port. The words "went up" and "went down" are ways of speaking: Jerusalem lies on high ground, which is why one goes up toward it.

The narrator is Luke, who summarizes the end of Paul's second missionary journey. Earlier, Paul had left Ephesus, where people asked him to stay longer. He wanted to reach Jerusalem for a feast, and he promised to return. Here the verse names the church at Jerusalem as the one he greeted, so the reader can see plainly which church he visited.

For today: Paul ministered far away, but he did not lose his bond with the church. Today we can care for that bond: greeting, visiting, and giving thanks for the brothers and sisters who have walked with us in the faith.
exp.18:8:
Some in Ephesus stubbornly refused to believe and publicly spoke against the Way, meaning faith in Jesus. So Paul left the synagogue, took his disciples with him, and held daily discussions in the lecture hall of Tyrannus. "Discussions" here means reasoning and talking through the message with people.

Luke, the author of Acts, describes what came after three months of teaching in the synagogue. Paul had spoken boldly about the kingdom of God, but the opposition grew. For that reason he sought another place. About Tyrannus, it is not known for certain whether he was a teacher or the owner of the hall; the text does not make this clear.

For today: when someone rejects the message harshly, there is no need to keep arguing without end. We can step away with respect, care for those who do want to learn, and keep serving faithfully in another place.
exp.14:15:
Here it says that God will raise up again the fallen tent of David, meaning his house, which is also understood as his family and kingdom. God promises to rebuild its ruins and restore it. The word "tent" here refers to a dwelling place.

James speaks at the council in Jerusalem. The question being debated was whether believers from other nations had to keep the law of Moses. He quotes the prophet Amos to show that God had already announced that the Gentiles too would seek the Lord. Christians have understood this restoration in different ways, but James connects it with the coming of the Gentiles to faith.

God keeps his promises in ways we do not always expect. Today we can trust that he continues to rebuild what has fallen, and we should welcome with joy those whom he calls, without placing on them burdens that he did not place.
exp.7:25:
The verse tells us that an angel of the Lord spoke to Philip and gave him a clear command: get up and go south, to the desert road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza. The angel speaks with the authority of the Lord himself, so Philip has no doubt about what he is being asked to do.

Notice the description of the road. The verse calls it the desert road. Some readers take this to mean the road itself runs through lonely, empty country, while others think it refers to the city of Gaza. The text allows for either reading, and what matters most is the picture it gives us of a quiet, out-of-the-way place.

Philip had just seen a remarkable revival in Samaria, where many people were believing the good news about Jesus. Now God sends him away from a crowd to an empty road. The one who speaks to him is an angel, sent by the Lord, and the purpose soon becomes clear: an encounter with an Ethiopian man who was reading the prophet Isaiah.

Today, God can lead us to places or situations that do not seem to make sense or to have any visible results. Obeying step by step, even when we cannot see the whole plan, places us where God is already at work in someone's heart.
exp.12:14:
After the reading from the Law and the Prophets was finished in the synagogue, the synagogue leaders (the men in charge of running the meeting) sent word to Paul and his companions. They addressed them as "brothers" and invited them to speak: if they had a word of encouragement for the people, they should say it.

Paul and Barnabas had just arrived in Antioch of Pisidia and went into the synagogue on the Sabbath. It was customary to invite visitors to speak after the readings. The ones speaking here are the synagogue leaders; Paul's response comes in the following verse.

For today: when a door opens to speak about God, it is wise to be prepared. Paul knew the Scriptures and was able to respond with clarity and encouragement.
exp.1:5:
When that loud sound rang out, a crowd came together in bewilderment, meaning they were confused and amazed, because each person heard the disciples speaking in his own language.

This took place on the day of Pentecost, in Jerusalem. Luke, the author of Acts, tells how the followers of Jesus were filled with the Holy Spirit and spoke in other languages. There were devout Jews from many nations who had traveled to the city for the feast. God was thus showing that the message of Jesus was for people from every nation.

Today we can remember that God wants his good news to reach everyone, in a language they can understand. We can speak about Jesus in simple words, with respect and affection, thinking of the person who is listening to us.
exp.27:13:
It says that Paul and his companions arrived at Puteoli, and there they found brothers in the faith. They invited them to spend the week with them. After that, they continued the journey and came to Rome. The word "found" in the verse simply means that they came upon them, and the word "so" here marks what happened next.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells this story of a journey in which he himself was taking part. Paul was a prisoner and was traveling to Rome to be judged before Caesar. Even so, the account shows that there were already Christians in Puteoli. It does not say how the faith arrived there; the Bible does not explain this. It is noticeable that the centurion allowed Paul that rest.

God takes care of us through other believers. Paul was traveling as a prisoner and tired, but he received company and rest. Today we can open our homes and our hearts to encourage someone who is going through a trial.
exp.1:0:
It says that when the day of Pentecost came, the followers of Jesus were all together in one place. The phrase "when the day of Pentecost came" means that the time of the feast had now arrived.

This is the beginning of the account in Acts 2, written by Luke. Pentecost was a Jewish feast celebrated fifty days after Passover. Jesus had already gone up into heaven and had told his disciples to wait in Jerusalem for the promise of the Holy Spirit. That is why they were together, waiting.

For today: value unity with other believers and patience in waiting on God. Seek to gather with your church or with a group of fellow believers, pray together, and trust that God keeps his promises in his own time.
exp.13:5:
They found out about a plot in Iconium to mistreat them and stone them. So they fled to the Lycaonian cities of Lystra and Derbe and to the surrounding region.

The word "mistreat" here means to abuse them or insult them publicly. The common people are the crowd.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells how the city of Iconium was divided over the message of the gospel. Some supported the apostles, and others sided with the Jews who rejected them. When the threat became real, the apostles went to another place, but they kept preaching, as the next verse shows.

For today: fleeing from danger is not always a lack of faith. Sometimes it is wisdom. When a door closes or becomes dangerous, we can look for another place where we can keep serving God faithfully.
exp.6:44:
Stephen tells the council that the fathers of Israel, led by Joshua, brought the tabernacle with them when they took the land. It was the tent they had received from their ancestors. God drove out the nations who lived there before them, and the tabernacle remained in the land until the time of David.

Stephen speaks before the Jewish council, defending himself against the accusations made against him. He surveys the history of Israel to show that God has never been limited to a building, and that the people often resisted God. Here he highlights that the tabernacle, a movable tent, accompanied the people for generations.

God keeps his promises and walks with his people, whether there are tents or temples. Today we can trust that his presence does not depend on a special place, but on his faithfulness toward those who seek him.
exp.20:26:
This verse tells how, when the seven days of purification were nearly over, some Jews from the province of Asia saw Paul at the temple. They stirred up the whole crowd and seized him. "Seized him" means grabbing hold of someone by force, as in an arrest. "Stirred up the whole crowd" means getting the crowd worked up with shouting and anger.

Luke, the author of Acts, narrates the moment. Paul had agreed to take part in a purification rite together with four other men, to show respect for Jewish customs. Even so, these Jews from Asia accused him falsely, and the following text says they believed he had brought a Gentile into the temple.

For today: even when we try to act with wisdom and peace, we can be misunderstood or accused without reason. We should not act on assumptions or join in the anger of the crowd; rather, let us seek the truth before we judge someone.
exp.14:7:
Peter says that God knows what is in the heart of every person, and that for this reason he could show approval of the Gentiles: God gave them the Holy Spirit just as he did to the believing Jews. The phrase "showed His approval" means that God demonstrated by his actions that he accepted them.

Peter speaks at the council in Jerusalem, before the apostles and elders. There was a strong debate: some insisted that Gentile believers had to be circumcised and follow the law of Moses in order to be saved. Peter recalls what happened in the house of Cornelius, where God himself showed that he accepted the Gentiles through faith.

For today: God sees the heart, not appearances, background, or customs. Before you judge someone or place on them burdens that God did not place, ask yourself whether God has already received them. Welcome with humility those who believe in Christ.
exp.11:5:
It says that on the night before Herod was to bring Peter to trial, Peter was sleeping between two soldiers, bound with two chains, while sentries stood guard at the entrance to the prison. Here "bring him to trial" means taking him to a public hearing, and the sentries are the men posted to watch the prison.

Luke, the author of Acts, narrates this moment. Herod Agrippa I had ordered James put to death and now had Peter in custody, waiting until the Passover had passed. Four squads of four soldiers guarded him in shifts. Meanwhile, the church prayed continually for him. The account shows that the situation was humanly hopeless.

For today: when everything seems closed and without a way out, we can rest in God and keep on praying. Peter slept in peace, and the church did not stop asking. God can act right in the darkest night.
exp.18:22:
This verse says that about that time in Ephesus a great disturbance broke out because of "the Way." "The Way" was a name used for the followers of Jesus, that is, Christianity in its earliest years. The word "disturbance" means a public riot or disorder.

The one telling the story is Luke, the author of Acts. Paul had been preaching in Asia for quite some time and was preparing to continue his journey. The verses that follow explain that the trouble began with Demetrius, a silversmith who lived by making small shrines of the goddess Diana. He saw that the Christian message put his business at risk.

For today: when the gospel makes people uncomfortable, it is wise to ask what lies behind people's reactions. Sometimes opposition comes from threatened interests or profits. Let us also examine our own hearts, so that money does not keep us from the truth.
exp.6:34:
This verse says that Moses, whom the people had rejected with the words "Who made you ruler and judge?", is the very one God sent to be their ruler and redeemer. God did this through the angel who appeared to him in the bush, the bush that was burning.

Here Stephen speaks before the Jewish council, going over the history of Israel. He wants to show that the people had already rejected the one God was sending them. Later he will compare this with Jesus, who was also rejected but chosen by God.

For today: sometimes what people reject or despise is exactly what God uses. Let us learn not to judge only by appearances or by the opinion of the majority, and to trust that God can work through people and ways we do not expect.
exp.13:21:
It says that Paul and Barnabas strengthened the souls of the disciples and encouraged them to keep holding on to the faith. They also told them that we must endure many hardships to enter the kingdom of God. "Strengthening" means building up and supporting, and "encouraging" means urging them on with care and conviction.

Luke tells that Paul and Barnabas returned to Lystra, Iconium, and Antioch, cities where they had recently faced opposition. Paul himself had been stoned in Lystra. They went back to care for the new disciples, who were facing similar pressures. Then they appointed elders in each church and commended them to the Lord.

Today, if you go through trials for following Christ, do not think that God has abandoned you. Seek the support of other believers, pray with them, and remain firm, trusting that God sustains you.
exp.9:0:
At Caesarea there lived a man named Cornelius. He was a centurion, that is, a Roman officer in charge of about a hundred soldiers. His unit was known as the Italian Regiment.

Here Luke, the author of Acts, introduces a new character. Cornelius was a Gentile, not a Jew, yet the verses that follow describe him as a man who already feared God, gave generously to those in need, and prayed. Luke introduces him because his story opens the door for the good news about Jesus to reach people outside Israel.

For today: God looks at a sincere heart, regardless of a person's background or occupation. No one is too far away for God to speak to them. Let us also be open to those who are seeking God.
exp.25:10:
Paul says that he often had the believers punished in the synagogues and tried to make them blaspheme, that is, to speak evil of Jesus. He was so filled with rage against them that he went after them even into foreign cities. "Raging fury" describes an intense, consuming anger, and "tried to make" means that he pressed them hard. The text does not say how many, if any, gave in.

Paul speaks before King Agrippa, a prisoner, and is making his defense. He wants to show that he once was a violent enemy of Jesus, acting with the authority of the priests. In this way he prepares the account of his encounter with Christ on the road to Damascus, where his life was completely changed.

For today: no one is so far away that God cannot reach them. If there is someone who has harmed you or opposes the faith, do not lose hope for that person. And if you yourself carry a dark past, remember that the grace of Jesus can transform you.
exp.16:3:
This verse tells the result of Paul's preaching in Thessalonica. Some of the Jews were persuaded and joined Paul and Silas. A large number of God-fearing Greeks also believed, that is, people who worshiped God without being Jews by birth. Quite a few leading women also believed. "Joined Paul and Silas" means that they became part of the group with the apostles.

The author, Luke, tells what happened after Paul, over three Sabbaths, showed from the Scriptures that the Messiah had to suffer and rise again, and that this Messiah was Jesus. Faith was born as they heard and examined the Word. But soon opposition came from other Jews, moved by jealousy.

For today: share your faith clearly and on the basis of the Bible, without becoming discouraged when some believe and others oppose. God can reach people of every kind and condition.
exp.9:10:
Peter, in a trance (a state in which God was showing him something in a special way), saw heaven open. Something like a large sheet was being let down to earth by its four corners. The word "vessel" in the older translations does not mean a cup, but a container or bundle, so this should be read as a large cloth lowered by its corners.

Peter was on the flat roof of a house in Joppa, praying around noon, and he was hungry. While the meal was being prepared, God gave him this vision. What follows shows that the sheet carried all kinds of animals. God was preparing Peter to bring the gospel to Cornelius, a man who was not Jewish.

For today: God can change our thoughts and prejudices when we pray with an open heart. Ask Him to show you whether you are leaving out someone whom He also loves and wants to reach.
exp.7:22:
Peter sees Simon caught up in bitterness and in sin. "Poisoned by bitterness" pictures something harmful and deadly soaking into a heart, and "captive to iniquity" speaks of being held prisoner by wickedness. Peter describes a heart that has been enslaved, not just a passing mistake.

Peter speaks with Simon the sorcerer, in Samaria. Simon had believed and been baptized, but he wanted to buy with money the power to give the Holy Spirit. Peter rebukes him firmly, but also calls him to repent and to pray that he may be forgiven. Some think Simon had not truly changed, since he asks others to pray for him; the text does not make this clear.

Today, this invites us to examine our motives before God. If we notice bitterness, ambition, or a desire to use spiritual things for our own benefit, let us not hide it. God calls us to repent with humility, and he offers us forgiveness and freedom.
exp.13:2:
Paul and Barnabas stayed in Iconium for a long time, speaking boldly for the Lord. The Lord affirmed the message of his grace by enabling them to perform signs and wonders, showing that the good news of his undeserved favor came from him.

Despite this, the phrase "despite this" means "in spite of that," that is, in spite of the opposition. To affirm the message means to support it and confirm that it is true.

Luke, the author of Acts, recounts the first missionary journey. Many Jews and Greeks believed, but others stirred up the Gentiles against the brothers. Paul and Barnabas did not flee at once; they stayed to strengthen the new believers. Soon afterward the city was divided, and there was an attempt to stone them.

For today: when there is opposition, do not lose heart or keep silent. Trust in the Lord, keep serving faithfully, and let God be the one who confirms his message.
exp.19:25:
Paul says that today he gives a solemn testimony before them. The phrase "I testify to you this day" means "I declare to you with seriousness." He affirms that he is "innocent of the blood of all men," that is, that he bears no guilt for anyone's ruin, because he fulfilled his duty of speaking to them.

Paul is taking leave of the elders of the church in Ephesus, gathered in Miletus, knowing that he will probably not see them again. The image comes from the watchman of the Old Testament, who was to warn of danger (Ezekiel 33). Paul explains in the following verse that he held nothing back: he announced to them the whole counsel of God.

Today, all of us who share our faith can ask ourselves whether we are speaking what God says with sincerity and love, without keeping silent about what is uncomfortable. It is not a matter of carrying the guilt of others, but of being faithful in what is ours to do, leaving the outcome in God's hands.
exp.16:26:
It says that God made everything so that people would seek him and, perhaps by reaching out, find him. It also makes clear that God is not far from each one of us. Reaching out for God is like feeling your way forward, the way someone searches in the dark.

Paul speaks in Athens, before philosophers at the Areopagus. The city was full of idols, and he explains to them that the true God created everything and does not live in temples built by human hands. He even quotes Greek poets to connect with his listeners and show them that worshiping images of gold or stone makes no sense.

For today: if someone has doubts or seeks God sincerely, they can approach him with confidence, because God does not hide himself. Pray simply, read the Gospels, and ask for light. And when you speak about your faith, begin with what the other person already knows, with respect.
exp.8:18:
This verse says that Saul ate and regained his strength. The Greek word behind "regained his strength" means to be made strong again, to be encouraged. After three days without eating or drinking, his body needed food. Then he spent several days with the disciples in Damascus, the followers of Jesus in that city.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells what happened after Saul met Jesus, was left blind, and was healed through Ananias. The disciples, whom Saul had earlier been persecuting, now receive him as a brother. This shows that his change was real and that the church accepted him.

God cares for both the body and the soul. After a powerful experience, resting, eating, and being with other believers helps us grow. We do not walk alone: we need a community that receives us and strengthens us.
exp.15:6:
It says that Paul and his companions came to the border of Mysia, in the northwest of Asia Minor, and tried to enter Bithynia, to the north. But the Spirit of Jesus would not permit them. "Tried" here simply means they made an effort to go, not that they were tempted to do evil. The phrase about the Spirit not permitting them means that the Spirit would not allow them to go.

It is part of the second missionary journey, and Luke, the author of Acts, tells what happened. Paul wanted to preach the gospel, but God closed two doors in a row (Asia and Bithynia). The Bible does not explain how the Spirit did it. Afterward came the vision that led them to Macedonia.

For today: even when you have good plans, keep your heart open to God's guidance. If one door closes, do not be discouraged; it may be that God is leading you to another place that is better.
exp.7:5:
This verse says that the people of Samaria paid close attention, all together, to what Philip was saying. Along with listening to him, they saw the signs he performed. The phrase "with one mind" means they were united, sharing one focus. "Signs" are miracles that pointed to God.

Luke, the author of Acts, recounts this after the persecution in Jerusalem that scattered many believers. Philip, one of the seven servants of the church, came to Samaria and proclaimed Christ. The miracles that follow, such as healings and deliverances, confirmed his message and brought great joy to the city.

Today we can learn to listen to God's word with attention and an open heart. Before we give our opinion or get distracted, let us take a moment to hear calmly what God wants to tell us, and let us seek to do this together with other believers.
exp.2:19:
God says he will send Jesus, the Christ, who has been appointed for you. The verse speaks of a future sending, and the phrase "who has been appointed for you" means that Jesus was set apart for them in advance by God's plan. Some understand this sending as the second coming of Christ; others see it as the fulfillment of the times of refreshing that God would bring. The text goes on to say that heaven receives him until the restoration of all things.

Peter speaks to the people in the temple, after God healed a lame man. He explains that Jesus, whom they rejected, was the promised Christ. He calls them to repent in order to receive forgiveness and to wait for what God will bring to pass.

For today: God fulfilled what he promised about the suffering of Christ, and he will also fulfill what remains. We can live with hope and repent with confidence, knowing that God is faithful to his word.
exp.9:4:
It says that Cornelius is to send some men to the city of Joppa to look for a man named Simon, who is also called Peter. "Send" means to dispatch them, and "call for" means to bring him or invite him to come. "Called" tells us that Peter was a second name by which this man was known.

A messenger from God speaks. Cornelius was a Roman soldier who prayed and helped the poor, and God saw his heart. The angel does not explain everything himself; he directs Cornelius toward Peter, who will tell him what he must do. In this way God prepares the meeting that will open the gospel to non-Jews.

For today: God often guides us step by step, frequently through other people. If you seek God sincerely, he is attentive and willing to be obeyed, even when you cannot yet see the whole plan.
exp.24:2:
They asked the new governor for a concession against Paul: that he would have Paul summoned to Jerusalem. The word "concession" here means a favor granted to someone who asks for it. The phrase "preparing an ambush" refers to a trap set in advance, and "to kill him along the way" shows that they planned to attack him during the journey.

Acts tells this as part of the story. Festus had just arrived as governor and visited Jerusalem. The chief priests and Jewish leaders took the opportunity to bring charges against Paul. Paul had been a prisoner in Caesarea for about two years. With this transfer they hoped for a chance to eliminate him, though they were asking for something that seemed lawful.

For today: wickedness sometimes disguises itself as a reasonable request. It is wise to have discernment and not be carried away by appearances. And when we face injustice, we can trust that God looks after his own, even when circumstances seem closed, as he did with Paul.
exp.27:11:
This verse tells us that the ship arrived at Syracuse, an important city on the island of Sicily, and that the travelers stayed there three days. The wording "putting in" simply means the ship pulled into the harbor, and "there" refers to that harbor.

The speaker is Luke, the author of Acts, who travels with Paul. Paul is being taken as a prisoner toward Rome to be judged before the emperor. After a shipwreck, they spent the winter on the island of Malta. Now they continue the journey on a ship from Alexandria. The Bible does not explain why they stopped for three days; it could have been because of the weather or matters concerning the ship, but this is not known for certain.

For today: God guides our path even in the pauses and delays we do not understand. When something seems to hold you back, trust that He is still leading you toward what He has promised, and use that time to rest and to serve.
exp.20:9:
Paul and his companions stayed in Caesarea for several days. While they were there, a prophet named Agabus came down from Judea. The travelers remained in Caesarea, and Agabus came down from Judea, since Jerusalem and Judea sit at higher elevation.

The narrator is Luke, who travels with Paul and writes as part of the group. Paul is heading toward Jerusalem and is staying at the house of Philip. Agabus has already appeared earlier in Acts as a prophet who foretold a famine. His arrival sets up the warning he will give about what awaits Paul in Jerusalem.

For today: God often speaks to us and prepares us through other believers. Let us learn to listen humbly to the counsel of mature brothers and sisters, and to ask for wisdom to know what to do with what we hear.
exp.5:2:
The apostles ask the whole church to select seven men from among themselves to be given a task. They must be people confirmed to be full of the Spirit and wisdom. The apostles say that they will assign this responsibility to them.

The twelve apostles are speaking. The church in Jerusalem was growing, and the believers who spoke Greek complained that their widows were not receiving the same care in the daily service. The apostles did not want to give up teaching the word of God, so they divided the work. The church chose seven, among them Stephen and Philip.

God also cares for his people through practical tasks, such as helping those in need. For this reason, those who serve in the church, even in simple things, must be people of good character and dependent on God. And all of us can help, sharing the work with humility.
exp.2:21:
Peter says that Moses told the ancestors of Israel that God would raise up a prophet for them from among their brothers, a prophet like Moses. The phrase "You must listen to Him" means you must listen to him and obey him. In other words, you must heed everything he tells you.

Peter is speaking in the temple in Jerusalem, after God healed a lame man. He is speaking to Jews, and he wants to show them that Jesus is the prophet promised in Deuteronomy 18:15. According to Peter, listening to Jesus does not contradict Moses but fulfills him.

For today: listening to Jesus is not just admiring him, but obeying him. Today you can read a passage from the Gospels and ask yourself, "What is Jesus asking of me here?" Then do one concrete thing to put it into practice.
exp.7:2:
This verse says that Saul was destroying the church. The word "destroy" means he was tearing it apart, and "prison" was the place where he locked up believers. He went from house to house, dragged off men and women, and put them in jail, without distinguishing anyone.

Luke, the author of Acts, records this after the death of Stephen, the first martyr. Saul had approved of that death. A fierce persecution then broke out in Jerusalem, and the believers were scattered. Luke shows how hostile Saul was, although later God would transform him and make him an apostle.

For today: God can use even the most painful things to spread his word, for those who were scattered kept proclaiming it. If you are going through a difficult situation, trust that God can still work. Pray also for those who oppose the faith: no one is beyond the reach of his grace.
exp.25:3:
Paul says that his way of life from his earliest childhood is known to all the Jews. From the beginning he spent it among his own people, and also in Jerusalem. The Berean wording says "lived," and "all the Jews know" means they are well acquainted with it.

Paul speaks before King Agrippa and the governor Festus, in Caesarea. The Jews accuse him, and he defends himself. To do so, he recalls his past: he was not a stranger or a rebel, but someone raised and trained in Judaism, with a reputation that many could confirm. In this way he prepares the way to explain why he now believes in Christ.

For today: a steady and honest life speaks for us. When someone questions us, our daily witness can give us credibility to share our faith with respect and without fear.
exp.7:18:
Simon asks the apostles: "Give me this power as well, so that everyone on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit." The word "power" here means authority or power over others. The phrase "lay hands on" means to place one's hands on someone in order to pray for them.

The speaker is Simon, a man from Samaria who had practiced magic before he believed. He saw that the Holy Spirit was given when Peter and John prayed with the laying on of hands, and he wanted that power. So he offered them money. Peter rebuked him sharply, because the gift of God cannot be bought. According to the text, his heart was not right. Interpreters debate how genuine his faith was, and the passage does not fully settle the question.

Today we can examine our motives in serving God. His power and his gifts are not for gaining fame, control, or personal profit. They are received with humility, as a gift from him.
exp.13:10:
He says that when the crowd in Lystra saw the miracle Paul performed in healing a man who could not walk, they shouted in their own language, Lycaonian: "The gods have come down to us in human form!" The word "semejantes" means "like" or "similar to," and the word "gentes" means "a crowd of people."

Those speaking are the people of Lystra, a city where they did not know the God of Israel. They spoke in their local language, so Paul and Barnabas may not have understood at first what they were saying. That is why they mistook the apostles for gods and wanted to offer them sacrifices. We do not know for certain which local legend influenced them.

Today, when God does something good through us, the glory belongs to Him. We should receive praise with humility and always point toward Him.
exp.7:29:
Philip ran up to the chariot and heard the man reading from the prophet Isaiah. Then he asked a simple question: "Do you understand what you are reading?" The word "ran" shows that Philip hurried over to him.

Philip spoke because the Spirit had told him to go near the chariot. The man is an Ethiopian official who was returning from Jerusalem. It was customary to read aloud, which is why Philip could hear him. Philip did not correct him harshly; with his question he opened a conversation, and the man answered humbly that he needed someone to guide him.

For today: reading the Bible is good, but understanding it is better. Do not be ashamed to ask questions or to ask for help from a pastor, a teacher, or a friend with more experience. And if someone near you is seeking God, approach them kindly and offer your help.
exp.18:15:
This verse says that the man with the evil spirit jumped on the seven sons of Sceva. He overpowered all of them. The attack was so violent that they ran out of the house naked and wounded. Some think that "naked" may mean that most of their clothing had been torn off them.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells this in Ephesus. God was doing miracles through Paul. These men, who were not believers, wanted to use the name of Jesus as a magic formula, saying "I command you by Jesus, whom Paul preaches." The evil spirit answered that it knew Jesus and Paul, but not them.

For today: faith in Jesus is not a phrase to repeat or something borrowed from others. It is a personal relationship with Him. It is not enough to know things about Jesus; He wants us to know Him and truly trust in Him.
exp.20:19:
When they heard Paul's report, the elders of Jerusalem glorified God. Then they said to him, "You see, brother, how many thousands of Jews have believed, and all of them are zealous for the law." The word "zealous" describes people who are very devoted and passionate about keeping something; here, the law of Moses.

James and the elders of the church in Jerusalem are speaking. First they celebrate what God has done among the non-Jews. But right away they explain to Paul a concern: rumors were going around that he was encouraging Jews to abandon Moses. That is why they give him this context before asking him for something.

For today: we can rejoice in what God is doing in others, even when they are different from us. And when there are tensions or rumors, it is good to speak with clarity and humility, seeking unity.
exp.20:21:
The elders of Jerusalem ask Paul: "What then should we do?" They tell him that the crowd will certainly hear that he has arrived. Their question shows their concern about how the crowd will react.

The ones speaking are James and the elders of the church in Jerusalem. Thousands of Jewish believers were very zealous for the law of Moses, and they had heard reports that Paul was teaching people to abandon it. So they propose a plan: that he take part in a purification vow with four men, to show that he too respects the law. Some think it was a good expression of love; others think it was a debatable concession.

For today: before a rumor grows, let us seek peace with humility and clear actions. We can yield in matters that do not harm the gospel, so as not to place unnecessary stumbling blocks before others.
exp.8:16:
Ananias obeys the Lord. He goes to the house where Saul is staying, places his hands on him, and calls him "brother." He explains that the Lord Jesus, the one who appeared to Saul on the road, has sent him so that Saul may see again and be filled with the Holy Spirit.

Saul had persecuted the Christians, and he was blinded after seeing Jesus on the road to Damascus. Ananias, a disciple, was afraid to go, but the Lord told him that Saul would be a chosen instrument to carry his name to the Gentiles. Here Ananias speaks, using the words the Lord entrusted to him.

For today: God may ask us to warmly welcome someone we find hard to accept. Ananias called his former enemy "brother." We can obey God and offer welcome and forgiveness, trusting that He can change anyone.
exp.11:21:
The people shouted that this was the voice of a god, not a man. The word "shouted" means that they cried out loudly, in approval and praise. They meant that his speech was so impressive that it seemed divine.

Herod Agrippa I had tensions with the cities of Tyre and Sidon, which depended on his kingdom for food. They sought peace through Blastus, the king's chamberlain. Herod, dressed in royal clothing, spoke to them from the judgment seat. The crowd praised him with their words, and he did not reject that praise or give the glory to God. For this reason the angel of the Lord struck him, according to the text that follows.

Today we can remember that every ability and every success comes from God. When someone praises us, let us give thanks to God in our hearts and humbly refuse any honor that belongs to Him alone.
exp.2:15:
This verse says that the lame man, whom everyone knew, was healed by the power of Jesus' name. That power came through faith in him. The phrase "whom you see and know" in the verse means "this man," and "complete healing" means he was made fully well, in the sight of everyone.

Peter speaks in the temple in Jerusalem to a crowd amazed at the healing of the lame man. He makes clear that they were not healed by their own power or holiness, but by Jesus, whom they had rejected and whom God had raised up. With this, Peter invites them to recognize what they did and to turn to God.

For today: when God does something good in your life, do not keep the credit for yourself or attribute it to your own effort. Recognize Jesus as the source and tell others about it with humility, so that they too may come to know him.
exp.23:0:
Five days later, the high priest Ananias came down to Caesarea with some elders and a lawyer named Tertullus. The verse's word "lawyer" tells us that Tertullus was trained to argue cases, so it is his role here that matters. He presented to the governor, Felix, the case against Paul.

The narrator is Luke, the author of Acts. Paul had been arrested in Jerusalem and sent to Caesarea because of threats against his life. The Jewish leaders traveled there to bring their accusation formally. They hired a skilled advocate, which shows how strongly they wanted to condemn him.

For today: sometimes opposition arrives well organized and with capable speakers. Paul did not defend himself with tricks, but with truth and trust in God. When you face injustice, try to respond with calm, honesty and faith, knowing that God knows your situation.
exp.6:24:
He assumed his brothers would understand that God was using him to rescue them from slavery, but they did not. Here, the word for "rescue" in the verse means deliverance. "Using him" means working through him. But the people did not see it that way.

The one speaking is Stephen, in his defense before the Jewish council. He reviews the history of Israel and shows that the people turned away from Moses before accepting him as their deliverer. In doing so, he hints that many of his own generation were also rejecting Jesus, the deliverer sent by God.

For today: sometimes God works in ways we do not recognize right away. Let us ask for humility to listen for his voice, even when it comes by unexpected means or at a time we did not expect. And if someone does not understand us when we serve God, let us trust that He is still carrying out his plan.
exp.4:10:
This verse says that great fear came over the whole church and over all who heard about these events. Here "fear" means a deep, reverent respect, mixed with awe and seriousness before God. "Church" refers to the gathered community of believers.

The one telling the story is Luke, the author of Acts. He recounts what happened with Ananias and Sapphira, who sold a property, pretended to hand over the full amount to the apostles, and lied about it. Peter confronted them, and both died. This is the first time Acts uses the word "church." Some see in this a sign of God's holiness at the beginning of the church; the text does not explain beyond that.

For today: God sees the heart, so it is worth living with sincerity. We can serve and give without pretending to be more than we are, remembering that God is holy and also merciful.
exp.15:21:
The crowd joined in the attack against Paul and Silas, and the officials ordered that they be stripped and beaten with rods. The text describes people rushing together in a sudden, violent attack. Being beaten with rods was a public physical punishment.

This happens in Philippi, a Roman city. The owners of a young slave girl were angry because Paul had driven a spirit out of her, and they no longer made money from her. They brought charges before the city authorities, stirring up prejudice against the Jews and appealing to the pride of being Romans. Luke tells us there was no fair trial, only a hasty reaction from the crowd and the judges.

For today: sometimes doing good brings injustice and suffering. Paul and Silas did not respond with bitterness, nor did they abandon their calling. We can trust that God is with us even when we are treated badly without reason.
exp.22:3:
The people standing nearby ask Paul a pointed question: how dare he insult the high priest of God? The word "insult" here means to speak harshly and disrespectfully against someone. "High priest" refers to the highest religious leader of the Jews.

Paul is before the Jewish council. Ananias had ordered him struck on the mouth without a trial, and Paul reacted by calling him a whitewashed wall, that is, someone who looks clean on the outside but is unjust within. Those present defend respect for the office. Then Paul says he did not know who the man was, and he points to the law that forbids speaking badly of a ruler of the people. Scholars debate why he did not recognize him; the Bible does not explain it.

We can defend justice without failing in respect. If we react in anger, it is wise to acknowledge it with humility and correct our course.
exp.18:24:
Demetrius, the silversmith, gathers the craftsmen who work in related trades. Here the phrase is "workmen in related trades" for the people he calls together. He reminds them that this business is their source of prosperity, that is, their income and their livelihood.

Demetrius, who made small shrines or little silver chapels of the goddess Diana (Artemis), is the one speaking. Paul had preached in Ephesus, and many were giving up their idols. Demetrius begins by talking about money, and then adds the religious issue. In this way he manages to stir up alarm among them all and unite them against Paul and "the Way," which was the name then used for the followers of Jesus.

For today: let us examine our motives. Sometimes we defend something with very spiritual words, when in truth we are looking after our wallet or our comfort. Let us ask God for an honest heart, one that loves the truth more than gain.
exp.22:11:
At daybreak, a group of Jews made a secret plan together and bound themselves with a solemn oath. They swore an oath not to eat or drink until they had killed Paul. The phrase "when daylight came" means "when morning arrived."

Luke, the author of Acts, reports this after Paul had been arrested in Jerusalem and a great commotion had broken out. That night the Lord had told Paul to take courage, because he would still bear witness in Rome. Later in the text, the number of those who had conspired is given as more than forty.

For today: human plans, even the most determined ones, cannot stop God's purposes. When we face opposition, we can trust that He watches over our path. We also learn not to make extreme promises driven by anger.
exp.27:18:
Paul explains that, because the Jews objected to his release, he felt compelled to appeal to Caesar, the emperor of Rome. The verse says "objected," so that word is used here, and "appeal" means asking a higher authority to review the case. He makes clear that he had no charge to bring against his people.

Paul is in Rome, a prisoner, and speaks with the Jewish leaders of the city. He wants them to know that he is innocent and that he has nothing against his nation. The Romans found in him no cause for death, but the objections of his own countrymen led him to appeal. He insists that his chain has to do with the hope of Israel.

For today: when you are treated unjustly, defend yourself with truth and firmness, but without holding a grudge. Paul sought justice without speaking badly of those who attacked him.
exp.26:20:
Paul stood up in front of everyone after many days without food, and told them it would have been better to have listened to him and not to have sailed from Crete. That way they would have avoided this disaster and loss they were now suffering, meaning the hardship and the damage they had brought on themselves. Paul was speaking to the men, and the advice he gave was the right advice.

Paul was traveling as a prisoner toward Rome. Before leaving Crete he had warned that the voyage would be dangerous (Acts 27:10), but the captain and the owner of the ship decided to go on. Now, in the middle of the storm and with everyone discouraged, Paul speaks. He does not do it to boast, but to gain their attention before giving them hope, as the next verse shows.

Listening to good advice in time saves us much pain. But if we have already made a mistake, God can still speak to us with hope. Let us learn to ask for direction and to listen with humility.
exp.12:24:
John was finishing his work when he asked the people, "Who do you suppose I am?" He answered that he was not that One. He said that another was coming after him, and that he was not worthy even to untie the sandals on his feet.

Paul speaks in the synagogue of Antioch in Pisidia. He surveys the history of Israel to show that Jesus is the promised Savior. He mentions John the Baptist because John was highly respected, and his testimony pointed clearly to Jesus. In this way, Paul prepares his listeners to receive the message of salvation.

John teaches us humility. He had fame and influence, but he did not seek to take the place of Christ. Today we can ask ourselves whether in what we do we seek applause or point to Jesus. Serving well means letting others see Him, not us.
exp.2:13:
Peter says that the people rejected Jesus, whom he calls "the Holy and Righteous One," that is, the one who is pure and always does what is right. Instead of Jesus, they asked that a murderer be released to them. "Rejected" means that they turned him down and refused to stand with him.

Peter speaks in the temple, before the crowd that was amazed to see a man who had been lame walking, a man who had just been healed. Peter makes clear that the miracle did not come from their power or goodness, but from Jesus. Firmly, yet seeking their repentance, he reminds them of what happened before Pilate.

For today: sometimes we prefer what is comfortable over Jesus. Today you can ask yourself in which decisions you are putting him first, and if you have gone wrong, return to him with humility, because God offers forgiveness.
exp.21:19:
Paul remembers the day Stephen was killed, whom he calls "Your witness," meaning someone who spoke about Jesus right up to the end. Paul was there, he gave his approval to that death, and he watched over the clothes of those who were killing Stephen. The phrase "giving my approval" means that he agreed with what was happening.

Paul speaks before a crowd in Jerusalem and tells them what Jesus said to him in the temple. He thinks that, because of his past as a persecutor, the people of the city would believe him. But Jesus answers that he will send him far away, to the Gentiles, and that stirs up the anger of the crowd.

For today: do not hide your past when God has changed you. Telling your mistakes and the grace you received honestly can help others. Even so, God decides how and where to use you.
exp.2:0:
This verse tells us that Peter and John were on their way up to the temple in Jerusalem one afternoon. It was the hour of prayer, the ninth hour, which is around three in the afternoon by our way of counting. They were going up because the temple stood on higher ground.

Here the narrator is Luke, the author of the book of Acts. The apostles kept going to the temple to pray, as the Jews of their time did. This simple detail prepares the story that follows: on the way they will meet a lame man who was asking for money, and God will work a miracle.

For today: having set times of prayer, and even better if we pray together with others, places us where God can use us. The great moments often come while we remain faithful in the everyday.
exp.14:22:
This verse is the opening of a letter. The leaders of the church in Jerusalem wrote it and sent it with Judas and Silas. They addressed their brothers who were not Jewish, the Gentiles, living in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia. The opening words were a common greeting in letters of that time, much like "Greetings" or "I hope you are well" today.

There had been a serious disagreement: some were saying that non-Jewish believers had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses. The apostles, the elders, and the whole church came together, reached an agreement, and wrote to give those brothers reassurance and clarity.

When there is confusion or conflict, it is good to answer with clarity, in writing if necessary, and with a kind manner. A friendly greeting can prepare the hearts of others to receive a difficult or important message.
exp.8:15:
It says that Jesus himself will show Saul how much he must suffer for the sake of Jesus' name. The word translated as "must" means "necessary," and the word about suffering means "endure." In other words, Saul would suffer for following and proclaiming Christ.

The Lord Jesus speaks in a vision that Ananias, a disciple in Damascus, has. Ananias was afraid, because Saul had persecuted the believers. Jesus reassures him: he has chosen Saul to carry his message to the Gentiles, to kings, and to the people of Israel. He tells Ananias ahead of time that this mission would bring suffering. Later, Paul spoke of the many hardships he went through, as he recounts in his letters.

Following Jesus can cost something: misunderstanding, rejection, or difficulties. If you are facing trials because of your faith today, remember that Christ does not leave you alone; he knows your path and sustains you in it.
exp.3:29:
Here the believers ask God to stretch out his hand in power, so that healings, signs and wonders take place. All of this would be done through the name of Jesus, whom they call "Your holy servant." The word "wonders" means astonishing deeds that show God's power.

The speakers are the early church in Jerusalem. Peter and John had just been released, after the authorities had ordered them not to speak about Jesus. The believers do not ask for revenge or for the threats to end, but for boldness to proclaim the word. They ask that God confirm the message with his power. Afterward, the place shook and everyone was filled with the Holy Spirit.

When you face pressure for your faith, pray as they did: not only that the problem will pass, but that God will give you courage and that his work will be seen. Fix your eyes on Jesus and on his honor, and not on your comfort.
exp.23:20:
Paul says that if his accusers want to point to anything wrong he has done, there is only one thing he shouted out while he stood before the council: "It is concerning the resurrection of the dead that I am on trial before you today." The word "called out" means he spoke suddenly and with force.

Paul speaks before the governor Felix, in Caesarea. The Jews from Jerusalem accuse him of causing trouble. He answers that they found no wrongdoing in him when he was before the council. The only thing he said there (Acts 23:6) was that he believed in the resurrection. In this way he shows that the real issue is one of faith, not crime.

For today: you can trust that God sustains you when your faith is misunderstood. Respond honestly and without hiding your hope in the risen Christ, without needing to fight or to return an insult.
exp.12:48:
This verse says that God's message spread throughout the whole region, like seed scattered across a field. The word "spread" here means carried far and wide. The "region" is the area around Antioch of Pisidia.

Paul and Barnabas had just proclaimed the gospel in Antioch. Many non-Jews believed with joy, and they told others what they had heard. Luke, the author of Acts, tells how the faith grew. Soon after, persecution came, but the message had already taken root.

For today: you don't need a big stage to share what God has done in you. When you talk simply and lovingly with your family, your neighbors, or your coworkers, God can make that seed grow much farther than you imagine.
exp.19:10:
Paul went back upstairs to the room where the believers were gathered, broke bread, and ate. Then he kept on talking with them until daybreak, and only then did he leave.

"Breaking bread" meant sharing a meal, probably the Lord's Supper together with an ordinary meal. The verse says Paul "ate," so he took food and enjoyed the meal with them. "Daybreak" is the first light of morning.

Luke, the author of Acts, recounts this in Troas. Paul was saying farewell to the believers because he was leaving on a journey the next day. Shortly before, the young Eutychus had fallen from a window and was given up for dead, but Paul embraced him and said that he was alive. After that, the gathering continued, the young man was brought back alive, and the people were greatly comforted.

For today: after a difficult moment, let us not abandon fellowship. God restores, and it is good for us to keep meeting together, sharing the table and listening to his word with gratitude and attention.
exp.15:38:
The magistrates of Philippi went in person to the prison and came to appease Paul and Silas, asking them to come out. After leading them out, they requested that the two men leave the city. Here "appease" means that they sought to calm them down and make peace with them.

Paul and Silas had been beaten and imprisoned without a trial. When Paul said that they were Roman citizens, the authorities became afraid, because they had violated their rights. Paul insisted that the officials themselves come to bring them out, so that it would be clear that they had been treated unjustly.

For today: we can ask for justice firmly and calmly, without seeking revenge. Paul guarded the good name of the gospel and protected the new believers in Philippi.
exp.17:0:
This verse says that, after what happened in Athens, Paul left that city and went to Corinth. The phrase "After this" points back to what had just taken place. The words "left" and "went to" describe his movement from one city to the other.

The narrator is Luke, the author of Acts, who tells of Paul's second missionary journey. Before this, Paul had spoken in Athens, with mixed results. Corinth was a large and busy trading city in Greece. The following passage shows that there he met Aquila and Priscilla, with whom he worked making tents.

For today: sometimes one stage ends and another begins, without our having everything clear. Paul did not stay stuck; he moved forward and worked with his hands. We can trust that God guides us through changes, and serve faithfully in everyday life wherever we are.
exp.17:25:
Apollos began to speak boldly in the synagogue. When Priscilla and Aquila heard him, they took him aside and explained the way of God to him more fully. "Boldly" means with courage and without fear. "More fully" means they explained it with greater clarity and accuracy.

Luke, the author of Acts, reports this in Ephesus. Apollos was a Jew from Alexandria, eloquent and well versed in the Scriptures, but he knew only the baptism of John. The text does not say precisely what he still lacked in understanding; many think it concerned what happened after Jesus' resurrection and the coming of the Spirit. Priscilla and Aquila, a married couple who were believers, corrected him with care.

Even someone who serves with enthusiasm and talent can keep learning. If someone corrects us with love and in private, we can receive it with humility. And if we must correct another, let us do it with respect, as they did.
exp.27:20:
The Jewish leaders in Rome tell Paul that they have not received any letters about him from Judea, and that none of the Jewish brothers who came from there has reported or even mentioned anything bad about him. The phrase "about you" simply means the letters concerned Paul, and "brothers" here refers to fellow Jews.

Paul has just arrived in Rome as a prisoner, and he calls together the leading Jews to explain his situation. They answer, probably sincerely, that they have no negative reports. Even so, they want to hear him, since they know that this movement is widely disputed everywhere. This opens the door for Paul to speak to them about Jesus.

For today: before judging a person or a belief, it is wise to listen to the person directly and examine things for ourselves, rather than relying on rumors or on what others say.
exp.19:12:
Luke tells us that he and his companions went ahead to the ship and sailed to Assos, a port on the coast of Asia Minor. There they would take Paul aboard. Paul had arranged to make that stretch of the journey by land, on foot.

The one telling the story is Luke, who travels with Paul and speaks using "we." He has just described the long night in Troas, when Paul taught and Eutychus was brought back to life. The Bible does not explain why Paul chose to go by land. Some think he wanted time alone to pray or reflect, but that is only a guess.

For today: not all of us need to walk the road in the same way. We can respect that God guides each person differently, and still stay united in the same purpose.
exp.24:11:
Festus, the Roman governor, confers with his council, the group of advisers who helped him make decisions. Then he answers Paul: "You have appealed to Caesar. To Caesar you will go!" With this he accepts Paul's request and declares it valid.

Paul had been held in prison in Caesarea for more than two years. The Jewish leaders were accusing him, and Festus, who had only recently arrived, wanted to win their favor and proposed that Paul be judged in Jerusalem. Paul, knowing he was in danger there, used his right as a Roman citizen and appealed to the emperor. Once the appeal had been made, the governor could no longer stop it. This opened the way for Paul to reach Rome.

God can guide our plans even along paths we do not choose. Paul acted wisely and used the lawful resources he had, while at the same time trusting in God. Let us do the same: think carefully, act with prudence, and rest in the knowledge that God is still at work.
exp.15:10:
Paul and his companions left the port of Troas and sailed straight to the island of Samothrace. The next day they reached Neapolis, the port of Macedonia. The phrase "straight to" describes a direct voyage, with no detours.

The one who tells the story is Luke, the author of Acts. Here he begins to write "we," which suggests that he had joined the group. Paul had seen a man from Macedonia in a vision at night, pleading for help, and the team understood that God was calling them. This verse shows that they obeyed right away. It marks the step of the gospel toward Europe, though the text does not say it in those words.

When we sense that God is guiding us, it is good to act promptly and simply, taking the next concrete step. We do not need to see the whole road to begin walking in faith.
exp.8:26:
This verse tells how Barnabas took Saul (Paul) and brought him to the apostles. He described to them how Saul had seen the Lord, who had spoken to him on the road to Damascus, and how Saul had spoken boldly in that city in the name of Jesus. The word "boldly" in this verse means with courage and without fear.

It is part of Luke's account in the book of Acts. Saul had persecuted the Christians, so in Jerusalem the disciples were afraid of him and doubted that his change was real. Barnabas, whose name means "son of encouragement" according to Acts 4:36, spoke in his favor. The Bible does not say why he had this willingness, only that he did it.

For today: sometimes a person who has changed needs others to believe in him. We can be like Barnabas: give someone a chance, listen with respect, and support those who seek to follow Christ, without being naive, but with mercy.
exp.4:41:
Acts 5:42 says that the apostles, every day, did not stop teaching and proclaiming the good news that Jesus is the Christ, the Messiah. They did this in the temple courts, a public place, and also from house to house, in a more personal setting.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells what happened after the Jewish council had beaten the apostles and ordered them not to speak about Jesus. They left rejoicing that they had been counted worthy to suffer for His name. Far from keeping quiet, they carried on with their work, because they believed they must obey God rather than men.

Today we can ask ourselves how to speak of Jesus in everyday life: with simple words, with kindness and steadiness, both in public places and at home. It does not take anything grand; it is enough to be faithful each day.
exp.21:11:
There was a man named Ananias, described as a devout observer of the law, meaning he was deeply committed to God and faithful to the Jewish law. He was highly regarded by all the Jews living in Damascus.

Paul speaks before a Jewish crowd in Jerusalem, defending himself after being arrested. He tells how he met Jesus on the road to Damascus and was blinded. In describing Ananias with such respect, Paul shows his audience that the man who received him and spoke to him on God's behalf was no enemy of the Jewish law, but a man respected by them as well.

For today: a faithful and steady life gives a testimony that opens doors. When we live with integrity in our community, God can use our good reputation to help others believe and receive his light.
exp.11:24:
This verse tells that Barnabas and Saul returned from Jerusalem after finishing their mission. They brought John, also called Mark, back with them. "When Barnabas and Saul had fulfilled their mission to Jerusalem" means that they had already completed the task they were sent to do there.

The narrator is Luke, the author of Acts. Before this, he recounted the death of King Herod and how the word of God kept growing. According to Acts 11:29-30, Barnabas and Saul had brought relief for the brothers in Judea. Now they return to Antioch, and Mark joins them. Luke thus prepares the next missionary journey.

God continues his work even when the powerful fall. And his work also advances through simple services, such as helping others. We can faithfully carry out what is entrusted to us and encourage others, as Barnabas did with Mark, to serve as well.
exp.17:16:
The crowd seized Sosthenes, the leader of the synagogue, and beat him in front of the judgment seat. But none of this was of concern to Gallio.

Gallio was the Roman governor in Corinth. The Jews had brought charges against Paul before him, but Gallio said it was a matter of their own law and drove them away. Some manuscripts say only "the crowd" without naming who it was, so it is not certain who beat Sosthenes. It is also not certain that this is the Sosthenes whom Paul mentions in 1 Corinthians 1:1.

Today we can learn that indifference toward injustice also has a cost. When we see abuse, it is not enough to shrug our shoulders. We can help, stand up for others, or speak with compassion.
exp.12:19:
Paul says that, after the land was divided among the tribes, God gave Israel judges for about 450 years, until the prophet Samuel. The number is approximate, which is why the verse says "about," and scholars work out the time span in different ways.

Paul is speaking in the synagogue at Antioch in Pisidia. He gives a summary of Israel's history to show that God was faithful throughout and that the whole story pointed forward to Jesus, the promised Savior from the family line of David.

For today: God works with patience over the years, even when we cannot see the full picture. When a season of your life seems long or confusing, remember that God is still guiding history, and also your story, with purpose and faithfulness.
exp.0:12:
The verse tells us that Jesus's disciples, after returning to Jerusalem, went up to a room on the upper floor of a house. The upper room is a room on the floor above. The phrase "where they were staying" means they were living there for a time. Then the names of the eleven apostles are listed in pairs. The name Simon the Zealot seems to indicate that Simon belonged to a group zealous for the cause of his people, though it may also simply mean that he was very fervent.

The narrator is Luke, the author of Acts. Jesus had just gone up into heaven from the Mount of Olives, and two angels had told the disciples that He would return. Jesus had instructed them to wait in Jerusalem for the promise of the Holy Spirit. No one knows for certain whether this upper room is the same as the room of the Last Supper; the Bible does not say.

When we do not know what comes next, we can do what they did: gather with other believers and wait in faith. This week, seek out someone from your church and pray together.
exp.21:15:
Here Ananias speaks to Saul (Paul) after his encounter with Jesus. He tells him not to wait any longer: he should get up, be baptized, and wash away his sins while calling on the name of the Lord. The question "what are you waiting for?" is a plain way of asking why Saul is still hesitating.

Paul recounts this story before a crowd in Jerusalem, at a time when he was being accused. He tells how God chose him to know His will, to see the Just One, and to be a witness. Ananias was a respected Jewish believer. Christians understand in different ways how baptism relates to forgiveness: some see it as the moment when forgiveness is received, others as the public sign of a forgiveness that comes through faith in Jesus.

If you already sense God's call, do not put it off out of fear or doubt. Take the step of faith that He shows you, and call on Jesus sincerely.
exp.9:25:
This verse tells how Peter helped Cornelius up after Cornelius had knelt before him. Peter said to him, "Stand up; I am only a man myself." The word "but" in the verse is the same as "but" in English, and Peter refused the reverence Cornelius was showing him.

Peter, who had just arrived at Caesarea, was speaking in the house of Cornelius, a Roman officer who sought God. Cornelius threw himself at Peter's feet and showed him a very great respect, almost as if he were a superior being. Some think it was a great show of reverence and others that it was true worship; the text does not make this clear. Peter stopped him because only God deserves worship.

For today: honor and respect the leaders of your church, but do not put them in the place of God. And if someone admires you, respond with humility, pointing to Christ and not to yourself.
exp.15:0:
Paul came to the cities of Derbe and then Lystra. There he found a disciple named Timothy. His mother was a Jewish woman who believed in Christ, but his father was a Greek.

The phrase about the old way of writing "to" does not apply to this reader's verse, so it is left out here.

The one who tells the story is Luke, the author of Acts. He recounts how Paul, on his second journey, goes back to visit the churches and finds this young man. The verses that follow say that the brothers spoke well of him, and that Paul wanted to take him along as a companion. Luke presents Timothy with his mixed background because that mattered for the work among Jews and Greeks.
