For today: God uses people with their family history just as it is. Also, a mother's faith can leave a deep mark. Encourage someone young and cultivate a good reputation among the brothers and sisters.
exp.9:7:
This verse says that Cornelius, after explaining everything he had seen and heard, sent the two servants and the soldier to the city of Joppa. The name of the city appears in the verse as Joppa, a port by the sea. The phrase "he explained what had happened" means that he kept nothing back from what the angel had told him.

The one who tells the story is Luke, the author of Acts. Cornelius was a Roman officer who feared God and prayed. An angel told him to send for Peter. Cornelius entrusted his plans to men he trusted and sent them with a clear mission.

For today: when God asks something of us, it is good to explain it clearly and honestly to those who help us. Cornelius obeyed without delay and shared all that he knew. We can do the same: obey with simplicity and surround ourselves with people who help us carry out what God places in our hearts.
exp.12:39:
Verse 40 says: "Watch out, then, that what was spoken by the prophets does not happen to you." The word "watch out" means "be careful" or "pay attention." Here the warning is a serious one, given with genuine care, so that no one overlooks what God is doing.

Paul is speaking in the synagogue at Antioch of Pisidia, to Jews and to Gentiles who feared God. He has just announced that through Jesus there is forgiveness of sins and justification for everyone who believes, something the law of Moses could not provide. He then quotes the prophet Habakkuk (1:5), who spoke of people who scorned the work of God and would not believe it.

For today: let us not harden our hearts when we hear the gospel. If God speaks to us through his Word, let us respond with faith and humility right now, without putting it off or assuming we already know everything.
exp.0:13:
These all kept on together in prayer, with one heart and purpose. They stayed faithful and did not give up. The eleven apostles were there, along with the women, Mary the mother of Jesus, and his brothers.

The author is Luke, who tells what happened after Jesus returned to heaven. Jesus had told them to wait in Jerusalem for the promise of the Holy Spirit. That is why they gather in the upper room, waiting and praying. It is striking that his brothers are there, since before this they did not believe in him (John 7:5). The Bible does not explain here how they changed.

For today: when we do not know what is coming, we can wait on God by praying with other believers. Steady prayer, held together in unity, sustains us and prepares us for what God will do.
exp.23:2:
Tertullus says that the Jews acknowledge Felix's work in every way and everywhere, and they are full of gratitude for it. "Gratitude" is the word that matters here, and the verse uses it directly. "Most excellent" was a title of respect for a Roman authority.

Tertullus is a speaker hired by the high priest Ananias and the elders to accuse Paul before the governor Felix. His speech opens with flattery to win the judge's favor before presenting the charges. Many scholars see here a common technique of the rhetoric of that era. What he says about "great peace" does not fully reflect reality, since the history of that time shows tensions in the region.

Let us take care with our words: sincere praise builds up, but flattery seeks personal advantage. Let us speak with truth and respect, without using compliments to manipulate anyone.
exp.8:2:
As Saul was on his way and drew near to Damascus, suddenly a light from heaven flashed all around him. The word "flashed" describes a bright burst of light, and "suddenly" means it happened all at once, without any warning.

The narrator is Luke, author of the book of Acts. Saul, who would later be known as Paul, was traveling with permission from the religious leaders to arrest believers in Jesus. He was full of anger toward them. At that moment, Jesus himself interrupts his journey, as the following verses show.

God can reach any person, even someone who seems farthest from Him. If you pray for someone who opposes the faith, do not lose hope. And if today you feel lost or mistaken, remember that Christ still comes to meet you with grace.
exp.1:36:
This verse tells us that those who heard Peter were deeply moved. "Cut to the heart" means they felt a strong pain inside, like a sharp wound in the conscience. So they asked Peter and the other apostles, "Brothers, what shall we do?"

It was the day of Pentecost, in Jerusalem. Peter had just preached that Jesus, whom they had crucified, was Lord and Christ, that is, the promised Messiah. Hearing this, they understood their guilt and sought how to respond to God. Peter will answer them right away with a call to repentance.

For today: when God's Word touches your conscience, do not ignore it or defend yourself. Do as they did: ask sincerely what you should do, and come to God with humility.
exp.4:0:
This verse says that a man named Ananias, together with his wife Sapphira, sold a piece of property. "Now" marks a shift in the story, so the account moves on from what came before. "Property" refers to land or ground that belonged to them.

The one telling the story is Luke, the author of Acts. In the previous chapter, several believers were selling their goods and handing the money over to the apostles to help those in need. This verse introduces a couple who do something similar, but the verses that follow show that they kept back part of the money and pretended to give it all. Their sin was not keeping a portion for themselves, but lying.

God desires sincerity more than appearances. We can give much or little, but we must give honestly. Today it is worth asking ourselves whether we serve and give to please God or to be admired.
exp.0:0:
In this verse the author says he had already written a first book, addressed to someone named Theophilus. In it he wrote about everything Jesus began to do and to teach.

The author of Acts, traditionally identified as Luke, here picks up his Gospel. Luke 1:3 also mentions Theophilus, a name meaning "friend of God." We do not know with certainty who he was; some think he was a real person of some standing, while others believe the name stands for any reader who loves God. Luke begins this second book by connecting it to the first, so that the story can continue after the resurrection.

For today: the work of Jesus did not end with the Gospel. He continues to work through his church, and you can be part of that story by living out and teaching what he taught.
exp.3:3:
It says that, although Peter and John were arrested, many of those who heard the message believed in Jesus. The group of believing men grew to about five thousand. The word "but" at the start shows the contrast with what came just before, and "grew" describes the number increasing. Some understand that the five thousand are added to those who were already there; others, that it is the total. The text does not fully make this clear.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells what happened after Peter and John healed a lame man in the temple and preached about the resurrection. The religious leaders, upset, had them put in prison for a night. Meanwhile, the people who had heard them kept responding with faith.

For today: sometimes it seems that opposition is going to stop the message, but the message can keep bearing fruit. You can share your faith simply and with confidence, without depending on everyone's approval, and leave the outcome in God's hands.
exp.22:7:
This verse explains the difference between two Jewish groups. The Sadducees said that there is neither a resurrection nor angels nor spirits. The Pharisees, on the other hand, acknowledged all of these. "Acknowledge them all" means that they accepted the resurrection as well as the existence of angels and spirits.

The author, Luke, makes this clear to explain what happened in the council. Paul was being judged and noticed that there were Sadducees and Pharisees present. By saying that he was being judged for his hope in the resurrection, he set off an argument between them. Some scholars see this as a clever move by Paul; others see it simply as a truth he really believed, one that divided the group.

For today: not every disagreement is equally important. Ask yourself which beliefs are central to your faith, such as the resurrection, and hold firmly to them with wisdom and calm.
exp.6:5:
This verse says that God spoke to Abraham and told him that his descendants would be foreigners in a land that was not theirs. There they would be enslaved and mistreated for four hundred years. "Descendants" refers to his children and their children after them, and "enslaved" means held as slaves.

Here Stephen is speaking, defending himself before the Jewish council. He is reviewing the history of Israel to show that God guides his people even in difficult times. He points back to the promise made to Abraham, which appears in Genesis 15:13. The "four hundred years" is a round figure; other texts give 430 years, and scholars explain that difference in several ways.

For today: God knows what is coming and does not abandon us in long seasons of hardship. We can trust that his promises still stand, even when they take a long time.
exp.25:9:
Paul says that in Jerusalem he put many believers in prison, people who were called "saints," that is, followers of Jesus. He did this with authority he had received from the chief priests. The words "I cast my vote against them" mean that, when they were condemned to death, he agreed with that decision and supported it. Some readers think this refers to a formal vote, while others understand him to be describing his general approval.

Paul speaks before King Agrippa and the governor Festus while he is himself a prisoner. He is telling his own story: before, he was a very convinced persecutor. By this he shows that his change was not a matter of a passing moment of enthusiasm, but the work of God, who met him and changed his life.

For today: no one is so far away that God cannot reach them. If you have done things you are ashamed of, God can forgive you and give you a new direction. And if you know someone who seems closed to faith, do not lose hope.
exp.10:21:
The verse tells us that news about what was happening in Antioch reached the church in Jerusalem. Here "news" is simply a report about events, and the church is the believers there. So the church decided to send Barnabas to Antioch to see for himself what was going on.

The account comes from Luke, the author of Acts. Some believers from Cyprus and Cyrene had spoken about Jesus to Greeks, that is, to people who were not Jewish, and many of them came to believe. It was something new, so the church in Jerusalem wanted to see it firsthand. They chose Barnabas, and the text describes him as a good man, full of the Spirit and of faith. It does not say he went with suspicion, and when he arrived he rejoiced.

For today: when God works in new or unexpected ways, let us not respond with suspicion, but with a humble heart, ready to rejoice in what God is doing.
exp.18:33:
When the crowd realized that Alexander was a Jew, they all shouted together for about two hours: "Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!" The shout itself is the key detail: the same chant went up from the whole crowd, and it went on for about two hours.

Luke, the author of Acts, describes the uproar in Ephesus, which the silversmiths stirred up. They sold small shrines of Artemis, and they feared losing their business because of Paul's preaching. The Jews pushed Alexander to the front, probably to distance themselves from the Christians, but the people rejected him for being a Jew. It is not known with certainty what Alexander intended to say.

For today: when the crowd's emotion takes over, reason goes quiet. Before joining a collective shout, let us stop and ask whether we truly know why we are doing it, and let us seek the truth calmly.
exp.4:33:
In the middle of the council, the Sanhedrin, a Pharisee named Gamaliel stood up. He was a teacher of the law, and all the people held him in high regard. He asked that the apostles be put outside the room for a short time.

The apostles had just said that they must obey God rather than men. The leaders were furious and wanted to kill them. Luke, the author of Acts, tells us that Gamaliel stepped in to calm the situation. Because of his standing, he asked that the apostles leave so the council could think more clearly. His exact motives are not explained, and we do not know whether he believed in them or was simply seeking prudence.

When everything heats up, a calm person can stop an unjust decision. Before reacting in anger, it is good to pause, listen, and think. Let us ask God for wisdom to be peacemakers.
exp.12:7:
The text tells us that Elymas the sorcerer opposed Paul and Barnabas. To oppose someone is to stand against them and push back against what they are saying. A sorcerer is a person who practiced magic or witchcraft. The verse also explains that this is what his name means.

Luke, the writer of Acts, describes the missionary journey on Cyprus. The proconsul Sergius Paulus, a sensible man, wanted to hear the word of God. Elymas, who stood close to him as an advisor, saw this as a threat to his own influence. So he tried to keep the proconsul from believing.

For today: sometimes people or interests will try to pull us away from the faith or from others who are seeking God. We can respond with courage and trust in God, and lovingly help those who are hungry for his word.
exp.14:28:
This verse says that believers who came from outside the Jewish community were to keep away from four things: food sacrificed to idols, blood, the meat of strangled animals (animals not bled properly), and sexual immorality. The words "If you keep yourselves from these" mean "if you take care to avoid these things," and "Farewell" is a closing greeting, like wishing someone well as they leave.

The apostles and elders gathered in Jerusalem wrote this letter to the believers in Antioch. They had been debating whether non-Jewish believers had to be circumcised and follow the law of Moses in order to be saved. They decided not to burden them with more, but asked them to take care to keep unity with the Jewish believers. Interpreters explain in various ways whether these instructions were moral or were meant for living together in community.

Today, we can ask ourselves which things call us to love and sensitivity toward other believers, even when they are not a requirement for salvation. Giving way in matters that are secondary helps to maintain unity.
exp.23:11:
Paul says that his accusers did not find him debating with anyone in the temple, or stirring up a crowd in the synagogues, or anywhere else in the city. The phrase "stirring up a crowd" refers to inciting a riot or gathering a mob to cause a disturbance.

Paul is in custody in Caesarea, before the governor Felix. Some Jews, together with the lawyer Tertullus, were accusing him of being a troublemaker and a leader of a sect. Paul defends himself with respect and with facts: he had been in Jerusalem only twelve days, and he had gone there to worship. He also points out that his accusers had no proof.

For today: our daily conduct can be the best defense of our faith. Living with calm, respect, and honesty, without looking for quarrels, gives us credibility when someone criticizes us. And if we are unjustly accused, we can answer with truth and serenity, not with anger.
exp.15:28:
This verse tells how the jailer called for lights, rushed into the inner cell, and fell down trembling before Paul and Silas. The phrase "calling for lights" means that he asked for torches or lamps. The word "fell" describes him throwing himself to the ground in fear and respect.

Paul and Silas were prisoners in Philippi. That night an earthquake opened the doors, and the jailer, believing the prisoners had escaped, was ready to take his own life. Paul stopped him with his voice. When he saw that no one had gone, the man was shaken by what was happening. How he understood all of this the text does not explain, but his next question shows that he was seeking salvation.

For today: when life shakes us and we are left without answers, it is a good time to draw near to God with humility and ask sincerely. He can use even crises to open our hearts.
exp.26:21:
Paul tells everyone on the ship to keep up their courage. He assures them that no one will lose their life; only the ship will be lost. The phrase "I urge you" can be understood as "I earnestly advise you," and "keep up your courage" means staying strong and confident.

Paul is a prisoner on his way to Rome, and the ship has been caught in a terrible storm for days. No one can see the sun or the stars, and they have already lost hope. Paul speaks after they failed to listen when he warned them not to set sail. Even so, he does not rebuke them harshly; he gives them a promise. He received it from an angel of God that very night.

God can give us peace in the middle of the storm, even when we cannot see a way out. We can trust his promises, and at times we will lose material things, but God cares for life and for his purposes. Today, when facing a crisis, pray and encourage others with that hope.
exp.18:40:
The verse you are reading says: "After he had said this, he dismissed the assembly." Here "assembly" refers to the gathered crowd, and "dismissed" means that he sent them home. The uproar ended.

The speaker is the town clerk, an official of the city of Ephesus. The people were furious because Paul's preaching was hurting the business of the silversmiths who made figures of the goddess Artemis. The clerk reminded them that they could get into trouble with Rome for stirring up a disturbance without cause, and that any complaint should be settled through the proper legal channels.

For today: calm and sensible words can put out an argument that is catching fire. Before reacting in anger, pause and think. God can even use unexpected people to bring peace and protect his own.
exp.15:5:
Paul and his companions traveled through the region of Phrygia and Galatia, but the Holy Spirit prevented them from speaking the message in the province of Asia. Here "Asia" refers to a Roman province in the west of what is today Turkey, not to the whole continent.

Luke, the author of Acts, is describing Paul's second missionary journey. They were strengthening the churches and sharing the decisions that had been reached in Jerusalem. Luke does not explain how the Spirit prevented them from going to Asia; the Bible does not give those details, and it is not wise to speculate. Later in the account, the Spirit guides them toward Troas and Macedonia.

For today: sometimes God closes a door without giving us reasons right away. If you seek his direction with prayer and humility, you can trust that it is not rejection, but guidance toward the right place, even if you cannot yet see it.
exp.13:19:
The passage tells that the disciples gathered around Paul, who was lying outside the city after being stoned. Then he got up and went back into Lystra. The next day he left with Barnabas for Derbe. In this version the words are "But" and "went back," so the verse reads plainly in modern English.

Luke tells this in the book of Acts. Paul and Barnabas were preaching in Lystra, and some Jews from Antioch and Iconium persuaded the crowd to stone Paul, believing him dead. The text does not say whether he died and was raised, or whether he was badly hurt and recovered; scholars read it both ways.

For today: suffering does not have to stop our calling. Paul did not stay behind; he moved forward with the help of other believers. When you face opposition or weariness, lean on your community of faith and take the next step with confidence in God.
exp.10:27:
This verse tells how a prophet named Agabus stood up and, through the Spirit, predicted that a great famine would sweep across the whole world. The word "world" here refers to the Roman world known at that time. The verse adds that this happened under the emperor Claudius.

Luke, the author of Acts, places this in Antioch, where there was a young and growing church. Prophets had arrived there from Jerusalem. Historians mention food shortages during the reign of Claudius, but it is not known precisely which years or which places were hit hardest. What matters here is the response of the believers: to help the brothers and sisters in Judea.

For today: when you become aware of a need, do not stop at worry alone. Act with generosity, each according to your means, and ahead of time if you can.
exp.25:7:
Paul asks his listeners a direct question: why would any of them consider it unbelievable that God raises the dead? The word "consider" means to think something over, and "unbelievable" refers to something that cannot be credited as true. Paul is not asking for blind faith. Instead, he invites them to think about whether rejecting the idea of resurrection makes sense, given that God is all-powerful.

Paul is speaking before King Agrippa and the governor Festus while he defends himself in a trial. The Jews accuse him because of his hope in God's promise, which included the resurrection. He reminds them that this hope was part of the faith of his own people. Many understand that his question points toward the resurrection of Jesus, which he will speak about shortly.

Today we can ask ourselves whether we limit God with our doubts. When something seems impossible to us, let us remember that God has power over life itself, and let us trust in Him with humility.
exp.23:17:
As Paul was carrying out his rite of purification in the temple, some Jews from the province of Asia found him there. He makes clear that he was not gathering a crowd or stirring up an uproar, that is, causing disorder or scandal. "Ceremonially clean" refers to a religious act of cleansing according to Jewish law.

Paul speaks before the governor Felix, defending himself against the accusations of the Jews from Jerusalem. He says he had come to bring aid and offerings to his people. His point is that he was not stirring up trouble. Moreover, the real accusers, the Jews from Asia, did not even appear at the trial, and this weakened the case against him.

For today: strive to live in such a way that your conduct speaks for you. When you are unjustly accused, a clear conscience and a peaceful life are a powerful witness. Act with simplicity, without seeking quarrels, and trust that God knows your heart.
exp.20:17:
The day after arriving in Jerusalem, Paul went with his traveling companions to see James, and all the elders of the church gathered there. The phrase "went with us to see James" means that he went to visit him. The elders were the leaders of the local church.

The one telling the story is Luke, who traveled with Paul (which is why the account speaks of "us"). Paul was arriving in Jerusalem after his third journey, bringing aid for the poor. This James is generally understood to be the Lord's brother, the leader in Jerusalem. Paul wanted to report in an orderly way what God was doing among the Gentiles.

For today: when we serve the Lord, let us do it in fellowship with other believers. Paul, although he had great experience, sought out the leaders, spoke with humility, and gave glory to God for what He had done. Giving an account and sharing testimonies strengthens the unity of the church.
exp.11:8:
Peter left the prison and followed the angel, but he was unaware that what was happening was real. He thought he was only seeing a vision.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells us that Herod had imprisoned Peter and wanted to bring him to trial. The church was praying for him. When God sets him free, Peter is so amazed that he does not believe it until the angel leaves and he comes to himself, in verse 11.

For today: sometimes God answers in ways we do not expect, and it can even be hard for us to believe it. Keep praying and obeying step by step, as Peter did, even when you do not understand everything. When God acts, give him thanks.
exp.15:27:
Paul calls out loudly to the jailer to stop him. He tells him not to harm himself, because everyone is still there. The word "called out" means that he shouted to get the jailer's attention, and "in a loud voice" means he spoke at full volume.

Paul and Silas were in prison in Philippi. An earthquake opened the doors and loosened the chains. The jailer, seeing the doors open, believed that everyone had escaped and wanted to take his own life with his sword, perhaps out of fear of the punishment he would face. Paul saw him and called to him in time. Shortly afterward, the jailer asked how he could be saved.

For today: Paul could have thought only of his own freedom, but he cared about the life of someone who was his jailer. We can ask ourselves who near us is suffering in silence, and offer a word at the right time, with kindness and without expecting anything in return.
exp.12:37:
Here, Paul tells his listeners that an important message is being made known to them: through Jesus, the forgiveness of sins is announced. The words "let it be known" mean "let this be clear to you" or "understand this well." "Brothers" is a respectful way of addressing them, like "my friends."

The one speaking is the apostle Paul, in the synagogue at Antioch of Pisidia, during his first missionary journey. He is speaking to Jews and to others who worshiped God. He has just explained that David died and his body decayed, but God raised up Jesus, and his body did not decay. That is why Paul presents Jesus as the only one who can offer forgiveness that is real.

For today: you do not have to earn God's forgiveness through your own effort. If you carry guilt, come before Jesus in faith and receive the forgiveness he offers.
exp.22:25:
This verse is the greeting that opens an official letter. Claudius Lysias writes it to Felix, the Roman governor. "To His Excellency" was a title of respect for a person in authority. "Greetings" was a common way to open a letter, like saying "Please accept my respectful greetings."

Claudius Lysias was the Roman commander in Jerusalem. He had rescued Paul from a mob, and now he had discovered a plot by more than forty men to kill him. For that reason he decides to send Paul away by night to Caesarea, under escort, and writes this letter to explain the case. The Bible does not say he was a believer, but God used his position to protect Paul.

God can care for us through means and people we do not expect, even ordinary authorities. We can trust that he works in everyday life, and we can also be respectful and clear when we deal with those who hold authority.
exp.22:33:
This verse says that the governor Felix read the letter sent to him by the Roman commander Claudius Lysias. Then he asked what province Paul was from. On learning that he was from Cilicia, he became informed about his origin. Here "learning" means that he gathered the information and became aware of it.

Paul had been taken by night from Jerusalem to Caesarea, because some Jews were plotting to kill him. Luke, the author of Acts, recounts the legal procedure with simplicity. Asking what province Paul was from was important because it could influence who should judge the case. Some think Felix could have sent him to another authority, but he decided to hear him himself.

For today: God can care for us even in procedures, paperwork, and decisions of authorities that seem cold or slow. We can act with order and truth, and trust that God continues guiding our story step by step.
exp.12:22:
From the descendants of King David, God brought Jesus into history as the Savior for Israel, just as he had promised. The phrase "from the descendants of this man" points to David's family line, and "God has brought" means that God himself set Jesus into the course of history at the right time.

Paul is speaking in the synagogue at Antioch of Pisidia. He tells the story of Israel to both Jews and God-fearing Gentiles, including the kings Saul and David. His purpose is to show that Jesus is not a surprise, but the fulfillment of what God had been promising for centuries. Then he mentions John the Baptist, who prepared the way.

For today: God keeps what he promises, even when it takes a very long time by our way of counting. You can trust his faithfulness when you are waiting for an answer, and remember that Jesus is his greatest promise fulfilled.
exp.8:39:
Peter had everyone leave the room where Tabitha's body lay. He knelt down and prayed. Then he turned toward her body and said, "Tabitha, get up!" She opened her eyes, saw Peter, and sat up.

Tabitha is her name in Aramaic, and Dorcas is the same name in Greek.

Peter was in Joppa because the disciples had sent for him when Tabitha died. The widows were weeping and showing him the clothing she had made for them, a sign of a life given to serving others. Peter does not act by his own power, but first prays. Luke, the narrator, tells the story, and many people came to believe in the Lord.

Before acting, Peter sought God in prayer. When we face situations that are beyond us, we can begin on our knees, in humility, trusting that God is the one at work and not ourselves.
exp.26:1:
We boarded a ship from Adramyttium, a port city in Asia Minor, and set out to sail along the coast of that region. Aristarchus, a believer from Thessalonica in Macedonia, was with us.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells the journey in the first person ("we"), so he was on board too. Paul was a prisoner being taken to Rome, because he had appealed to Caesar. This ship was not going directly to Italy; it was only one stage of the way, and they would have to change ships later.

For today: even in difficult times, God often gives us faithful companions. Aristarchus chose to travel with Paul even though Paul was a prisoner. We can be that kind of friend to someone who is suffering, and be thankful for those who stand beside us.
exp.16:21:
Paul is standing in the middle of the Areopagus, a meeting place in Athens, and he speaks to the Athenians. He tells them that he sees they are very religious in every way. The original word can mean "very religious" or "very respectful of the gods," so the reader's translation uses the more positive sense. Scholars do not agree on whether Paul meant it as a mild criticism or as a polite greeting.

Paul is the speaker. The philosophers of Athens had brought him there because his new teaching about Jesus and the resurrection caught their attention. Paul had seen the city full of idols, and he opens his speech by noting their deep interest in spiritual things, then speaks to them about the true God.

For today: before we share our faith, we can observe with respect what people believe and seek. In this way we find an honest starting point for speaking to them about Christ with kindness.
exp.17:19:
The Jews in the synagogue at Ephesus, who had listened to Paul, asked him earnestly to stay longer with them. But he declined. "He declined" means that he did not agree to stay.

Paul was coming from Corinth, on his way to Syria. He stopped at Ephesus and spoke with the Jews in the synagogue. They showed interest, but he was in a hurry to reach Jerusalem for the feast, and he promised to return if God willed it. Scholars do not agree on which feast it was. We also do not know for certain all of his reasons.

For today: a good opportunity does not always mean that we should stay. Paul said no kindly and left the door open, saying he would come back if God willed it. We can decide calmly, praying, and placing our plans in God's hands.
exp.27:21:
The Jewish leaders in Rome tell Paul that they want to hear directly what he thinks. They explain that they already know people everywhere are speaking against this group, that is, the followers of Jesus. The phrase "want to hear" in the verse means that they are eager to hear from him, and the phrase "speaking against" means that people are criticizing it.

Paul has just arrived in Rome as a prisoner, and he calls together the leading men of the Jews to explain that he is bound because of the hope of Israel. They have not received letters or bad reports about him. So they respond with curiosity, although they have already heard criticism of Christianity. Afterward, Paul gives them a whole day to explain the kingdom of God to them.

For today: before repeating what others say about something or someone, let us listen firsthand. And if we speak of our faith, let us do it with patience and with the Bible, as Paul did.
exp.8:29:
Luke, the author of Acts, recounts what happened after Saul (Paul) came to faith in Christ. He spoke boldly about Jesus in Jerusalem and argued with Greek-speaking Jews, who then tried to kill him. When the believers learned of this plot, they took him down to Caesarea, a port city, and sent him off to Tarsus, his hometown. Their words "learned of this" mean that they realized the danger he was in.

To protect someone is not cowardice but love and wisdom. Today we can care for those who serve God, and we can also accept help and counsel when our zeal puts us in danger. God works both in courage and in prudence.
exp.23:7:
Tertullus says that the tribune Lysias ordered Paul's accusers to come before Felix. He also says that by questioning Paul himself, Felix will be able to learn the truth about all the charges against him. The word "questioning" here means investigating. The verse does not make clear whether "all our charges" refers to charges against Paul or to Lysias, and scholars understand it both ways.

Tertullus, the lawyer for the Jewish leaders, speaks before the governor Felix in Caesarea. He wants Felix to condemn Paul. So he presents the facts in his own favor: he says Lysias acted with violence, although in reality he rescued Paul from a mob.

Today, when facing a conflict, do not settle for just one version. Listen calmly, look for the facts, and be wary of accounts that favor only the person telling them.
exp.6:27:
A Hebrew man asks Moses whether he means to kill him too, just as he killed an Egyptian yesterday. Here "yesterday" refers to the day before. The word "shoved" means he pushed him hard and pushed him away with contempt.

Stephen repeats these words in his defense before the Jewish council, summarizing the history of Israel. He tells how Moses wanted to help his people, but was rejected by his own. Stephen shows that Israel had already rejected the one God had placed to deliver them. Afterward, Moses fled to Midian, and God called him forty years later.

God can use the one others reject, and his timing is not ours. If your good desire to help was poorly received, do not lose heart: God is still at work and prepares the right moment.
exp.23:21:
Felix, after hearing Paul and his accusers, already knew quite well about "the Way," the Christian movement. Here the Way simply means a group or movement, not something negative in itself. Felix put off the hearing, meaning he postponed the case. He said he would decide it when the commander Lysias arrived, the officer who had sent Paul under guard.

Paul had been accused before Felix in Caesarea by Jewish leaders. He defended himself by saying he was being judged for believing in the resurrection. Historical evidence suggests that Felix had spent years in the region, which would explain why he knew something about Christianity. Some think his delay was prudence, others that it was evasion or personal interest; the text does not fully clarify this.

Today, postponing an important decision about God is not neutral. Felix listened, but let the moment pass. If God speaks to you through his Word, respond with humility and do not leave it for later.
exp.4:26:
This verse tells us that the apostles were brought in and made to stand before the council, that is, the Sanhedrin, the highest court of the Jews. The high priest then began to question them. The reader's wording "made them stand before" describes the apostles being placed in front of all the judges.

The one telling this account is Luke, the author of Acts. The apostles had been in prison, but an angel led them out of the jail, and they went back to teaching in the temple. The leaders had ordered them not to speak about Jesus. That is why the high priest questions them, and right away Peter answers that we must obey God rather than men.

For today: if following Christ brings you pressure or criticism, do not be afraid. Respond with respect and calm, but stay firm in what God has commanded you. Ask him for courage and wisdom to speak gently and without fear.
exp.21:12:
Ananias came to where Saul was, stood beside him, and said, "Brother Saul, receive your sight." At that very moment Paul says he was able to see, and he looked up at Ananias.

Paul is speaking to a Jewish crowd in Jerusalem, after being arrested. He wants to explain how his life changed when he met Jesus. Ananias was a respected Jew, faithful to the law, and for that reason his testimony gave weight to the account.

For today: Ananias called "brother" the man who had once persecuted the believers. God can use us to welcome with warmth and trust someone who seems distant or even hostile, and so open a way for that person to come to know Jesus.
exp.1:11:
All the people who were listening were astonished and did not know what to think. The first word here means greatly surprised, and the second means perplexed, unable to make sense of what was happening. They asked one another, "What does this mean?"

We are at Pentecost, in Jerusalem. The Holy Spirit had just filled the disciples, and they were speaking of the wonderful works of God in languages they had never learned. Those who listened were Jews and converts who had come from many countries, and each one heard them in his or her own language. Luke, the author of the book, tells that some were amazed and others mocked. Then Peter would stand up to explain to them.

For today: when God does something we do not understand, let us not mock it or dismiss it right away. Let us do as those who asked with sincerity did: look for answers in the Bible and listen with humility.
exp.2:6:
Peter took the lame man by his right hand and helped him up. At that very moment, the man's feet and ankles were made strong. The phrase "made strong" here means that they were steady and firm. The word "at once" in the verse means that it happened right away.

Luke, the author of Acts, tells what happened at the temple gate called Beautiful. There the man, who had been lame since birth, was begging for money. Peter, together with John, had no money, but he offered him something better: healing in the name of Jesus. The gesture of taking him by the hand shows closeness and compassion.

For today: many times we can help others more with who we are than with what we have. A gesture of closeness, a prayer, or an outstretched hand can lift someone up, and all the credit still belongs to God.
exp.8:17:
At that instant, something like scales fell from Saul's eyes, and his sight was restored. Then he got up and was baptized.

Luke is the author, who tells what happened after Jesus appeared to Saul on the road to Damascus. Saul had been left blind. God sent Ananias, a disciple, to pray for him. Once his sight was restored, Saul accepted baptism as a sign of his new faith. The text says "something like scales," so it is a comparison; we do not know exactly what it was.

For today: God can change any person, and He also uses ordinary believers, like Ananias, to help. Obey when He asks you to go to someone, even if it frightens you, and welcome with love the one who is beginning to believe.
exp.21:16:
Paul says that, when he had returned to Jerusalem and was praying at the temple, he fell into a trance. That experience describes a moment when his attention was completely taken up by God and he received a vision, as if his mind had been lifted away from what surrounded him.

Paul speaks before an angry crowd in Jerusalem, defending himself after his arrest. He recounts his conversion and his life after it. This took place in the temple, a place the Jews considered sacred, and that is why Paul mentions it: he was still a devout Jew when Jesus spoke to him. Scholars do not agree on exactly when this visit to Jerusalem took place.

Prayer is not only speaking, it is also making room to listen. God may have guided Paul precisely when he stopped to pray. Let us set aside a few minutes of silence today to listen.
exp.9:35:
He says that God sent his message to the people of Israel, and that this message announced the gospel of peace through Jesus Christ. Then he adds that Jesus is Lord of all. The phrase "the word" refers to the message God sent, and the earlier context about God accepting people is about his favor toward those who fear him and do what is right.

The apostle Peter is speaking in the house of Cornelius, a Roman officer who was not a Jew. God had shown Peter that the gospel was also for other peoples. That is why Peter explains that the good news, sent first to Israel, has in Jesus a Lord who rules over every person, regardless of their origin.

Today we can remember that Jesus is not only the Lord of my church, my family, or my culture. If He is Lord of all, I must treat every person with respect and love, and share with them the peace that Christ offers, without prejudice.
exp.7:21:
Peter tells Simon to repent, which means to change his mind and turn away from his wickedness. He also tells him to pray to the Lord, asking that God might forgive him for the intent of his heart. The words "perhaps He will forgive you" express that forgiveness is possible, not that God is unwilling.

Peter is the speaker. Simon, a man who had practiced sorcery in Samaria before, saw that the apostles gave the Holy Spirit through the laying on of hands, and tried to buy that power with money. Peter rebukes him firmly, but opens a door for him: repentance. The word "perhaps" does not necessarily show doubt about God's goodness; it may show that Peter could not see into Simon's heart. The text does not say how Simon's story ended.

Today we can learn that God looks at our intentions, not only at our actions. If we discover crooked motives, such as wanting to use spiritual things to gain prestige or profit, the best thing is to acknowledge it early and sincerely ask God for forgiveness.
exp.12:31:
Paul and Barnabas announce good news: God made a promise to the ancestors of Israel, and now it has come true. The word translated as "gospel" means good news, and the verse you are reading says "good news" in the same sense.

Paul is speaking in the synagogue at Antioch of Pisidia, on a Sabbath. He goes over the history of Israel and arrives at Jesus. He has just said that God raised him up and that many witnesses saw him. Now he explains that this resurrection is the fulfillment of what God promised centuries before. The verses that follow support this with texts from the Old Testament.

For today: God keeps what he promises, even when it takes a very long time. You can trust his word in moments of waiting. And like Paul, you can share that hope with others simply, by telling what God has done in Christ.
exp.7:10:
This verse says that the people of Samaria paid close attention to Simon, because for a long time he had astounded them with his sorcery. "They paid close attention to him" means they listened to him very carefully. "Astounded" here means fascinated, as if caught up by something that impresses them.

Here Luke, the author of Acts, tells what happened when Philip came to Samaria. He explains why so many people followed Simon: he presented himself as someone great, and his tricks and signs had won everyone over, from the least to the greatest. Afterward, the people believed Philip's message about Jesus.

For today: let us not follow someone only because they impress or amaze us. Let us examine whether what they teach points to Jesus and agrees with the Bible, and not simply to that person's fame.
exp.10:0:
This verse says that the apostles and the brothers throughout Judea soon heard that people who were not Jews, called "Gentiles," had also received the word of God. The word "heard" means that the news reached them. "Gentiles" were those who did not belong to the people of Israel.

The book of Acts is written by Luke. Earlier, in chapter 10, Peter had preached in the house of Cornelius, a man who was not Jewish, and God gave them the Holy Spirit. Now the news reaches Judea. The verses that follow show that not everyone reacted with joy, since some questioned Peter for having had dealings with them.

Today we might ask ourselves whether we rejoice when God works in people who are different from us. Before we criticize or doubt, it is wise to listen with humility and to recognize that God's grace is for everyone.
exp.18:7:
It says that Paul went into the synagogue in Ephesus and spoke boldly there for three months. The word "boldly" here means speaking without fear and with confidence. "Arguing persuasively" does not mean fighting, but reasoning and discussing with good arguments, trying to convince people with sound reasons. His subject was the kingdom of God, that is, God's rule and work through Jesus.

Luke, the writer of Acts, tells how Paul came to Ephesus on his third journey. First he met about twelve disciples who received the Holy Spirit. Then he went to the synagogue, where the Jews were, because they knew the Scriptures. Afterward, some became stubborn and refused to believe, so Paul continued teaching in another place.

For today: we can speak about our faith with boldness, but with respect, patience and good reasons, without forcing anyone.
exp.16:14:
The brothers from Berea who were traveling with Paul escorted him all the way to Athens to keep him safe. Their care for him is shown in the way they took responsibility for his journey. Then they received instructions to tell Silas and Timothy to join Paul as soon as possible, and afterward they returned to Berea. "As soon as possible" here means as quickly as they could manage.

Luke, the author of Acts, narrates Paul's journey. Some Jews from Thessalonica came to Berea and stirred up the crowds, so the brothers sent Paul away from there. Silas and Timothy stayed behind to keep strengthening the young church. Paul arrived alone in Athens and waited there for his companions.

For today: God takes care of his own through brothers and sisters who accompany, protect, and serve without seeking recognition. Think about who needs your company or your help today, and offer it simply.
exp.17:27:
This verse says that Apollos argued forcefully against the Jews, and he did it in public, where everyone could see. He used the Scriptures (what we today call the Old Testament) to prove that Jesus is the Christ, that is, the promised Messiah. The phrase "in public debate" describes open argument, and "proving from the Scriptures" means he backed up his case with what the Bible said.

The author is Luke, who tells how Apollos, a Jew from Alexandria and a skilled student of the Bible, came to Achaia. Earlier, Priscilla and Aquila had explained the way of God to him in more detail. The brothers supported him with a letter of recommendation, and he helped the believers greatly.

For today: learn the Bible well, and accept correction from others with humility. Then speak about Jesus with passion, but with respect and based on the Word of God.
exp.14:30:
This verse says that the believers in Antioch read the letter from the apostles and rejoiced because of the encouraging message it brought them. The word "encouraging" here speaks not only of comfort in sorrow but also of strength, hope, and peace of heart. And "rejoiced" means filled with joy.

Context: In Jerusalem, the apostles and elders gathered to decide whether the non-Jewish believers should keep the law of Moses. They sent this letter with Judas and Silas to bring clarity and unity. The people of Antioch rejoiced because they were not burdened with an unnecessary weight, and because the church in Jerusalem accepted them.

For today: When there are doubts or tensions in the church, let us seek solutions with humility, prayer, and the Word. And when someone gives us a clear and encouraging word, let us thank them and share it with others.
exp.8:33:
Peter speaks to Aeneas, a man who has been paralyzed, and tells him that Jesus Christ heals him. He tells him to get up and put away his mat, and Aeneas gets up at once.

The words "put away your mat" mean that he should roll up or set aside the mat where he had lain for so long. "Immediately" means right away.

Peter was visiting the believers in Lydda, and there he found Aeneas, who had been bedridden for eight years. Notice that Peter does not say that he himself heals him, but that Jesus Christ does. Afterward, many in Lydda and Sharon saw the healed man and turned to the Lord.

For today: when God works in your life, give the credit to Jesus and not to yourself. And if He lifts you out of a difficulty, live in such a way that others see His power and draw near to Him.
exp.19:3:
The verse lists the men who travelled with Paul: Sopater son of Pyrrhus, from Berea; Aristarchus and Secundus, from Thessalonica; Gaius, from Derbe; Timothy; and Tychicus and Trophimus, from the province of Asia. Their names and home towns show that Paul's companions came from several places across the region.

Luke, the author of Acts, writes this account. Paul had changed his route through Macedonia because some Jews had set a trap for him. Many think these men represented different churches and perhaps carried the offering for Jerusalem, but this verse does not say so.

Today: Paul did not walk alone. God uses teams of people from different places. He seeks brothers and sisters with whom to serve, and you too can be a faithful companion to others.
exp.6:1:
These words are the beginning of Stephen's defense. "Brothers and fathers, listen to me" is a respectful way of asking for attention. It says that the God of glory appeared to Abraham while he was still in Mesopotamia, before he lived in Haran.

Stephen speaks before the Jewish council, after the high priest asked him whether the accusations were true. He decides to begin with the history of Israel. He starts with Abraham, whom God called before the temple existed or the promised land was in their possession.

Today we can remember that God acts and speaks wherever we are, not only in places set apart. If He called Abraham in a foreign land, He can also draw near to you in your present situation. Listen to Him with faith and an open heart.

sum.19: Paul travels through Macedonia and Greece, and in Troas he brings Eutychus back to life. The young man had fallen asleep and dropped from a window during Paul's long message. Then, in Miletus, Paul says goodbye to the elders of Ephesus. He reminds them of how he served among them, encourages them to take care of the church, to watch out for false teachers, and to give generously. Everyone weeps as they say goodbye.
sum.13: In Iconium, Paul and Barnabas preached, and many believed, but opposition forced them to flee to Lystra, where a man who had been lame was healed and the people wanted to worship them as gods. They pointed to the living God, and then Paul was stoned and got back up. They went back to strengthen the disciples, telling them that they would enter the kingdom of God through many hardships.
sum.17: In Corinth, Paul works with Aquila and Priscilla and proclaims Christ to the Jews. When they reject him, he turns to the Gentiles. God encourages him in a vision, and he stays there for a year and a half. Afterward he travels on, and Priscilla and Aquila instruct Apollos more fully, and he vigorously argues that Jesus is the Christ.
sum.3: Peter and John are arrested for proclaiming the risen Jesus, but Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, boldly declares that salvation is found only in Jesus. The leaders order them to stop speaking, but they answer that they must obey God. The church prays together, receives boldness, and generously shares its possessions.
sum.0: After rising from the dead, Jesus appeared alive to his apostles over a period of forty days. He told them to wait in Jerusalem for the Holy Spirit, who would make them his witnesses. Then he went up into heaven, and two men dressed in white said that he would return. The disciples prayed together, and they chose Matthias to take the place of Judas.
sum.27: After the shipwreck, Paul and his companions are warmly welcomed on the island of Malta, where he survives a viper's bite and prays for the sick, who are healed. Then they arrive in Rome, and Paul, a prisoner but with some freedom, explains the kingdom of God to the Jews. Some believe and others do not, and he preaches without hindrance for two years.
sum.22: Paul defended himself before the council. When he saw that the Pharisees and Sadducees were divided, he spoke about the resurrection, and a great uproar broke out. The Lord encouraged him, saying that he would also testify in Rome. When a plot by more than forty men was discovered, Paul was taken safely to Caesarea, before the governor Felix.
sum.23: Paul is accused before the governor Felix by the high priest Ananias and the orator Tertullus. But Paul defends himself calmly: he says he did not stir up anyone, that he serves God, and that he hopes for the resurrection. Felix keeps him in custody, listens to him speak about Jesus and a coming judgment, becomes frightened, and hopes for money. Two years later, he leaves Paul in prison to win favor with the Jews.
sum.9: An angel tells Cornelius, a Roman captain who prays and helps the poor, to send for Peter. In a vision, God shows Peter that he must not call anyone impure. When Peter tells them about Jesus, the Holy Spirit falls on the non-Jewish listeners, and Peter orders that they be baptized.
sum.2: Peter and John heal a lame man who was begging at the temple gate. In the name of Jesus, they make him well, and he walks in, leaping and praising God. Amazed, the crowd gathers around them, and Peter explains that the power did not come from their own ability but from Jesus, whom the people handed over, yet whom God raised from the dead. He invites them to repent and turn back to God so that their sins may be forgiven and they may receive blessing.
sum.6: Stephen, accused before the council, goes over the history of Israel: Abraham, Joseph, and Moses, and how the people often resisted God. Then he accuses his listeners of resisting the Holy Spirit and of betraying the Righteous One. Enraged, they stone him, while he sees Jesus at the right hand of God and prays for his enemies.
sum.1: On the day of Pentecost, the Holy Spirit fills the disciples, and they begin speaking in other languages. Peter explains that Jesus, who was crucified and then raised from the dead, is Lord and Christ. About three thousand people repent and are baptized. The believers live together in unity: they learn, pray, share bread and their possessions, and praise God.
sum.26: Paul travels as a prisoner toward Rome, and a violent storm leaves everyone without hope for many days. Through an angel, God promises him that no one will die, and so it happens: the ship is destroyed, but all 276 people reach land safely. The chapter shows Paul's faith and God's care in the midst of danger.
sum.24: Festus arrives in Jerusalem, and the Jewish leaders ask that Paul be brought there, planning to kill him on the way. Festus judges him in Caesarea, finds no proof of the charges, and Paul appeals to Caesar. Afterward, Festus presents the case to King Agrippa, who wants to hear Paul.
sum.7: After Stephen's death, a fierce persecution scattered the believers, and they preached the word wherever they went. Philip preached in Samaria with great joy. Simon the magician believed, but he wanted to buy the gift of God, and Peter rebuked him. Then Philip explained Isaiah to the Ethiopian eunuch, and the eunuch was baptized.
sum.14: Some teachers from Judea were saying that Gentiles had to be circumcised to be saved, so the apostles and elders gathered in Jerusalem. Peter and James explained that God saves by his grace, and they sent a letter asking only for a few abstentions. Afterward, Paul and Barnabas argued over John Mark and separated so that each could keep serving.
sum.15: Paul takes Timothy along, and the Spirit guides them to Macedonia, where Lydia and the jailer in Philippi believe and are baptized along with their households. Paul and Silas suffer beatings and imprisonment, yet they sing to God, and He works with power. The chapter teaches that God opens hearts and that salvation comes through believing in Jesus Christ.
sum.10: Peter explained to the believers in Jerusalem that God himself had shown him, through a vision and through the Holy Spirit, that non-Jewish people could also receive the gospel, and they praised God. Later the church grew in Antioch, where the disciples were first called Christians, and they sent help to the brothers and sisters in Judea.
sum.5: As the church was growing, there were complaints because some Greek-speaking widows were not receiving their fair share of the daily food distribution. The apostles had the community choose seven men full of the Spirit, including Stephen, to take charge of this service. Then Stephen was falsely accused of blasphemy and brought before the council, where his face looked like the face of an angel.
sum.21: Paul spoke to the crowd in Hebrew and told them about his life. He had persecuted believers, until Jesus appeared to him on the road to Damascus and sent him to bear witness. When he mentioned that God was sending him to the Gentiles, the crowd became furious. The commander ordered that Paul be flogged, but Paul said he was a Roman citizen, and they released him.
sum.20: Paul traveled on toward Jerusalem, and several believers, including the prophet Agabus, warned him that he would be imprisoned there. But he was determined to follow the Lord's leading. At the temple, some Jews from Asia falsely accused him and stirred up the crowd. The Roman commander rescued him, had him bound with chains, and allowed him to speak to the crowd.
sum.25: Paul makes his defense before King Agrippa. He tells how he was once a Pharisee and a persecutor of Christians, until Jesus appeared to him on the road to Damascus and sent him to preach repentance and faith to both Jews and Gentiles. Festus says that Paul is out of his mind, but Paul speaks the truth. Agrippa and the others find him innocent.
sum.11: Herod had James put to death and imprisoned Peter, but the church prayed without ceasing, and an angel miraculously brought Peter out of the prison. Peter went to the house where the people had been praying, and they were amazed to see him. Afterward Herod died because he did not give glory to God, and the word of the Lord continued to grow.
sum.18: In Ephesus, Paul baptized twelve disciples of John, who received the Holy Spirit, and he taught for two years while God worked miracles through his hands. The name of Jesus was honored, and many gave up sorcery. But Demetrius, a silversmith, stirred up the city because he was losing profits, until the city clerk calmed the crowd.
sum.8: Saul, who had been persecuting Christians, meets Jesus on the road to Damascus and is left blind. He is later healed and baptized by Ananias. He begins preaching that Jesus is the Son of God, escapes a plot against his life, and is accepted by the apostles thanks to Barnabas. After that, Peter heals Aeneas and raises Dorcas from the dead.
sum.16: Paul preached about Jesus in Thessalonica and Berea. In Berea some believed, but in Thessalonica others stirred up trouble. Paul then went on to Athens. There, before the philosophers, he spoke about the God who made everything, who does not live in temples, and he called everyone to repent, because there will be a judgment, which was confirmed by the resurrection of Jesus. Some mocked him, and others believed.
sum.12: The Holy Spirit sets apart Barnabas and Saul, and the church in Antioch sends them out. In Cyprus the governor, a proconsul, believes. In Pisidian Antioch, Paul preaches that Jesus, a descendant of David, was raised from the dead and offers forgiveness and justification to everyone who believes. Many Gentiles believe with joy, but some Jews stir up persecution and drive them out of the region.
sum.4: Ananías and Safira lie about the money from their sale, and both of them die, and great fear comes over the church. The apostles perform miracles and are put in prison, but an angel frees them, and they keep on teaching. Before the council they say that one must obey God rather than men, and they leave rejoicing that they suffered for Jesus.
